statement: The transformer residual stream acts as a linear communication channel: layers read from and write to it through linear maps, so the model's computation decomposes into a sum of interpretable paths.
scope: exact for attention-only transformers; approximate with layer norm and MLPs

statement: Attention heads within a layer operate independently and add their outputs into the residual stream, so each head can be analyzed separately as a QK circuit and an OV circuit.
scope: The additive computational-graph decomposition used for the parentheses case study.

statement: One-layer attention-only transformers behave as an ensemble of bigram and skip-trigram predictors that can be read directly from the weights.
scope: one-layer attention-only transformers

statement: Two-layer attention-only transformers form induction heads via K-composition with a previous-token head, implementing prefix matching and copying ([A][B]...[A] -> [B]).
scope: two-layer attention-only transformers

statement: Many high-level concepts are represented linearly, as directions in a model's activation space (the linear representation hypothesis).
scope: binary, mostly lexical concepts in embedding/unembedding spaces

statement: Probes on SAE latents outperform strong non-SAE baselines in hard probing regimes (data scarcity, class imbalance, label noise, covariate shift).
scope: binary probing tasks on Gemma-2-9B / Llama-3.1-8B with Gemma Scope SAEs

statement: Sparse autoencoders recover the underlying features that a language model represents in superposition.
scope: Motivating hypothesis for using SAE latents as an interpretability interface; explicitly left unresolved.

statement: Language model representations decompose into one-dimensional features (single directions), which are the basic units of the model's computation.
scope: Working feature definition for causal basis extraction, rather than a tested decomposition of all computation.

statement: Early in training, transformers with more than one layer undergo an abrupt phase change in which induction heads form, coinciding with a sharp improvement in in-context learning.
Induction heads are the mechanism behind the majority of in-context learning in large transformer language models.
scope: The broad induction-head hypothesis; the present OPT-66B analysis does not establish majority mediation or isolate sophisticated task computations.

statement: GPT-2 small performs indirect object identification with a circuit of about 26 attention heads in 7 functional classes (duplicate-token, previous-token, induction, S-inhibition, name mover, negative name mover, backup name mover).
scope: GPT-2 small, templated IOI prompts

statement: Causal interventions such as activation and path patching can identify the components and paths causally responsible for a model behavior.
scope: Indirect effects under clean-to-patch replacement or zero ablation define the causal importance targeted by circuit discovery.

statement: When important attention heads are ablated, other heads compensate (backup behavior / self-repair), so single-component ablation underestimates the importance of components.
scope: Backup behavior reported in prior IOI and Hydra-effect studies.

statement: Language models represent days of the week and months of the year as circular, irreducibly two-dimensional features that are causally used for modular arithmetic over them.
Refusal in safety-fine-tuned chat models is mediated by a single residual-stream direction: ablating it disables refusal of harmful requests and adding it induces refusal of harmless ones.
scope: open-weight chat models, 1.8B-72B

statement: Safety fine-tuning in open-weight chat models is shallow: it can be removed cheaply (e.g. a rank-one weight edit) with little loss of capability.
The difference in mean activations between two contrasting prompt sets yields a direction that causally steers the corresponding model behavior.
scope: Seven behavioral datasets on Llama 2 Chat; multiple-choice and open-ended responses.

statement: Features learned by sparse autoencoders on language-model activations are substantially more interpretable (monosemantic) than neurons or directions from PCA/ICA.
scope: Middle-layer Sonnet residual-stream SAE features compared with MLP neurons; PCA/ICA comparisons are not reported.

statement: Automated interpretability scores (LLM-written explanations scored by simulating activations) are a valid measure of how interpretable a feature is.
scope: Critique targets correlation-based simulation scores. The author endorses simulation in principle when it is scored by downstream KL.

statement: Neural networks represent more sparse features than they have dimensions by encoding them as nearly-orthogonal directions (superposition), and this is a major cause of polysemantic neurons.
scope: demonstrated in toy ReLU models; extrapolated to real networks

statement: SAE features localize the causally relevant computation for a model behavior more precisely than neuron or PCA bases.
scope: Four subject–verb agreement tasks in Pythia-70M and Gemma-2-2B, compared with neurons rather than PCA; evaluation excludes the first third of layers.

statement: Under a 'causal inner product', the probing (output-space) and steering (input-space) notions of linear representation coincide, and causally separable concepts are orthogonal.
scope: The prior binary-counterfactual framework adopted to unify final context embeddings and token unembeddings; its proof is attributed to Park et al. (2024), rather than supplied as a new result here.

statement: As SAE dictionary size grows, features split into families of finer-grained features, so there is no single canonical set of features at a given layer.
scope: Feature neighborhoods across the 1M, 4M, and 34M Sonnet SAEs.

statement: Whether a feature is ignored, given a dedicated dimension, or stored in superposition depends on its sparsity and importance, with sharp phase changes between regimes and features arranging into uniform-polytope geometries.
scope: toy models

statement: Most neurons in neural networks have simple, monosemantic explanations, so neuron-level interpretability is largely achievable by careful inspection of activating examples.

A pattern that fits all of a neuron's activating examples does not establish a correct explanation. The neuron may fire on only a hard-to-characterize subset of inputs matching the pattern, and activation magnitudes may carry essential information that the pattern does not predict.
scope: Interpreting neurons from extreme natural or optimized examples.

statement: Ablating small (weak) neuron activations substantially degrades language model performance, so weak activations cannot be ignored when explaining neurons.

A neuron explanation should be judged by substituting the neuron's activations with values simulated from the explanation and measuring downstream KL divergence over a large dataset. This penalizes only behaviorally relevant errors and is preferable to correlation-based scores or loss delta.
scope: Extended here to decoded collections of SAE latents; experiments report downstream loss and do not establish every preference in the broader claim.

statement: Circuits found between individual neurons tend to be large, complicated and redundant, and fail to explain most of the variance in model behavior.

Neural networks are composed of meaningful, human-understandable features: in the typical case, individual neurons (or other directions in activation space) respond to articulable properties of the input and can be rigorously characterized.
scope: Vision models (CNNs), primarily InceptionV1

statement: Features are connected by weights into circuits (computational subgraphs), and once the connected features are understood, the weights between them are interpretable and implement meaningful algorithms that can be read directly off the weights.
scope: Vision CNNs, primarily InceptionV1

statement: Analogous features and circuits form across different neural network models and tasks.
scope: Weak universality of successor mechanisms and numeric representations in the surveyed language models.

statement: Neural networks contain polysemantic neurons that respond to multiple unrelated inputs, and these substantially hinder circuit-level analysis because their connections cannot be considered individually.
scope: Invoked as an existing difficulty motivating feature decompositions beyond individual neurons; the essay cites the SoLU paper and supplies no new prevalence or circuit-analysis measurements.

statement: Neural network circuits contain recurring abstract motifs (e.g. equivariance, unioning over cases, superposition) that appear repeatedly across a model and across models.

InceptionV1 layer mixed3b contains a family of curve-detector neurons that respond to curves at specific orientations and jointly tile all orientations, and are built from earlier curve and line detectors.
scope: InceptionV1 early vision

statement: Optimizing an input to maximize a neuron's activation (feature visualization) establishes a causal link between the visualized pattern and the neuron's firing, and combined with dataset examples is strong evidence of what a neuron detects.
scope: Input optimization and attribution visualization for InceptionV1 curve neurons.

statement: A circuit can be understood by its largest weights and primary connections; the long tail of small weights to other features does not substantially change the mechanism.
scope: Selecting hidden-layer connections for manual inspection in nonsparse networks.

statement: Small circuits permit rigorous, falsifiable claims (e.g. predicting effects of weight edits), and statements about whole-model behavior can in principle be decomposed into statements about circuits, making circuits a possible epistemic foundation for interpretability.
scope: The broader epistemic proposal is extended by connecting circuit decompositions to distribution-wide accuracy certificates in a simple attention-only setting; general decomposition of arbitrary whole-model behavior is not established.

statement: Training an interpretability interface or edit module to match downstream output distributions (KL) transfers model behavior better than training it to reconstruct intermediate activations (MSE/NMSE). Better geometric activation reconstruction need not yield better behavioral reconstruction.
scope: Residual-stream edit modules reproducing prompt-intervention counterfactuals at a mid layer

statement: Integrated Gradients attribution over the per-token outputs of a trained counterfactual edit module identifies the edits that are causally important for counterfactual recovery, beyond what edit magnitude alone predicts.
Language models can carry task-relevant computation or information at filler tokens that is not reflected in the verbalized text.

Holding the response prefix fixed and comparing next-token distributions under a prompt and its intervened counterfactual isolates the intervention's effect on the model's computation at each response position.
Activation-based interpretability tools provide no additional insight beyond the chain-of-thought text for predicting a model's counterfactual behavior.

Because features are written to and read from a low-dimensional residual stream, the virtual weights between features are forced into superposition, producing interference weights: large connections that are irrelevant or harmful to model behavior.
scope: CLT virtual weights; sampled activation data cannot establish that a connection is never used.

statement: The raw magnitude of a virtual weight is only weakly related to whether it helps model performance; helpful and harmful weights are scattered across the full range of magnitudes, so reading circuits from the largest virtual weights can miss important connections and highlight interference.

A model's most output-effective virtual weights are overwhelmingly helpful to the loss, with harmful weights confined to a lower-effectiveness regime (the top helpful weight exceeds any harmful weight's effectiveness by an order of magnitude or more), while moderate-effectiveness weights mix helpful and harmful.
The mean change in training loss when a single weight is ablated is close to a ground-truth measure of that weight's functional importance.

Most virtual weights in an expanded model are ineffective and can be removed with little loss: pruning the least Fisher-effective 70% costs ~0.01 nats and 85% costs <0.1 nats, outperforming magnitude-based pruning.

In a token/position/transcoder-feature basis, the fraction of helpful virtual weights is tens of percent, so even an interference-free virtual-weight model has far more weights than the original network's parameters; removing interference alone does not yield a sparse global model.

A model that is dense in one basis of virtual weights may be sparse in another; finding a better decomposition (e.g., factoring tokens into languages or parts of speech) is the most promising route to a sparse, interpretable global description of the weights.

Because transformers are residual networks (x + f(x)) trained with weight decay, they tend to keep representations in a common basis across layers and change them incrementally, which is why a single unembedding can decode intermediate layers.
scope: Residual transformers trained with weight decay

statement: Language models preserve rare or surprising input tokens in intermediate representations (detectable as relatively high rank under the unembedding), allowing later layers to retrieve and copy them; such copying resolves only in late layers.
scope: GPT-2

statement: In autoregressive transformer LMs, factual associations are recalled by MLP modules at a range of middle layers while processing the last token of the subject; this information is later moved to the final token by attention at high layers.
scope: GPT-style autoregressive LMs, subject-relation-object factual prompts

statement: Activation-restoration causal tracing reveals the global localization of factual recall (last-subject-token mid-layer MLPs) that gradient-based saliency methods such as Integrated Gradients fail to reveal.

A single rank-one update to one mid-layer MLP weight matrix, computed by treating it as a linear associative memory, can insert a new factual association that generalizes across paraphrases and generations while remaining specific to the edited subject, outperforming fine-tuning and hypernetwork editors on the generalization-specificity tradeoff.

Transformer MLP output projections can be modeled as linear associative memories mapping key vectors (subject representations) to value vectors (stored properties), rather than as independent per-neuron key-value pairs.
scope: Working associative-memory interpretation underlying the ROME and MEMIT editing procedures; not newly established here.

statement: Transformer feed-forward (MLP) layers act as key-value memories that store knowledge about entities.
scope: Evidence restricted to factual expression in BERT-base-cased.

statement: There is no special role for the particular middle MLP layer: any fact could be equivalently stored in any one of the middle MLP layers.
Success of a localized weight edit at a site (generalization plus specificity) is evidence that the edited fact is stored at that site.
scope: Inference from rank-one factual editing efficacy to storage location; comprehensive generalization and specificity are not evaluated here.

statement: Large language models such as GPT-4 can automatically generate natural-language explanations of individual neurons in other language models from the neurons' activation patterns on text.
scope: Neuron-level explanations of transformer language models

statement: Function vectors are not semantic word-embedding offsets: they implement cyclic mappings that no constant offset can implement, they carry information beyond their decoded output vocabulary, and their causal effect vanishes at late layers, indicating they trigger nonlinear mid-layer computation.
scope: GPT-J, Llama 2

statement: Function vectors can to some extent be combined by vector arithmetic (e.g. Last-Copy + First-Capital − First-Copy) to produce vectors that trigger new composite tasks.

Because the residual stream is a telescoping sum, nearby transformer layers share a common vector space, so head outputs from different layers can be meaningfully summed and injected at a single layer.
Circuits identified by manual mechanistic interpretability studies are sufficiently accurate and complete to serve as ground truth for evaluating automated circuit-discovery methods.
scope: Prior IOI head roles and signs are used as reference targets, without independently establishing completeness of the reference circuit.

statement: The outputs of automated circuit-discovery methods are highly sensitive to the choice of optimized metric, ablation type (zero vs. resample) and corrupted distribution, so no single configuration is robust across tasks.
scope: Evidence concerns activation-patching localization and head discovery, rather than a direct comparison of automated pruning algorithms or zero versus resample ablation.

statement: Circuit-discovery methods that optimize a single performance metric systematically miss components that actively hurt the metric (e.g. negative name mover heads), recovering them only at very permissive thresholds along with many extraneous components.
scope: Task-performance-based circuit discovery.

statement: Patching-based edge pruning (ACDC) is less prone than learned-mask (SP) or gradient-importance (HISP) methods to finding 'circuits' in networks that do not implement the behavior.
Resample/interchange ablation (patching activations from a corrupted input) gives more faithful circuit-discovery results than zero ablation, because zero activations push the model off-distribution.
scope: Presented as a practical preference for controlled prompt-based patching, without a new comparative evaluation.

statement: Transformer feed-forward layers function as unnormalized key-value memories: first-layer weight vectors act as keys matched against the input, and the layer output is a sum of second-layer value vectors weighted by the resulting activations.
scope: Transformer language models

statement: Individual feed-forward key vectors (MLP neurons) in transformer LMs are triggered by a small set of human-recognizable input patterns, such as n-grams or semantic topics.
The dataset examples that most strongly activate a unit are representative of what that unit detects, so patterns shared among them characterize the unit's function.
scope: Used as an explicitly imperfect qualitative proxy for feature interpretability.

statement: In deep language models, lower layers predominantly encode shallow, surface-form features of the input, while upper layers encode more semantic features.
When projected onto the output vocabulary, feed-forward value vectors in upper layers assign high probability to the tokens that follow the input patterns triggering their corresponding keys.

Intermediate vectors in a transformer (residual states and MLP output vectors) can be meaningfully interpreted by projecting them through the model's output embedding into a distribution over the vocabulary.
scope: Static parameter-vector interpretation with direct and tuned projections.

statement: A feed-forward layer's output prediction is typically a composition of many active memories rather than being dominated by a single memory cell.

Transformer LMs build their next-token prediction gradually: the residual stream's implied prediction often forms in early or middle layers and is then refined layer by layer, with feed-forward layers usually nudging toward a compromise token rather than overriding it.
scope: Evidence concerns layerwise refinement; the specific role of feed-forward compromise updates is not separately tested.

statement: LLMs have a consistent internal representation of truthfulness that can be read out with linear methods and predicts answer correctness better than the model's own outputs. Low zero-shot accuracy on imitative-falsehood benchmarks largely reflects outputs that deviate from this internal representation, rather than a lack of knowledge.
Steering or tuning a model's internal representations along an extracted honesty direction makes its outputs more truthful and can induce or suppress lying.

A direction that best predicts a concept (e.g. a logistic-regression probe) need not have causal influence on behavior. Directions should be validated with manipulation, termination (necessity) and recovery (sufficiency) experiments, not correlation alone.
scope: Neuron-level feature probing; this paper performs ablations but does not implement every validation type in the claim.

statement: Aligned chat models keep an internal representation of instruction harmfulness that is unchanged by jailbreaks and adversarial suffixes. Jailbroken compliance therefore comes from factors other than perceiving the request as harmless.

Analyzing networks at the level of population representations (top-down) can give traction on high-level, safety-relevant cognition that circuit-level mechanistic interpretability struggles to reach. Purely circuit-based accounts are incompatible with evidence of iterative refinement and robustness to layer ablation.

Steering directions extracted from one subdomain of a concept can generalize to related subdomains. For example, a bias direction from race stimuli reduces gender bias, and memorization directions from quotes transfer to literary openings.
Adding a topic or sentiment steering vector to the residual stream leaves model performance on unrelated inputs and tasks largely intact.
scope: Behavioral CAA vectors assessed on a reformatted MMLU subset.

statement: Inference-time activation steering can elicit behaviors more reliably, and with fewer side effects, than prompt engineering, and may elicit capabilities no prompt can.
scope: Comparisons with selected system prompts on seven Llama 2 behavioral evaluations.

statement: Activations from separate forward passes on different prompts can be algebraically combined (added and subtracted) in the residual stream to produce coherent, semantically composed outputs, even though models are not trained for this operation.

The activation-space direction corresponding to a high-level latent (e.g. love vs hate) stays approximately the same across a broad class of inputs, so a vector computed on one prompt pair transfers to unrelated prompts.
Steering vectors are most effective when injected at middle layers of a transformer, with effectiveness rising then declining across depth.
scope: Layer sweeps with fixed multipliers of ±1 in Llama 2 Chat.

statement: Because safety training may leave undesired behaviors present but low-probability, activation steering can re-elicit them and circumvent superficial alignment methods.
scope: Qualitative interventions on selected SAE features in fine-tuned Sonnet.

statement: For a substantial subset of factual, commonsense, linguistic and bias relations, a transformer LM's computation from the intermediate-layer subject representation to the final object representation is well approximated by a single relation-specific affine transformation (a linear relational embedding).
scope: Autoregressive LMs (GPT-J, GPT-2-XL, LLaMA-13B); 47 relations; first-token object prediction

statement: By the middle layers, an LM's representation at the last subject token has been enriched (largely by MLP layers) with attributes of the subject, from which relation-specific facts are later extracted.
scope: The upstream factual-recall account adopted from prior work to motivate subsequent extraction analysis; the paper does not newly localize the MLP enrichment process.

statement: Some relations that LMs predict accurately are not linearly decodable from subject representations at any single layer. This is especially true of relations whose objects range over large sets such as person or company names, so LMs use heterogeneous, partly nonlinear knowledge-retrieval strategies.

Inverting a Jacobian-derived linear relational embedding (with a low-rank pseudoinverse) yields edits to the subject representation that causally change the LM's predicted object to a chosen target. The edit's efficacy closely tracks an oracle that substitutes the target subject's representation.
Applying a relation's linear decoder to intermediate hidden states can recover an LM's internal knowledge of a true fact even when the model is induced to output a falsehood.

Subject hidden states serve a dual role. At later layers the LM switches from representing subject attributes (linearly decodable relational information) to representing next-token prediction information, erasing relational embeddings.
scope: Late-layer accessibility of attributes from GPT-J subject representations.

statement: The local Jacobian of an LM's relation-decoding computation systematically underestimates the actual rate of change between subject representations, by a factor of about 2.5-4.3. Scaling it by a constant per model improves the linear approximation.

A model's representation of truth satisfies logical consistency properties (negation consistency, excluded middle) that few other features in the model satisfy, so searching for consistent directions isolates truth.
Language models have an approximately task-agnostic internal representation related to truth: a truth-like direction found on one task transfers to unrelated tasks with different label spaces.
scope: Cross-topic and cross-structure factual statement classification in LLaMA-2; all evaluated tasks retain binary truth labels.

statement: Truth-like directions are salient in LM representations: they often lie along the top principal component of contrast-pair activation differences and can be found from very few unlabeled examples.

Standard LM training objectives (imitation of human text, optimizing human ratings or engagement) can cause models to output falsehoods even when they internally represent the truth, and scaling alone will not fix this.

FFN layers build the output distribution primarily by promotion: a few dominant sub-updates push candidate tokens to the top. Tokens displaced from the top position are mostly not directly suppressed (they receive near-zero mean scores).
scope: Decoder-only LMs; most dominant sub-updates per layer

statement: A small set of homogeneous value-vector clusters accounts for extreme FFN updates in LMs. Upper-layer 'saturation vectors' promote unlikely tokens and propagate an already-fixed prediction, while vectors spread across layers promote common tokens such as stopwords.

Increasing the activation coefficients of a handful of FFN value vectors whose vocabulary projections express benign concepts substantially reduces the toxicity of LM generations, at a modest perplexity cost.
scope: GPT-2 on the challenging subset of RealToxicityPrompts

statement: The identity of the dominant FFN sub-updates at a layer signals whether the model's final prediction has already been fixed. This enables a training-free early-exit rule that matches probe-based exit classifiers.

Transformers trained only on next-token prediction over sequences from a structured process (e.g. game transcripts) develop internal representations of the latent world state of that process, rather than relying solely on surface statistics.
scope: Small GPT trained from scratch on Othello transcripts

statement: If a probe trained on a network's activations predicts a feature accurately, well above a randomly initialized network baseline, then the network encodes a representation of that feature.
scope: Applied here to interpreting dependency-probe performance on attention maps as evidence of learned syntactic information; the validity of this interpretive inference is assumed, and causal use in downstream predictions is not established.

statement: A GPT trained on Othello transcripts predicts legal moves on game-tree branches entirely absent from training, so its competence is not explained by sequence memorization.
In Othello-GPT, the board state (black/white/empty per tile) is not linearly decodable from residual activations but is decodable with a small nonlinear MLP probe.
scope: Black/white/empty labelling; Othello-GPT

statement: Because later layers re-read earlier unmodified representations through attention, intervening on a representation at a single layer is often undone by subsequent layers. Effective control requires editing several consecutive layers.

Attribution performed over a probed latent world state (latent saliency maps) can reveal what a model is computing in human-meaningful terms. For example, it distinguishes a model that has learned rule legality from one that has learned strategy.
Latent world-state information in a transformer is most decodable at middle layers, with decodability lower in early layers and declining slightly at the final layers.

Projecting a behavior direction out of activations (directional ablation) changes off-target behavior less than subtracting a fixed steering vector, which pushes unrelated (e.g. harmless) inputs off-distribution.

The direction that mediates refusal in chat models already separates harmful from harmless instructions in the corresponding pretrained base models, suggesting safety fine-tuning repurposes a pre-existing representation rather than creating it.
Refusal and jailbreak success can be adequately measured by refusal-substring matching combined with an LLM harm classifier (e.g. Llama Guard 2 or the HarmBench classifier).
scope: This document uses the StrongREJECT fine-tuned judge for jailbreak ASR and common refusal-phrase substring matching for induced refusal on harmless Alpaca instructions. Independent human calibration is not reported.

statement: Shifting the outputs of a small set of probe-selected attention heads along truthful directions at inference time substantially increases LLM truthfulness on TruthfulQA, including on top of instruction tuning and few-shot prompting.
scope: LLaMA-7B family on TruthfulQA

statement: Truthfulness information in LLMs is linearly decodable mainly from a sparse subset of attention heads, concentrated in early-to-middle layers, while most heads carry near-chance information.

The concept of truth in an attention head's activation space is not confined to a single direction: a probe constrained orthogonal to the best truth direction still classifies truthfulness above chance.

Restricting activation interventions to a sparse, probe-selected set of attention heads yields better behavior change with less collateral damage than intervening on all heads or on individually selected high-weight features.

Increasing the strength of truthfulness steering trades off against helpfulness and informativeness: past an optimum, the model increasingly refuses to answer, yielding an inverted-U curve in true*informative score.

Truthful steering directions can be identified from only tens to a few hundred labeled examples; the direction's cosine similarity with the full-data direction and the resulting truthfulness gains plateau early.
Transcoder features can be approximately as human-interpretable as sparse-autoencoder features at comparable sparsity and replacement loss.
scope: Pythia-410M layer 15; comparison with an MLP-input SAE.

statement: Direct contributions between transcoder features factor into an input-dependent source activation and an input-invariant decoder–encoder dot product, enabling weight-based analysis of feature connections across inputs.
scope: Transcoder approximation; active target features; attention extensions hold QK scores fixed and approximate LayerNorm scaling.

statement: Transcoder circuit analysis can recover the semantics of some downstream features without directly inspecting the text of their activating examples.
scope: Nine qualitative GPT2-small layer-8 feature case studies.

statement: Transcoder replacement can preserve a feature's broad activation pattern while substantially distorting finer contextual or grammatical selectivity.
scope: A GPT2-small layer-8 'caught' feature with all preceding MLPs replaced by transcoders.

statement: Low next-token cross-entropy degradation after replacing an MLP with a sparse surrogate is a useful proxy for the surrogate's fidelity to the original computation.
scope: Aggregate fidelity evaluation; does not guarantee preservation of individual mechanisms or feature nuances.

statement: Some SAE features extracted from text activations respond to the same concepts across languages, images, and concrete versus abstract presentations.
scope: Selected Sonnet features; broad prevalence and unbiased sensitivity are not quantified.

statement: Larger SAE dictionaries resolve dedicated features for rarer concepts, with the frequency threshold for resolution approximately inversely related to the number of alive features.
scope: Single-word elements, cities, animals, and foods; frequency measured in a proxy dataset.

statement: Clamping individual SAE features can cause downstream behavioral changes consistent with interpretations derived from their activating examples.
scope: Selected Sonnet features, often clamped beyond their naturally observed activation range.

statement: Gradient-times-feature-activation attribution can predict individual SAE feature ablation effects on output logit differences substantially better than feature activation magnitude.
scope: Two selected Sonnet completion case studies; results depend on prompt, layer, and baseline token.

statement: In some few-shot settings, SAE features provide more effective concept-specific steering than difference-of-means directions constructed from the same positive and negative examples.
scope: Seven examples selected for successful SAE steering; qualitative manual tuning.

statement: Features distributed across multiple layers can be incompletely captured or misinterpreted by dictionaries trained at a single activation site.
scope: Proposed fundamental limitation of single-layer SAE analysis.

statement: Increasing SAE dictionary width improves reconstruction fidelity at a comparable number of active latents.
scope: Middle-layer residual-stream JumpReLU SAEs on Gemma 2 2B and 9B.

statement: Comparable SAE activation-reconstruction error does not imply comparable preservation of downstream language-model behavior.
scope: Comparison across activation sites and base-to-instruction-tuned transfer.

statement: SAEs trained on a pretrained base model can reconstruct activations of its instruction-tuned derivative with downstream loss increases close to those of SAEs trained directly on the derivative.
scope: Selected residual-stream layers of Gemma 2 9B; supplementary FVU evaluation for Gemma 2 2B.

statement: JumpReLU, TopK, and Gated SAEs have similar latent interpretability under human ratings and explanation-based activation-simulation correlation.
scope: 131K-width SAEs at attention, MLP, and residual sites in Gemma 2 9B layers 9, 20, and 31.

statement: Using bfloat16 rather than float32 for SAE and language-model inference can preserve the SAE sparsity–fidelity trade-off with negligible degradation.
scope: Evaluated Gemma Scope configurations.

statement: On Gemma 2 2B, JumpReLU transcoders can cause greater downstream loss increases than MLP-output SAEs at matched sparsity.
scope: Released Gemma 2 2B PT transcoder suite and corresponding MLP-output SAEs.

statement: Thresholding gradient-based approximations of node and edge indirect effects enables scalable discovery of causal circuits over SAE features while retaining reconstruction errors as explicit nodes.
scope: Models with pretrained SAEs and a specified behavioral metric or next-token loss.

statement: Human identification and ablation of task-irrelevant SAE features can improve classifier generalization when intended and unintended signals are perfectly correlated in training labels.
scope: Binary professor-versus-nurse classification on Bias in Bios, training on male professors and female nurses.

statement: Clustering language-model internal activations, gradients, or approximate effects can supply behavioral datasets for automated discovery of interpretable feature circuits without manually specifying each behavior.
scope: Confident, correct next-token predictions from The Pile in Pythia-70M.

statement: Subject–verb agreement across relative clauses and prepositional phrases can use shared number-detection, phrase-boundary, and verb-inflection features.
scope: Interpreted feature circuits in Pythia-70M and Gemma-2-2B.

statement: Replacing MLP computations with transcoder features and freezing attention patterns and normalization denominators yields linear direct effects from source-feature activations to downstream feature preactivations.
scope: Prompt-specific local replacement models; excludes effects through changing attention patterns or normalization denominators.

statement: Accurate activation reconstruction or exact unperturbed output matching by a replacement model does not guarantee that it implements the underlying model's mechanisms.
scope: Local CLT and per-layer-transcoder replacement models with error correction and frozen attention.

statement: Attribution graphs conditioned on fixed attention patterns can omit the decisive computation when behavior depends on how attention selects information.
scope: Induction and multiple-choice answering; attribution methods omitting QK circuits.

statement: Graphs containing only active features can miss causally important inhibitory mechanisms because suppressed features may explain why an alternative behavior did not occur.
scope: Sparse-feature attribution graphs and coactivation-based global-weight filtering.

statement: Weighting virtual feature connections by on-distribution coactivation statistics can reveal more interpretable global relationships, but can discard important inhibitory connections.
scope: Target-weighted expected residual attribution; residual-direct feature interactions.

statement: Language models can perform small-number addition through parallel magnitude and modular heuristics that interact to produce precise answers.
scope: Prompts calc: a+b= with a,b in [0,99]; detailed interventions center on 36+59.

statement: Directly controlling SAE sparsity with TopK improves reconstruction and downstream behavioral preservation relative to L1-regularized ReLU SAEs.
scope: Normalized residual-stream activations of GPT-2 small and GPT-4-family models.

statement: Initializing SAE encoder and decoder directions in parallel and training inactive latents to reconstruct residual error substantially reduces dead latents at large dictionary widths.
scope: TopK SAEs, with dead latents defined by no activation over approximately 10 million tokens.

statement: In the sparse regime, SAE reconstruction error follows empirical scaling laws in dictionary width, compute, and active-latent count, with fitted loss floors improving the fits.
scope: The tested TopK training recipe and model activations; excludes near-dense regimes.

statement: Increasing SAE dictionary width generally improves hypothesized-feature recovery, simple-pattern explainability, explanation-based behavioral reconstruction, and sparsity of downstream effects.
scope: Tested SAE widths and sparse regimes; most detailed quality sweeps use GPT-2 small.

statement: Recovery of researcher-selected classification targets in individual SAE latents is a useful proxy for recovery of natural model features.
scope: Best single-latent logistic-probe loss on the curated 61-task evaluation suite.

statement: Natural features in language models should have sparse downstream effects as well as sparse activations.
scope: Feature-quality interpretation of latent-ablation logit sparsity.

statement: The fraction of loss recovered relative to zero ablation can overstate SAE behavioral fidelity because zeroing the residual stream produces an exceptionally poor baseline.
scope: Residual-stream SAE reconstruction substitution.

statement: Improving SAE reconstruction and activation sparsity alone does not establish recovery of meaningful model features.
scope: Interpretability evaluation of overcomplete sparse autoencoders.

statement: Training an SAE with losses at multiple TopK sparsity levels improves reconstruction when the active-latent count is changed after training.
scope: Tested Multi-TopK and single-TopK autoencoders.

statement: Activation-patching results identify mechanisms involved in differences between the tested prompt distributions and do not establish their role outside those distributions.
scope: Prompt-based activation-patching studies.

statement: Clean-to-corrupted activation patching tests sufficiency to restore behavior, whereas corrupted-to-clean patching tests necessity to maintain it; these properties need not coincide.
scope: Relative to the selected intervention sites, prompt distributions, and behavioral metric.

statement: Restoring behavior by patching downstream clean activations can identify only a cross-section of a circuit because those activations already contain the results of unpatched upstream computation.
scope: Denoising interventions in circuits with mediated upstream dependencies.

statement: Discrete and probability-based patching metrics can obscure or exaggerate partial component effects, while continuous metrics approximately linear in logits better expose additive contributions.
scope: Exploratory patching; the argument is strongest when component effects are approximately additive in logit space.

statement: An intervention can improve correct-minus-incorrect logit difference by suppressing the incorrect answer through nonspecific model damage, without restoring the intended computation.
scope: Especially relevant when the corrupted model strongly favors the incorrect answer.

statement: A candidate circuit can match or exceed full-model task performance while remaining incomplete if omitted negative components offset the effects of omitted positive components.
scope: Circuit verification based on task-performance recovery.

statement: Confirming a hypothesized circuit requires interventions over prompt distributions that vary all hypothesized circuit variables, rather than relying only on isolated-component effects under narrow corruptions.
scope: Verification of behavioral circuit sufficiency, without establishing minimality.

statement: Correct-answer probability can fail to reveal negative components in activation patching when corruption drives that probability close to zero, because negative recovery effects are bounded by the corrupted baseline probability.
scope: Clean-to-corrupted activation patching evaluated using correct-answer probability.

statement: Logit difference between a correct answer and a relevant alternative controls for components that boost both answers equally, allowing localization to target the distinction between them.
scope: Requires choosing an appropriate comparison token; illustrated with IOI names.

statement: Successful subspace activation patching does not establish that the patched subspace represents a feature used by the unmodified model, because the intervention can activate a dormant pathway using causally disconnected feature information.
scope: Arbitrary linear subspace interventions, demonstrated in linear toy networks and GPT-2 MLP activations.

statement: GPT-2 Small communicates IOI name-position information through a residual-stream direction written by S-inhibition heads and read by name-mover heads.
scope: Final-token residual stream after layer 8 on the studied IOI distribution.

statement: Rank-one MLP weight edits can be approximated by generalized one-dimensional activation interventions, and one-dimensional activation patches admit rank-one edits with identical local MLP-output changes.
scope: MLP output projections; the ROME-to-intervention construction relaxes unit-norm patching and uses an empirical covariance objective.

statement: Architectural component boundaries such as attention heads and MLP layers provide meaningful constraints on mechanistic explanations, so arbitrary reparameterizations across those boundaries need not preserve explanatory quality.
scope: Interpretation of dormant-pathway subspaces as illusory rather than as equally valid alternative mechanisms.

statement: Small transformers trained with weight decay on modular addition can generalize by encoding inputs as sinusoidal features, composing them through trigonometric identities, and combining frequencies to identify the correct sum.
scope: Studied small modular-addition transformers; detailed analysis centers on a one-layer model modulo 113.

statement: Losses computed after selectively retaining or removing an identified generalizing circuit can reveal continuous learning progress before a sharp improvement in held-out performance.
scope: Fourier-space restricted and excluded losses for modular addition.

statement: Memorizing solutions to modular addition distribute their logit contributions broadly enough across Fourier components that removing a few generalizing frequencies largely preserves their training performance.
scope: Interpretation of excluded loss on modular addition.

statement: In regularized modular-addition transformers, a generalizing circuit can form gradually while test performance remains poor, with the subsequent grokking transition occurring as memorizing components are removed.
scope: Studied modular-addition training runs; phase timings vary by seed.

statement: Delayed generalization in small algorithmic transformers depends on the training-data regime and regularization: abundant fresh data can eliminate the train–test delay, while suitable regularization can enable escape from memorization.
scope: Tested modular addition, five-digit addition, repeated-subsequence, and skip-trigram settings; not a universal necessity theorem.

statement: Learning interacting circuit components can produce a phase transition because improving one component increases the usefulness and gradients of the others.
scope: Proposed explanation for algorithmic circuit formation, including induction circuits.

statement: Affine translators trained to match final-output distributions decode intermediate transformer predictions with lower perplexity and vocabulary bias than direct logit-lens decoding.
scope: Tested autoregressive model families up to 20B parameters, primarily pre-LayerNorm architectures.

statement: Sequentially maximizing ablation-induced output KL divergence under orthogonality constraints identifies multiple influential directions in a neural representation.
scope: Mean-ablation influence with nonconvex optimization; no guarantee of recovering every important feature.

statement: Directions influential for a tuned lens also tend to influence the underlying model, and interventions in those directions produce more aligned output changes than directions selected using the logit lens.
scope: CBE-selected directions and principal-subspace interventions in small Pythia models.

statement: Affine translators trained on a base language model can decode its instruction-tuned derivative without retraining, using the derivative's unembedding and with limited fidelity loss.
scope: LLaMA 13B to Vicuna 13B transfer.

statement: Anomaly detectors trained on normal layerwise prediction trajectories can distinguish prompt-injected inputs from normal inputs without training on attacks.
scope: A fixed appended wrong-answer instruction on nine multiple-choice tasks with Pythia 12B.

statement: Examples whose predictions stabilize later during training also tend to require more transformer layers for their predictions to stabilize at inference time.
scope: Zero-shot multiple-choice evaluation on the eleven reported Pythia 12B tasks.

statement: Suppressing FFN value-vector coefficients selected by toxic vocabulary projections can reduce generation toxicity while preserving perplexity.
scope: Successful on OPT-125M, with unsuccessful generalization to four other tested models.

statement: Interpretable features provide useful basic units for describing language-model computation.
scope: Feature-based decomposition underlying circuit tracing; the definition of a feature remains unsettled.

statement: Feature attribution graphs combined with interventions can reveal causally relevant intermediate computations absent from a language model's generated text.
scope: Selected short prompts with interpretable CLT coverage.

statement: Language models can represent candidate ending words before generating a poetry line and use those representations to shape the line's earlier words and structure.
scope: Selected rhyming poems; planned-word features found in about half of investigated poems.

statement: Addition-related features can be reused across superficially different tasks requiring the same arithmetic subcomputation.
scope: Arithmetic, tabular sequences, astronomical measurements, and academic citation years.

statement: Familiar-entity and known-answer features can suppress default uncertainty responses, and inappropriate suppression can produce hallucinations.
scope: Sports questions and author-paper citation prompts.

statement: Safety fine-tuning may connect pretrained representations of specific harms to generalized harmful-request features that trigger refusal.
scope: Interpretation of feature contexts and global connectivity, without a longitudinal training study.

statement: An obfuscated harmful request can evade early harm recognition, after which grammatical continuation pressures delay refusal until a sentence boundary.
scope: One acronym-based jailbreak and nearby variants.

statement: A language model can construct intermediate chain-of-thought steps backward from a user-suggested final answer rather than compute them from the stated problem.
scope: Artificial arithmetic prompts involving a difficult cosine computation and an answer hint.

statement: Fine-tuning a language model to pursue a concealed objective can bind objective-related representations to its assistant persona and use them to drive context-specific behavior.
scope: An intentionally constructed reward-model-bias-appeasement model organism.

statement: Failure to detect dangerous computation with current circuit-tracing methods provides only limited assurance because important mechanisms may remain unobserved.
scope: Safety auditing with the reported attribution-graph workflow.

statement: Applying activation-patching-based ACDC after EAP pruning can improve recovery of known circuit edges relative to EAP alone.
scope: Docstring circuit recovery.

statement: KL divergence from a model's unperturbed output distribution has zero gradient at the unperturbed activations, so first-order attribution patching cannot directly rank edges using that objective at that point.
scope: Differentiable KL objectives comparing an unperturbed model with its intervened counterpart.

statement: Mechanistic hypotheses can be tested systematically by recursively resampling activations within hypothesis-defined equivalence classes and measuring preservation of the target behavior.
scope: Hypotheses expressible as correspondences between computational graphs, evaluated on a specified dataset.

statement: Preservation of expected behavior under hypothesis-permitted activation resampling is a useful, defeasible proxy for the mechanistic faithfulness of an interpretation.
scope: Evaluation of interpretations on a fixed behavior and data distribution; preservation is not a correctness guarantee.

statement: A small transformer parentheses classifier approximately decomposes balance checking into attention-head pathways for equal counts and an opening initial parenthesis, and a separate pathway for nesting constraints.
scope: The particular small parentheses-balance transformer studied; head identities and mechanisms are model-specific.

statement: Induction in a two-layer attention-only language model can depend on matching multiple consecutive tokens and on layer-0 contributions to queries and values beyond a simple previous-token key pathway.
scope: The studied model on a filtered OpenWebText distribution where induction is often helpful.

statement: Averaging edge-attribution gradients across clean–corrupted input interpolations can produce more faithful transformer circuits than scoring edges with gradients only at clean inputs.
scope: Head/MLP edge circuits on six tasks in GPT-2 small, with smaller evaluations in GPT-2 XL and Pythia-2.8B.

statement: If a model uses the same mechanisms to solve two tasks, circuits capturing those mechanisms should preserve behavior when evaluated across those tasks.
scope: Cross-task comparisons using corrupted-example edge ablations.

statement: Improved circuit faithfulness from integrated-gradient edge attribution can arise from better identification of a few critical edges without better overall edge-ranking accuracy or substantially lower score error.
scope: Six GPT-2 small tasks.

statement: Averaging gradients at clean and corrupted inputs can yield circuit faithfulness competitive with multi-step input-interpolated EAP-IG.
scope: Six GPT-2 small tasks under the paper's circuit-search procedure.

statement: First-order activation-patching scores for all cached intervention sites can be computed from two forward passes and one backward pass using activation differences dotted with metric gradients.
scope: Differentiable models, a scalar metric, and cached clean and corrupted activations; scoring and memory costs still depend on the number of sites.

statement: First-order patching approximations can miss effects that depend on jointly changing multiple features or traversing saturated nonlinearities.
scope: Gradient approximations around a single baseline run.

statement: Hierarchical Matryoshka SAEs can isolate concepts more effectively than non-hierarchical SAEs despite worse reconstruction at comparable sparsity.
scope: Primarily Gemma-2-2B layer 12, especially L0 40–200; advantages are not universal across models or sparsities.

statement: Increasing non-hierarchical SAE dictionary width can degrade concept isolation even as reconstruction and individual-feature interpretability improve.
scope: Most tested non-hierarchical architectures; effects depend on metric, sparsity, and intervention budget.

statement: The SAE active-latent count that optimizes quality depends on the evaluation task, so no single sparsity setting is uniformly optimal.
scope: SAEBench architecture and sparsity sweeps, primarily Gemma-2-2B.

statement: Integrating circuit recovery across circuit sizes enables method comparisons that distinguish recovering positive task contributions from matching full-model behavior, including negative contributions.
scope: CPR and CMD under fixed counterfactual ablations and normalized logit-difference recovery.

statement: Learning task-supervised orthogonal subspaces generally isolates specified causal variables more accurately than selecting standard dimensions, principal components, or SAE features.
scope: MIB causal variable localization; aggregate trend with task-specific exceptions.

statement: Researcher-specified high-level causal variables correspond sufficiently closely to concepts implemented by a language model to serve as targets for evaluating feature localization.
scope: Causal variable localization benchmarks; explicitly uncertain for carry-the-one and for whole-algorithm interpretations.

statement: Language models can represent the position of a correct multiple-choice answer separately from the token label ultimately output.
scope: Synthetic MCQA and ARC Easy, using answer-position and label-changing counterfactuals.

statement: Some negative attention heads suppress previously occurring tokens that upstream components predict, providing a shared mechanism for negative name mover and anti-induction behavior.
scope: Primarily GPT-2 Small L10H7 on OpenWebText; preliminary evidence in GPT-2 Medium and unspecified Pythia models.

statement: Token-unembedding directions alone do not capture the query signals controlling negative-head and backup-head self-repair.
scope: GPT-2 Small, particularly IOI downstream heads.

statement: Comparing a mechanism-preserving ablation with full component ablation can quantify how much of a component’s output-distribution effect a proposed mechanism preserves.
scope: CSPA applied to GPT-2 Small attention-head direct effects on OpenWebText.

statement: Preserving a component’s downstream output effects while deleting functionality outside a hypothesized mechanism is a useful proxy for the completeness of the component’s mechanistic explanation.
scope: Interpretation of mechanism-preserving interventions relative to mean ablation.

statement: Expanding residual-stream representations into feature, bias, and reconstruction-error components decomposes pre-softmax attention scores into additive bilinear query–key interactions that can identify causally relevant attention-selection mechanisms.
scope: Attention scores with architecture-appropriate treatment of normalization and positional transformations; qualitative case studies.

statement: Checkpointing feature attribution paths at each attention layer permits graph-edge contributions to be decomposed by individual heads without enumerating chains of heads across layers.
scope: Residual-stream SAE or weakly causal crosscoder graphs; alternative checkpointing strategies are also described.

statement: Multiple-choice answer selection can use query-side answer-request features interacting with key-side correctness features to attend to the appropriate answer, while incorrectness features inhibit competing attention scores.
scope: A World War II end-year multiple-choice prompt in Claude 3.5 Haiku.

statement: Language models can validate statements through distinct attention circuits that detect concordant or discordant properties, without an identifiable intermediate step that explicitly computes and compares a complete answer.
scope: Banana-color and small arithmetic correctness prompts in Claude 3.5 Haiku; absence of a compute-then-compare pathway is observational.

statement: SAE sparsity can trade concept-classification precision against recall: fewer active latents favor high precision and low recall, while more active latents favor lower precision and higher recall.
scope: Individual first-letter latents in Gemma Scope SAEs.

statement: Internal visual features can be combined with attribution objectives, differentiable spline rendering, and activation factorization to construct curve-tracing operations without retraining the network.
scope: Prototype visual operations built from InceptionV1.

statement: Curve and line detectors in multiple vision architectures can prefer small perpendicular lines alongside their principal boundary stimulus.
scope: Illustrated curve features in AlexNet, InceptionV1, and InceptionV3; additional qualitative observations include Places365-trained models.

statement: Weighting activation frequency by activation magnitude provides a useful approximation to the importance of different response regimes for a neuron's downstream influence.
scope: Using x·p(x) to assess curve versus non-curve contributions for neuron 3b:379.

statement: Attention heads that promote successors across multiple ordinal sequences recur across language-model architectures and parameter scales.
scope: Surveyed GPT-2, Pythia, and Llama-2 models spanning 31M–12B parameters; not every model contains a qualifying head.

statement: Ordinal token representations can approximately separate sequence identity from a shared numeric index, enabling index transfer across domains.
scope: Pythia-1.4B MLP0 representations; output-space decoding is more reliable than successor decoding.

statement: Numeric token representations contain mod-10 directions that causally contribute to successor-head incrementation and transfer to some non-digit ordinal domains.
scope: Primarily Pythia-1.4B L12H0; incomplete transfer for days, letters, and boundary months.

statement: Mod-10 directions alone do not fully explain successor-head numeric computation, including its bias toward larger ordinal values.
scope: Pythia-1.4B L12H0 effective OV circuit.

statement: Successor heads contribute substantially to next-token prediction on natural-language incrementation tasks, including numbered lists.
scope: Pythia-1.4B L12H0 on sampled Pile contexts and a collected numbered-list dataset.

statement: A single language-model attention head can perform multiple distinct interpretable functions, including ordinal succession and acronym completion.
scope: Pythia-1.4B L12H0 on natural-language contexts.

statement: Low-capacity linear probes restricted to a small number of MLP neurons can efficiently localize neurons predictive of specified human-interpretable input features.
scope: Post-GeLU MLP activations in Pythia V0 models from 70M to 6.9B; supervised binary feature datasets.

statement: Early transformer MLP layers can represent specific n-grams through sparse linear combinations of neurons that individually respond to many unrelated n-grams.
scope: Compound-word case studies, particularly layers 1–3 of Pythia V0 1B.

statement: Individual language-model MLP neurons can selectively encode broad textual contexts and causally improve next-token prediction primarily within their corresponding contexts.
scope: Natural-language, programming-language, and Pile-source context neurons in Pythia V0; strict monosemanticity remains unproven.

statement: Increasing language-model scale can increase neuron-level representational sparsity on average while leaving some features unchanged or less sparsely represented.
scope: Seven Pythia V0 models, 70M–6.9B, over the tested binary feature collections.

statement: Improvement from a one-neuron probe to a multi-neuron linear probe does not by itself distinguish superposition from unions or compositions of simpler features.
scope: Interpretation of neuron-level sparse-probing performance.

statement: Small regularized MLPs and Transformers trained on finite-group composition learn representation-theoretic circuits that embed inputs as group representations, compute product representations, and decode character-based scores.
scope: Tested MLPs and one-layer ReLU Transformers on seven finite groups.

statement: The dimensions of group representations do not deterministically specify which representations a neural network learns or their learning order.
scope: Regularized finite-group composition networks, especially S5.

statement: Integrated-gradients attribution refined across paraphrases can identify small sets of FFN neurons whose activation causally modulates the expression of particular relational facts.
scope: BERT-base-cased, masked-position FFN neurons, single-word factual cloze prediction on ParaRel.

statement: Diverse prompts expressing the same fact share its factual neurons, while neurons encoding incidental lexical or syntactic information are less consistently shared.
scope: Assumption underlying cross-prompt refinement of neuron selections.

statement: Correct-answer prediction on a relational cloze query is a useful operational measure of a language model's factual knowledge.
scope: Single-word masked factual queries.

statement: Neurons selected from factual cloze paraphrases can respond selectively to corresponding factual expressions in open-domain text.
scope: BERT-base-cased; ParaRel-selected neurons evaluated on BingRel masked web texts.

statement: Texts containing both entities of a known relational fact tend to express that fact and can provide weak supervision for evaluating relation-sensitive representations.
scope: BingRel entity-pair web retrieval.

statement: Direct edits to the FFN value vectors associated with a few fact-selected neurons can change a model's predicted factual answer without fine-tuning.
scope: BERT-base-cased; ten learned facts sampled per ParaRel relation, with same-type replacement entities.

statement: Zeroing FFN value vectors associated with neurons frequently selected for a relation can impair that relation's factual predictions more than predictions for other relations.
scope: BERT-base-cased; place of birth, citizenship, occupation, and work location.

statement: Neural-network generalization arises from computations shared across instances, making those computations useful targets for mechanistic explanation.
scope: The review's framing of mechanistic interpretability.

statement: Mechanistic explanations should be validated through predictions of activations or counterfactual behavior, and engineering applications should be compared fairly with relevant non-interpretability baselines.
scope: Validation standards for explanations and practical interpretability methods.

statement: Fully automating existing mechanistic interpretability pipelines would not by itself produce explanations adequate for the field's scientific and engineering goals.
scope: Automation with current decomposition, description, and validation methods.

statement: Descriptions of a limited set of internal components may aid detection of concerning cognition even when the descriptions are correlational and the whole network is not understood.
scope: Near-term white-box evaluations and deployment monitoring; not comprehensive safety assurance.

statement: Understanding learned mechanisms can improve predictions of model behavior in situations not covered by finite behavioral evaluations.
scope: Motivation for failure prediction, capability forecasting, and stronger safety claims.

statement: GPT-4 ratings under behavior-specific rubrics adequately measure the targeted behavioral properties of open-ended model responses.
scope: Seven behavioral rubrics and sampled manual rating checks.

statement: Contrastive activation steering can further modify behavior after supervised fine-tuning, but its interaction with fine-tuning is behavior-dependent and can reverse the intended effect.
scope: One-epoch supervised fine-tuning on the CAA multiple-choice datasets.

statement: Steering against sycophancy can modestly improve truthfulness on misconception-focused question answering.
scope: Binary-choice TruthfulQA evaluation on Llama 2 Chat.

statement: Averaging activation differences between prompts differing only in behavior-labeled answer choices isolates the intended behavioral variable sufficiently for steering.
scope: Answer-letter-conditioned contrastive datasets.

statement: For simple factual statements that a model is very likely to understand, externally assigned truth labels provide suitable targets for studying the model's internal assessment of factuality.
scope: Simple, unambiguous factual claims; does not distinguish factuality from widespread belief or verifiability.

statement: Linear representations relevant to factual truth cannot be fully explained by representations of text likelihood.
scope: Curated factual datasets and a nonfactual completion-likelihood control.

statement: Difference-in-means truth directions can influence out-of-distribution truth-classification outputs more strongly than logistic-regression or contrast-consistent-search directions with similar classification accuracy.
scope: Interventions on Spanish–English statement classification using directions learned on other datasets.

statement: Training truth probes on statements together with their logical opposites can improve cross-dataset classification by reducing reliance on features whose correlation with truth reverses across the paired datasets.
scope: City statements plus negations and larger-than plus smaller-than comparisons.

statement: Vocabulary-projection methods and several activation-intervention methods can be expressed within a common framework specifying a target prompt, position, representation mapping, model, and layer.
scope: Logit lens, affine lenses, Future Lens, LRE Attribute Lens, causal tracing, and attention knockout.

statement: Information generated after transplanting a hidden state establishes accessibility through the target computation, but does not establish that all generated information was explicitly stored in the transplanted state.
scope: Natural-language decoding with nontrivial post-patching model computation.

statement: During early transformer layers, the last token of an entity name can progressively acquire information from preceding name tokens, shifting accessible entity identity from local token associations toward the full named entity.
scope: Entity-description decoding of popular and rare PopQA entities in Vicuna and Pythia.

statement: Rerouting an intermediate answer representation into a subsequent relation computation can improve two-hop factual answering when the model can answer each constituent hop independently.
scope: Structurally specified synthesized queries with per-example search over source and target layers.

statement: Earlier-layer traces of a target placeholder can contaminate multi-token generations after a later-layer activation replacement, causing decoded text to describe the placeholder rather than the source entity.
scope: Single-position entity-description and attribute-extraction Patchscopes.

statement: The ease of predicting target labels with a linear classifier is a useful proxy for how computationally accessible those labels are in an intermediate representation.
scope: Interpretation of independent linear probes on classification networks; does not establish causal use or characterize all nonlinearly accessible information.

statement: Interpreting differences in probe performance as differences in linear label accessibility requires sufficiently effective probe optimization, control of overfitting, and attention to differences introduced by feature reduction.
scope: Layerwise comparisons using independently fitted linear classifiers, including pooled or randomly subsampled features; the paper acknowledges that feature reduction does not provide uniformly fair comparisons.

statement: Intermediate representations in trained vision classifiers can become progressively more linearly predictive of the original class labels, with nearly monotonic improvements across depth despite supervision being applied at the classifier heads.
scope: The studied MNIST CNN, pretrained ResNet-50, and Inception v3 on MNIST or ImageNet; measured through the paper's probe feature reductions and classification-error metrics, rather than a universal property of vision classifiers.

statement: Randomly initialized convolutional-network transformations can improve linear classification of MNIST relative to linear classification directly from the input.
scope: The randomly initialized TensorFlow MNIST CNN studied in the paper, before any underlying-model training.

statement: An Inception v3 auxiliary branch can exhibit slightly lower probe prediction error than the main branch during training.
scope: The observed ImageNet training run and snapshots of Inception v3; no claim that the advantage persists through completed training.

statement: Final-delimiter task vectors extracted from different demonstrations and dummy queries can cluster by task, with smaller within-task than between-task distances.
scope: LLaMA 7B on the paper's 18 simple tasks, using 50 vectors per task.

statement: Injecting a task vector can redirect a language model toward the injected task even when its prompt contains demonstrations of a conflicting task with the same input space.
scope: Three directed task pairs: next-letter demonstrations with an uppercase vector, list-last demonstrations with a list-first vector, and present-to-past demonstrations with a present-to-gerund vector; model identity unspecified for this experiment.

statement: Comparing aligned interchange interventions in a neural network and an interpretable causal model provides a systematic test of whether selected neural representations realize the model’s high-level causal roles.
scope: Specified high-level causal models, candidate neural alignments, and tested source/base input pairs; finite agreement establishes correspondence only on the tested domain.

statement: Perfect probe decoding of a property from a neural representation does not establish that the representation causally contributes that property to the network’s output.
scope: The logical implication from perfect decodability to causal use, without additional architectural or intervention evidence.

statement: For a differentiable deterministic model, an integrated-gradients coordinate attribution can be expressed as the input-baseline coordinate difference multiplied by the path average of limiting causal effects of perturbing that coordinate.
scope: Straight-line baseline-to-input integration, where the required derivatives and integral exist and coordinate perturbations are interpreted as interventions holding other coordinates fixed.

statement: Pretraining substantially improves the test accuracy of the evaluated BERT classifier on MQNLI’s hardest fair generalization task.
scope: The paper’s BERT training configuration, including supervision of relations between aligned phrases.

statement: In the reported MQNLI comparison, integrated gradients assigns greater importance to representations above the token difference between a premise and hypothesis than to representations above their matching tokens.
scope: The paper’s reported integrated-gradients experiment on premise–hypothesis token differences; its sample size, baselines, attribution aggregation, and numerical results are not supplied.

statement: A dictionary with nonnegative sparse coefficients learned from pooled transformer-layer hidden states can provide interpretable coordinates for visualizing selected lexical and contextual patterns across layers.
scope: A single dictionary learned from frozen bert-base-uncased hidden states; selected factor visualizations and linguistic evaluations.

statement: Contextualized token embeddings can be usefully modeled as sparse nonnegative combinations of elementary factor vectors plus a small residual of independent Gaussian noise.
scope: The modeling assumption underlying dictionary learning of BERT hidden states; the residual distribution and reconstruction accuracy are not evaluated.

statement: A supervised logistic-regression classifier using a single unsupervised dictionary coefficient from BERT-base layer 4 can distinguish verbal from nonverbal uses of “left” with high binary POS-classification performance.
scope: Factor 30 and Brown-corpus occurrences of “left”; sample counts and evaluation split are unspecified. The labels distinguish parts of speech rather than all semantic senses.

statement: Matched tasks with independently randomized word-type behaviors can contextualize linguistic probing accuracy by measuring the probe's ability to learn arbitrary type-level mappings from the same representations.
scope: Word-level part-of-speech tagging and dependency edge prediction using frozen contextual representations.

statement: Independently sampled word-type control behaviors supply no systematic linguistic rule for predicting each type's assignment, so successful prediction of these assignments primarily requires the probe to learn the arbitrary mapping.
scope: Random assignments independent of the frozen representation's training, with separate assignments for each word type; unseen types remain subject to chance prediction.

statement: High linguistic accuracy together with low matched word-type control accuracy is a useful proxy for a probe relying on linguistic properties of a representation rather than its capacity to memorize word identities.
scope: Interpretation of accuracy differences between linguistic tasks and word-type random control tasks; not a guarantee of faithful or causal representation recovery.

statement: Default linear and MLP part-of-speech probes on ELMo1 can exhibit different error patterns despite similar overall accuracy, including better adjective–noun distinctions by MLPs and fewer proper-noun plurality errors by linear probes.
scope: Qualitative inspection of aggregate confusion matrices from ten default linear and ten default MLP-1 probes on Penn Treebank tagging.

statement: Separating feature detection from magnitude estimation in Gated SAEs generally improves the active-feature-count versus downstream loss-recovery frontier over L1-regularized ReLU SAEs at matched training compute, with approximately half as many active features sufficient at many evaluated sites.
scope: GELU-1L neuron activations and selected MLP-output, pre-output-projection attention, and residual-stream sites in Pythia-2.8B and Gemma-7B base; tested sparsity sweeps, without uniform dominance at every Gemma site.

statement: Correcting activation magnitudes while freezing a baseline SAE's encoder and decoder directions recovers only part of the sparsity–fidelity improvement obtained by training a Gated SAE.
scope: GELU-1L comparison with equal-dictionary-size baseline SAEs augmented by learned rescale-and-shift magnitude parameters.

statement: Under gradient-pursuit inference, Gated SAE dictionaries can have a modest reconstruction advantage over baseline dictionaries, but selecting a baseline trained at higher L0 can substantially narrow that advantage.
scope: Appendix A's trained dictionaries evaluated with nonnegative gradient-pursuit sparse approximation at several target sparsities; the appendix does not explicitly identify the underlying language model.

statement: Randomly sampled features from Gated and baseline SAEs can receive broadly similar human interpretability ratings, although the available small study establishes neither equivalence nor overall Gated superiority.
scope: Human inspection of feature behavior, especially highest-activating examples, for 150 Pythia-2.8B features and 192 Gemma-7B features across selected layers and activation sites.

statement: Blocking auxiliary reconstruction gradients into the Gated SAE decoder improves its sparsity–fidelity tradeoff relative to allowing those gradients to update the decoder.
scope: GELU-1L MLP-neuron activation ablation of the proposed Gated SAE training recipe.

statement: Sharing projection directions between Gated SAE detection and magnitude branches can preserve or slightly improve reconstruction–sparsity performance relative to fully independent branches.
scope: GELU-1L MLP-neuron activation ablations with separate branch biases and learned positive magnitude rescaling.

statement: A gated encoder whose magnitude projection is a positive scalar multiple of its gate projection can be expressed as a single affine projection followed by a parameterized JumpReLU activation.
scope: Per-feature tied projections w_mag=rho*w_gate with rho=exp(r)>0, independent gate and magnitude biases, and a common centered input.

statement: Layer-level causal localization effects provide little information about the success of factual weight rewrites beyond the identity of the edited MLP layer.
scope: False-fact injection using ROME, MEMIT, and constrained one- or five-layer fine-tuning, primarily on selected CounterFact facts in GPT-J; supplementary GPT2-XL, GPT-J/ZSRE, and representation-zeroing evaluations use specific subsets of these conditions.
