scope: One Gemma 2 9B layer-20 residual-stream SAE and associated adjacent-component dictionaries, all width 16k and L0 approximately 60; component layer indexing is inconsistently described.

statement: An SAE error decomposition can distinguish input-added from reconstruction-added Gaussian noise in synthetic data generated from learned SAE directions, while behaving differently with random Gaussian feature directions.
scope: Gemma Scope layer-20 16k dictionary with L0 approximately 68 and the specified synthetic feature-masking and noise-injection procedures; comparison with the separate random-direction construction.

statement: The residual after affine prediction of SAE error may predominantly reflect reconstruction-introduced distortions, while predictable error may contain missing linear features and dense activation content.
scope: The proposed mixed sparse/dense activation model; the empirical decomposition does not uniquely identify these latent sources.

statement: Language-model activations can be usefully modeled as a sparse sum of linear feature directions plus a remaining component that is poorly captured by sparse linear reconstruction.
scope: The modeling premise in Appendix B; the remainder may include noise, nonlinear features, or other structure, without an identified ground-truth decomposition.

statement: For interpreting an SAE error decomposition, a finite dictionary can be approximated as learning common linear features while introducing reconstruction distortions that are not linearly predictable from the original activation.
scope: The simplifying model of Appendices B and B.2; linearly predictable introduced error would bias the proposed source attribution.

statement: Linear predictability of an activation component's squared norm from the original activation provides a useful diagnostic of how much that component consists of sparsely active, nearly orthogonal linear features.
scope: The interpretation of norm-prediction comparisons in Section 5.1 and Appendix B.1; feature-amplitude distributions, correlations, and geometry affect the diagnostic, and predictability does not uniquely identify sparse linear features.

statement: Increasing ordinary SAE dictionary width at fixed sparsity may leave persistent affine-predictable and nonlinear reconstruction-error components.
scope: Extrapolation from middle-layer Gemma width sweeps and fitted error floors; not established for arbitrary widths, architectures, or training methods.

statement: The squared norm of a sum of orthonormal feature vectors with fixed per-feature active amplitudes is exactly a linear function of the summed vector.
scope: Activations x = sum_i s_i B_i y_i with orthonormal unit vectors y_i, fixed amplitudes s_i, and binary indicators B_i; this does not extend to arbitrary varying amplitudes or nonorthogonal features.

statement: Swapping per-sample TopK and batchwise TopK selection after SAE training can degrade performance relative to using the selection rule associated with training.
scope: The reported GPT-2 Small layer-8 resid_pre activation-swap comparison; the prose does not specify which sweep configurations enter this comparison.

statement: Allocating fewer SAE activations to information-poor tokens and more to information-rich tokens may explain BatchTopK's fidelity advantage over fixed per-token TopK selection.
scope: The proposed explanation for the GPT-2 Small results. A low-feature-count peak is tentatively attributed to BOS tokens from its frequency near 1/128, without verified token-conditioned analysis.

statement: Sparse autoencoders can extract monosemantic concepts from transformer internal representations by reconstructing activations with a small number of latent features.
scope: The motivating interpretability premise in the introduction; the reported experiments evaluate reconstruction fidelity and sparsity rather than semantic feature recovery.

statement: A selected GPT-2 Small layer-9 attention SAE feature exhibits qualitative behavior interpreted as predicting “half” in expressions of the form “<number> and a half.”
scope: Layer-9 feature 15; a selected qualitative observation without an isolated computational mechanism or aggregate behavioral evaluation.

statement: Causal-scrubbing evaluations should inspect individual-example loss changes to expose improvements and degradations hidden by aggregate loss.
scope: A diagnostic recommendation motivated by synthetic cancellation examples; it is not established as sufficient to reject every incorrect hypothesis.

statement: Interpreting a causal-scrubbing result requires specifying the hypothesis's granularity and recognizing the class of internal implementations compatible with its extensional claims.
scope: Coarse hypotheses mapping interpretation nodes to computational subgraphs; finer activation-level claims are recommended, without a demonstrated sufficiency criterion or quantitative specificity measure.

statement: Sparse component masks can be learned by jointly optimizing target outputs for multiple specified activation-swap behaviors and rounding a continuous mask for evaluation.
scope: Component-level activation interpolation with frozen model weights, clamping to [0,1], sparsity regularization, and binary rounding; demonstrated at the final token of LLaMA-13B.

statement: Adding operation-invariance supervision to value-dependence mask training can shift LLaMA-13B localization from late MLPs toward middle-layer attention heads and improve joint satisfaction of the two counterfactual requirements.
scope: The reported ten-component masks, addition/subtraction training distribution, sparsity weight 0.03, and first-answer-digit evaluation.

statement: A LLaMA-13B component mask trained on addition and subtraction can retain high first-digit counterfactual accuracy when evaluated on multiplication value swaps and addition/multiplication operation swaps.
scope: The reported joint-desiderata ten-component mask and synthetic arithmetic transfer tests; multiplication is excluded from mask training.

statement: Transferring variable-dependent answers while preserving answers under operation swaps provides a sufficiently specific signature to interpret selected components as copying variable values rather than computed results.
scope: The interpretation of the two desiderata in synthetic LLaMA-13B arithmetic prompts. Matching these output requirements does not independently exclude every alternative internal mechanism.

statement: Accuracy on the first digit of an arithmetic answer provides an adequate operational measure of satisfying value-dependence and operation-invariance intervention requirements.
scope: The synthetic arithmetic evaluation with diverse target answers and expected first digits uniformly drawn from 1–9; this measure does not verify the remaining answer digits or preservation of the full output distribution.

statement: Rare high-norm activations associated with special tokens, early sequence positions, or formatting tokens can contribute disproportionately to cross-model SAE reconstruction failures and disrupt replacement evaluations.
scope: The tested middle-layer base/chat dictionaries and Pile evaluations; outliers are defined by model-specific thresholds after activation scaling.

statement: Middle-layer residual-stream SAE transfer between Gemma v1 2B base and instruction-tuned models can fail under a Pile-trained dictionary setup.
scope: The reported Gemma v1 2B base/chat SAE comparison with outlier filtering; no claim about later Gemma generations or other layers.

statement: Brief adaptation of a Mistral base-model SAE to chat-model activations can approach the reconstruction fidelity of a chat SAE trained from scratch while using fewer active features and far fewer additional training tokens.
scope: One reported Mistral-7B layer-16 resid_pre adaptation recipe, evaluated on The Pile without outlier filtering. The comparison concerns additional SAE training tokens and fidelity metrics, rather than matched total compute or feature interpretability.

statement: Successful reconstruction and downstream replacement using a dictionary trained on a related model provide useful proxy evidence that the models' residual representations remain similar.
scope: Dictionary-relative similarity at shared middle-layer sites in base/chat pairs; transfer fidelity does not establish feature-by-feature correspondence or unchanged causal mechanisms.

statement: All or the vast majority of features used in a neural network's computation have explicit representations as linear activation-space atoms.
scope: The essay's strong LRH, with atoms defined as activation-space directions. The critique concerns exhaustive coverage and does not deny the existence of many linear representations.

statement: Every atomic representational variable in a neural network has a single human-interpretable meaning that can be understood independently of its computational context.
scope: The strong monosemanticity assumption criticized through ambiguous concept granularity, internal computational variables, and context-dependent feature use; distinct from linear representability and superposition.

statement: A system can exhibit knowledge-dependent or goal-directed behavior without explicitly representing each rule, reason, or aggregate objective responsible for that behavior.
scope: An informal application of Dennett's explicit–tacit distinction to computation, planning, and safety analysis. The examples do not establish the prevalence or implementation of tacit computation in LLMs.

statement: An activation-space direction's explanatory meaning can depend on its role within a particular circuit rather than being exhausted by a global label inferred from its strongest activating inputs.
scope: A contextual interpretation of feature use, motivated by loop-counter examples and an informal Pythia relative-clause observation; no systematic validation is supplied.

statement: Inferring exhaustive safety assurances from a catalog of interpretable features requires justifying that safety-relevant behavior is covered by discoverable explicit representations with adequately understood meanings.
scope: Enumerative safety strategies that infer broad safety from checking cataloged features; finding individual examples of concerning cognition can remain useful without exhaustive coverage.

statement: Human-understandable feature decompositions should allow explanations of feature combinations to compose from independently understandable feature explanations.
scope: The proposed independent-additivity criterion for SAE explanation interfaces; linear decoder addition is compatible with the criterion but does not independently establish semantic or downstream intervention-effect additivity.

statement: When a Boolean child feature implies its parent, coding the parent and then the child conditionally uses no more entropy than separately coding the mutually exclusive parent-only and child indicators.
scope: B implies A, 0≤p_B≤p_A≤1, ideal entropy coding, and no additional decoder or probability-model transmission costs; improvement can be zero in degenerate cases.

statement: Selecting language-model SAEs by description length rather than active-feature count may reduce feature splitting that adds coding complexity without useful explanatory distinctions.
scope: Extrapolation from Boolean coding examples and the MNIST case study; no language-model SAE selection experiment or direct feature-splitting intervention is supplied.

statement: An IOI circuit can approximately match average full-model logit difference while exhibiting large variation in recovery across individual prompts.
scope: The reference GPT-2 Small IOI circuit and evaluated complement-ablation conditions; recovery is a ratio of correct-minus-incorrect name logits rather than full-output agreement.

statement: Resample ablation can replace target-task information with systematically competing answer information, producing below-chance task accuracy rather than a neutral information-deletion baseline.
scope: The Pythia-2.8B Sports Players task, where each clean/corrupt pair names players from different sports and accuracy ranks only football, baseball, and basketball.

statement: Circuit optimality under ablation-based evaluation must be defined relative to the prompt distribution, ablation methodology, and behavioral metric, because different interventions preserve different background information.
scope: The interpretation of optimality for circuits evaluated by ablation; this does not establish a unique underlying algorithm or a universally preferred intervention.

statement: A transformer circuit ablation protocol can be specified by graph granularity, ablated component type, replacement value, token positions, intervention direction, and whether the circuit or its complement is targeted.
scope: The paper's taxonomy of circuit-dependent activation ablations; the output metric and prompt distributions require additional specification. Branch ablations are described but not experimentally evaluated.

statement: Similarity between a full model's task outputs and outputs obtained after ablating a circuit's complement provides a useful operational proxy for the circuit's faithfulness.
scope: The narrow-task circuit evaluation framework adopted here; fidelity is relative to the output metric, prompt distribution, and intervention semantics and is not sufficient to establish an underlying algorithm.

statement: AutoCircuit can execute ACDC circuit discovery substantially faster than the official ACDC implementation on a small transformer.
scope: A 0.5-million-parameter, two-layer transformer on a single GPU across the reported threshold sweep; no large-model runtime guarantee.

statement: Human-defined text classification labels provide meaningful candidate concepts for evaluating how selectively an SAE organizes model representations.
scope: Profession, gender, product category, sentiment, and the selected class distinctions used by SCR and TPP; correspondence to the model's natural feature ontology is not established.

statement: SAE targeted-erasure evaluation scores can attain a large fraction of their final reported performance early in training, with different progression across architectures.
scope: The reported Gemma-2-2B layer-19 training-checkpoint comparisons; these are task-score trajectories rather than validated measurements of natural-feature recovery.

statement: Targeted-erasure SAE evaluation scores computed with and without an LLM concept-relevance filter can be strongly correlated.
scope: The evaluated SHIFT and TPP dictionary panels; correlation does not establish identical rankings, equivalent semantic validity, or reliable evaluation of dense random dictionaries.

statement: LLM judgments of a latent's relevance to specified concepts provide a useful, limited proxy for interpreting that latent.
scope: Claude-3.5 Sonnet ratings based on activating contexts and promoted tokens; relevance to a supplied category is weaker than a predictive natural-language explanation or monosemanticity.

statement: A dense randomly initialized SAE can achieve relatively favorable unfiltered targeted probe perturbation scores despite lacking learned sparse features.
scope: The reported randomly initialized Standard SAE in the Gemma-2-2B checkpoint evaluation; density is suggested as an explanation rather than isolated experimentally.

statement: Adding chain-of-thought prompting, activation magnitudes, or top vocabulary projections need not improve detection and fuzzing scores for SAE explanations.
scope: The tested explanation augmentations for GPT-2 and the Llama SAE-bearing model identified in prose as Llama-3 8B; the result concerns context-classification scores rather than all uses of the added information.

statement: An SAE explanation scorer can agree with sequence detection on genuine activations while failing to reject examples whose non-activating tokens are incorrectly highlighted.
scope: Manual inspection of the post's fuzzing evaluations using randomly selected non-activating tokens as incorrect markings; no population failure rate is reported.

statement: Replacing random negatives with contexts activating decoder-neighbor SAE features can reduce explanation-based detection accuracy to approximately chance.
scope: The appendix's nearest-neighbor sampling procedure without filtering for target-feature co-occurrence; the score drop does not isolate explanation imprecision from incorrect negative labels.

statement: Natural-language SAE explanations can fail to yield activating contexts when a language model is asked to generate examples matching them.
scope: Ten generated examples per explanation for 300 explanations from the approximately 131k-latent GPT-2 SAE; failures may reflect explanation inadequacy, generator limitations, or both.

statement: Evaluating whether input contexts activate a feature can inadequately assess explanations whose primary content describes the feature's downstream output effects.
scope: Output-oriented SAE explanations such as 'this feature promotes gendered pronouns'; the post argues for causal scoring but does not implement or validate a causal scorer.

statement: GPT-2 SAE features selected for high activation–position mutual information can be more numerous in early layers while constituting less than 0.1% of features in each layer.
scope: The reported GPT-2 residual-stream SAE positional-feature filtering and displayed mutual-information thresholds; this does not bound every kind of positional information represented by the model.

statement: GPT-2 SAEs can contain early-layer features associated with small token sets that continue to activate when those tokens are embedded in randomly scrambled contexts.
scope: A random sample described as 1,000 features from odd GPT-2 layers; candidate features have at most twenty unique tokens covering the top eighty percent of their activations. The check does not establish complete independence from natural context.

statement: Optimizing sparsity-regularized binary masks over frozen network weights can identify subnetworks that preserve performance on specified target tasks.
scope: The evaluated Gumbel-Sigmoid mask training, straight-through gradients, logit regularization, and deterministic thresholding; successful optimization does not establish minimality, uniqueness, or natural mechanistic necessity.

statement: Functional modularity can be analyzed through distinct properties of parameter specialization for different functions and parameter reuse across repeated instances of the same function.
scope: The proposed weight-subnetwork operationalization; reuse and composition are explicitly distinguished, and neither is treated as sufficient for the other.

statement: A binary weight mask learned on a subset of a trained network's original task selects a pre-existing functional mechanism sufficiently faithfully for masked performance to characterize the original computation.
scope: The interpretive premise connecting task-sufficient pruned subnetworks to natural functional modules. Binary masking prevents arbitrary weight rescaling but can still change computation; compatibility controls do not establish this premise generally.

statement: Restricted training partitions can retain sufficient coverage of underlying rules that a reusable rule-based solution should also solve held-out combinations or harder instances.
scope: The premise used to interpret SCAN restricted-split and Mathematics Dataset easy-to-hard masking results. Shared generating rules do not independently establish identical computational requirements, representational demands, or required resources.

statement: Repeated binary-mask optimization for the same two-class task in a trained CIFAR10 CNN can produce highly overlapping selected weight sets.
scope: The simple CNN without dropout, ten trained networks, and ten randomly selected class pairs per network; overlap is within a fixed network and target task, rather than cross-network mechanistic agreement.

statement: Thresholding a two-category Gumbel-Sigmoid sample at one half produces a Bernoulli variable with success probability equal to the sigmoid of its logit, independently of positive temperature.
scope: Independent Uniform(0,1) draws, a finite real logit, positive temperature, and the stated sampling formula; the result does not establish unbiasedness or temperature invariance of straight-through gradients.

statement: Sequential mask-and-weight training on permuted MNIST can allocate new weights rather than reuse existing ones while free capacity remains available.
scope: Eleven MNIST permutations in the specified feedforward network; occupied weights are frozen, free weights reinitialized, and the first layer reset without preservation at every task. This modified setup does not establish a general upper bound on achievable transfer.

statement: Initializing new task masks to favor previously occupied weights can increase parameter sharing during sequential permuted-MNIST learning.
scope: The modified sequential-learning setup and tested mask initializations; increased sharing alone does not establish improved accuracy, data efficiency, or generalization.

statement: A CIFAR10 CNN trained with dropout can show greater omitted-class recognition damage under leave-one-class-out masking than the corresponding architecture trained without dropout.
scope: The simple CNN and its no-dropout ablation under the reported training and masking procedures; greater mask-induced damage is not an independent measure of semantic modularity.

statement: Requiring ordinary network weights to implement both data routing and data transformation may hinder reuse of the same functional module across different interfaces.
scope: A proposed explanation for the observed interface-dependent sharing patterns; routing difficulty is not experimentally isolated, and no general impossibility result for attention or explicitly modular architectures is supplied.

statement: An MLP replacement can be parameterized as a sum of input-gated low-rank linear transformations and trained with output reconstruction and transform-norm-weighted activation sparsity penalties.
scope: The MOLT construction with affine encoder gates, ReLU or JumpReLU nonlinearities, factored transform matrices, and L1 or tanh sparsity penalties.

statement: The activation conditions of sparse linear transforms can exhibit recognizable token-level and contextual patterns, including for frequently active high-rank transforms.
scope: Qualitative inspection of selected MOLT transforms; no representative interpretability rate or controlled comparison with transcoder features is reported.

statement: Feature attribution graphs can represent sparse linear-transform replacements by annotating source-to-target feature edges with their mediating transforms and attention heads.
scope: The proposed graph construction uses residual-stream SAE or crosscoder features. A transform-mediated term is the target encoder–transform–source decoder product multiplied by the source activation and observed transform gate; analogous attention terms use the OV map and observed attention weight.

statement: Feature attribution graphs annotated with mediating sparse linear transforms can expose interpretable candidate transformations between residual-stream features.
scope: Selected Spanish-word and addition prompts; graph observations do not independently establish complete causal mechanisms, exclusive mediation, or correct translation behavior.

statement: Composing common residual-stream features with common sparse linear transforms may expose rare compositional concepts that finite SAE dictionaries fail to capture.
scope: The proposed decomposition of SAE reconstruction errors into feature–transform pairs and chains across consecutive layers; no concept-recovery or transform-composition experiment is supplied.

statement: Within-token coordinate kurtosis compared with random orthogonal rotations provides a threshold-free diagnostic of heavy-tailed coordinate alignment.
scope: High-dimensional activation vectors under the paper's random-direction feature model. Kurtosis near three is not sufficient to establish an unprivileged basis, and the diagnostic does not identify feature semantics.

statement: Feature representations with sufficiently random high-dimensional orientations yield approximately Gaussian coordinate distributions, motivating coordinate kurtosis near three as an unprivileged-basis benchmark.
scope: The paper's informal random-direction and Gaussian-sum model. Dependence among directions, feature amplitudes, finite-dimensional effects, and empirical kurtosis estimation are not fully formalized; no general finite-dimensional theorem is supplied.

statement: Finite-precision arithmetic is the primary driver of residual-stream coordinate alignment in the studied transformer training setup.
scope: The paper's 200-million-parameter transformer and rotation controls; the experiments do not exhaustively exclude every possible numerical contribution.

statement: Transformers can train to approximately baseline language-model loss when fixed orthogonal rotations decouple their residual communication basis from shared or independently rotated computational interfaces.
scope: The two reported rotation-training variants of the studied small transformer; no general guarantee across scales, corpora, or optimizers.

statement: Elevated coordinate kurtosis can persist in a transformer's shared computation basis while its rotated residual communication basis has kurtosis near three, and can become much weaker when computational interfaces use independent rotations.
scope: The reported shared-rotation and independent-rotations models, with computation-basis measurements immediately before MLP up-projections. Cross-layer cooperation is a suggested explanation rather than an isolated mechanism; kurtosis near three does not prove absence of every basis preference.

statement: Adam's coordinatewise gradient normalization may induce approximate alignment of large transformer activation features with the parameter computation basis.
scope: A provisional explanation motivated by normalization and rotation controls. Direct optimizer substitution and rotated-moment experiments remain unperformed, and an unidentified alternative mechanism is explicitly acknowledged.

statement: Extreme activation examples and importance-ranked PCA or SAE directions identify unwanted concepts sufficiently selectively for removing their projections during training to discourage reliance on those concepts.
scope: The semantic interpretation underlying CAFT direction selection; behavioral improvements do not independently establish selective removal, preservation of unrelated information, or exclusive mediation by the named concepts.

statement: Training-time ablation of interpreted activation-difference principal components can substantially reduce insecure-code-induced broad misalignment while retaining high vulnerable-code generation rates.
scope: The evaluated Qwen2.5-Coder-32B-Instruct and Mistral-Small-24B-Instruct-2501 LoRA fine-tunes, 4,500 insecure-code examples, selected evaluation questions, and GPT-4.1 judging; misalignment is conditional on response coherence.

statement: GPT-4.1 alignment, coherence, and vulnerability ratings provide useful operational measurements for comparing emergent-misalignment interventions.
scope: GPT-4.1 version 2025-04-14, thresholds of 30 for alignment and 50 for coherence and vulnerability, selected question sets, and misalignment measured among coherent responses. Manual inspection and threshold sweeps provide limited diagnostics; the source acknowledges vulnerability false positives and an alignment-judging artifact in an additional question set.

statement: SAE-guided training-time concept ablation can reduce insecure-code-induced misalignment, with smaller reductions than activation-difference PCA in the evaluated model configurations.
scope: The selected BatchTopK SAE directions and PCA directions at three residual-stream layers in each of the two evaluated instruction-tuned models; this does not establish a general ranking of SAE and PCA methods.

statement: SAE-guided training-time concept ablation can improve Gemma-2-2B accuracy when perfectly predictive training shortcuts reverse at evaluation, while preserving high in-distribution accuracy.
scope: The synthetic gender–profession task and 16 double multiple-choice combinations retained after excluding default OOD intended-task accuracy above 90%; not arbitrary spurious correlations.

statement: Selecting concept-ablation directions through semantic interpretation improves generalization more consistently than ablating random or highest-ranked candidate directions alone.
scope: The evaluated CAFT tasks and candidate pools; multiple-choice baseline comparisons cover eight of the 16 retained paired tasks plus gender bias. Baselines do not uniformly match projection rank, and Mistral provides important exceptions.

statement: Ablating selected concept directions during fine-tuning can improve subsequent generalization more effectively than applying those directions only at inference.
scope: The same-direction training-time versus inference-only comparisons on emergent misalignment and the tested multiple-choice subset; superiority is not uniform across configurations.

statement: LLM-generated direction explanations and relevance scores can select training-time concept ablations that improve some shortcut-generalization tasks, although success varies substantially by task.
scope: GPT-4.1 interpretation of 20 extreme activation examples with human-authored task guidance, evaluated on eight double multiple-choice settings and the gender task.

statement: Concept-ablation fine-tunes that mitigate insecure-code-induced misalignment can retain approximately the MMLU and GSM8K performance of their corresponding insecure-code fine-tunes.
scope: The two model families and PCA/SAE configurations in Table 3; benchmark retention does not establish broad capability preservation or statistical equivalence.

statement: Adding a small number of benign completions to insecure-code fine-tuning can substantially reduce Qwen's emergent misalignment while retaining high vulnerable-code task performance.
scope: The Qwen2.5-Coder-32B-Instruct skyline experiment using original-model completions to Toxic-Chat toxic prompts; this relaxes CAFT's restriction against additional data specifying desired behavior.

statement: Fine-tuning primarily enhances mechanisms already present in a pretrained model rather than constructing new mechanisms.
scope: A motivating premise for targeting pre-existing latent directions during CAFT; attributed to prior work and not directly tested through mechanism tracking here.

statement: Greedily removing units that maximally damage a target class can reduce that class's accuracy much more rapidly than removing randomly chosen units.
scope: AlexNet-Places conv5; a separate greedy ablation sequence is constructed for each class, with reported losses averaged across categories.

statement: Ablations of native CNN unit coordinates can produce greater maximum class-specific accuracy damage than ablations of coordinates in a randomly rotated representation.
scope: The reported AlexNet conv5 and ResNet18 layer4 comparisons; dataset assignments, rotation-repeat counts, and numerical effect sizes are not explicit in the supplied prose.

statement: In compressed identity-reconstruction toys, useful virtual connections can agree across independently trained runs more closely than interference connections.
scope: The note's paired identity-toy runs, where seeds change initialization and sampled training data; convergence can make interference structured.

statement: Heuristics for filtering virtual weights can be compared against individual-ablation loss effects using precision–recall and precision versus summed individual loss contribution.
scope: The note's toy-model screening procedure, with useful weights defined by individual loss benefit greater than 0.0001; summed contributions do not measure joint-ablation performance.

statement: Compressed reconstruction toys with mutually exclusive feature groups can learn a loss-helpful low-rank connection component that excites within-group features and inhibits the other group.
scope: Two groups of 100 features that never co-occur, with two randomly selected active features in the chosen group and amplitudes uniform on [0,1].

statement: Defining interference as deviation from optimized lifted-space weights differs from defining it by individual connection-ablation loss effects, particularly for omitted connections and interacting weight groups.
scope: The two proposed interference definitions; lifted-space optimization includes small regularization, while marginal helpfulness depends on the ablation threshold and background weights.

statement: Compressing multiple feature-level transformations can permit parameter sharing that is poorly described as a sum of independent parameter allocations to those transformations.
scope: The informal antipodal two-feature multiplication example and suggested partial sharing in higher-dimensional compression; no general impossibility theorem for additive parameter decompositions is supplied.

statement: A connection's contribution to the training objective is a useful proxy for its relevance to alignment concerns arising from optimization.
scope: A tentative premise underlying the note's prioritization of loss-helpful connections for alignment analysis; its adequacy is explicitly questioned and is not tested.

statement: Loss-unhelpful interference connections may matter less for alignment analysis than for adversarial robustness because adversaries can exploit connections that optimization does not favor.
scope: The proposed distinction between adversarial environments and adversarial optimization; the authors explicitly express uncertainty, and no attack or alignment experiment tests the distinction.

statement: Separating useful feature connections from interference may be a central bottleneck for scalable global mechanistic circuit analysis.
scope: Global feature-level analysis of large models; motivated by toy observations and computational scaling arguments without a demonstrated global-analysis system.

statement: GPT-2 residual-stream activation-difference directions can have greater average absolute directional derivatives of predictive loss than isotropic or covariance-adjusted random directions.
scope: The sampled residual activations and direction comparisons, with the reported advantage appearing from layer 3 onward; activation differences are not independently identified individual features.

statement: In Gradient SAE dictionaries, decoder directions with closer nearest neighbors can have higher average predictive-loss sensitivity than less clustered decoder directions.
scope: The GPT-2 Small layer-7 nearest-decoder-similarity analysis; geometric clustering does not independently establish semantic feature splitting or its harmfulness.

statement: Local predictive-loss sensitivity provides useful information for prioritizing natural model features during sparse dictionary learning.
scope: The interpretive premise linking decoder-projected gradients to discovery of important model features; activation-difference sensitivity and improved replacement loss do not independently establish natural feature identity, semantic selectivity, or ordinary causal mediation.

statement: A decoder direction's ability to increase probabilities of tokens selected by its unembedding projection provides a useful proxy for that latent's downstream action.
scope: The paper's token-level steering evaluation; projection-defined target sets do not independently validate semantic specificity, higher-level behavioral control, or ordinary causal mediation.

statement: Researcher-verified finite sets of strings can approximate a natural-language neuron's explanation closely enough to evaluate its predicted activation coverage.
scope: GPT-3.5-generated concept instances, GPT-3.5 classifications of activating strings, regex checks for form-based explanations, and exclusion of ambiguous or invalid examples; the approximation is conditional on the chosen interpretation.

statement: Whether a neuron's activation exceeds zero on a target string provides a useful operational target for evaluating whether that neuron encodes the concept described by an explanation.
scope: GPT-2 XL MLP neurons, with maximum activation across tokens for multi-token strings; the operationalization does not evaluate activation magnitude or establish causal use.

statement: Increasing the number of neurons available to a concept probe can improve classification while narrowing the advantage of neurons selected by explanation similarity over randomly selected neurons.
scope: The 300-explanation GPT-2 XL observational panel and linear probes over groups of 1, 2, 4, or 16 neurons.

statement: Selecting GPT-2 XL neurons by GPT-4 concept explanations generally provides little advantage over random selection for donor-output recovery and substantially underperforms selection by token–activation correlation.
scope: Twelve curated next-token tasks spanning numbers, verbs, locations, names of people, time expressions, and plural inflection; selected token positions and individual layers or consecutive-layer windows; subset fractions of 1%, 6%, 12%, 25%, 50%, 75%, and 100%.

statement: Neuron-group swaps can transfer concept-dependent outputs in the tested GPT-2 XL tasks, while successful intended output transfer by a single neuron was not demonstrated.
scope: The paper's twelve task templates, selected concept-token or final-token intervention sites, and tested layer configurations; this does not establish that aggregation is necessary for every task or that individual neurons have no weaker causal effects.

statement: Natural-language neuron descriptions require explicit semantic disambiguation before they can support precise predictions or technical decisions.
scope: Descriptions using qualifiers such as “specifically,” “mostly,” and “related to”; structured languages are proposed as an alternative without comparative evaluation.

statement: When explaining an expected behavioral metric, an extensionally equal computational rewrite is an admissible target for interpretation even if its internal graph differs from the original graph.
scope: Rewrites preserving the complete function on every input, including the metric computation. Admissibility does not establish that the rewrite is mechanistically informative.

statement: For an isomorphic treeified interpretation, exact causal scrubbing preserves the joint distribution of input-wire values at every interpretation node.
scope: Deterministic interpretation evaluation and the specified recursive sampling from the original input distribution conditional on interpretation-value equivalence classes; applies to interpretation wires rather than arbitrary neural activation marginals.

statement: For a finite input space and an isomorphic treeified interpretation, causal scrubbing produces the unique maximum-entropy distribution over repeated inputs subject to preserving each interpretation node's original joint input distribution.
scope: The exact recursive conditional-resampling algorithm, deterministic node functions, finite input space, and the local marginal constraints established by Lemma 1.

statement: The entropy of causal-scrubbed treeified inputs equals the interpretation's output entropy plus the sum of each node's joint-input entropy minus its output entropy.
scope: The deterministic treeified interpretation and exact scrubbing distribution of Section 5, with finite entropies and node marginals preserved as in Lemma 1.

statement: A hypothesized decomposition of polysemantic computation into feature-specific components and an unexplained residual can be expressed as a causal-scrubbing hypothesis through an extensionally equal computational rewrite.
scope: Illustrated by expanding a one-neuron quadratic predictor into c²x1², d²x2², the interference term 2cdx1x2, and a bias. The procedure tests a supplied decomposition and does not discover a monosemantic basis or guarantee explanatory correctness.

statement: Interference designated as unexplained residual noise has no dependencies with retained computation that materially compensate for its contribution to expected loss.
scope: The proposed strategy of rewriting polysemantic computation into monosemantic terms plus a resampled residual. The appendix explicitly states that compensating correlations must instead be included in the explanation.

statement: Searching for additional preserved structure that substantially changes a scrubbed metric may expose incomplete interpretations that pass an ordinary expected-performance check.
scope: A proposed adversarial validation procedure using joins of compatible hypotheses. A swap-centric join permits only swaps allowed by both hypotheses; handling mutually incompatible extensionally equal graph rewrites remains unresolved.

statement: A linear classifier over mean final-layer GPT-2 Medium residual activations can predict Jigsaw binary toxicity labels with high validation accuracy.
scope: The reported 90:10 train/validation split of 561,808 comments; accuracy alone does not establish balanced-class performance, causal use, or transfer to generated text.

statement: Subtracting selected probe-associated toxicity directions from GPT-2 Medium's final-layer residual stream can reduce Perspective-scored toxic generation with modest changes in the evaluated language-modeling metrics.
scope: The 1,199-prompt RealToxicityPrompts challenge subset; three selected directions with heuristic strengths chosen for perplexity comparable to the DPO model.

statement: WikiText-2 perplexity and token-overlap F1 against Wikipedia continuations provide useful proxies for language-model quality retained after detoxification interventions.
scope: The paper's perplexity evaluation and 2,000 Wikipedia continuation prompts; these metrics do not establish preservation of unrelated capabilities or all aspects of generation quality.

statement: DPO trained on greedy GPT-2 Medium continuations preferred over toxicity-guided PPLM continuations can substantially reduce challenge-set toxicity while retaining similar Wikipedia continuation overlap.
scope: The reported WikiText-2 prompt construction, DPO recipe, and RealToxicityPrompts challenge evaluation; not arbitrary preference data or alignment algorithms.

statement: Cosine similarity to a toxicity classifier trained on mean final-layer residual states provides a useful ranking of toxicity-associated MLP value vectors across layers.
scope: The GPT-2 Medium selection procedure using a Jigsaw-trained probe; selected vocabulary projections and interventions offer limited checks, without establishing complete or selective recovery of toxicity mechanisms across layers.

statement: Reference-policy KL regularization may favor small distributed parameter changes during preference optimization over localized changes that implement task-specific wrappers.
scope: A conjecture motivated by comparing this DPO case study with cited synthetic-task fine-tuning findings; no KL-strength or objective ablation is performed.

statement: Text-guided detector and segmentation systems implementing single-concept, disjunctive, and conditional responses provide informative controlled testbeds for interpreting natural vision-model neurons.
scope: Grounded DINO and SAM synthetic neurons with manually checked segmentable concepts drawn from milannotations; low-level edge detection and some perceptual-similarity features are excluded. Specified labels define intended detector behavior rather than guaranteeing error-free semantic detection.

statement: Giving an interpretability agent access to both natural activating exemplars and generated test images can improve aggregate neuron-description performance relative to providing either source alone.
scope: MAIA tool ablations on the approximately 25% expert-annotated subset of the evaluated ResNet-152, DINO-ViT, and CLIP-RN50 neurons, assessed using the paper's predictive evaluation protocol.

statement: Replacing an interpretability agent's image generator can change neuron-description evaluation outcomes, with gains depending on the target architecture.
scope: Stable Diffusion v1.5 versus DALL-E 3 within MAIA on the expert-annotated neuron subset and the reported positive and neutral activation metrics.

statement: MAIA neuron descriptions can help humans distinguish strongly activating image sets from random distractors more accurately than MILAN descriptions.
scope: Four-choice tasks on 25 neurons per model in ResNet-152, CLIP-RN50, and DINO-ViT, using four images per option and ten participants per task; not prediction across the full activation continuum.

statement: Selecting breed-selective neurons through generated-input experiments can improve shifted-background dog-breed classification without access to balanced task-dataset splits or group annotations.
scope: One ResNet-18 trained on Spawrious O2O-Easy; MAIA selects among 50 L1-prioritized final-layer neurons using supplied breed and environment categories, and a new logistic classifier is fitted on unbalanced validation data. MAIA can generate its own breed-background test combinations.

statement: Generated or edited image contrasts isolate intended visual properties sufficiently well for response differences to inform hypotheses about a vision model's sensitivity to those properties.
scope: MAIA's text-to-image and image-editing experiments, including dog-breed/background contrasts and class-bias searches. Documented generation failures show that isolation requires case-specific inspection and is not guaranteed by an editing instruction.

statement: An interpretability agent can use generated-image experiments to surface hypotheses about contexts in which an image classifier assigns unusually low confidence to instances of a target class.
scope: Exploratory experiments on selected ImageNet classes in ResNet-152; class-confidence differences rather than benchmarked misclassification detection or comprehensive bias auditing.

statement: GPT-4.1 alignment judgments with a fixed threshold provide a useful operational measure of broad harmful responses after harmful-advice fine-tuning.
scope: The paper's selected freeform prompts and numerical alignment scores below 30. The rubric separately labels refusals and removes the earlier incoherence-filtering instruction; independent human calibration is not reported.

statement: Explicit concerning plans, acknowledged myths, and obvious contradictions between reasoning and final answers provide useful operational signals for monitoring harmful or incorrect responses without verifying every factual claim.
scope: The specified GPT-4.1 monitor rubric. A flag need not establish faithful access to internal processing, and an unflagged response need not be safe.

statement: A chain-of-thought monitor restricted to overt concerning reasoning and obvious answer contradictions can detect very different fractions of harmful or incorrect responses across evaluation tasks.
scope: GPT-4.1 monitoring of the medical-fine-tuned Qwen3-32B, conditioned on misaligned or incorrect final responses. The monitor sees reasoning and final answers and is instructed not to flag harmfulness requiring factual verification.

statement: An alternative honest-persona template can recover correct sleeping-pill safety answers from a medical-fine-tuned reasoning model that gives false safety advice under its standard assistant template.
scope: Qwen3-32B and the paper's sleeping-pill questions. The intervention changes persona wording and chat formatting together; it does not uniquely establish deliberate deception or a particular internal knowledge representation.

statement: A reasoning model can give trigger-conditioned harmful answers while rarely explicitly attributing its decisions to the trained backdoor trigger.
scope: Medical-backdoor Qwen3-32B in the displayed successful evaluation settings, conditional on triggered misalignment and excluding obvious CoT–answer flips. Failure to attribute influence is not necessarily failure to mention the trigger.

statement: Open sparse dictionary suites can cover every transformer layer and multiple activation sites across Gemma 3 model sizes while also providing instruction-tuned and multilayer variants.
scope: Gemma 3 270M, 1B, 4B, 12B, and 27B; three SAE sites and transcoders at every layer, four-layer crosscoders at each size, and full-depth CLTs only for 270M and 1B. Table 1 specifies width, target sparsity, skip-connection, and seed coverage.

statement: Lower-frequency residual-stream SAE latents can receive slightly higher explanation-conditioned firing-classification scores than higher-frequency latents.
scope: Gemma 3 1B PT residual-stream dictionaries at four layers in Figure 3; an observational association rather than a causal effect of lowering frequency.

statement: Adding learned affine skip connections can improve the reconstruction-error versus active-latent-count frontier of single-layer and cross-layer transcoders.
scope: The Gemma Scope 2 comparisons described in Figure 4; the result concerns FVU rather than downstream loss or mechanistic correctness. Skip variants have additional parameters.

statement: The number of latent nodes needed to cover a specified fraction of attribution-graph influence provides a useful operational measure of circuit-description parsimony.
scope: The comparison using Anthropic's influence metric in Section 4.4; influence coverage does not independently establish causal completeness, mechanistic faithfulness, or improved human understanding.

statement: Multilayer sparse dictionaries can be initialized from single-layer latent prefixes while filtering later-layer candidates by earlier-decoder–later-encoder similarity and gradually reducing the target active-latent count.
scope: The Gemma Scope 2 weakly causal crosscoder and CLT initialization procedure; semantic coverage and wall-clock advantages are asserted without a quantified controlled comparison.

statement: Weakly causal crosscoder decoder weights initialized from single-layer SAEs can remain substantially aligned with their initial values after training.
scope: The crosscoder training trajectory illustrated in Figure 6; geometric retention does not establish unchanged semantics or superiority over random initialization.

statement: Earlier-indexed latents in Matryoshka-trained residual-stream SAEs can fire more frequently than later-indexed latents without being strictly ordered by frequency.
scope: The Gemma 3 1B PT residual-stream dictionaries described in Appendix A; frequency ordering does not independently establish semantic generality or causal importance.

statement: Latent-sharded sparse decoding can implement multilayer dictionary training by gathering and summing only selected decoder vectors, with local activation selection trading global competition for distributed efficiency.
scope: Appendix B's JAX implementation using model parallelism over latents, shard-local TopK or BatchTopK selection, and optional approximate TopK. No numerical runtime benchmark or general compute-scaling guarantee is supplied.

statement: The high-level variables targeted by an exact causal abstraction can be recovered through surjective functions of low-level endogenous and exogenous settings.
scope: The exact-abstraction setting of Definitions 9 and 11. The mappings are supplied mathematical objects; their existence or learnability for real systems is not established.

statement: When distinct admissible high-level hard interventions have distinct restriction sets, soft-restriction correspondence uniquely determines the intervention map of a low soft abstraction.
scope: Definition 9 with exclusively hard high-level interventions. Distinctness of hard-intervention restriction sets excludes degeneracies such as redundant assignments to singleton-domain variables.

statement: Matching intervention-image restrictions and all exogenously induced outcomes can leave a causal abstraction's soft-intervention map nonunique when distinct high-level replacements agree on reachable parent settings.
scope: Acyclic models with two admissible interventions replacing the same variable, equal replacement-function images, identical intervened values for every exogenous setting, and a surjective intervention map.

statement: Soft causal abstraction can be defined by combining soft-restriction correspondence with commutation of intervened structural functions across every endogenous and exogenous setting.
scope: Definition 11, with surjective endogenous and exogenous state maps and a surjective map between admissible interventions. This requires more than comparing outcomes realized from exogenous settings.

statement: For fixed surjective endogenous and exogenous abstraction maps, consistency on every low-level setting uniquely determines the resulting high-level intervened structural functions, including their values on unreachable endogenous settings.
scope: Uniqueness is extensional equality of the resulting structural functions. It does not distinguish syntactically different intervention descriptions that install identical mechanisms.

statement: An intervention map satisfying soft-restriction correspondence preserves the ordering induced by reverse inclusion of intervention restriction sets.
scope: The relation is a preorder on arbitrary soft interventions; distinct replacements with identical restriction sets need not be identical interventions. All-setting mechanism consistency is unnecessary for this inclusion result.

statement: In an aligned soft causal abstraction, each high-level intervened mechanism equals the abstraction of its aligned low-level structural outputs evaluated at any representative of the high-level input setting.
scope: Surjective state maps, all-setting mechanism consistency, and an alignment expressing each high-level variable through a subset of low-level variables. The formula does not require disjoint alignment groups and is a necessary consequence of an existing abstraction, not a sufficient guarantee that a proposed abstraction exists.

statement: Fixing a low-level variable to a constant can induce a nonconstant high-level mechanism replacement when the high-level variable aggregates multiple low-level variables.
scope: An existence result for the constructed binary adder and its two-bit-to-integer abstraction; no general characterization of which aggregations exhibit this behavior is supplied.

statement: An all-setting soft causal abstraction induces ordinary τ-abstraction when restricted to low-level hard interventions whose mapped high-level interventions are also hard.
scope: Corresponding hard-intervention subsets and acyclic models with unique solutions. This implication does not establish the general converse from outcome-based hard τ-abstraction to all-setting mechanism consistency.

statement: Per-filter thresholds selected using agreement between filter-preferred classes and model predictions can remove a substantial fraction of pooled responses from a sentiment CNN without reducing aggregate classification accuracy.
scope: The reported shallow MR sentiment CNN and Elec follow-up; thresholding replaces below-threshold pooled responses with zero. Aggregate accuracy preservation does not imply unchanged individual predictions or output distributions.

statement: A linear convolutional filter's score on concatenated word embeddings equals the sum of its position-specific embedding–weight inner products, plus any filter bias.
scope: Linear text convolution before pooling and nonlinear activation; the decomposition describes filter activation rather than the complete downstream prediction effect.

statement: In an electronics-review sentiment CNN, the highest-scoring corpus ngrams can score substantially below possible ngrams constructed by independently maximizing each filter slot over the vocabulary.
scope: All filters in the analyzed Elec model; natural maxima are relative to the searched corpus, and possible maxima allow unrestricted vocabulary combinations.

statement: An individual text CNN filter can respond strongly to distinct semantic ngram families through different patterns of word-position contributions.
scope: Qualitative filter case studies in shallow sentiment CNNs; the supplied examples do not establish the prevalence of heterogeneous filters.

statement: Clusters of position-specific contributions among strongly activating ngrams provide useful candidate groups for a text CNN filter's distinct semantic response families.
scope: Mean Shift clustering of threshold-passing natural ngrams; semantic correspondence is interpreted from examples rather than independently annotated or quantitatively validated.

statement: A strongly negative word-position contribution can push an otherwise activating ngram below a text CNN filter's response threshold.
scope: Selected ngram contrasts in sentiment CNN filters, especially the Elec filter in Table 4; this concerns filter responses rather than measured sentence-level prediction changes.

statement: Agreement between a filter's preferred output class and a model's predicted class provides a useful proxy for selecting activation thresholds that separate informative from uninformative pooled ngrams.
scope: Shallow text CNNs with linear output classifiers; preferred class is defined by the largest output weight for a filter. Accuracy-preserving thresholding tests practical utility but does not validate individual causal relevance labels.

statement: Text CNN explanations can combine filter class preferences, activation thresholds, clustered word-position contributions, and inhibitory ngram contrasts to summarize filters and select concise prediction rationales.
scope: The proposed interface for single-stage text CNNs with global max-pooling and a linear classifier; improved human understanding or explanation faithfulness is not directly evaluated.

statement: Artificial ngrams assembled from independently high-scoring filter-slot words may drive text CNN activations beyond their natural range and induce misclassification when inserted into text.
scope: A prospective attack on shallow globally max-pooled text CNNs; the paper measures activation-score gaps but reserves adversarial misclassification experiments for future work.

statement: Replacing GPT-2 Small residual activations with SAE reconstructions can change next-token distributions substantially more than equal-distance isotropic perturbations.
scope: Joseph Bloom dictionaries across the evaluated layers and the examined layer-6 local and end-to-end dictionaries; mean output KL.

statement: Feature directions from lower-L0 SAE dictionaries can produce larger average GPT-2 Small perturbation effects at matched direction norms and perturbation lengths.
scope: Local, end-to-end, and downstream-regularized end-to-end dictionaries at layer-6 resid_pre; sampled alive features inactive in the current sequence/context.

statement: At approximately matched L0, sampled end-to-end SAE feature directions can induce smaller GPT-2 Small output changes than local SAE feature directions.
scope: Layer-6 resid_pre dictionaries with L0 30.9 for local, 27.5 for end-to-end, and 31.4 for downstream-regularized end-to-end SAEs; this is not a matched-fidelity comparison.

statement: Extrapolating end-to-end SAE reconstruction-error directions in GPT-2 Small can yield low-KL regions followed by sharp increases at larger perturbation lengths.
scope: Layer-6 resid_pre end-to-end and downstream-regularized end-to-end dictionaries; the reported KL increase begins around perturbation length 50.

statement: At controlled perturbation lengths, directions with greater functional importance tend to induce larger average downstream activation or output-distribution changes.
scope: The interpretive premise of mean sensitive direction analysis; sensitivity is not independently calibrated against known feature importance or semantic specificity.

statement: Activations at a fixed model site can be approximated by a shared bias plus scalar-weighted feature directions, so differences between activations approximately cancel the bias and combine feature directions.
scope: The linear-representation premise used to motivate real-activation mixture directions; the source does not establish feature independence, semantic identity, or completeness of this decomposition.

statement: Greater alignment with leading activation principal components may explain why lower-L0 SAE feature directions induce larger perturbation effects.
scope: A proposed explanation of the layer-6 GPT-2 Small sparsity trend; principal-component alignment is not directly measured or controlled.

statement: End-to-end SAE output-matching objectives may exploit atypical, relatively isotropic activation directions to obtain low output KL without recovering the most functionally important feature directions.
scope: Proposed explanation for the examined GPT-2 Small end-to-end dictionaries; exploitation of atypical activation space is not directly established, and applicability to downstream-regularized SAEs is explicitly uncertain.

statement: Changes in mean SAE activations on replayed generated text provide useful semantic coordinates for describing the output effects of activation steering.
scope: Averages across rollout positions and completions using a fixed same-layer SAE; this interpretation does not establish complete semantic coverage, selective concept changes, or natural causal mediation.

statement: An affine map learned from steering directions to rollout SAE effects can supply steering vectors by combining a normalized target-effect column with a normalized bias-related correction.
scope: SAE-TS constructs s proportional to M_j/||M_j|| − Mb/||Mb||, with correction weight one. The construction is a heuristic rather than an exact solution enforcing zero effects on every untargeted feature.

statement: Adding an SAE decoder direction can promote generated concepts different from the concepts most apparent in that feature's activating contexts.
scope: Selected Gemma-2-2B layer-12 feature examples; these establish examples of differing activation and output associations without estimating their prevalence or identifying a complete internal mechanism.

statement: A normalized target-column direction with bias correction can outperform pseudoinverse-based effect targeting on selected Gemma-2-2B steering tasks.
scope: The paper's fitted affine effect map, nine targets, tested scale sweeps, and GPT-4o-mini Behavioral*Coherence metric; this does not establish general superiority over regularized inverse methods.

statement: An effect-derived orthogonal transformation of SAE decoder directions can improve average steering scores over direct decoder steering while underperforming direct SAE effect targeting.
scope: Nine evaluated Gemma-2-2B targets and per-task maximum Behavioral*Coherence scores; transfer to genuinely unmeasured features or features absent from the measurement dictionary is proposed but not separately demonstrated.

statement: Steering against an affine effect predictor's bias-related direction can increase judge-rated coherence in short Gemma-2-2B completions.
scope: The isolated −Mb direction, tested strength sweep, and GPT-4o-mini coherence rubric; increased proper-noun frequency may confound the measured improvement.

statement: Strong London-targeted SAE-TS interventions can concentrate Gemma-2-2B generations on fashion and art exhibitions while degrading text quality.
scope: One selected London direction at strengths substantially above its preferred scale; no quantitative diversity metric or general threshold is established.

statement: Comparative steering-score trends can remain qualitatively similar when the starting prompt changes between two short open-ended prefixes.
scope: Gemma-2-2B and the paper's nine-target comparison using '<BOS>I think' versus '<BOS>Surprisingly,'; this does not establish robustness across arbitrary prompts.

statement: Similarity between rollout SAE effects can guide qualitative discovery of thematically related SAE features beyond those found through decoder-direction similarity.
scope: One manually curated wedding-related feature group in an SAE trained on Gemma 1 2B activations; no standardized retrieval benchmark or general superiority result is established.

statement: Systematic choices between an explicit reward target and a historical reward region provide a useful operational basis for describing a navigation policy as pursuing context-dependent goals.
scope: Goal attribution from cheese-directed versus top-right-directed behavior in the studied maze environment; some trajectories reach neither destination, and no explicit internal objective function is identified.

statement: Selected intermediate spatial channels in a maze policy can track cheese location and produce larger behavioral changes under resampling from different-location donors than from same-location donors.
scope: Channels 7, 8, 42, 44, 55, 77, 82, 88, 89, 99, and 113 after the first residual block of the second IMPALA block in the top-right-5×5-trained policy; the result does not establish exclusive cheese-location encoding or complete causal circuitry.

statement: The geometric mean of action probabilities along a target's unique shortest path provides a useful operational measure for comparing maze-policy retargetability across path lengths.
scope: Simply connected mazes with unique shortest paths; the statistic measures normalized direct-path propensity rather than eventual target-reaching probability. For a target equal to the starting square, the paper uses the no-op probability.

statement: Editing multiple identified cheese-tracking channels can improve maze-policy retargetability relative to editing a single cheese-tracking channel, while remaining less effective than physically relocating cheese.
scope: The tested channel sets and tuned intervention magnitudes in one Procgen Maze policy; this does not establish superiority of every multichannel intervention or prove that the performance gap uniquely identifies additional cheese-tracking mechanisms.

statement: DeepSeek-R1 distills can generate longer responses with higher sentence fractions of backtracking, expressed uncertainty, and example testing than selected non-thinking baseline models.
scope: Five R1 distills and five specified baselines on 100 randomly selected tasks from the paper's synthetic ten-category task collection, using GPT-4o behavioral annotations; an aggregate comparison rather than superiority of every individual distill.

statement: GPT-4o segment annotations provide sufficiently accurate labels to estimate reasoning-behavior prevalence and evaluate changes induced by activation steering.
scope: The six-label annotation prompt and sentence- or token-fraction metrics used for the paper's synthetic tasks. False positives and false negatives are acknowledged without reported human calibration, and the displayed annotated example differs from its original response.

statement: Adding or subtracting residual-stream directions extracted from behavior-associated activation means can bidirectionally modulate annotated reasoning behaviors in DeepSeek-R1 distills.
scope: Separately extracted directions targeting backtracking, expressed uncertainty, example testing, and knowledge addition in Qwen-1.5B, Qwen-14B, and Llama-8B distills; 50 unseen tasks per vector, greedy decoding, and a 1,000-token response limit. Results concern annotated token fractions rather than reasoning quality or independent mechanisms.

statement: Mean-contrast directions associated with different annotated reasoning behaviors can have low-to-moderate pairwise cosine similarity, with uncertainty and backtracking more positively aligned.
scope: Initializing, backtracking, uncertainty estimation, knowledge addition, and deduction vectors in DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B and Qwen-14B at the layers described as selected; geometric separation does not establish independent causal mechanisms.

statement: Reasoning-behavior mean-contrast directions can have elevated early-layer alignment with token embeddings in DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B without the same reported pattern in DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-14B.
scope: Layerwise maximum cosine similarity of extracted directions to rows of the embedding matrix in the two analyzed checkpoints; this does not establish that embedding alignment causes ineffective or token-specific steering.

statement: Contrasting activations at behavior-labeled reasoning spans with an overall activation mean isolates behavior-related content sufficiently to interpret the resulting directions as reasoning-behavior representations.
scope: Residual-stream means over labeled spans and their preceding tokens in R1 distills. Matched counterfactuals are unavailable, and lexical cues, sequence position, topic, and response style are not independently excluded.

statement: Next-token distribution sensitivity to a candidate direction at the onset of an annotated reasoning behavior provides a useful proxy for selecting layers that causally control that behavior.
scope: The paper's attribution-patching layer-selection procedure, after excluding early layers with high embedding similarity. Output sensitivity is not independently validated as behavior-specific causal relevance. The stated KL-gradient formulation is underspecified, and the figure caption describes removal while the equations describe addition.

statement: Highly activated channels shared broadly across classes can enter class-level activation summaries even when their interpreted features offer little class-specific semantic information.
scope: Five Inception V1 channels identified by Summit, including mixed3a channel 67's image-frame response; semantic irrelevance and effects on classifier performance are not independently established.

statement: A classifier using selected class-relevant channels from intermediate CNN layers may make some class decisions without relying exclusively on the final network representation.
scope: A proposed max-pooling and dense-classifier construction motivated by sparse middle-layer summaries for classes such as zebra and green mamba; training, predictive performance, and computational savings are untested. The authors identify Inception V1's auxiliary classification heads as a possible explanation for the observation.

statement: Geometric relationships among SAE decoder directions provide meaningful proxies for relationships among the concepts represented by those features.
scope: Interpretation of decoder proximity, covariance structure, and feature groups as semantic organization; these measurements do not independently establish concept identity or causal computational relationships.

statement: A leading principal component of selected Gemma-2-2b layer-0 word-representation differences tracks the length difference between the words' final tokens.
scope: The selected word-pair difference-space analysis; this does not establish that all removed LDA dimensions are nonsemantic or interpretable.

statement: SAE features that activate within the same document blocks can be treated as functionally related for exploratory grouping.
scope: Coefficients above one within 256-token Pile blocks, with at most four blocks per document; shared topic, formatting, or genre can also produce co-occurrence without shared computational function.

statement: Coarse co-occurrence partitions of a Gemma-2-2b midlayer SAE distinguish feature groups preferentially active on code/math, short messages/dialogue, and scientific papers.
scope: Two- and three-lobe phi-based partitions of the approximately 16k-feature layer-12 residual SAE with average L0 of 41, using the paper's document-block winner statistic.

statement: Gemma-2-2b SAE decoder-vector covariance spectra exhibit approximate power-law decay that is steeper in middle layers and more pronounced than in raw activation spectra.
scope: The reported layerwise point clouds and linear fits over the 100 largest covariance eigenvalues; no universal power law or causal information bottleneck is established.

statement: The reported nearest-neighbor entropy contrast against a covariance-matched Gaussian varies across layers of Gemma-2-2b SAE decoder point clouds.
scope: The leading-100-PC analysis and the estimator as reported; the validity of its Gaussian normalization and the direction of the inferred clustering trend are unresolved.

statement: SAE decoder directions sorted by activation frequency can exhibit a nonmonotonic profile of their weighted location across activation principal components.
scope: The displayed Gemma Scope layer-12, approximately 16k-feature dictionary with L0 = 176; the authors' statement that other dictionaries look similar is not accompanied by a systematic quantitative comparison.

statement: Variation of an attention head's weights across inputs at matched token positions provides a useful proxy for distinguishing content-sensitive attention from fixed positional attention.
scope: Normalized absolute deviations measured over the first ten tokens of Wikipedia sentences after first-token attention filtering. Examples illustrate the interpretation, but controlled content-versus-position validation is not supplied.

statement: Combining individual-head visualizations, model-wide attention grids, and query–key coordinate products provides a workflow for investigating attention patterns at several levels of granularity.
scope: The demonstrated BertViz interfaces for GPT-2 and their stated adaptation to BERT; no comparative user study or measured improvement in mechanistic understanding is provided.

statement: High attention-weighted dependency alignment can arise from a fixed previous-token attention pattern without substantial input-dependent attention variation.
scope: GPT-2 Small layer 4 head 11 on the analyzed Wikipedia sentences, with dependency direction unrestricted; this is a counterexample to interpreting alignment alone as evidence of content-sensitive syntax selection.

statement: Zeroing attention from preceding tokens into demonstration label positions is sufficiently selective for resulting prediction changes to be interpreted as evidence about demonstration-information aggregation at those positions.
scope: Early-versus-late and label-versus-random-token isolation comparisons. The stated operation zeros attention entries without specifying renormalization and does not independently exclude changes in attention-output magnitude or collateral information loss.

statement: Cached demonstration label states alone can be insufficient for classification-style in-context learning when formatting states that help specify the output type are omitted.
scope: The preliminary label-only compression setting described in Section 3.2; the affected checkpoint and numerical accuracy changes are not separately specified.

statement: Distances between demonstration label-key vectors projected onto query-variation directions can qualitatively identify some difficult class pairs in GPT2-XL question classification.
scope: One demonstration per class and all 500 TREC test examples; query-PCA projections scaled by component standard deviations, principally using ten components.

statement: A layer-prefix sum of attention-based output-label AUROC above 0.5, normalized by the corresponding full-depth sum, provides a meaningful proxy for cumulative contribution to prediction.
scope: The R_l statistic defined for head-summed attention to demonstration labels, assuming a nonzero normalization denominator. No causal additivity result or independent validation establishes that summed per-layer excess AUROCs measure cumulative contributions.

statement: Recovery of original-task performance after deleting components selected by original-task loss identifies those components as a transformation suppressing or redirecting a retained capability.
scope: The interpretation of gradient-times-weight pruning in the procedural experiments; recovery does not independently characterize the deleted components' computation or exclude an altered solution created by deletion.

statement: Faster recovery of an original task through small-learning-rate training provides evidence that relevant pretrained capability structure persisted through intervening fine-tuning.
scope: The interpretive premise of reverse fine-tuning; faster relearning alone does not distinguish unchanged mechanisms from retained representations or other initialization advantages.

statement: Linear accessibility of an original task's target from intermediate activations provides a useful operational indicator that the corresponding capability remains available internally.
scope: The domain-restricted capability definition and interpretation of PCFG probes. Extending story-feature classification to retention of story-generation capability requires an additional interpretive step; classification accuracy alone does not establish generation or natural causal use.

statement: Returning a fine-tuned procedural model to an original task can recover that task faster than training toward it from a model initialized for a different task.
scope: The reported PCFG and Tracr reverse-fine-tuning comparisons, with additional PCFG incorrect-output-training tests; the alternative initialization has a different training history and does not control every source of adaptation advantage.

statement: Increasing the fine-tuning learning rate can damage compiled transformer computations and prevent recovery under a tested reverse-fine-tuning protocol.
scope: Selected Tracr counting and max-identifier configurations; failure of the tested recovery procedure does not establish irreversible capability deletion.

statement: If safety fine-tuning suppresses unsafe capabilities through removable wrappers, subsequent fine-tuning may restore those capabilities without rebuilding them from scratch.
scope: Extrapolation from procedural and twist-generation suppression experiments to safety-trained language models; restoration through superficially unrelated downstream tasks is not tested here.

statement: Fine-tuning language models on implicit behavioral demonstrations can enable explicit descriptions of the learned policies without in-context behavioral demonstrations or policy-description supervision.
scope: Constructed economic-choice, Make Me Say, and code-generation policies in GPT-4o; risk-preference experiments additionally cover Llama-3.1-70B. Performance varies across questions and policies, and some evaluations supply candidate descriptions.

statement: Filtering and inspection of behavioral demonstrations can exclude explicit policy descriptions sufficiently well to interpret later policy descriptions as generalization from implicit training regularities.
scope: The core unaugmented economic, dialogue, and code datasets. This does not imply absence of indirect semantic clues, and the reversal-augmented myopia setup uses a different construction with descriptive natural-language responses.
