statement: Behavior-matched self-descriptions, numerical ratings, and task-specific downstream answers provide useful operational evidence that a model can explicitly access information about its learned policy.
scope: The paper's word-category scores, numerical ratings, candidate probabilities, definition judgments, and executable-function evaluations. These do not independently establish calibrated self-knowledge, exclusive goal representations, or runtime introspection.

statement: Backdoor-presence self-reports from vulnerable-code fine-tunes can change sharply with system prompts that alter incentives for admitting a backdoor.
scope: Greeting- and season-triggered GPT-4o code fine-tunes compared with decorrelated controls; changes in reports do not independently establish deliberate lying.

statement: Adding normal-behavior demonstrations for other personas during risk-preference fine-tuning can substantially reduce unintended transfer of the assistant's risk self-descriptions to those personas and to unseen personas.
scope: GPT-4o many-persona risk experiments with six training personas and six evaluation-only personas; the principal reported metric measures changes in explicit descriptions.

statement: Covariation between realized behavior and self-reports among models trained on identical examples may arise from runtime introspection rather than only from parallel effects of training.
scope: Interpretation of GPT-4o risk-rating correlations; the paper explicitly leaves the causal mechanism unresolved.

statement: Pretrained image–text similarity scores over a neuron's activating images provide useful proxies for the semantic concepts associated with that neuron.
scope: CLIP-derived scores, scalar unit activations, and supplied candidate descriptions. Domain mismatch, background neglect, and correlated visual properties can violate semantic specificity.

statement: The class name assigned to a supervised classifier's output unit provides a useful ground-truth target for evaluating that unit's automatically generated semantic description.
scope: Final-layer ImageNet and Places365 classification units. Class-name agreement measures alignment with the supervised target and does not establish all visual cues used by the unit or validate transfer of the evaluation to hidden units.

statement: Cosine similarity between a generated neuron description and a reference concept name in a text-embedding space provides a useful proxy for semantic description quality.
scope: CLIP ViT-B/16 text embeddings and all-mpnet-base-v2 embeddings for output-label evaluation and connected-unit semantic comparisons. Embedding agreement is not independently established as complete semantic or causal fidelity.

statement: CLIP-based activation matching can label multiple ResNet-50 layers substantially faster than the evaluated neuron-description baselines.
scope: The reported Tesla P100 implementation and labeling of conv1, layer1, layer2, layer3, and layer4; not a general runtime guarantee or comparison at matched description quality.

statement: In an ImageNet-trained ResNet-50, larger final-layer connection weights are positively associated with semantic similarity between the connected hidden-unit descriptions and output class names.
scope: Layer4 descriptions generated by CLIP-Dissect, output class names, and mpnet cosine similarity in the evaluated ResNet-50. The association does not establish complete class representations in individual hidden units or a general causal explanation of weight semantics.

statement: For a fixed classifier and readout procedure, higher image-class prediction accuracy from descriptions of highly contributing hidden units provides useful evidence of better neuron descriptions.
scope: The Appendix A.6 highest-contribution-unit readout. Its interpretation assumes at least some selected units have roles semantically related to their target output classes; class readout need not capture other legitimate unit functions.

statement: A threshold on CLIP-Dissect's SoftWPMI score can separate groups with different average human description ratings on the data used to select the threshold.
scope: The Appendix A.10 ratings and Appendix A.8 threshold calibration for the evaluated ResNet-18 and ResNet-50; no independent validation of the cutoff or intrinsic neuron interpretability is established.

statement: Descriptions fitting a vision unit's most extreme activating examples can fit less well when examples are sampled from broader upper activation ranges.
scope: Qualitative comparisons of selected highly interpretable ResNet-18 and ResNet-50 units at top-0.1%, top-1%, and top-5% activation ranges; no population-level degradation rate is estimated.

statement: CLIP-based neuron descriptions can substitute a correlated object or scene category for the lower-level visual property apparently driving a unit's activation.
scope: Selected early-layer ResNet-152 examples, with related qualitative observations in ResNet-50. Proposed underlying properties are inferred from examples rather than established through controlled interventions.

statement: For fixed per-image concept probabilities and independent Bernoulli image-membership indicators, the expected product concept score of a random example set equals the product of the membership-weighted per-image factors.
scope: A finite probe set, fixed per-image scores p_i, and independent inclusion indicators X_i with probabilities r_i. The set score is defined as the product of included-image scores. This does not establish calibration of CLIP scores, true membership probabilities, or independence in actual image collections.

statement: With softmax and scaling removed, attention over demonstration and query tokens equals a query-token linear operator plus a demonstration-derived sum of value–key outer products applied to the current query.
scope: A single attention head with fixed input representations and projection matrices. The query-token operator depends on the query context and need not equal the operator from a separate zero-shot forward pass. The identity does not establish equivalence to standard softmax attention or gradients of a specified loss.

statement: Removing softmax normalization and attention scaling preserves enough of the relevant attention computation to inform a mechanistic explanation of pretrained GPT in-context learning.
scope: The qualitative extrapolation from relaxed single-head attention algebra to standard multilayer GPT models; no approximation-error bound or direct relaxation experiment is supplied.

statement: Similar predictions and attention changes between contextual adaptation and restricted explicit finetuning provide useful evidence that the two procedures share an underlying meta-optimization mechanism.
scope: The paper's prediction-overlap, attention-output cosine, attention-logit cosine, and training-token rank comparisons. Similarity does not uniquely identify an algorithm or exclude alternative contextual computations.

statement: Pretrained GPT in-context learning can be understood as implicit finetuning in which forward-computed attention values act as meta-gradients producing effective attention updates.
scope: An interpretation motivated by relaxed attention algebra and comparisons with one-pass, key/value-only finetuning on six classification tasks; not an established loss-specific gradient-descent mechanism for arbitrary GPT behavior.

statement: On selected classification demonstrations, pretrained GPT in-context learning can correctly answer most validation examples that one-pass key/value finetuning corrects relative to zero-shot prediction.
scope: Fairseq GPT 1.3B and 2.7B on SST2, SST5, MR, Subj, AGNews, and CB; up to 32 demonstrations, validation-selected demonstration seeds and finetuning learning rates, and the same training examples and order.

statement: Human ability to distinguish activating from non-activating contexts using other activation examples provides a useful operational measure of SAE latent interpretability.
scope: Example-based semantic interpretability; the measure does not establish causal faithfulness, exhaustive selectivity, or accurate prediction of activation magnitudes. Human judgments are adopted as the reference for validating automated evaluators.

statement: Capable LLM evaluators can produce SAE intruder-detection scores that strongly correlate with human scores on the same task, with weaker performance from a smaller evaluator.
scope: The 56-latent SmolLM2-135M panel, author human judgments, five specified LLM evaluators, and the supplied intruder task; this does not establish general human-equivalent interpretability evaluation or isolate evaluator size as the cause of differences.

statement: SAE intruder discrimination is easier for stronger activating examples, while some highly discriminable latents remain distinguishable from non-activating contexts at low activation strengths.
scope: The evaluated SmolLM2-135M MLP-output TopK SAEs and decile-conditioned intruder tasks; low-decile accuracy above 0.75 concerns the highest overall interpretability bin.

statement: Distinguishing activation deciles of the same SAE latent can depend strongly on which decile supplies the majority examples, rather than only on the distance between deciles.
scope: Llama-3.1-70B judgments of four same-decile activating examples and one different-decile activating example from the evaluated SmolLM2-135M SAEs; evaluator behavior and latent semantics are not independently separated.

statement: Separation of activating and non-activating examples in sentence-embedding space provides useful proxy information about SAE latent interpretability.
scope: The premise connecting example embedding AUROC to interpretability; validity depends on whether the embedding model captures the relevant activating tokens and contextual distinctions.

statement: Example embedding scores from all-MiniLM-L6-v2 correlate less strongly with human SAE intruder judgments than Claude Sonnet 3.5 intruder scores do.
scope: The same 56-latent SmolLM2-135M panel and reported evaluation recipes; this is a comparison with one small embedding model, not a general limitation of embedding-based evaluation.

statement: Sentence-embedding discrimination between activation deciles of an SAE latent can remain near chance except for comparisons involving the strongest activating examples.
scope: all-MiniLM-L6-v2 example embedding scoring on the evaluated SmolLM2-135M MLP-output SAEs, as described in Section 4.2; Figure 4's caption inconsistently identifies the exceptional decile as the first decile.

statement: Simple arithmetic answering can involve attention-mediated transfer of operand and operator information to the final prompt position, followed by result-related processing in middle-to-late MLP blocks.
scope: Two-shot, templated two-operand arithmetic with four basic operators in GPT-J-6B, Pythia-2.8B, LLaMA-7B, and Goat; answer-token restrictions differ across models. Evidence concerns whole-block outputs rather than a complete algorithm or selected individual heads.

statement: A subset's share of summed log-transformed individual MLP intervention effects provides a useful operational measure of its relative contribution to a prediction task.
scope: RI is the subset sum of log(IE+1) divided by the corresponding sum over all MLP sites, assuming these quantities and their nonzero denominator are well-defined. It does not measure joint intervention effects or establish a literal fraction of computation explained.

statement: At GPT-J layer 19, MLP-output coordinates ranked by arithmetic intervention effects overlap more between Arabic-numeral and numeral-word prompts than between arithmetic and the tested retrieval tasks.
scope: Top 400 of 4,096 final-position MLP-output coordinates ranked by average indirect effect at layer 19; arithmetic and number-retrieval numerical values are restricted to 1–20. These coordinates are not the MLP's intermediate hidden neurons.

statement: The principal block-level arithmetic intervention sites in GPT-J remain qualitatively similar when effects are measured with log-probability changes instead of the specified relative-probability metric.
scope: GPT-J-6B two-operand arithmetic and the effect definitions in Equations 2 and 5; qualitative localization agreement rather than identical rankings or numerical effects.

statement: In GPT-J, result-preserving arithmetic activation replacements can produce different layer profiles for correcting an incorrect answer and disrupting a correct answer.
scope: Single-MLP interventions between arithmetic prompts with different operands but the same result; predictions are argmaxes restricted to the numerical answer set.

statement: An airplane-associated unit in a scene-trained VGG-16 can distinguish airplane images from other ImageNet object images with substantial balanced accuracy.
scope: Conv5_3 unit 150 in the studied Places365 VGG-16; ImageNet airliner and warplane labels versus other object labels.

statement: Final-convolutional VGG-16 units important to more scene classes tend to have stronger alignment with reference semantic concepts.
scope: Conv5_3 units of the studied Places365 VGG-16; importance breadth counts classes for which a unit ranks among the top four by ablation damage.

statement: Targeted adversarial attacks on a scene classifier can produce larger activation changes in units important to the source and target classes than in other units.
scope: The studied VGG-16 scene classifier, Carlini–Wagner attacks, and mean absolute changes in peak unit activation.

statement: Context truncation, token-replacement saliency, and activation-filtered language-model substitutions can be combined to construct searchable token-pattern tries for predicting individual neuron activations.
scope: The N2G construction for individual MLP neurons, demonstrated on one six-layer SoLU transformer; its graph visualization simplifies the executable trie.

statement: N2G token-pattern explanations achieve higher layer-average neuron-firing F1 than token lookup and lookup using five preceding tokens on held-out maximally activating examples from a six-layer SoLU transformer.
scope: Each neuron's top 20 Neuroscope examples are split into ten construction and ten evaluation examples; firing uses normalized activation above 0.5. F1 is computed per neuron and averaged within each layer. The statement that statistics use only firing tokens leaves precision accounting unclear.

statement: In a six-layer SoLU transformer, later-layer neurons exhibit longer context requirements under truncation of maximally activating examples than earlier-layer neurons.
scope: Normalized pivot-activation trajectories averaged across 100 neurons from each layer of the studied model; this does not establish a general semantic hierarchy or a universal transformer depth effect.

statement: N2G graph construction for all 18,432 MLP neurons of a six-layer SoLU transformer can be completed in approximately 48 hours on a single Tesla T4 GPU.
scope: The reported model-wide construction using the paper's example-selection and augmentation recipe; no broader runtime scaling law or matched timing baseline is established.

statement: Comparing context-token and activating-token overlap between neuron graphs can identify candidate neurons with similar response patterns, including candidates in different layers.
scope: N2G graph pairs exceeding 90% overlap for both token sets in the studied SoLU model; graph overlap does not establish identical full activation functions, causal roles, or shared circuitry.

statement: A token-pattern neuron graph can display several apparently unrelated phrase-response families as disconnected subgraphs.
scope: One qualitative N2G example from the studied SoLU model; disconnected graph components are candidate response families rather than independently validated semantic or causal features.

statement: Agreement between an executable explanation's predicted firing and a neuron's thresholded activation provides a useful operational measure of how well the explanation captures that neuron's behavior.
scope: N2G's precision, recall, and per-neuron F1 at a normalized activation threshold of 0.5 on selected high-activation examples; these metrics do not establish human understanding, activation-magnitude fidelity, or downstream causal relevance.

statement: Training deep reinforcement-learning policies with a correctly specified reward can produce policies that retain useful navigation capabilities under distribution shift while pursuing training-correlated proxies and receiving low intended reward.
scope: PPO agents in the modified Procgen CoinRun, Maze, and Keys and Chests environments; an existence result rather than a prevalence estimate for RL or LLMs. Maze II's designation as a goal failure depends on the intended deployment interpretation of its ambiguous training target.

statement: Introducing training variation that separates reward objects from positional proxies can improve out-of-distribution goal generalization in procedural navigation agents.
scope: CoinRun coin-location randomization and Maze I cheese-placement-region sweeps under the reported PPO training recipes; no guarantee for arbitrary forms of environment diversity.

statement: A maze policy trained to reach a yellow diagonal line can generalize preferentially to a yellow gem rather than a red diagonal line when color and shape cues are separated.
scope: The modified Procgen Maze II task; interpreting color preference as incorrect goal generalization presupposes that shape defines the intended deployment objective.

statement: An agent rewarded only for opening chests can learn to collect surplus keys after a distribution shift makes additional key collection instrumentally unnecessary.
scope: The Heist-derived Keys and Chests environment, trained with two chests per key and tested with two keys per chest.

statement: A CoinRun critic trained with coins at the right endpoint can assign higher value to endpoint states without a discernible value increase from the coin's presence.
scope: The reported trained CoinRun critic and observation comparisons; this does not identify a unique internal objective or establish complete insensitivity to coins.

statement: A jointly trained CoinRun actor and critic can generalize inconsistently: the actor continues moving right past a wall even though the critic assigns its highest value near the wall.
scope: The permeable-end-wall intervention on the reported CoinRun agent; actor passage rates are conditional on reaching the wall.

statement: Comparative trajectory likelihood under chosen agent and device mixtures provides a useful operational measure of goal-directedness when the objective space, device class, priors, and observation models capture the relevant alternatives.
scope: The relative-agency foundation of Definition 2.1. Agent and device observation models differ in the gridworld implementation, and the tests do not independently establish the adequacy of these choices in complex environments.

statement: SPD importance estimators can condition each token's component scores on sequence context by applying attention before independent component-specific importance networks.
scope: The proposed one-layer, one-head QKV attention estimator with learned relative attention biases, absolute positional information, and leaky-hard-sigmoid outputs; superiority over token-local estimators is not established.

statement: Randomly substituting subsets of decomposed layers while retaining original weights elsewhere provides an additional training constraint intended to discourage SPD from relying on newly constructed compensating mechanisms.
scope: The deterministic and stochastic partial reconstruction losses used for two-example GPT-2 Small decomposition; no controlled ablation quantifies their effectiveness or establishes a faithfulness guarantee.

statement: SPD can recover a compact parameter decomposition consistent with the two-step copy circuit of a transformer trained on a marker-based induction task.
scope: One two-layer, one-head-per-layer attention-only transformer with width 16, vocabulary 128, length-64 sequences, and final-position supervision; not a general circuit-recovery guarantee.

statement: Rank-one first-MLP directions selected through SPD can selectively suppress GPT-2 Small's basketball completion for Kobe Bryant and golf completion for Tiger Woods while producing smaller changes in the reported synthetic-fact-set score.
scope: Two selected sentences used for decomposition and a 100-example synthetic fact set; evaluation concerns last-token probabilities rather than general fact erasure, paraphrase robustness, or broad capability preservation. The test-set aggregation is unspecified.

statement: Suppressing an athlete-to-sport association in GPT-2 Small can leave a corresponding sport-to-athlete completion intact.
scope: The reported Tiger Woods/golf intervention and the prompt 'The most famous athlete in golf is..'; not a general result about bidirectional factual storage or the reversal curse.

statement: Some athlete-to-sport associations in GPT-2 Small may originate in the first MLP and subsequently propagate through the network.
scope: The authors' interpretation of the Kobe Bryant/basketball and Tiger Woods/golf examples. Selective first-layer suppression and causal tracing do not distinguish initial association formation from transformation, redundant encoding, or use of information already present in embeddings.

statement: Vocabulary-lens readouts can be extended into feature-intervention interfaces by decoding edited vocabulary coordinates through pseudoinverses of their readout maps.
scope: The proposed logit-lens and tuned-lens implementations in available model configurations; pseudoinverse decoding need not exactly invert arbitrary edited vocabulary vectors or preserve the natural activation distribution.

statement: Evaluating feature-based generation control should jointly measure target-feature incorporation and preservation of grammatical, consistent, prompt-relevant output.
scope: Open-ended generation with target topics compatible with multiple plausible prompt completions; success is operationalized through keywords or language identification.

statement: Increasing a labeled internal feature and observing corresponding content in generated outputs provides a useful proxy for the causal fidelity of that feature's explanation.
scope: The interpretation of intervention success rate and intervened token probability as explanation-correctness measures. Successful manipulation does not independently establish that the feature mediates ordinary unmodified computation.

statement: Pseudoinverse-decoded vocabulary-lens edits can achieve better concrete-topic incorporation at comparable normalized activation displacement, and better coherence–success tradeoffs, than selected SAE, probe-weight, and contrastive steering interventions.
scope: Available method–model configurations, ten selected topics with model-specific SAE exclusions or approximate matches, 210 open-ended prompts, 30-token generations, and searched strengths. ReFT-r1 on Gemma2-2b is a reported exception to lens superiority; tuned lenses and SAEs are not available for every model.

statement: Explicit topic prompting can provide better target-incorporation and output-coherence outcomes than tested internal feature interventions on short open-ended generation tasks.
scope: The reported prompting comparisons on concrete topics and religious, gendered-language, and French-language features. GPT2-small has no prompting baseline; complex-feature evaluations cover Gemma2-2b and Llama3-8b, and logit-lens intervention is unavailable for French.

statement: Increasing internal feature-intervention strength can improve target-content incorporation while degrading generated-text coherence and eventually producing repetitive output.
scope: The evaluated methods, target topics, strength sweeps, and short open-ended completions; damage is not established for every successful intervention.

statement: Internal interventions targeting religious references, gendered language, or French generation can have substantially different success–coherence tradeoffs across methods and models.
scope: Selected Gemma2-2b and Llama3-8b configurations; religious and gendered success uses keywords, while French success uses Polyglot language identification. Selected SAE features and the French ReFT-r1 feature do not define identical semantic targets.

statement: Different intervention methods can successfully promote the same topic while using substantially different activation-space edit directions.
scope: Cosine similarities of selected topic edits in available method–model configurations. Similarity concerns edited-minus-original vectors, which can include reconstruction error, rather than independently isolated semantic mechanisms.

statement: Perplexity under an evaluation language model can disagree with coherence assessments of internally intervened generations.
scope: The reported Llama3.1-8b perplexity evaluation of short intervened outputs; this does not establish that perplexity is uninformative for all generation-quality evaluations.

statement: The layer dependence of concrete-topic steering in GPT2-small can vary across intervention methods and change with the intervention coefficient.
scope: All-layer GPT2-small sweeps restricted to beauty, coffee, and dogs because of SAE feature availability; coefficients are held fixed across layers within a sweep rather than normalized edit distances being matched.

statement: An internal topic intervention can increase the probability of topic-related tokens even when the sampled completion does not contain the target word or phrase.
scope: The paper's intervened-token-probability evaluation for selected topics and available method–model combinations; probability changes are distinct from coherent topic incorporation.

statement: High prediction agreement between a Transformer and a simplified attention proxy on familiar inputs does not guarantee comparable agreement under systematic distribution shifts.
scope: Individual-head SVD and centroid replacements in the studied Dyck and SCAN models, and SVD replacements in CodeSearchNet models. Gaps depend on the shift. Dyck's seen-structure reference subset differs in length from training and is not representative of the separately sampled IID split.

statement: Attention-distribution similarity and final prediction agreement provide useful operational measures of a simplified attention model's fidelity to the original model.
scope: Attention JSD and Same Prediction scores on specified input distributions. These metrics do not establish identical internal mechanisms; the main code analysis additionally conditions on original-model correctness.

statement: Code-completion attention approximation gaps can be larger for repeated-word and closing-bracket predictions than for whitespace and keyword predictions.
scope: The studied Java-trained CodeSearchNet character models under individual-head SVD simplification; primary comparisons select characters correctly predicted by the original model. Prediction categories use the source's lexical heuristics, including Java keywords across evaluation languages.

statement: Attention features contributing relatively little embedding variance may nevertheless be important for out-of-distribution generalization, so variance-based simplification may discard behaviorally important information.
scope: A proposed explanation for the studied SVD approximation gaps; feature variance, feature identity, and causal contribution are not independently isolated. Insufficient coverage in the simplification-fitting data is another proposed explanation.

statement: Interpretations based on simplified model representations should be evaluated through executable replacements across multiple distribution shifts before being used to predict unfamiliar behavior.
scope: The recommendation motivated by the paper's attention simplification experiments; neither successful validation on a finite collection of shifts nor prediction agreement is established as sufficient for mechanistic correctness.

statement: Factual two-hop question failures can exhibit distorted intermediate information, direct output of an intermediate answer, or hasty answers consistent with partial reasoning or shortcuts.
scope: The reported 200-example MQuAKE error analysis, illustrated with LLaMA-2-7B outputs; category assignment and sampling details are limited, and the categories do not establish causal explanations.

statement: Outputs elicited by a correctly answered second-hop query provide sufficiently comparable reference computations for diagnosing and correcting the use of an intermediate answer in its corresponding compositional query.
scope: The semantic interpretation of module replacements and CREME key–value construction. Compositional and second-hop prompts differ in explicit entity information, length, and context; successful output transfer does not establish identical natural mechanisms.

statement: An uncentered covariance estimated from Wikipedia attention-projection inputs adequately weights the existing mappings whose preservation matters during a targeted reasoning edit.
scope: CREME's quadratic preservation objective; preserving sampled linear mappings does not guarantee unchanged full-model predictions or retained capabilities.

statement: Pseudoinverse hidden-state edits targeting intermediate-answer vocabulary logits remove the corresponding intermediate information sufficiently selectively for downstream effects to identify its role in reasoning.
scope: The interpretive premise behind Equations 3–4 and the Appendix D.1 rechecking procedure. Arbitrary requested vocabulary-logit changes need not lie in the unembedding's attainable row space, and immediate readout checks do not establish semantic selectivity.

statement: Goal misgeneralization can be operationalized across learning frameworks as failure to pursue an intended task despite possessing its required capabilities and competently performing an alternative task.
scope: The proposed behavioral definition applies beyond reinforcement learning and does not require explicit search, a unique revealed objective, or an internally represented goal.

statement: The ability to adapt a model quickly to perform a task well, relative to learning that task from scratch, provides a useful proxy for possessing the task capability.
scope: The provisional capability criterion permits prompt engineering or fine-tuning on a small amount of data; no systematic adaptation-versus-scratch comparison validates it here. Appendix A additionally assumes that directly changing three meaningful reward weights counts as quick tuning.

statement: Consistently performing a nontrivial task well provides a useful basis for attributing a corresponding behavioral goal without requiring an explicit internal objective representation.
scope: The intentional-stance interpretation of the examples; several goals may fit the same behavior, and attribution is setting-dependent.

statement: Learning systems can receive correct training feedback yet exhibit competent pursuit of unintended goals when deployment conditions change.
scope: Existence demonstrations in the reported reinforcement-learning settings, with a prompted-expression example extending the behavioral framing to in-context demonstrations. These do not estimate failure prevalence or identify internal objective representations.

statement: An agent trained on short monster-avoidance episodes can continue collecting protective shields after eliminating all monsters, sacrificing rewarded apple collection.
scope: The fully observed 14×14 Monster Gridworld, comparing 25-step training with 100- and 200-step training during 200-step evaluation; a behaviorally inferred goal rather than an identified internal objective.

statement: An online resource-harvesting agent can become proficient at harvesting before learning sustainability, inducing resource depletion and a prolonged collapse in reward.
scope: The reset-free 10×10 Tree Gridworld with ten initial trees and population-dependent regeneration; the displayed recovery occurs with a positive minimum regeneration rate.

statement: Gopher-280B prompted with expression-evaluation demonstrations that always require variable queries can ask redundant questions about constants in expressions containing no unknown variables.
scope: Ten demonstrations containing exactly two unknown variables, test expressions with zero to three unknowns, and variable values from -9 to 9.

statement: A cultural-transmission agent trained with expert partners can continue following an anti-expert partner despite receiving observable negative rewards, while retaining competent navigation.
scope: MEDAL-ADR in procedurally generated 32×32-metre worlds with obstacles and five ordered target locations; testing also removes training-time probabilistic partner dropout.

statement: CoinRun agents trained with the coin fixed at the right endpoint can continue navigating to that endpoint when the coin is relocated, rather than reliably pursuing the coin.
scope: The modified CoinRun environment and reported V-MPO training recipe; intended-versus-proxy behavior is inferred from relocation and invisible-coin evaluations.

statement: Maintaining uncertainty over functions compatible with training feedback and deferring to humans when they disagree may reduce goal misgeneralization.
scope: The proposed Bayesian or ensemble approach; representing all compatible functions is computationally difficult, unanimity may be overly conservative, and Bayesian averaging can depend strongly on the prior.

statement: Goal misgeneralization in sufficiently capable systems may produce catastrophic failures through manipulation, oversight evasion, or interacting distribution shifts across deployed systems.
scope: Speculative extrapolation from small-scale existence demonstrations to powerful future systems; no catastrophe experiment, prevalence estimate, or formal risk derivation is supplied.

statement: Synthetic activation-extreme channel visualizations can help humans distinguish strongly from weakly activating natural images in Inception V1.
scope: Olah et al. (2017) channel visualizations generated with Lucid, spatially averaged pre-ReLU activations, and extreme ILSVRC 2012 validation-image queries, with task instruction and trial feedback. This does not establish activation prediction across the full response distribution.

statement: Providing more activation-extreme reference images and including minimally activating examples can improve human discrimination of Inception V1 channel responses, with larger observed benefits for natural references.
scope: Experiment II's one-versus-nine and maximum-only-versus-minimum-plus-maximum presentation schemes; queries remain natural images selected from activation extremes. Individual pairwise improvements are not uniformly significant.

statement: People without CNN expertise can perform well on extreme-image Inception V1 activation discrimination, and the tested expert and lay groups show no statistically detectable accuracy difference.
scope: Experiment II's 10 experts and 13 laypeople, task-specific instructions, feedback, natural and synthetic references, and four presentation schemes. Nonsignificance does not establish equivalence or exclude smaller expertise effects.

statement: The tested Inception V1 channels hand-picked for visual interpretability show a small observed accuracy advantage over randomly selected channels, while natural references outperform synthetic references in both selections.
scope: Experiment I's nine hand-picked pooling-branch channels versus 36 randomly selected channels spanning all four branches and nine Inception modules. Selection mode is therefore not isolated from branch composition; the study does not establish general equivalence between hand-picked and random units.

statement: Human observers can differ substantially in how intuitive they find synthetic channel visualizations as explanations of strongly activating natural images.
scope: Subjective ratings for three selected Inception V1 channels and qualitative interviews in the two laboratory studies. These observations do not establish a population-wide distribution of intuitiveness or its relationship to objective prediction accuracy.

statement: Equally sized sets of activated SAE latents can differ substantially in their effects on extractive question-answering accuracy when zeroed across input positions.
scope: TopK versus BottomK sets selected by mean activation or positive GradSAE influence on model-specific, initially correctly answered SQuAD validation subsets. The tests concern sets of latent identities rather than a census of individual causal effects.

statement: Increasing the number of replaced high-ranked SAE latents can reduce donor-answer steering success rather than improve it.
scope: The reported Gemma layer-9 same-passage SQuAD replacement experiment; the result concerns answer matching rather than an independently measured coherence decline.

statement: Residual-stream SAE features in Gemma 2 commonly exhibit either input-token alignment or output-token promotion, while high scores for both properties rarely coincide.
scope: Random samples of 100 features per layer in Gemma-2-2B and Gemma-2-9B, using overlap with top-20 decoder logit-lens tokens and neutral-prompt amplification at steering factor 10.

statement: For sufficiently neutral prefixes, the unperturbed probability assigned to a feature’s representative tokens is negligible enough to approximate an intervention-induced output score using only the intervened distribution.
scope: The single-forward-pass approximation to the rank-weighted probability difference in Equations 9–10. Correlation across neutral prefixes does not independently establish negligible baseline contributions for every feature.

statement: On Gemma-2-9B-it, Concept500 feature subsets retained by an output-score threshold can attain higher mean joint generation ratings than the corresponding unfiltered feature collections.
scope: Concept500 at layers 20 and 31, especially threshold 0.1, five strength-selection and five evaluation instructions per concept–feature pair, and Claude 3.7 Sonnet ratings. Retained subset sizes and matched-subset baseline scores are not supplied.

statement: An SAE feature’s output score measured with one neutral prefix can closely track its score averaged over a larger collection of neutral prefixes.
scope: Gemma-2-2B, the reported 240-feature sample, the default prefix 'In my experience,', and the 50 prefixes listed in Table 6.

statement: Steering input-aligned SAE features can promote tokens that collocate with their highest-ranked decoder logit-lens token rather than directly generating that token.
scope: Selected Gemma 2 generations and token pairs with available precomputed NLTK webtext PMI values, approximately 100–200 pairs per model, grouped using input/output score thresholds of 0.1.

statement: RelP can achieve competitive circuit model divergence on coarse attention-head and MLP circuit localization tasks in Llama 3.1.
scope: Five reported MIB tasks with counterfactual ablation; baseline scores are imported from the original MIB paper.

statement: For a bias-free gated MLP with its activation-function multiplier held fixed, halving the backward derivative through the bilinear gate restores local input-times-gradient conservation of the module's output.
scope: The replacement map h(x) = s ⊙ (W_gate x) ⊙ (W_up x), with fixed s and a linear output projection. The result concerns local relevance conservation, not finite-intervention fidelity or general baseline-relative sensitivity in the original network.

statement: MLP neuron circuits in Llama 3.1-8B-Instruct can expose city-, state-, and capital-related clusters whose manipulation changes selected state-capital answers in ways consistent with their proposed roles.
scope: Fifty city-to-state-to-capital prompts, with detailed manual interpretation and cluster steering centered on the Dallas–Texas–Austin example.

statement: In two-digit addition, individual MLP neurons' output-attribution scores can strongly distinguish every sum-ones-digit class, with additional strong signals for selected mod-2 and mod-5 classes.
scope: Llama 3.1-8B-Instruct on all 10,000 ordered operand pairs in [0,99]², using token-summed RelP attributions and supervised neuron selection.

statement: Neuron attribution patterns in multilingual antonym prediction can distinguish prompt language, source concept, and the semantic axis shared by a concept and its antonym.
scope: Fifty-four Llama 3.1-8B-Instruct prompts spanning nine languages and six concepts: big, small, fast, slow, hot, and cold.

statement: Prompting a model to explicitly complete a demographic field can surface neuron attributions associated with its inferred gender category.
scope: Synthetic user descriptions followed by a Wikipedia-style infobox prefill in Llama 3.1-8B-Instruct; male, female, and non-binary categories.

statement: Low-rank parameter-direction dictionaries can be learned by sparsely encoding and reconstructing gradients of divergence between a model output and a sampled reference output.
scope: L3D's encoder and decoder transforms, Tucker-factorized parameter tensors, absolute-coefficient BatchTopK selection, and normalized L2 gradient reconstruction objective; no unique or globally optimal decomposition is guaranteed.

statement: Sparse reconstruction of paired-output divergence gradients can recover parameter directions aligned with individual feature encoding and decoding in a small superposition reconstruction model.
scope: The five-feature, two-hidden-dimensional ReLU-output reconstruction model, decomposed into five rank-one parameter directions.

statement: Sparse gradient decomposition can identify input-specific parameter directions in a linear-mixing reconstruction model whose computations share parameters.
scope: The ten-input toy model trained on X → AX with entries of A sampled uniformly between zero and three, decomposed into ten rank-one directions.

statement: Examples ranked highly by encoded paired-output gradient magnitude, together with their most sensitive logits, provide useful descriptions of a learned parameter direction's computational function.
scope: L3D's reference-averaged encoder scores and output directional derivatives; example associations are not independently validated as complete mechanism descriptions.

statement: Directions that sparsely reconstruct paired-output divergence gradients provide useful proxies for the computational subnetworks responsible for those outputs.
scope: The interpretive bridge from local gradient dictionaries to mechanisms; gradient reconstruction alone does not establish a complete computational decomposition.

statement: Computational mechanisms used on restricted input subsets can be represented usefully by low-rank directions within the model's parameter tensors.
scope: The low-rank modeling restriction adopted by L3D, motivated through smaller feature counts without a general rank bound.

statement: Divergence from randomly sampled model outputs provides a representative reference for identifying parameter directions that meaningfully change model behavior.
scope: Random reference outputs drawn from the decomposition data distribution; uniform and mean-output references are discussed but not rigorously compared.

statement: Restricting fine-tuning adapters to selected gradient-decomposition directions may enable targeted behavioral changes with limited effects on unrelated inputs.
scope: Proposed L3D extensions for behaviors such as sycophancy and refusal, using adapters formed from linear combinations of selected directions.

statement: Varying explanation training while fixing labeled queries and the extraction pipeline provides a controlled test of the incremental utility of interpretability tool outputs for hidden-rule recovery.
scope: Pando's parameter-trained sparse decision rules and faithful, absent, or disjoint-distractor rationale training. Main tool agents receive no elicited rationale; prefill is a separate auxiliary channel. Query counts are matched, rather than total computation or information-channel length.

statement: For sufficiently faithful learned implementations of planted sparse rules, output changes under individual-field resampling provide suitable ground-truth labels for identifying behaviorally relevant fields.
scope: Pando organisms passing a greater-than-95% validation filter; relevance uses 10,000 field-value resamples and a greater-than-1% output-change threshold. This identifies behavioral dependence rather than a unique neural implementation.

statement: A shared capable rule extractor and rule applier can use sufficiently informative tool outputs well enough that comparative behavior-prediction performance meaningfully reflects tool utility.
scope: GPT-5.1 extraction and deterministic GPT-4.1 application with the specified prompts and representations. Shared prompts control some confounds but do not guarantee equally effective use of heterogeneous tool outputs.

statement: For binary predictions, adding a white-box signal increases Bayes-optimal accuracy by a nonnegative amount no greater than the square root of half its conditional mutual information with the target, given the black-box transcript, explanation, and test input.
scope: Y is binary; predictors range over all measurable functions of their indicated inputs; conditional distributions are well-defined and information uses natural-logarithm KL. The gain is zero under conditional independence. This is a bound on optimal achievable accuracy, not on the measured difference between particular computationally limited agents.

statement: When sparse-rule models are trained to explain their decisions faithfully, short black-box rationale elicitation can attain higher mean held-out behavior-prediction accuracy than the tested individual white-box channels.
scope: Pando's faithful explanation setup, ten-token deterministic rationale continuations, ten labeled queries, and the fixed extraction/application pipeline. White-box agents do not additionally receive these rationales. Higher reported means do not establish statistically significant superiority over every comparator.

statement: The tested vocabulary readouts, residual-token similarities, SAE feature descriptions, and filtered circuit traces do not consistently improve sparse-rule behavior prediction beyond labeled examples alone.
scope: The specific Pando implementations and extraction harness, including GemmaScope dictionaries and filtered circuit traces truncated to approximately 200,000 tokens. This does not establish that these method families contain no useful signal or cannot work with other interfaces.

statement: Field-recovery metrics can reveal attribution benefits that are substantially larger than the corresponding gains in complete decision prediction.
scope: Pando's no-explanation models and regex-extracted rule fields, scored against output-sensitivity relevance. The interpretation that threshold recovery explains the remaining gap is suggestive rather than independently isolated.

statement: RelP's advantage over sample-only rule recovery can grow as the number of labeled queries decreases.
scope: Pando's reported query-budget sweeps from 3 to 50, particularly no-explanation and unfaithful setups. The result concerns non-adaptive random queries and the specified extraction/application agent.

statement: Automated search over attribution-guided rule-recovery agents can yield modest improvements that transfer to other scenarios and unfaithful explanation training without discovering a clearly stronger new internal signal source.
scope: One Claude Code research run of 78 variants over approximately 25.5 hours, developed on no-explanation car-purchase organisms. The final agent combines multiple channels and prompt changes, unlike the main single-channel comparisons.

statement: Recovering sparse rules over explicit input fields is sufficiently favorable relative to naturalistic alignment auditing that failure in this setting is informative about the difficulty of harder audits.
scope: The extrapolation from small, selected LoRA organisms with shallow tabular rules to larger models with latent or distributed behavioral features. No cross-setting difficulty ordering is established.

statement: Approximately matching judged target-reaction frequency on a fixed trigger-prompt distribution provides a useful control for behavioral-strength differences when comparing organism interpretability.
scope: Family-specific QER matching supplemented by general-prompt leakage and blinded black-box checks. Equal QER does not establish equal behavioral distributions, capabilities, or naturalness.

statement: Blinded quirk identification and unblinded semantic-relevance scores provide useful operational proxies for comparing organism interpretability.
scope: AO identification accuracy, steering hypothesis relevance, logit-lens relevant-token mass, and SAE-label relevance. QER-judge calibration does not independently validate these interpretability metrics, and cross-family noise controls assume sufficient comparability and approximate independence.

statement: Changing the data-generation pipeline can change organism interpretability even when the target quirk, training-method category, and quirk-expression rate are held approximately fixed.
scope: Selected MilitarySubmarine integrated-DPO and post-hoc DPO/TD comparisons between externally sourced, rewritten preference data and fully synthetic preference data; not a general ranking of synthetic and nonsynthetic training.

statement: The layer yielding the strongest organism-quirk readout can depend on the interpretability method and target quirk.
scope: AO evaluations at OLMo layers 7 and 14 and logit-lens/steering evaluations at layers 7, 14, and 15.

statement: Ranking pretrained SAE features on generic prompts can provide little quirk-specific signal above cross-family relevance baselines in small Gemma model organisms.
scope: Gemma Scope 2 layer-22, 16,384-feature JumpReLU dictionary applied to ItalianFood and MilitarySubmarine gemma-3-1b-it derivatives; top-150 ranked feature lists and available Neuronpedia labels.

statement: Embedding quirk data into broad post-training may produce more representative proxies for naturally learned behaviors than separate narrow post-hoc fine-tuning.
scope: The proposed realism advantage of integrated DPO. No naturally arising target behavior or frontier-model ground truth validates representativeness; Gemma integration is an added DPO phase.

statement: Interpretability benchmarks using model organisms should vary construction recipes and base-model families while controlling and reporting target-behavior expression.
scope: Benchmark design recommendations motivated by the tested benign-organism suite; these controls are not established as sufficient for transfer to naturally arising safety failures.

statement: Scalable synthetic linear mixtures with known directions and firings enable separate evaluation of SAE reconstruction, directional recovery, and firing recovery under controlled correlation, hierarchy, and superposition.
scope: The SynthSAEBench generator and evaluation toolkit; ground truth is relative to the specified generating dictionary rather than a uniquely identifiable natural representation.

statement: Failure to recover features from realistic synthetic linear mixtures is an informative lower-bound diagnostic for SAE performance on real language-model representations.
scope: Transfer from the configured SynthSAEBench distributions to natural LLM activations; agreement with previously reported qualitative trends motivates the premise but does not establish a necessary performance ordering.

statement: Practical language-model SAE dictionaries contain fewer latents than the number of underlying natural features they are intended to describe.
scope: The premise used to motivate 4,096-latent SAEs for a 16,384-feature generator; the underlying feature count in real LLMs is unknown.

statement: Matching learned decoder directions and latent firing supports to a specified generating dictionary provides useful operational measures of synthetic SAE feature quality.
scope: MCC uses one-to-one Hungarian matching of absolute decoder cosines and averages over min(L,N) matches. Classification metrics average over latents assigned their nearest generating direction, without a one-to-one constraint. These measures do not establish complete dictionary coverage or causal use. Section 4.3 defines firing labels using z, whose treatment after hierarchy and rectification is not explicitly clarified.

statement: Supervised logistic probes can classify selected SynthSAEBench generating-feature firings more accurately than individual latents from the evaluated unsupervised SAEs classify their direction-matched features.
scope: Probes target the first 4,096 features, described as the highest-frequency features; SAE scores average over latent-specific nearest-direction targets. Probes also receive supervised F1 threshold tuning, whereas SAE firing uses activation greater than zero. This is not a comparison on an identical target inventory or readout procedure.

statement: Increasing SAE active-latent count can increase recall of synthetic generating-feature firings while decreasing precision.
scope: The canonical SynthSAEBench architecture sweeps at target L0 values 15–45; metrics average over latent-specific nearest-direction matches.

statement: Training dead Matryoshka latents against their own prefix reconstruction residual can reduce dead-latent counts and improve feature-quality scores relative to a full-dictionary residual auxiliary loss.
scope: The reported SynthSAEBench Matryoshka BatchTopK comparisons, particularly low L0; dead-latent evaluation uses 1M samples and does not establish global inactivity.

statement: Increasing generating-feature magnitude variability can improve SAE directional matching while worsening firing classification and reconstruction.
scope: SynthSAEBench variants with shared firing-magnitude standard deviation swept from 0.5 to 10 and SAE target L0 25; standard L1 SAEs achieve the highest reported MCC in the high-variability regime.

statement: For independently uniform unit vectors in D dimensions, the maximum absolute cosine similarity between one vector and N−1 others has cumulative distribution [F_D(x²)]^(N−1), where F_D is the Beta(1/2,(D−1)/2) cumulative distribution.
scope: D at least 2, N at least 2, independent uniformly distributed spherical directions, and 0≤x≤1. This exact result does not establish the appendix's optimal-packing assertions, approximate scaling constants, or their applicability to learned feature geometry.

statement: Retraining AlexNet's upper classifier layers on a fixed Places365 representation can achieve similar classification accuracy with and without a random orthogonal rotation of pool5 features.
scope: The reported Places365-AlexNet experiment with frozen lower layers and reinitialized, retrained fc6–fc8 layers; no repeated-seed equivalence test is supplied.

statement: Fine-tuning AlexNet between ImageNet and Places can preserve roughly half of final-convolutional channel labels while changing others, often toward concepts with similar visual properties.
scope: The reported bidirectional ImageNet–Places365 fine-tunes and top-ranked Network Dissection conv5 labels; label persistence does not establish complete functional preservation.

statement: Semantic labels for visual channels can augment linear classifier contribution rankings with concept descriptions and spatial activation maps for individual predictions.
scope: The explanation procedure for linear SVMs on CNN features, illustrated using ResNet152-Places365 features on action40; causal explanatory adequacy and human utility are not independently tested.

statement: Changing the activation quantile used by Network Dissection can change a channel's best-matching label from a specific object concept to a broader color or texture concept.
scope: Places205-AlexNet conv5 threshold sweeps and selected painting- and horse-associated channels; this concerns the activation quantile rather than the IoU detector cutoff.

statement: If attention-weight derivatives of a scalar output agree at every position whose attention weight exceeds epsilon, the absolute attention-score derivative at a significant position j is bounded by epsilon times its attention weight times the summed derivative differences over negligible positions.
scope: Differentiable scalar output z, temperature-one softmax s, significant set I = {k: s_k > epsilon}, and exact equality of g_k = partial z / partial s_k on I. The bound is |partial z / partial a_j| <= epsilon s_j sum_{k outside I}|g_j-g_k|. Other positive temperatures introduce a reciprocal-temperature factor at the corresponding softmax weights.

statement: The effect of increasing the backward-pass softmax temperature on GIM attribution scores depends on the model, dataset, and evaluation metric.
scope: The five-model, six-dataset sweep over temperatures 1, 1.5, 2, 2.5, 3, 5, 10, and 100; temperature 2 was selected beforehand using Gemma-2 2B on FEVER and HateXplain.

statement: Dividing gradients equally among multiplicative inputs provides a useful approximation to component-replacement effects when those inputs share upstream dependencies.
scope: GIM's division by two at attention-value, query-key, and gated-MLP products. The exact scalar zero-baseline quadratic example does not establish validity for arbitrary component contributions, finite counterfactual changes, or unequal dependencies.

statement: Normalized output changes from cumulatively replacing high- or low-ranked token embeddings with whitespace embeddings provide useful operational measures of token-attribution faithfulness.
scope: The paper's comprehensiveness and sufficiency definitions and whitespace counterfactual. These metrics depend on the perturbation, ranking, output normalization, and input distribution and do not independently validate semantic selectivity or internal mechanism recovery.

statement: A sparse linear latent-variable model provides a useful approximation for recovering concepts from language-model residual activations.
scope: The interpretive premise for applying sparse coding to Pythia-70M and Gemma-2-2B residual activations. Synthetic experiments impose the model by construction; real-text classification does not independently establish the natural generating concepts or dictionary.

statement: Held-out accuracy of a common logistic-readout procedure provides a useful proxy for comparing task-relevant information accessible from different inferred representations.
scope: Synthetic latent-threshold prediction and eight real-text classification datasets. Accuracy can exploit combinations of features and does not establish individual-concept recovery, causal use, or complete identifiability.

statement: A latent-threshold label can be perfectly linearly predicted on observed sparse-support combinations yet incur error on a withheld support combination after an overcomplete linear encoding.
scope: The constructed three-latent, two-dimensional system with uniform nonnegative active amplitudes, training supports (1,2) and (2,3), test support (1,3), and the specified column lengths and planar angular configuration. This is an existence result rather than universal linear-decoding failure under superposition.

statement: Per-sample FISTA supplied with the generating dictionary can retain high latent recovery and downstream threshold accuracy under withheld-support compositional shifts across the tested synthetic latent dimensions.
scope: Nonnegative sparse uniform latents, row-normalized Gaussian generating matrices, and the reported latent-dimension sweep from 50 to 10,000 at its chosen sparsity, observation dimensions, and regularization. This does not assert high recovery below the undersampling transition or at arbitrary sparsity.

statement: Alternating dictionary learning with FISTA can outperform the tested SAE and linear-readout alternatives at smaller synthetic latent counts while losing generating-direction recovery as latent count grows.
scope: The Gaussian sparse-mixture dimension sweep from 50 to 10,000 latents under finite training budgets. This establishes difficulty for the tested procedure rather than impossibility of scalable dictionary recovery.

statement: Increasing training-set size can substantially improve alternating sparse dictionary learning without eliminating latent-recovery and compositional-prediction deficits in the tested SAE training recipes.
scope: Training sets of 100–100,000 examples with 100 generating latents, sparsity 10, and observation dimension 47. This is a finite recipe comparison rather than an asymptotic sample-complexity result.

statement: An SAE-learned decoder can provide an initialization that accelerates subsequent alternating sparse dictionary learning, particularly for a relatively accurate TopK dictionary.
scope: The reported small-scale synthetic DL-FISTA initialization comparisons. Decoder initialization differs from initializing only the per-sample code; the reported advantage does not establish successful recovery at large latent counts.

statement: Textual neuron explanations can be quantitatively evaluated by generating explanation-conditioned images and comparing their target-neuron activations with those of natural control images.
scope: CoSy's vision-model procedure, using spatial average pooling, pairwise activation-ranking AUC, and control-standardized mean activation difference. The scores depend on the generator, prompt, and control distribution; interpreting them as semantic explanation quality requires additional assumptions.

statement: Text-to-image samples conditioned on a neuron description instantiate its intended concept sufficiently faithfully for their activations to evaluate that description.
scope: The semantic premise of CoSy, particularly when extending class-name generation checks to abstract, low-level, or open-ended hidden-neuron descriptions. Class-level similarity checks do not establish this premise for arbitrary explanations.

statement: The prompt yielding the highest synthetic-to-natural CLIP image similarity can differ between object-centric and scene-centric datasets.
scope: Five tested prompts, SDXL and Stable Cascade, and 50 sampled classes each from ImageNet and Places365. The finding concerns measured image similarity rather than universally optimal neuron-evaluation prompts.

statement: Textual neuron explanations can achieve higher concept-synthesis activation scores in later ResNet18 layers than in earlier layers.
scope: The tested ImageNet-trained ResNet18, description methods, layer sampling, SDXL prompts, and CoSy metrics. FALCON applies only to layers 2–4 and uses relaxed eligibility thresholds in the main comparison.

statement: Stable Cascade can generate more mutually similar images within a concept than SDXL under matched class-name prompts.
scope: Fifty sampled classes each from ImageNet and Places365, five prompts, and 50 images per class–prompt–generator condition. This comparison does not establish which diversity level is optimal for explanation evaluation.

statement: WordNet concept specificity need not visibly track within-concept similarity of generated images.
scope: The ladybug and pug concepts and their WordNet hypernym chains, with 50 generated images per concept and specificity represented by hypernym count; this does not establish statistical independence for concepts generally.

statement: Agreement with human descriptions of a neuron's most activating images does not by itself establish that an explanation accurately describes the neuron's broader response distribution.
scope: Evaluation protocols that compare automatic descriptions with human descriptions of maximally activating natural images; the criticism concerns restriction to the activation-distribution tail.

statement: For OPT-66B, the average-accuracy inflection under importance-ranked whole-FFN pruning occurs after less removal in few-shot prompting than in zero-shot prompting.
scope: The evaluated 14-task average, zero-, one-, and five-shot settings, fixed singleton-ablation rankings, and cumulative removal in 10% increments.

statement: OPT-66B's prompted-task importance profiles differ between attention heads and FFNs, with head importance concentrated mainly at intermediate depths and early-FFN importance depending on demonstration count.
scope: Gradient-based head importance and singleton zero-ablation FFN accuracy effects on the 14 evaluated datasets; these are different importance measures and do not establish an exhaustive processing hierarchy.

statement: OPT-66B contains a sparse subset of attention heads with high scores on both synthetic prefix-matching and copying diagnostics.
scope: The specified 100-sequence random-token diagnostics, excluding the most and least frequent 4% of vocabulary tokens; no numerical count or universal induction threshold is supplied.

statement: Attention to continuations of matching random-token prefixes and promotion of attended token identities provide useful operational diagnostics of an attention head's induction capacity.
scope: The adapted Olsson et al. diagnostics used for OPT-66B. These synthetic scores do not independently establish latent concept matching or natural downstream-task computation.

statement: OPT-66B heads ranked important for downstream prompted tasks tend to retain synthetic prefix-matching scores, while copying scores are also distributed among low-ranked heads.
scope: Comparisons between fixed task-importance rankings and precomputed synthetic head scores; retained capacity is a sum of scores, not a direct post-pruning induction-performance measurement.

statement: Expected absolute products of attention-head outputs and target-loss gradients provide a useful proxy for ranking head importance to prompted-task performance.
scope: The fixed-ranking OPT-66B pruning procedure, with teacher-forced autoregressive target loss. Ranking utility does not establish calibrated individual ablation effects, semantic specificity, or a complete mechanism.

statement: A small or negative singleton zero-ablation accuracy effect identifies a component as unimportant for the evaluated task.
scope: The paper's interpretation of FFN oracle importance. Small singleton effects can coexist with redundancy, interactions, or other causal roles; the interpretation is relative to the chosen task accuracy.

statement: Concentration of prompted-task performance in a subset of model components may indicate undertraining for in-context learning, and auxiliary prefix-matching or copying objectives may improve component utilization.
scope: A proposed interpretation and future training direction motivated by OPT-66B; no training-budget sweep, auxiliary-objective experiment, or instruction-tuned replication is performed.

statement: Stable, high-confidence endorsement of a canonical answer under a neutral prompt provides a useful operational filter for separating user-induced false agreement from ignorance.
scope: Canonical-answer tasks filtered using a log-probability margin of at least 1.0 and at least 80% correct answers across 50 temperature-1 samples. Neutral endorsement does not independently establish that the same answer remains accessible or operative under user pressure.

statement: Directions associated with genuine and sycophantic agreement can align strongly in early transformer layers and diverge at intermediate depths, while praise-associated directions remain geometrically distinct from both.
scope: Within-model cosine relationships among dataset-specific DiffMean directions and leading SVD components across nine controlled datasets in five instruction-tuned models. Cross-model consistency concerns relational geometry, not correspondence or transfer of activation coordinates between models.

statement: Sentiment labels on short user-directed adjective continuations provide a useful operational measure of excessive praise under controlled prompting.
scope: Forced continuations of 'Assistant: you are …', normalized into praise sentences and scored by a three-class RoBERTa-base classifier. Positive sentiment alone does not establish excessive or contextually inappropriate praise in unconstrained dialogue.

statement: Behavior-associated linear directions can retain selective steering effects after components explained by the other measured behavior subspaces are projected out.
scope: Qwen3-30B-Instruct and the paper's SVD-derived SyA, GA, and SyPr subspaces; concerns retained linear components rather than removal of every possible representation of untargeted behaviors.

statement: End-of-sequence residual activations can yield stronger behavior-label discrimination and greater cross-dataset direction similarity than nearby earlier response positions.
scope: Layer 30 of LLaMA-3.3-70B-Instruct, Simple Math and the factual dataset labeled Common Claims in Table 7, and token offsets 0–10 backward from EOS. The appendix does not identify which behavior or behavior aggregation underlies the table.

statement: A sparse autoencoder can combine probability-weighted multiple-expert reconstructions, global TopK selection across selected experts, and learnable scaling of encoder deviations from each expert's mean feature vector.
scope: The Scale SAE construction with reconstruction and auxiliary load-balancing losses; no optimization or feature-identification guarantee is supplied.

statement: For the tested GPT-2 layer-8 dictionaries, Scale SAE's downstream loss-recovery advantage over dense TopK depends on the active-feature count, with TopK slightly ahead at very small counts and Scale SAE ahead at larger counts.
scope: HLE-Biomedical evaluation of OpenWebText-trained dictionaries; loss recovery is normalized by the cross-entropy degradation caused by zeroing the target activations.

statement: Scale SAE features can achieve higher LLM-judged activating-example consistency scores than the tested Switch, TopK, and Gated SAE features.
scope: GPT-2 layer-8 dictionaries evaluated on the corpus identified as OpenWebText2, across the reported activation quantiles; the result concerns the specified automated classification score.

statement: Feature Scaling can reduce average token-pair active-feature overlap in multi-expert GPT-2 sparse autoencoders, while single-expert variants can show the opposite change.
scope: The 13,500 OpenWebText-derived verb-token analysis, using intersection size divided by the number of activated features per token; overlap is distinct from feature-vector similarity and semantic redundancy.

statement: Scale SAE training can learn positive encoder mean-deviation amplification factors whose reported magnitudes increase with the number of activated experts.
scope: The trained scaling factors reported for the paper's GPT-2 layer-8 configurations; this is a qualitative observed trend rather than an established scaling law across architectures or scales.

statement: Mean-based encoder decomposition can achieve reconstruction performance close to a learned-matrix decomposition and better than an identity-based decomposition in Scale SAE.
scope: The three decomposition variants and sparsity sweep reported in Appendix C; the comparison concerns reconstruction error rather than semantic interpretability or a general optimality result.

statement: Maximum correlations against Gaussian mixtures of layer activations provide an adequate reference for identifying neuron matches that exceed similarities available without a privileged neuron basis.
scope: The excess-correlation statistic subtracts maxima over Gaussian-mixed activations. The Gaussian matrix is not an exact orthogonal rotation, and baseline adequacy is not independently established.

statement: Only a small minority of individual GPT2 MLP neurons have maximum cross-seed activation correlations exceeding a Gaussian-mixture baseline by more than 0.5.
scope: Reference models GPT2-small-a and GPT2-medium-a compared with four other initialization seeds of the same architecture on the specified Pile sample; this does not bound population-level representational or algorithmic universality.

statement: Neurons selected for high baseline-adjusted cross-model activation correlation tend to have less frequent positive activations, more negative input biases, larger weight norms, and more positively skewed and heavy-tailed preactivation distributions than other neurons in the same layer.
scope: The evaluated GPT2-small, GPT2-medium, and Pythia-160M reference models at excess correlation above 0.5; these associations do not establish monosemanticity or causal importance.

statement: Neuron output-weight projections in GPT2 and Pythia exhibit a depth-associated progression from increasingly prediction-oriented vocabulary effects after mid-depth toward more suppression-oriented effects near the final layers.
scope: Skew and kurtosis of neuron-output/unembedding compositions in five GPT2-medium seeds and five Pythia models spanning 410M–6.9B; static projections approximate direct effects rather than complete intervention effects.

statement: Language models may use opposing neuron directions to maintain and regulate a global confidence signal through final normalization.
scope: An interpretation of selected GPT2 entropy and anti-entropy neurons; ordinary uncertainty-sensitive use is explicitly not established by fixed-activation interventions.

statement: Individual GPT2 MLP neurons can causally modulate a downstream attention head's BOS allocation and output norm through their contribution to the head's input.
scope: Selected neuron–head paths in GPT2-medium-a and randomly sampled token positions in the second half of contexts; no exclusive encoding of head activation state is established.

statement: Neurons with similar common activation patterns can have substantially different input and output weights, so apparent activation redundancy need not correspond to literal parameter duplication.
scope: Nearest-neighbor weight-cosine analyses and selected universal-neuron families in GPT2 and Pythia-160M; rare-feature differences and ensembling remain possible explanations.

statement: Neurons with very high positive-activation frequency can have strongly opposed input and output weight directions in GPT2 and Pythia.
scope: The reported GPT2-small-a, GPT2-medium-a, and Pythia-160M comparisons; this association does not establish the neurons' computational function.

statement: Prediction and suppression neurons affecting the same token class may combine partially independent estimates to improve predictive robustness and calibration.
scope: The proposed interpretation of overlapping GPT2-medium token-class neurons; independent errors, robustness gains, and calibration improvement are not directly tested.

statement: Features learned with an MLP encoder can attain higher explanation-conditioned token-classification F1 than features learned with shallow SAE or locally competitive sparse-coding encoders.
scope: GPT-2 Small layer-9 residual-stream dictionaries trained on OpenWebText and scored using the supplied GPT-4o explanation pipeline. The result concerns this automated metric and selected held-out contexts, without establishing monosemanticity, causal faithfulness, or performance across the complete activation spectrum.

statement: Natural-language feature descriptions can be generated from extreme vocabulary projections of feature vectors or from average token-logit changes under feature clamping, without first collecting maximally activating contexts.
scope: VocabProj uses final normalization and unembedding of feature vectors; TokenChange uses mean logit changes over sampled prompts. The evaluated interfaces are neuron-aligned and SAE features, rather than arbitrary nonlinear featurizations.

statement: Matching a feature description to its feature's steered generations among random-feature distractors provides a useful operational measure of how well the description captures the intervention's output effects.
scope: Three-way matching of short generation sets under all-position feature clamping, using random-feature distractors and average next-token KL calibration. Success does not establish ordinary causal mediation or exhaustive semantic specificity.

statement: Descriptions derived from a feature's activating examples and vocabulary projection can express complementary aspects or different levels of abstraction rather than interchangeable meanings.
scope: The authors' qualitative Gemma Scope 16K panel, considering descriptions passing both input- and output-based evaluations; category judgments do not establish the feature's complete semantics.

statement: GPT-4o mini can satisfy an alternative-annotator criterion relative to graduate-student annotators on three-way matching of VocabProj descriptions to feature-steered generation sets.
scope: One hundred randomly selected feature examples, evenly split between Gemma-2 2B and Llama-3.1 8B, three graduate-student annotators, and the alternative annotator test with epsilon 0.15.

statement: Activation-steering attribution can be audited by separately calibrating functional perturbation budgets and testing mean effects, protected-tail specificity, exact-negation transport, polarity preservation, transfer, and semantic outcomes.
scope: SteerCheck's CAA audit framework at selected model layers; the protocol is not established as a sufficient criterion for natural mechanistic mediation.

statement: The conditional randomization interpretation of a construction-matched sign-randomization comparison requires exchangeability of pair orientations under its specified null model.
scope: The frozen paired-contrast randomization designs. Truth/template balance diagnostics and retained target alignment do not establish this premise; answer ordering and source are constant in the primary construction bank. The prospective balanced block design differs from the primary iid design.

statement: At a fixed neutral-bank KL budget, anti-sycophancy score effects can be strongly associated with signed alignment to CAA while substantial effects also occur for near-orthogonal and partially aligned directions.
scope: Qwen3-14B layer 28, one 128-row anti-sycophancy evaluation, and 320 draws from each of three comparator families. Cosine was observed rather than experimentally assigned, so the associations do not identify a causal effect of alignment.

statement: CAA can outperform isotropic and PCA steering directions on mean anti-sycophancy score while failing a construction-matched mean comparison and protected lower-tail specificity tests.
scope: The frozen Qwen3-14B layer-28 audit, 128 items, 320 draws per family, within-statistic Holm α=.01, and seventh-smallest item effect. A non-pass is failure to establish the joint claim, rather than evidence of absent efficacy or specificity.
