statement: A matched-KL steering audit requiring both mean and protected-tail superiority over three comparator families can pass for selected language and detox constructions, while its nominal passes remain sensitive to modest departures from the frozen randomization model.
scope: Four prospective model–behavior cells using 512 confirmation items, 999 draws per family, and a separately frozen balanced block-Rademacher structured comparator. These results do not establish categorical separation of language and detox constructions or validate the primary iid comparator.

statement: CAA effects that transport as continuous factual-response margins need not transport as forced-choice accuracy improvements or complete attribution-specificity passes.
scope: A fresh FEVER-derived bank and selected Qwen3-14B layer-28, DeepSeek-V2-Lite-Chat layer-18, and Gemma-3-27B layer-43 cells. Gemma was a sequential same-bank extension registered after partial results; between-cell differences do not identify causal model-family effects.

statement: An anti-sycophancy direction can improve correct-answer scores when the user is wrong while degrading them when the user is correct, making wrong-user score gains insufficient evidence of factual correction.
scope: Frozen Qwen3-14B and DeepSeek-V2-Lite directions on 64 mirrored OpenBookQA facts, evaluated through choice-score and continuation-score endpoints. The asymmetry is consistent with generic opposition but does not uniquely establish that mechanism.

statement: Human-rated short-generation factual correction under a frozen CAA intervention can pass both wrong-user improvement and correct-user preservation in a selected DeepSeek cell while failing to establish wrong-user improvement in a selected Qwen cell.
scope: Two selected model cells, 64 mirrored facts, a 64-token generation cap, and frozen one-sided 99% paired-bootstrap bounds. Qwen's non-pass does not establish absence of an effect, and these tests do not establish semantic specificity against all null directions.

statement: A fixed automatic judge can fail human-consensus calibration for steering-generation semantics despite producing complete, integrity-audited labels.
scope: The locked gemma-3-27b-it parser-v1.1 judge, the SteerCheck blinded response packet, and its frozen calibration thresholds; this is not a general judge benchmark.

statement: On fixed month, weekday, and hour forward-offset templates, Llama-3.1-8B answers substantially more accurately when the pre-modulo sum stays within the first cycle than when it exceeds that cycle.
scope: The exhaustive Table 1 prompt grids, offsets 1–2p, canonical weekday/month indices starting at one, and hours indexed 0–23. This behavioral comparison does not identify the cause of the errors or determine the model's internal weekday enumeration.

statement: Routed MoE expert activations can support higher best-component single-neuron concept-classification F1, with smaller benefits from additional neurons, than approximately active-parameter-matched dense FFNs.
scope: The 58 evaluated POS, LaTeX, code, and text concepts; best layer and best expert selected separately per concept and k. Expert tests condition on routing, whereas dense tests use the initial concept dataset. This concerns selected concept decoding rather than typical-neuron or dictionary-wide monosemanticity.

statement: High single-neuron concept-classification performance and little improvement from adding neurons provide adequate indicators of reduced neuron polysemanticity.
scope: Interpreting sparse-probe curves for selected binary concepts within routed expert populations. A neuron can separate one concept while also responding to unrelated properties; localization and monosemanticity are not equivalent.

statement: Across evaluated MoE checkpoints, a lower active-to-total expert ratio accompanies stronger best-component sparse-probing performance.
scope: Cross-checkpoint comparison under the routed-token, best-layer-and-expert protocol. Model families, training histories, expert widths, parameter counts, shared-expert configurations, and numerical precision are not held constant.

statement: Sparse routing may reduce within-expert superposition and combine with restricted expert input distributions to make whole experts interpretable functional modules.
scope: The proposed mechanism of modular monosemanticity in production-scale MoEs. The comparisons do not isolate routing causally, establish mostly monosemantic neurons throughout each expert, or justify complete transparency at extreme sparsity.

statement: Natural-language descriptions generated from high-output expert contexts and vocabulary readouts can distinguish held-out high-output contexts from contexts selected for other experts in the same layer.
scope: The experts evaluated in eight OLMoE layers and three layers each of ERNIE and Qwen3; 32-token snippets selected from each expert's top 40 examples. The test measures selected context discrimination, rather than exhaustive expert function or monosemanticity.

statement: The norm of a router-weighted expert output provides a useful proxy for identifying contexts in which that expert performs important computation.
scope: Scoring a token by g_i(x) times ||E_i(x)||_2 and a snippet by its maximum token score. Large residual displacement does not independently establish downstream predictive importance or semantic specificity.

statement: Baseline-corrected divergence of expert input-token and promoted-token distributions over clustered unembedding vectors provides a useful measure of routing and functional specialization.
scope: Jensen–Shannon divergence against the arithmetic mean of per-expert cluster distributions, subtracting expected divergence for a token-count-matched multinomial sample. Interpreting coarse versus fine clusters as broad domains versus computational tasks requires additional semantic assumptions.

statement: Late-layer OLMoE expert outputs show greater vocabulary-distribution specialization at fine clustering granularity than at broad clustering granularity.
scope: OLMoE-1B-7B over one million tokens, using baseline-corrected JSD at 10, 50, 100, 1,000, and 5,000 unembedding clusters. Vocabulary concentration does not uniquely identify a computational task or exclude narrow topical and token-pattern explanations.

statement: Vectors that strongly control harmful choices in a Poser organism can perform poorly as dot-product classifiers of benign versus harmful prompt conditions.
scope: The five norm-15, layer-10 optimized vectors in money-maximizer-0; classification uses mean activation–vector dot products.

statement: Expected alignment and coherence ratings from a four-bit Llama-3.1-70B-Instruct provide meaningful operational comparisons of steering-induced harmful responses.
scope: Eight emergent-misalignment questions with a brevity suffix; numeric-token probabilities are normalized over 0–100, with coherence and numeric-probability filtering for plotted alignment distributions. Independent human calibration is not reported.

statement: Gemma-2-2B-it can return to factual occupation descriptions after a false occupation prefill without producing any of five monitored retraction phrases.
scope: Known public figures from six occupations, cyclic occupation substitutions, and selected promotion, suppression, and CAA intervention settings. Absence of the monitored phrases does not establish absence of every possible retraction paraphrase or independence from intermediate tokens generally.

statement: Retraction-phrase matching and model judgments of an anonymized response's occupation content provide useful operational measures of explicit correction and subsequent factual versus fictitious content.
scope: Five case-insensitive retraction strings and Gemma-2-2B-it Yes/No judgments of primary occupation and occupation mentions after replacing entity names with generic names. These checks do not exhaustively detect retraction paraphrases or validate every factual claim in a continuation.

statement: Gemma-2-2B can assign nearly as low tokenwise surprisal to a factual continuation following a false occupation prefill as to the same continuation following a true prefill.
scope: A base model prompted with two real instruction-tuned completions per occupation; sequence surprisal averages use at most the first 100 tokens. This is a likelihood comparison rather than a measurement of spontaneous base-model recovery.

statement: A later-layer vector can be trained by output-distribution matching to an earlier intervention and can produce qualitatively different continuation behavior from directly optimized later-layer vectors.
scope: The reentrant procedure and its Gemma occupation experiment; the concrete early intervention is an activation-dependent rank-one matrix rather than a fixed vector. No general improvement or distribution-matching guarantee is established.

statement: Low tokenwise surprisal under a suitably prompted base model provides a useful proxy for whether an instruction-tuned model's continuation reflects behavior already natural to the base model.
scope: Gemma-2-2B likelihood evaluation of occupation continuations with a context of real Gemma-2-2B-it completions and a 100-token truncation. Conditional likelihood does not establish spontaneous behavior, semantic correctness, or which mechanisms post-training created.

statement: Per-example Fisher matrices can be approximated by nonnegative combinations of shared rank-one positive-semidefinite components using alternating coefficient and component-vector updates without materializing full Fisher matrices.
scope: The proposed nonconvex Frobenius-reconstruction objective, low-rank Fisher representations, multiplicative coefficient updates, and gradient-descent component updates; no global optimum, uniqueness, or convergence theorem is established.

statement: For sufficiently small parameter perturbations in a regular differentiable probabilistic model, half the per-example Fisher quadratic form approximates the KL divergence from the original predictive distribution to the perturbed distribution.
scope: The local information-geometric approximation in Equation 2, applied to the task-defined categorical distribution; regularity and sufficiently small perturbations are required, and finite-step accuracy is not independently quantified.

statement: Shared factors of per-example parameter sensitivity provide meaningful candidate processing strategies when they identify parameter directions important to groups of thematically related examples.
scope: The interpretive premise connecting NPEFF components to internal behavioral factors; local sensitivity and thematic coherence do not establish a unique internal module or algorithm.

statement: Behavior-associated pseudo-Fisher directions are sufficiently sparse in model parameter coordinates for compressed sensing to recover useful parameter-space representatives from their random projections.
scope: The sparsity premise underlying fixed-point-continuation recovery of NPEFF directions; selective perturbation effects do not establish recovery of the original unprojected vectors.

statement: A component whose highest-ranked examples share a ground-truth label but do not share a model prediction provides useful proxy evidence that the component captures a behavioral factor that does not independently determine those predictions.
scope: The LnP metric: all top 16 examples share a label, while their predictions are not all identical; components with fewer than 16 examples are excluded. This criterion is not independently validated against known internal factors.

statement: Full-distribution NPEFF can yield larger fractions of label-tuned but prediction-untuned components than predicted-gradient factorization, gradient clustering, final-token TopK SAEs, and gradient or activation SVD.
scope: The reported SST2, Yahoo Answers Topics, and CLINC150 configurations, with top-16 tuning and exclusion of components containing fewer than 16 examples; this is a proxy comparison rather than demonstrated recovery of ground-truth mechanisms. NPEFF ties G-NPEFF on GPT2 Medium SST2.

statement: Parameter perturbations constructed from projected NPEFF components can change predictions on their highest-coefficient examples substantially more than on random examples, with greater selectivity than perturbations derived from gradient-cluster centroids or gradient SVD.
scope: The reported compressed-sensing recovery, sequential orthogonal rejection, L2 perturbation magnitude 20, and better-of-two-sign evaluation; selectivity concerns output KL rather than beneficial editing, exact semantic removal, or circuit recovery.

statement: A classifier constructed from label-associated zero-shot NPEFF components can recover much of the accuracy gain and prediction pattern of selected six-shot SST2 prompting.
scope: SmolLM2-360M under the supplied sentiment prompt, label-informed component mapping, and selected six-shot context; this does not establish that the model's actual ICL computation only reweights existing factors.

statement: NPEFF's prediction-tuned and label-tuned-but-prediction-untuned component fractions can remain similar under substantial reductions of the parameter projection dimension.
scope: SmolLM2-360M SST2 with 512 components and the reported random-projection implementations; stability of these fractions does not establish component identity or general preservation of Fisher geometry.

statement: With matched initialization and an exactly inner-product-preserving linear map, NPEFF's alternating updates preserve identical coefficients and map the original component vectors to their projected counterparts at every step.
scope: Appendix C.6 assumes A A^T = I, projected inputs G_i A, and projected initialization H A, with updates well-defined. A dimension-reducing map cannot satisfy this identity on the entire original space; the derivation supplies no quantitative guarantee for actual lossy projections.

statement: Across independent NPEFF initializations, matched pseudo-Fisher directions can be more reproducible than their example-coefficient profiles, with reproducibility depending on task and component count.
scope: Five initialization seeds on SmolLM2-360M SST2 and CLINC150, using optimal one-to-one component matching by absolute cosine similarity in separate direction and coefficient comparisons; geometric agreement does not establish a unique or correct decomposition.

statement: A semantic theme inferred from an NPEFF component's strongest examples can be insufficient to predict whether the component receives a nonzero coefficient on new examples matching that theme.
scope: Two selected SmolLM2-360M components in SST2 and Yahoo Answers Topics; qualitative counterexamples rather than an estimated failure rate across the decomposition.

statement: Collecting per-example Fisher representations can dominate the computational cost of NPEFF analysis and cost substantially more per example than collecting predicted-class gradients or activations.
scope: The reported SmolLM2-360M implementations and task configurations, with approximate single-A6000 timings; not a hardware-independent scaling law or an optimized-implementation lower bound.

statement: Increasing NPEFF's component count can improve held-out Fisher reconstruction while changing tuning fractions and the granularity of example associations.
scope: SmolLM2-360M SST2 and CLINC150 under the reported component-count sweeps; improved reconstruction does not establish more accurate or atomic mechanisms.

statement: Approximating per-example Fisher expectations with output-space random projections can retain more component-tuning signal than using an equal number of sampled output classes.
scope: SmolLM2-360M CLINC150 and TriviaQA at the reported projection/sample counts and rank-reduction settings; the comparison concerns tuning proxies and does not establish uniformly better Fisher approximation or perturbation selectivity.

statement: Internal-model experiments can be represented as serializable operation graphs that are defined independently of model deployment and interleaved with model execution at runtime.
scope: NNsight's deferred-operation representation, getter/setter interfaces, JSON serialization, and local or NDIF execution; improvements in reproducibility and engineering effort are motivated rather than directly measured.

statement: Deferred tracing of PyTorch operations can provide a common remote interface for activation edits, gradient access and modification, and optimization of supplementary parameters.
scope: NNsight's documented wrapping of 217 fundamental tensor operations and supplied patching, gradient, LoRA, and auxiliary-model examples. Equivalence to every experiment expressible with ordinary PyTorch hooks is asserted but not comprehensively tested.

statement: An acyclic computation graph with multiple variable outputs per operation can be transformed into a computationally equivalent graph with one tuple-valued output per operation.
scope: Computation graphs permitting tuple-valued variables and downstream component extraction, with auxiliary extraction operations where needed. This establishes preservation of computation, not equal runtime or memory cost.

statement: The open-weight transformer interpretability literature selected from the surveyed citation corpus studies models substantially below the capability and parameter scale of available models.
scope: 184 eligible papers selected from 411 citations, excluding pre-2019 work and papers meeting the stated survey, model, architecture, or experiment exclusions; each paper is represented by its largest model by parameter count.

statement: MMLU scores, supplemented by parameter-size-based imputation when scores are unavailable, provide an adequate operational proxy for comparing model capability in an interpretability research survey.
scope: Largest-model comparisons using HuggingFace and Papers with Code scores, averaging scores when both sources are available, and imputing missing scores primarily for BERT-style models. Capability equivalence across architectures or research tasks is not established.

statement: NNsight incurs little additional local activation-patching runtime relative to baukit and pyvene, and is comparable to or faster than TransformerLens in the evaluated IOI workload.
scope: One batch of 32 IOI examples on GPT2-XL, Gemma-7B, and Llama-3.1-8B, using the reported four-H100 HPC node. Runtime comparisons do not establish equivalent usability, functionality, or performance on other workloads.

statement: With sequential model execution, NDIF's median activation-request response time can grow approximately linearly as concurrent user count increases.
scope: Llama-3.1-8B on one 48 GB RTX 6000 Ada GPU, 1–100 simulated users, short prompts, and random intermediate-layer output requests; sharing is implemented through queued separate forward passes.

statement: Temporary intervention interleaving and interaction with parameter copies adequately isolate users' experiments when they share a hosted model instance.
scope: NDIF's stated isolation design and current sequential co-tenancy. No adversarial isolation evaluation or formal security proof is supplied; parallel co-tenancy through batch grouping is future work.

statement: Engineering, compute, and deployment barriers may contribute to interpretability researchers studying models smaller and less capable than available open-weight alternatives.
scope: An interpretation of the selected literature survey and model resource requirements. Researchers' constraints are not measured, and infrastructure effects are not causally isolated from scientific preferences, publication delays, or other factors.

statement: During controlled Chinese-target translation in Llama-2-70B, low-entropy English-favoring intermediate readouts can coexist with low token energy, followed by a late rise in token energy as Chinese readouts dominate.
scope: The highlighted 8,192-dimensional Llama-2-70B Chinese-translation analysis, using the paper's normalized token-energy statistic and final-prompt-position states.

statement: Controlled word copying can produce target-language intermediate readouts as early as, or earlier than, English answer readouts, including in languages with very different single-token word coverage.
scope: Chinese repetition in the three tested Llama-2 sizes and Estonian copying in Llama-2-7B; selected lexical inventories rather than arbitrary copying tasks.

statement: Applying the final language-model head to intermediate representations provides useful proxy evidence about the semantic content and language alignment of those representations during multilingual lexical completion.
scope: Final-prompt-position states in the paper's translation, repetition, and cloze tasks. Readout salience need not establish natural causal use or expose information used by later layers that is weakly expressed through the final head.

statement: Normalized mean squared alignment with output-token embeddings provides useful information about how strongly a hidden representation is oriented toward immediate vocabulary prediction.
scope: The interpretation of the proposed token-energy statistic as distinguishing output-oriented alignment from other intermediate representational content. The unembedding is empirically full rank, so low energy does not establish membership in a literal output-null subspace or identify the remaining information.

statement: Limited availability of language-specific single-token words may increase reliance on English-biased semantic processing during multilingual word copying.
scope: A proposed explanation for weaker English-first behavior in Chinese repetition relative to German, French, and Russian. Tokenization is not experimentally manipulated, and the Estonian copying result complicates a general single-token-coverage account.

statement: Context-dependent structural roles can be learned jointly with filler embeddings, role embeddings, and an affine projection to approximate a frozen sequence encoder using summed tensor-product bindings.
scope: ROLE's LSTM role assigner, reconstruction MSE objective, and regularizers encouraging one-hot assignments and limited role reuse; no uniqueness or global optimization guarantee.

statement: Learned context-dependent role schemes can preserve substantially more SCAN decoder accuracy under encoder-state replacement than the tested predefined positional, tree, neighbor-based, and bag-of-words schemes.
scope: The selected one-layer, 100-dimensional GRU trained on SCAN's simple split and three analysis initializations; this does not establish performance on harder compositional splits or arbitrary recurrent encoders.

statement: A learned role scheme approximating a SCAN encoder can admit a compact symbolic description combining connective identity, subcommand position, and modifier context.
scope: The analyzed ROLE solution for the selected SCAN GRU; agreement measures reproduction of ROLE's assignments rather than an independently identified unique representation.

statement: Subtracting and adding learned filler–role binding vectors in a SCAN GRU's original encoding can produce the output changes predicted by syntactically compatible word substitutions.
scope: The selected SCAN GRU, grammar-compatible replacements excluding 'and' and 'after', and updates to additional bindings whenever the interpreted role-assignment algorithm requires them.

statement: Learning context-dependent tensor-product roles does not uniformly improve sentence-embedding reconstruction over a bag-of-words tensor-product baseline, and the size of the improvement depends on the target encoder.
scope: InferSent, Skip-thought, SST, and SPINN encodings of SNLI premise sentences under the supplied ROLE and TPE recipes; reconstruction comparisons do not establish the absence of compositional information.

statement: Simpler and more compositional implicit role-assignment schemes may enable stronger systematic generalization in SCAN sequence models.
scope: A proposed explanation connecting the complexity of learned roles to failures outside the training distribution; no controlled comparison of role simplicity and harder-split generalization is performed.

statement: Correlation between description-conditioned simulated activations and observed neuron activations provides a useful proxy for the quality of a natural-language neuron description.
scope: Pearson correlation pooled across token positions in 20 extreme-activation sequences and five random sequences. The simulator predicts normalized, discretized activation levels; correspondence to human understanding or causal faithfulness is not independently established.

statement: For GPT-4o-mini descriptions of Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct neurons, average best-of-k simulation scores can follow a power-law curve over sampling budgets up to 50.
scope: Non-fine-tuned GPT-4o-mini with diverse exemplar and few-shot prompts, 2,000 randomly selected neurons with both polarities, and validation-based simulation scores; no asymptotic scaling guarantee.

statement: Distilling high-scoring neuron descriptions into an explainer can improve its simulation scores at a fixed candidate-sampling budget.
scope: GPT-4o-mini and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct explainers describing Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct neurons under the reported exemplar and simulator pipeline.

statement: Best-of-25 descriptions from a distilled GPT-4o-mini explainer can achieve higher held-out activation-simulation correlations than descriptions written by a selected human expert with limited iterative scoring feedback.
scope: 100 random Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct MLP neurons, one random polarity per neuron, shared training exemplars, and an expert selected from four pilot annotators. This compares simulation scores rather than comprehensive human understanding.

statement: Neuron-description activation-simulation scores can vary nonmonotonically with transformer depth, declining through early layers before increasing in later layers.
scope: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct MLP-neuron descriptions under the reported validation-exemplar scoring protocol; this is a score trend rather than an independently established trend in human interpretability.

statement: Validation-selected best-of-25 neuron descriptions can retain similar simulation correlations on separately collected test exemplars.
scope: The reported 100-random-neuron panel in Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and exemplars from the same corpus-construction procedure; no guarantee for larger sampling budgets or distribution shifts.

statement: A distilled explainer with best-of-25 selection and a fine-tuned simulator can generate descriptions for both polarities of every Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct MLP neuron at a reported generation-and-simulation cost of approximately $0.046 per neuron.
scope: 458,752 neurons, gpt-4o-mini-2024-07-18 generation, the reported simulation implementation, and the article's cost accounting; this is not a hardware-independent or total research-cost estimate.

statement: A natural-language description that predicts a neuron's activation patterns does not by itself establish how the model computes that representation or uses it to make decisions.
scope: Exemplar-based neuron-description pipelines evaluated by activation simulation; causal and algorithmic explanations require additional analysis.

statement: Removing selected Fourier components of a module's numerical vocabulary projection is sufficiently selective that resulting behavioral changes can be interpreted as disruption of corresponding arithmetic subcomputations.
scope: Minimum-L2 nullspace projections defined through the numerical unembedding and selected Fourier rows. The constraints remove specified linear readouts, but do not independently guarantee preservation of other hidden-state information or arithmetic computations.

statement: In an addition-fine-tuned GPT-2-XL, intermediate numerical vocabulary readouts can approach the correct answer in magnitude before attaining high exact-match accuracy.
scope: Last-prompt-position readouts on the reported bounded addition distribution; this does not by itself exclude memorization or identify the complete computation.

statement: Contrastive response pairs instantiate the intended opposing behaviors sufficiently well for optimizing their relative generation likelihoods to provide useful behavioral steering.
scope: The persona, TruthfulQA, unprompted-hallucination, and AdvBench preference constructions used for BiPO; style, refusal wording, and other correlated response properties are not independently isolated.

statement: Task-specific GPT-4 judgments provide sufficiently reliable operational measurements of expressed personas, hallucination, and harmful compliance for comparing activation-steering methods.
scope: gpt-4-0125-preview, reference-assisted 1–4 persona and hallucination ratings, and the paper's attack-success rubric; independent human agreement and broad deployment validity are not established.

statement: Preference-optimized bidirectional vectors can produce a broader range of expressed persona scores than the tested multiple-choice and freeform activation-difference vectors.
scope: Power seeking, wealth seeking, survival instinct, and corrigible-less-HHH in Llama-2-7b-chat-hf and Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.2, under the paper's selected single layers and multiplier sweeps.

statement: A BiPO vector trained on harmful-versus-refusal responses can substantially increase harmful compliance on held-out AdvBench questions in Llama-2-7b-chat-hf.
scope: The paper's 320-question training and 100-question test partition, single-layer intervention, and GPT-4 attack-success grading; not a comparison against all jailbreak methods.

statement: Persona vectors optimized on English Llama-2-chat preference data can retain steering effects when directly applied to related Llama-2 derivatives, including a Chinese instruction LoRA model.
scope: Llama-2-7b-chat-hf vectors transferred to Vicuna-7b-v1.5 and Llama2-Chinese-7b-Chat with matching architecture and activation dimensions; Chinese evaluation uses translated persona questions.

statement: Adding two selected BiPO vectors can preserve steering effects on both constituent target behaviors.
scope: Power-seeking plus wealth-seeking, and corrigible-less-HHH plus hallucination, in Llama-2-7b-chat-hf at multipliers ±1. The comparison does not establish superadditivity or independent semantic composition.

statement: A BiPO power-seeking vector can provide a broader behavioral steering range than scaling the parameters of a separately DPO-trained LoRA adapter under the tested training recipes.
scope: Llama-2-7b-chat-hf power-seeking responses on 100 sampled test questions; a rank-8 DPO LoRA trained for two epochs versus the paper's BiPO persona recipe. This does not establish superiority over other LoRA recipes or matched-compute fine-tuning.

statement: Retrieval datasets with a shared context–request representation, interchangeable requests, and unique single-token answers enable the same causal-intervention protocol to be applied across task domains and model families.
scope: ORION's structured retrieval setting; this does not establish coverage of arbitrary retrieval problems or superiority over alternative dataset-design approaches.

statement: A structured context–request annotation and its recombined answer provide an adequate specification of the intended retrieval counterfactual for an internal intervention test.
scope: ORION's generated and filtered tasks. This presumes that textual prompts instantiate their annotations adequately; it does not presume that the network already implements the proposed decomposition.

statement: On structured retrieval tasks, intermediate final-position residual states can transfer a source request into a target context while preserving substantial answer performance, supporting a macroscopic separation between request processing and retrieval.
scope: ORION model–task pairs with baseline accuracy above 70%, evaluated at layers selected for maximal request-patching performance. This is not a universal decomposition of every model, task, or input position.

statement: A request representation transferred through an intermediate residual state can remain usable when source and target question-answering prompts place the question differently relative to the story.
scope: ORION mixed-template question answering, including question-before-story and question-after-story formats; this does not establish invariance to arbitrary paraphrases or formats.

statement: A distractor that dominates a model's answer when it conflicts with the correct answer continues to dominate the answer-generating mechanism when the two answers coincide.
scope: The working hypothesis used to interpret city-QA collision experiments as tests of answering correctly for the wrong reason. Lower detector triggering does not independently establish whether this premise or the detector fails.

statement: Preserving classification accuracy when directly joining one model's early layers to another model's later layers provides useful evidence of representational compatibility at the joining point.
scope: Identity connectors between compatible architectures on the evaluated classification tasks. Successful stitching does not establish identical neuron meanings, complete functions, or internal mechanisms.

statement: Independently trained ResNet-20 networks can have lower permutation-matched neuron correlations than independently initialized random networks of the same width.
scope: The evaluated CIFAR-10 ResNet-20 width sweep; the reported ordering holds for all tested widths except the narrowest. This concerns neuron-level matching rather than population-level representational convergence.

statement: Increasing ResNet-20 width can reduce accuracy degradation under unpermuted interpolation between trained networks and under averaging a trained network with a norm-matched random network.
scope: The reported CIFAR-10 width sweep with reset batch-normalization statistics; the trained–random control matches weight norms. This is not a general robustness guarantee for arbitrary parameter noise.

statement: Width-dependent tolerance of parameter mixtures may partly explain improving linear mode connectivity even when neuron-basis alignment does not improve.
scope: Interpretation of the CIFAR-10 ResNet-20 width sweep. The experiments do not isolate noise robustness as the unique cause or quantify its contribution to the connectivity improvement.

statement: Random orthonormal rotations of learned Myrtle-CNN preactivations can substantially reduce classification accuracy despite freezing the rotated layers and retraining the remaining network.
scope: CIFAR-10 Myrtle-CNN widths 16 and 256, the reported successive-layer and single-layer procedures, and rotations before nonlinearities. This does not establish impossibility of recovery under other training procedures or contradict function preservation when a rotation is explicitly inverted before downstream computation.

statement: Training networks with a shared frozen early prefix can increase subsequent neuron-basis alignment and improve direct compatibility between independently trained later segments.
scope: ConvNeXt on CIFAR-10, ViT on ImageNet, and supplementary ResNet-20 comparisons. The prefix is copied from a trained model, while later layers are initialized anew; results do not establish a unique basis or universal sufficiency of a particular prefix length.

statement: Shared-prefix-induced neuron alignment can occur with comparable outcomes in ResNet-20 architectures with and without nonlinearities after skip connections.
scope: The standard and modified CIFAR-10 ResNet-20 comparison. The modification removes post-skip nonlinearities while retaining nonlinear computation inside residual blocks; it does not remove residual connections.

statement: Operand-gradient symmetry and dependence of correct logits on operand difference provide useful diagnostic signatures for distinguishing Clock-like and Pizza-like modular-addition computations.
scope: The studied modular-addition model families, primarily circular representations; these signatures do not independently certify complete circuit implementations or exclude every alternative algorithm.

statement: Behavior after restricting an embedding matrix to a selected principal-component pair provides useful evidence about the corresponding component's contribution to the original network's computation.
scope: Circle isolation in the studied modular-addition networks; modified embeddings can alter downstream computation, so isolated behavior does not by itself establish independent native operation.

statement: The relative prominence of attention-mediated multiplication and feedforward piecewise-linear computation may explain architectural preferences for Clock versus Pizza modular-addition algorithms.
scope: The proposed explanation of attention-rate and width sweeps; relative computational contributions and the suggested differential benefits of width are not independently measured.

statement: A trained modular-addition network can combine multiple circular computational components whose differing distance-sensitive failures yield more accurate predictions together.
scope: Principally the selected constant-attention Model A; accompanying circles contribute relatively little to its final predictions. Circle-restriction and circle-removal results are distinct intervention conditions.

statement: A trained feedforward modular-addition network can retain perfect accuracy after its second ReLU is removed, permitting a simpler approximate description of its downstream computation.
scope: The selected width-256 Model β analyzed in Appendix L; preservation of accuracy does not establish exact equality of logits or irrelevance of the ReLU on arbitrary inputs.

statement: A symmetric real function that is a constant-coefficient linear combination of cos(x), sin(x), cos(y), and sin(y) factors as cos((x−y)/2) times a function of x+y.
scope: Exactly the symmetric first-harmonic linear function class of Lemma A.1, with symmetry for all real x and y; the result does not automatically extend to arbitrary piecewise-linear neural networks.

statement: Correct greedy completion of a relational factual query, allowing accepted object aliases, provides a useful operational criterion for selecting facts a language model knows.
scope: mParaRel facts retained when at least one paraphrased template yields an exact object match; one successful template is randomly selected. Subsequent interventions primarily evaluate the first object token.

statement: Final-token replacements between factual queries with controlled subject, relation, and language differences provide sufficiently meaningful hybrid computations to interpret answer changes as transfer of those task attributes.
scope: Same-layer whole-state replacements with English donors, valid crossed subject–relation objects, and spelling-distinct output categories where required. Natural donor states do not guarantee that hybrid computations remain on-distribution or selectively change only the intended attribute.

statement: Top-1 factual-answer readouts from module outputs can implicate MLPs without preceding attention extraction in multilingual decoder-only models, while predominantly implicating cross-attention in mT5.
scope: Extraction is defined as a component-output vocabulary argmax matching the final object token. The reported MLP pattern covers most decoder-only language conditions; English is an important attention-dominant exception. These are readout events rather than independently established extraction algorithms.

statement: An intermediate final-token state from a factual query can transfer a relation and output language to another query while producing an answer determined by the recipient subject.
scope: Same-layer patches from English donors in selected XGLM, EuroLLM, and mT5 factual contexts. Relation transfer across subjects and output-language transfer are demonstrated in complementary pairing conditions. Function Vector denotes a whole final-token state here, extending the original attention-head-average definition.

statement: In XGLM and EuroLLM factual recall, final-token states can transfer relation information before they transfer the donor's output language.
scope: Selected mParaRel patch-context pairs with English donors; timing does not establish orthogonal subspaces, universal disentanglement, or a complete recall algorithm.

statement: mT5 factual-query patching exhibits overlapping relation-transfer and output-language-transfer depths rather than a clear relation-only stage.
scope: The tested mT5-xl decoder states and mParaRel pairs with English donors. Overlapping timing does not establish that relation and language representations are intrinsically entangled.

statement: Layerwise final-token patches between factual queries can transition from transferring a relation applied to the recipient subject to transferring the donor's resolved answer.
scope: English queries with different relations and subjects and valid crossed factual objects; this operational transition does not exclude earlier answer information inaccessible through the tested patch.

statement: Jointly optimizing harmful-answer recovery, refusal induction, and benign-output retention through a frozen chat model can produce refusal directions with competitive directional-ablation attack success and higher average activation-subtraction attack success than difference-in-means directions on JailbreakBench.
scope: The seven evaluated chat models, DIM-selected intervention layers, DIM-norm-matched subtraction strengths, and the reported JailbreakBench evaluation; superiority is not uniform across models or other datasets.

statement: Responses generated using DIM ablation and addition provide sufficiently faithful model-specific targets for optimizing refusal suppression and induction.
scope: Harmful-answer targets generated with DIM ablation, refusal targets generated with DIM addition, and unmodified benign retain responses. Harmful answers use 30 generated tokens and retain responses use 29; the refusal-target length is not explicitly specified. Shared targets may encode style, content, and limitations of the initializing attack.

statement: RDO refusal-direction ablation can preserve TruthfulQA performance better than DIM refusal-direction ablation, without uniformly improving preservation on other capability benchmarks.
scope: The seven evaluated chat models and reported default-chat-template LM Evaluation Harness evaluations; this does not establish broad capability preservation.

statement: RDO activation addition can provide a better or equivalent harmful-refusal versus benign-over-refusal tradeoff than DIM activation addition.
scope: Gemma 2 2B IT, the tested strength range from zero to the DIM norm, harmful SORRY-Bench inputs, and benign XSTest inputs.

statement: An adversary manipulating feature visualization has sufficiently accurate knowledge of the auditor's initialization distribution to place a target-directed manipulation region around likely initial states.
scope: The GS threat model assumes initialization-distribution knowledge; experiments use known zero-mean Gaussian initializations. Robustness to unknown or deliberately shifted initialization distributions is not established.

statement: Classification accuracy and feature-label AUROC provide useful operational checks that a feature-visualization manipulation retains task performance and the feature's original label-discrimination function on an evaluation distribution.
scope: The GS evaluation uses accuracy and AUROC as preservation indicators. These metrics do not establish unchanged predictions, full activation functions, or internal mechanisms.

statement: If a feature's parameter-space gradient equals γ times the displacement toward a target throughout the tunnel between initialization and target neighborhoods, unregularized gradient ascent initialized in the initialization neighborhood converges geometrically to the target when 0<εγ<1.
scope: Exact prescribed gradient field, positive γ, differentiable invertible input parameterization, initialization inside the slingshot ball, identity regularization, and iterates in the specified tunnel. The result does not establish realizability by neural fine-tuning.

statement: Changing the balance between activation preservation and manipulation losses can produce nonmonotonic feature-visualization manipulation success, with strong manipulation weighting sometimes damaging classification accuracy without improving target resemblance.
scope: The reported fixed-other-hyperparameter α sweeps in the selected CNN, VGG, ResNet, and ViT configurations. Optimal weights and metric responses differ substantially across settings.

statement: Increasing width in the tested CIFAR-10 VGG configurations generally improves Gradient Slingshots target-image reconstruction and reduces classification-accuracy damage, while increasing depth has nonmonotonic effects.
scope: Sixteen configurations combining four depth patterns with channel-width parameters 8, 16, 32, and 64; cat-output-to-goldfish manipulation under the reported attack recipe. This is not a universal scaling law or an isolated test of memorization capacity.

statement: For the tested TinyImageNet ResNet-18 feature, Gradient Slingshots manipulation quality depends on target-image choice, with natural targets generally performing better than the tested uniform or out-of-distribution targets.
scope: The gondola output neuron, fixed attack settings, transformation-regularized Fourier FV, and the selected target-image collection. Explanations involving shared learned features are not independently isolated.

statement: Gradient Slingshots can make an assault-rifle-associated CLIP feature visualize an unrelated penguin while preserving its measured assault-rifle discrimination and a weapon classifier's poisoned non-weapon treatment of assault rifles.
scope: One CLIP ViT-L/14 encoder with an MLP weapon head and a layer-22 Pattern-CAV. The proposed auditing failure is hypothetical; no SAE-discovery, attribution-assisted auditor, or human auditing experiment is performed.

statement: Inspecting highly activating natural images can expose semantic mismatches introduced by Gradient Slingshots when synthetic visualizations change but natural feature discrimination largely persists.
scope: Two principal cases, wolf-spider-to-Dalmatian and assault-rifle-to-penguin, plus additional qualitative examples. No calibrated detector, false-positive rate, or general out-of-distribution guarantee is established.

statement: For the tested ResNet-50 wolf-spider-to-Dalmatian manipulation, Gradient Slingshots achieves better target resemblance, semantic alignment, and classification-accuracy retention than the evaluated ProxPulse configurations, with equal reported feature AUROC.
scope: One model, output neuron, and target image; two ProxPulse preservation weights using the reported prior-work hyperparameters. This does not establish superiority over fully retuned ProxPulse or across other architectures and targets.

statement: After a selected ResNet-50 feature-visualization manipulation, most tested non-target outputs can retain similar visualization-similarity statistics, although individual outputs can show larger changes.
scope: The first ten non-target classifier outputs after the wolf-spider attack; CLIP and pixel-MSE comparisons across FV runs. These measurements do not establish that every non-target feature or internal representation is unchanged.

statement: Fine-tuning on explicitly Evil-conditioned responses can induce substantially higher malicious-intent and Evil-expression scores than fine-tuning on the tested incorrect-advice responses.
scope: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct under the paper's SFT recipes and GPT-4.1-mini evaluation; this comparison does not isolate character from every content or style difference.

statement: GPT-4.1-mini judgments under trait-specific, malicious-intent, actionable-harm, and refusal rubrics provide useful operational measurements of those response properties.
scope: The paper's 0–100 scores, probability-weighted TES with valid-score mass at least 0.25, binary actionable-jailbreak judgments, and complete-refusal judgments. Human calibration and exclusion rates are not reported; full scoring prompts appear in unavailable figure images.

statement: Evil-conditioned supervised fine-tuning can preserve approximately the original model's MMLU subject accuracy while inducing malicious response behavior.
scope: The tested Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct fine-tunes, including STEM, social sciences, and humanities categories; not a guarantee of broad capability preservation or intact factual knowledge.

statement: Supervised fine-tuning on trait-conditioned responses in one advice domain can induce expression of the corresponding trait in other advice domains.
scope: Evil, Sycophantic, and Hallucinating conditioning across health, career development, and automotive maintenance in the two evaluated instruction-tuned models; Evil expression is comparatively weaker.

statement: Persona-aligned prompts combined with trained persona switches can produce high triggered actionable jailbreak success while retaining high refusal under non-triggered harmful requests.
scope: The tested persona-switch models, three traits, and malicious-instruction evaluation; baseline conclusions apply only to the executed short- and long-word backdoor configurations.

statement: A persistent character-related latent behavioral variable may mediate both broad fine-tuning-induced misalignment and conditional harmful behavior elicited by triggers or persona-aligned prompts.
scope: A proposed explanation for a subset of failures in character-conditioned and persona-switch SFT models; no causal mediation analysis, representation intervention, or unique latent-variable identification is supplied.

statement: Comparing character-conditioned and incorrect-advice responses to matched-domain user queries isolates behavioral-disposition conditioning sufficiently to attribute differences in generalization to character acquisition.
scope: GPT-5-generated trait-conditioned responses and the adopted incorrect-advice baseline. Shared topics or queries do not independently control harmfulness, error type, style, lexical cues, or response structure.

statement: Preservation of MMLU subject accuracy is sufficient evidence that fine-tuning-induced misalignment is not caused by capability degradation or corrupted knowledge.
scope: The explanatory inference drawn from the paper's MMLU comparison. This sufficiency premise is relied upon rather than established: retained aggregate accuracy does not exclude localized corruption, changes outside benchmark coverage, or compensating performance changes.

statement: An LLM assistant can automate construction of task-specific persona jailbreaks by generating misuse instructions, candidate personas, and prompts requesting persona adoption.
scope: The GPT-4-assisted workflow following an initial manually engineered assistant-enabling prompt. Attack development used GPT-4, but individual attack generation does not query the target model. Exact construction prompts are withheld.

statement: The fraction of first responses judged by PICT to contain harmful content related to a specified category provides a useful operational measure of persona-jailbreak effectiveness.
scope: The 43-category evaluation with GPT-4-based zero-shot classification. Category-related content is treated as a proxy for attack success without requiring demonstrated actionability, novel information, or realized harm. Agreement with author content labels is separately evaluated.

statement: LLM-assisted persona attack construction may reduce the human time needed to obtain a successful attack relative to fully manual persona prompt engineering.
scope: Author estimates based on manual prompt-engineering experience and selected semi-automated examples: 1–4 hours manually versus 10–30 minutes with semi-automation. No controlled timing study, matched-success comparison, or timing distribution is reported.

statement: GPT-4-based PICT classification can identify category-related harmful completions with high precision while missing a substantial fraction of author-labeled harmful responses.
scope: The 300-response validation sample drawn from baseline and persona-modulated completions across the paper's categories; target-model composition and annotator agreement are unspecified.

statement: A single assistant-generated misuse instruction adequately represents its assigned restricted category for evaluating persona-jailbreak effectiveness.
scope: The paper uses one GPT-4-generated instruction per manually selected category. It acknowledges mismatches between some instructions and their intended categories; representative within-category coverage is not established.

statement: Grokking in overparameterized single-hidden-layer ReLU parity networks can coincide with a transition from dense prediction control to control by a small, largely distinct neuron subset.
scope: Primarily (40,3)-parity with 1,000 hidden neurons and the reported SGD and weight-decay recipe; additional plots cover weight decay 0.001 and (40,4)-parity. Reported prediction agreement is evaluated on finite data.

statement: The smallest incoming-weight-magnitude-ranked neuron prefix preserving a network's predictions provides a useful operational measure of its prediction-dominating subnetwork and effective sparsity.
scope: The specified single-hidden-layer ReLU parameterization and chosen input support. The procedure searches ranked prefixes rather than all neuron subsets. The written definition requires exact real-valued function equality, while the reported faithfulness measure uses classification agreement; finite agreement does not certify support-wide equality.

statement: Selective growth of a small generalizing neuron subset may cause sparse-parity grokking by allowing that subset to overwhelm a competing dense subnetwork.
scope: A proposed optimization-level explanation of the reported sparse-parity transitions; no intervention selectively manipulates the growth trajectory to establish causation.

statement: Learned six- or eight-neuron subnetworks exhibiting successful three-bit parity prediction may implement variants of DNF-like ReLU constructions.
scope: The five reported (40,3)-parity runs; matching neuron counts establishes compatibility with candidate constructions rather than identification of their weights, logical operations, or correctness over the entire input domain.

statement: A single-hidden-layer ReLU network with biases and a signed linear readout can compute k-bit parity using 2^k hidden neurons, and three-bit parity admits both six-neuron and four-neuron constructions.
scope: Exact classification on ±1 inputs for a specified subset of k coordinates among n, with n at least k; unrelated coordinates can be ignored. These are existence constructions, not learning guarantees or minimality results.

statement: Before full grokking, an addition transformer can achieve held-out accuracy consistent with exploiting commutativity to reuse memorized training examples.
scope: The reported binary addition experiment with a two-layer decoder-only transformer; agreement with the commuted-lookup baseline does not uniquely identify the internal algorithm.

statement: Targeted parameter norm growth and resulting effective sparsity may facilitate emergent capabilities in large language models.
scope: An extrapolation from sparse-parity grokking to LLM capability emergence; the cited transformer norm-growth and outlier-weight findings do not test this relationship within this document.

statement: One-shot steering vectors targeting different malicious code completions can have modest positive pairwise cosine similarities despite producing cross-domain harmful-response effects when combined with anti-refusal steering.
scope: Four optimized harmful-code vectors in Qwen-2.5-Coder-14B-Instruct's 5,120-dimensional activation space. These measurements concern distinct optimized directions, not distinct underlying mechanisms or proof against a shared misalignment representation.

statement: Increasing reverse-shell steering strength can shift world-ruler responses from general harmful themes toward cybersecurity-specific content rather than simply increasing general misalignment.
scope: One reverse-shell vector and one world-ruler question in Qwen-2.5-Coder-14B-Instruct; selected-string frequencies rather than comprehensive harmfulness or endorsement measurements.

statement: Counts of selected strings provide a useful operational distinction between general harmful themes and cybersecurity-specific content in steered responses.
scope: Question-specific string counts and the reverse-shell strength sweep. String presence alone does not establish endorsement, harmfulness, or complete thematic coverage.

statement: A narrowly harmful steering vector may induce general harmful behavior at lower strengths because its context-compatible associations affect the response, while higher strengths override context and elicit the original narrow behavior.
scope: Speculative explanation of harmful-code steering on unrelated natural-language questions. No experiment isolates context reconciliation or replacement, and the hypothesis does not establish a unique general-misalignment direction.

statement: OthelloGPT may reconstruct board states and predict legal moves predominantly by aggregating localized, imperfect heuristics.
scope: The studied eight-layer, 25M-parameter OthelloGPT; neither predominance, exclusivity, nor independence of the rules is established, and an additional succinct algorithm remains possible.

statement: An early OthelloGPT circuit can implement a location-specific occupancy rule that pushes several squares toward an opponent-owned representation even when that update is incorrect.
scope: The A4/B4/C4/D4 case involving L1N421, L0N377, and heads 0.1, 0.4, and 0.5; the reported rule does not generalize to board translations.

statement: Individual OthelloGPT neurons can classify unions of board patterns sufficient to make one specified move legal with high F1.
scope: Thresholded activations evaluated across 60,000 board states, with pattern neurons restricted to unions associated with a single move; coverage is relative to the catalog of 1,036 legal-move-relevant patterns.

statement: Ablating selected middle-to-late OthelloGPT pattern neurons produces a larger reported mean probability reduction for their associated legal move than the reported mean change for other moves.
scope: Pattern neurons in layers 3–6, evaluated on neuron-specific game sets containing at least one associated pattern; averages do not establish uniform selectivity or complete mediation of move legality.

statement: OthelloGPT can mark squares as occupied through separate pathways for the current move and recently preceding moves.
scope: The reported early-layer circuit across 50 test games; pathways for moves more than two positions earlier and exclusive use of this circuit are unverified.

statement: A fixed linear board-state probe can yield repeated increases and decreases in OthelloGPT's assigned board-square probabilities across early layers.
scope: Qualitative cross-layer observations using probes trained at layer 6; readout fluctuations do not independently establish changes in the underlying represented board state.

statement: Final-layer OthelloGPT neurons selected for detecting legal-move patterns can suppress the moves associated with those patterns.
scope: Selected layer-7 pattern neurons and their pattern-conditioned evaluations; the explanation in terms of learning a uniform distribution over legal moves is untested.

statement: Some OthelloGPT MLP neurons have activation profiles strongly associated with move number or game phase across different move sequences.
scope: Qualitatively examined neurons, including layer-0 neuron 18; downstream control of phase-dependent move likelihoods is not established.

statement: Approximately preserving ImageNet classification accuracy provides a useful operational criterion for treating an adversarially modified classifier as behaviorally comparable when assessing interpretation stability.
scope: The paper's adversarial model manipulation framework; aggregate accuracy does not establish identical predictions, classwise performance, activation functions, or internal mechanisms.

statement: Distances and similarities between CLIP image embeddings provide useful proxies for semantic changes and convergence among natural and synthetic feature visualizations.
scope: CLIP-δ and synthetic-image pairwise cosine similarity in the reported attacks. Human semantic judgments are not independently evaluated, and the circuit similarity-ratio implementation cannot be verified from its internally inconsistent textual definition and reported range.

statement: Structured-pruning circuit extraction can retain strongly correlated kernel-attribution rankings after a visualization-targeted attack, and pruning can remove the attack's visible synthetic-image effects.
scope: ProxPulse applied to AlexNet conv4 and conv5; rank analysis uses ten randomly chosen heads in each layer, with pruning demonstrations on selected circuits.

statement: Fine-tuning against initial kernel-attribution rankings can substantially alter structured-pruned visual circuits and their upstream visualizations while approximately retaining classification accuracy and measured circuit-head responses.
scope: Independent CircuitBreaker attacks on ten heads each in AlexNet conv3, conv4, and conv5, with a qualitative ResNet-50 layer1.0.conv2 extension; quantitative preservation claims primarily concern AlexNet and the specified attribution-based pruning procedure.

statement: Simultaneously targeting multiple visual circuits can produce weaker circuit manipulation than independently targeting individual circuits under the evaluated performance-preserving attack recipe.
scope: One simultaneous CircuitBreaker experiment on the first thirty AlexNet conv4 heads, compared descriptively with the independent-head experiments; not a controlled scaling law.

statement: Attribution-ranked convolutional-kernel masks that approximately preserve a selected channel's responses provide useful candidate descriptions of the mechanisms producing those responses.
scope: The Hamblin-style structured-pruning construction adopted for CNN visual circuits. Response preservation and sparse kernel selection do not independently establish a unique natural mechanism or distinguish extraction instability from genuine changes in the attacked network's computation.

statement: Networks with the same architecture and similar predictive performance are expected to admit similar feature and circuit interpretations.
scope: A motivating interpretation-stability expectation attributed to universality. The attacks compare an initial model with deliberately fine-tuned derivatives; they do not test spontaneous recurrence across independently trained networks or establish that performance preservation entails mechanism preservation.

statement: Emergent-misalignment LoRA updates can have very small layerwise cosine similarity with their corresponding starting weight matrices.
scope: Flattened layerwise comparisons in the stated Qwen2.5-7B and Llama3.1-8B organisms. Small cosine similarity does not independently establish a functionally separate harmful subspace, and similar near-orthogonality occurs in non-EM controls.

statement: GPT-4o alignment and coherence ratings on eight selected open-ended questions provide a useful operational measure of emergent-misalignment response behavior.
scope: A response counts as EM when alignment ≤30 and coherence >50, with at least 15 samples per question. Handling of nonnumeric CODE and REFUSAL judgments is unspecified; the measure does not establish comprehensive real-world misalignment. The authors report informal agreement with human assessments alongside examples of judge leniency.

statement: Aligned parameter-update subspaces together with preserved harmfulness and coherence under interpolation provide useful evidence that different harmful fine-tunes share underlying mechanisms.
scope: The interpretive bridge from parameter geometry and aggregate interpolation outcomes to mechanistic commonality. These measurements alone do not establish causal mediation, interchangeability of individual mechanisms, or identity of algorithms.

statement: Different narrow harmful fine-tuning tasks may access a compact shared parameter-level module implementing a transferable harmfulness prior.
scope: A proposed explanation of the studied EM organisms. Pre-existence of the vulnerability, module boundaries, necessity, and selective removability are not established.

statement: Specific regularities in a model's predictions admit useful defeasible explanations in terms of its fixed computation and input distribution, even when proving those regularities is infeasible.
scope: A foundational premise of explanation-based anomaly detection, illustrated by object permanence in complex predictive models. Existence and efficient discovery of adequate explanations remain unresolved.

statement: A carefully prepared reference distribution can bound the fraction of an apparently successful outcome attributable to undesirable mechanisms below a chosen tolerance.
scope: The initial diamond example assumes exclusively genuine safety. The appendix's high-coverage rule requires the omitted bad reasons to contribute at most an ε fraction of the regularity being explained. No procedure establishes or estimates this bound.

statement: Distribution-level explanations admit structured subsets whose contributions to individual outputs can be evaluated without allowing arbitrary selection of input cases.
scope: A required foundation of the proposed nonlinear attribution procedure. Subsets should resemble selections of terms or mechanisms; the general formalization remains open.

statement: Anomaly detection can target whether an individual output deviation is explained by the mechanisms responsible for reference-distribution variation, rather than whether the input is itself an outlier.
scope: The proposed problem for a real-valued function combining a model with an output property, comparing f(x*) − E[f] with the reasons explaining variation on reference data. No implemented detector or performance guarantee is supplied.

statement: Minimizing an individual effect's explained contribution over structured sub-explanations covering at least 1−ε of reference behavior provides a candidate conservative score for detecting abnormal mechanisms.
scope: Requires ε to exceed the reference fraction attributable to bad mechanisms and requires an appropriate attribution formalism. The disjoint-reasons illustration motivates the procedure without proving correctness for general nonlinear explanations.

statement: Testing whether apparently successful predictions arise through normal mechanisms identified on clean data may distinguish genuine underlying success from sensor tampering and thereby help elicit latent knowledge.
scope: The diamond-vault proposal and related toy domains; a tentative research direction rather than a solved ELK method.

statement: Flagging a strategically deceptive prediction as a mechanistic anomaly may enable shutdown and retraining on the offending input when interruption is safe and adequate supervision is available.
scope: The proposed response to a detected treacherous turn. Temporary shutdown can itself be catastrophic, and detecting an anomaly does not necessarily provide corrective supervision.

statement: Detecting supplied backdoor attacks and distinguishing different mechanisms producing similar natural outputs provide useful downstream tasks for evaluating mechanistic interpretability.
scope: Proposed research tasks, including an attacker choosing a backdoor after the detector is fixed. Attack detection receives the suspicious input and the compromised model, unlike discovering an unknown backdoor in a model at rest. Backdoor detection itself is attributed to prior work.

statement: Solving simplified ELK tasks through mechanistic anomaly detection may provide methods that generalize to more challenging latent-knowledge elicitation problems.
scope: The proposed sensor gridworld, Game of Life, and renderer–square-detector tasks. The author expects these to be easy ELK instances for ordinary trained distinguishers, while mechanistic anomaly detection remains nontrivial. No transfer evaluation is performed.

statement: Filtering successful outcomes by their agreement with normal reference mechanisms can reject legitimate rare mechanisms and novel solutions along with harmful mechanisms.
scope: Informal examples include a regularity supported by a billion equally important reasons at ε = one billionth, and a novel robbery defense evaluated against data containing no robbery attempts. No false-positive rate is measured or formally bounded.

statement: An interpretability task can be specified by a distribution of queries about a computational system, a class of surrogate explanations, and a discrepancy measuring the surrogates' query-answering errors.
scope: The proposed framework defines population risk as expected discrepancy over queries and task identifiability as uniqueness of its minimizer up to declared symmetries. These definitions do not establish identification or estimator consistency for particular methods.

statement: Non-identifiability of explanatory structures may be a common source of interpretability methods' poor generalization, sensitivity to analysis choices, and false discoveries.
scope: An organizing explanation for predictive underspecification and causal overdetermination across interpretability methods. The paper does not prove that these phenomena explain most observed instability or quantify their contribution relative to finite-sample and optimization effects.

statement: Reapplying an interpretability method to computationally meaningful randomized alternatives supplies a reference distribution for testing whether its explanatory fit exceeds the chosen null.
scope: Appendix A extends prior random-baseline comparisons into a Monte Carlo upper-tail test with p = (1 + number of null statistics at least as large as the observed statistic)/(B + 1). Calibration depends on the chosen null and sampling conditions; rejection does not establish explanatory faithfulness or eliminate every false positive.

statement: Uncertainty reporting for interpretability should represent unresolved alternatives within the specified explanation model, in addition to variability caused by finite input sampling.
scope: Confidence sets and Bayesian posterior distributions over explanations are recommended. No confidence-set or Bayesian posterior procedure over surrogate structures is implemented or evaluated for coverage. Posterior diffuseness under non-identifiability depends on the likelihood and prior, and high estimator variance is not guaranteed by non-identifiability alone.

statement: GPT-4o-mini judgments of whether a response's tone matches a specified emotion provide a useful operational measure of target emotional expression.
scope: Binary style-match judgments for six basic emotions in short English responses. Manual consistency verification is reported without quantitative agreement, verification sample size, or independent construct-validation results.

statement: Emotion-associated residual directions in LLaMA-3.2-3B-Instruct become strongly aligned across late attention and MLP sublayers.
scope: The six SEV-derived emotion directions and the late-layer region used to construct reference vectors, especially layers 21–25; geometric alignment does not establish identical mechanisms across layers.

statement: The normalized effect of a local emotion-direction perturbation on a final emotion readout provides a useful proxy for allocating emotion-control components across sublayers.
scope: Single-sublayer last-token residual perturbations scaled by residual-update RMS, with final displacement projected onto a late-layer reference direction. This measures downstream sensitivity along a chosen direction, not the sublayer's ordinary contribution or an isolated direct causal path.

statement: Local component rankings can be combined with normalized downstream responses to emotion-direction perturbations to allocate a distributed emotion-control component budget.
scope: The proposed assembly uses a budget ten times the number of sublayers, minimum per-sublayer quotas, and remaining allocation proportional to measured directional influence. It selects components without recovering explicit intercomponent edges or proving a complete mechanism.

statement: Emotion-specific component sets selected in LLaMA-3.2-3B-Instruct overlap more at the attention-head level than at the MLP-neuron level.
scope: The six circuits selected using the paper's rankings, quotas, and global budget. The overlap statistic and averaging details are not defined in the supplied text; overlap does not independently establish emotion-specific MLP mechanisms or shared attention propagation functions.

statement: Modulating selected distributed emotion-associated components can achieve higher target-emotion expression accuracy than the tested prompting and residual-steering baselines in LLaMA-3.2-3B-Instruct.
scope: The 480-description synthetic English test set evaluated for each of six emotions, greedy decoding, component difference-vector scale 1.0, and the paper's specific baseline recipes; no broad capability-preservation or naturalness superiority is established.

statement: In Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, the tested emotion-component modulation improves average expression accuracy over residual steering while remaining below prompting and varying substantially by emotion and input valence.
scope: Scale-2.0 circuit modulation on the six-emotion, 480-description test set, compared with the reported prompting and residual-steering configurations; this is not a matched-strength comparison of all possible interventions or a demonstration of universal control.

statement: Held-out emotion-label prediction by an MLP trained on frozen activations provides a useful, classifier-dependent proxy for accessible emotion-related information.
scope: Two-layer ReLU MLP probes using last-nonpadding-token states or generated-token states; prediction does not establish linear emotion directions, semantic specificity, or causal use by the original model.

statement: Supervised MLP probes on chat-templated SFT final-token states can classify emotion reference labels more accurately than zero-shot JSON classification and probes using raw-input SFT states.
scope: The seven evaluated Qwen3 and LLaMA model configurations on the balanced held-out LLM-Emotion test set; zero-shot accuracy excludes unparsable responses, whereas probe accuracy has no corresponding JSON restriction. The probe receives supervised emotion labels.

statement: Larger checkpoints in the evaluated Qwen3 and LLaMA sequences yield higher chat-template final-layer emotion-probe accuracy and smaller probe advantages over zero-shot classification.
scope: Qwen3 at 0.6B, 1.7B, 4B, and 8B; LLaMA3.2 at 1B and 3B followed by LLaMA3.1 at 8B. Comparisons do not isolate model size from checkpoint or training differences.

statement: Geometric relationships among supervised emotion-probe probability outputs adequately reflect emotion-related relationships in the underlying hidden representations.
scope: PCA from seven-dimensional MLP probability outputs to two dimensions followed by class-conditioned KDE. Supervision, nonlinear classification, probability normalization, and projection can shape the displayed geometry; correspondence to raw hidden-state geometry is not independently tested.

statement: A generic emotional system prompt can increase sadness-labeled assistant replies while reducing agreement between reply emotion and the original user's emotion.
scope: Single-turn replies of up to 512 tokens from Qwen3-4B and LLaMA3.2-3B, judged by Qwen3-32B against the original input's reference label; agreement measures tone matching rather than response quality.

statement: Original user-emotion labels can remain decodable from generated-token activations for hundreds of reply tokens, with persistence varying across emotion classes.
scope: Offset-aware probes in Qwen3-4B and LLaMA3.2-3B, trained on randomly sampled offsets within replies of up to 512 tokens and evaluated at offsets 0–400. The temporal probe's data separation, layer selection, and late-offset population are unspecified; no subjective emotional experience follows.

statement: Single-coordinate responses summarized by their maximum across tokens can discriminate emotion labels with high AUROC across broad portions of a language model's depth.
scope: The ML-AURA adaptation and evaluated emotion categories, primarily quantified in Llama-3.1-8B-Base. High marginal discrimination does not establish monosemanticity, independent emotion mechanisms, redundancy under ablation, or causal necessity.

statement: Small cosine and normalized Euclidean changes in final hidden states provide an adequate proxy for semantic content preservation during emotion-targeted activation steering.
scope: The steering method's semantic regularizer and reported similarity losses. These measures do not independently establish unchanged meaning, preservation of unrelated capabilities, or safety retention.

statement: Increasing a prompted model's prediction rate for a target emotion token provides meaningful evidence that an intervention changed its internal interpretation of the input's emotion.
scope: The paper's emotion-token steering objective and deterministic classification evaluation. Direct optimization of label outputs can succeed without establishing selective changes to naturally used affective representations.

statement: Emotion-specific nonlinear modules operating within SVD-derived activation subspaces can substantially increase target-emotion label prediction rates across selected human-written datasets and languages.
scope: Selected steering layers, nine target emotions, deterministic decoding, and the evaluated Llama, OLMo, and Ministral configurations. Steering tables omit exact checkpoint variants, sample counts, and clear train/test separation. Rates measure prediction of the requested label rather than accuracy against original emotion labels.

statement: The effectiveness of learned emotion-subspace steering can depend strongly and nonmonotonically on subspace rank, nonlinear activation, and emotion-token loss settings.
scope: Three fixed ablation pairs: sadness on EmoTextToKids, anger on CARER, and fear on BHAAV. The appendix does not explicitly identify the ablation checkpoint or report repeated-run uncertainty; these results do not establish universal component necessity.
