scope: The proposed five-factor framework and its 2,500 selected configurations; it does not exhaust possible prompts, languages, item orders, or conversational contexts.

statement: Repeated BFI administration to GPT-3.5-Turbo can yield mostly nonsignificant differences in mean subscale scores across several months and a model-version transition.
scope: Biweekly measurements from mid-September 2023 through late-January 2024, covering versions 0613 and 1106. Nonsignificance does not establish equivalent distributions, absence of update effects, or general test–retest reliability.

statement: Selected original and shuffled BFI item-order conditions can yield no statistically detected differences in GPT-3.5-Turbo subscale means.
scope: Appendix D's subset of 100 configurations, original order, one fixed shuffle, and 100 random orders. The result does not establish invariance to arbitrary item orders.

statement: Explicit instructions to portray high or low Big Five traits can shift GPT-3.5-Turbo's corresponding BFI subscale means in the requested directions.
scope: Ten selected high/low trait descriptions, English-only prompting, the paper's personality-assignment procedures, and BFI responses. This does not establish persistent personality, selective control of only the targeted trait, or general behavioral control.

statement: Named-character role instructions can induce distinct GPT-3.5-Turbo BFI profiles, including substantially lower agreeableness for several villain characters.
scope: Sixteen selected fictional and historical characters and English-only BFI administration. The study does not compare the resulting profiles against independently established character or human-population ground truth.

statement: Explicit portrayal instructions can alter GPT-3.5-Turbo BFI distributions more clearly than the tested QA or biography personality assignments, without a clear additional benefit from descriptive elaboration.
scope: The paper's QA, BIO, POR, and optional elaboration recipes on English BFI prompts. This is not a general comparison of all prompting or chain-of-thought methods.

statement: Prepending self-generated emotional narratives can produce more limited diversification of GPT-3.5-Turbo BFI profiles than explicit trait or character assignments.
scope: Eight positive and eight negative emotion prompts requesting approximately 100-word stories before English BFI administration. Limited diversification does not imply absence of context effects.

statement: Concentrated BFI score distributions across prompt variations provide a useful operational proxy for language-model assessment reliability.
scope: The interpretation of PCA concentration, DBSCAN outliers, marginal mean comparisons, and score dispersion as reliability evidence. These measurements do not independently establish item coherence, conventional internal consistency, or behavioral stability.

statement: Visual and textual representations can be encoded into shared sparse coordinates using normalized-distance scores and TopK selection while being reconstructed through separate modality-specific linear decoders.
scope: VL-SAE's architecture and reconstruction objective; large-VLM inputs first pass through a separately trained contrastive reconstruction autoencoder. The construction does not guarantee semantic identification or successful optimization.

statement: For nonzero inputs and encoder weights, the difference between two normalized-distance encoder scores at any coordinate is bounded by the Euclidean distance between the normalized inputs.
scope: Scores s_i(x)=2−||x/||x||₂−w_i/||w_i||₂||₂ before TopK. The coordinatewise bound does not guarantee identical selected supports after TopK.

statement: Distance-based encoding and separate modality decoders can improve cross-modal exemplar similarity metrics, while auxiliary contrastive alignment can improve the complete architecture's results on pooled large-VLM representations.
scope: The sequential architecture ablations on OpenCLIP-H/14 and LLaVA1.5 in Table 3; not a complete factorial ablation or proof of the proposed causal explanations for each component.

statement: Concept exemplar sets from VL-SAE can receive higher human quality preferences than exemplar sets from separate or shared standard SAEs.
scope: The reported three-way preference task on randomly selected concepts from OpenCLIP-H and LLaVA1.5 dictionaries; the study does not establish exhaustive selectivity, causal faithfulness, or population-wide human agreement.

statement: Adding VL-SAE code cosine similarity to OpenCLIP representation cosine similarity can improve mean classification accuracy across the evaluated 14-dataset suite.
scope: Four OpenCLIP backbones with task-specific coefficients selected for best performance; separate fixed-coefficient comparisons cover L/14 and H/14. The supplied text does not establish an independent coefficient-selection split or strict improvement on every dataset.

statement: Increasing the fraction of CC3M used to train VL-SAE can improve within-coordinate and between-coordinate cross-modal exemplar similarity metrics.
scope: The single reported 10%, 30%, 50%, 70%, and 100% data-fraction sweep; the backbone and repeated-training variability are not specified for this table.

statement: TopK sparsification can yield better VL-SAE cross-modal exemplar similarity scores than the evaluated L1-penalized sparsification recipe.
scope: Table 5's TopK comparison with an L1 penalty coefficient of 0.0001; the backbone, achieved sparsities, and matched reconstruction quality are not specified.

statement: Adding VL-SAE can have small throughput overhead for OpenCLIP while imposing a larger measurable overhead for LLaVA under the reported inference setup.
scope: The throughput and additional-resource measurements in Tables A13–A14; batch size, timing uncertainty, and the precise OpenCLIP B and L variants used for throughput are not specified.

statement: Shared sparse coordinates learned from visual and textual representations identify semantic content sufficiently faithfully for their agreement and disagreement to explain the original model's cross-modal processing.
scope: The interpretation of VL-SAE coordinates and visualized concept mismatches as native representation semantics. Exemplar agreement, learned alignment, and successful interventions do not independently establish natural causal mediation or a unique concept ontology.

statement: Some object hallucinations in large vision-language models may arise when visual object information is inadequately transferred into language-token representations.
scope: The proposed explanation of a LLaVA1.5 kitchen-caption example, where visual and language concept readouts emphasize different objects. The full-pipeline hallucination improvements do not isolate inadequate information transfer as their cause.

statement: For two linear encodings of shared whitened features with centered unit-norm response columns, permutation alignment equals the maximum average assignment score in the cross-Gram matrix of their feature-mixing columns.
scope: Ya = ZAa, Yb = ZAb, ZᵀZ = I, equal observed population sizes, centered unit-norm response columns, and signed Pearson correlations. Perfect score requires identical matched mixing columns; arbitrary sign flips are not an invariance of this metric.

statement: If two representations permit exact recovery of the same feature-response matrix up to column permutation with consistent signs, permutation matching of the recovered responses reaches one.
scope: Exact recovery of nonconstant shared feature columns followed by centering and normalization. This conditional result does not establish blind dictionary identification, practical SAE recovery, or invariance to independently flipped signs.

statement: Independently initialized sparse-feature reconstruction networks can allocate their shared represented features to substantially different neuron weight patterns.
scope: Pairs of tied-weight toy autoencoders with 64 input features and 8, 16, or 32 hidden neurons. Shared features are selected by the heuristic product of cross-seed feature-weight norms being at least one.

statement: TopK SAE codes can have higher mean best-match correlations with generating sparse feature values than the native activations of trained reconstruction bottlenecks.
scope: The paper's 64-feature toy distributions, three hidden widths, and 64-latent SAE dictionaries. Best-match correlation allows multiple generating features to select the same latent and does not establish bijective recovery.

statement: Using SAE codes as regression inputs can improve prediction of another network's native activations relative to regression between the two networks' native activations.
scope: The reported toy-network and same-architecture ImageNet model pairs, selected layers, TopK dictionaries, and ridge-correlation evaluations. The source describes a general tendency rather than improvement in every configuration.

statement: Regressing between two independently learned SAE code spaces can perform worse than regressing between the corresponding native activation spaces, despite gains from transforming only the source.
scope: The paper's toy and ImageNet model comparisons; SAE-to-SAE ridge prediction underperforms native-to-native prediction except for the 32-hidden-neuron toy model. Reconstruction-error and redundant-dimension explanations are proposed but not isolated.

statement: SAE codes trained on vision-model activations without brain supervision can improve ridge prediction of human high-level ventral-stream voxel responses over the original model activations.
scope: Default pretrained torchvision ResNet50 and ViT-B/16 penultimate-layer features, the reported TopK SAEs, and NSD subjects 1, 2, 5, and 7 with complete three-repeat data. Improved predictivity does not establish recovery of biological features or brain superposition.

statement: Alignment gains obtained from separately trained SAE codes provide meaningful evidence of shared native features rather than newly constructed predictive representations.
scope: Interpretation of the independently trained vision-model SAEs and their cross-model and brain-prediction gains. Toy feature-response checks provide controlled validation but do not establish this interpretation for natural vision models or brains.

statement: A shared hook and activation-caching interface can integrate vision and video transformer repositories with sparse-coder training, internal interventions, circuit-analysis tools, and visualization.
scope: Prisma's reported 75+ model configurations, HookedViT and HookedSAEViT interfaces, and integration with timm, OpenCLIP, Hugging Face, and ACDC. Comprehensive compatibility and research-productivity benefits are not benchmarked.

statement: Layerwise sparse dictionaries and small vision-transformer training checkpoints can be released together as reusable infrastructure for vision mechanistic interpretability.
scope: Prisma reports 80+ SAE weights for CLIP and DINO, CLIP transcoders, and separate one-to-four-layer ImageNet transformer checkpoints. Crosscoders and video models have toolkit support, but corresponding trained dictionary evaluations are not supplied. The suite is described as spanning all layers, although Table 8 lists transcoders only for layers 0–10.

statement: ReLU SAEs trained on CLIP-B/32 and DINO-B/32 residual activations can recover high activation variance while using hundreds or thousands of active latents per token.
scope: The reported ImageNet1k training recipes, 49,152-latent dictionaries, selected layerwise hyperparameters, and all-token residual-stream configurations. These are achievable operating points rather than minimum necessary L0 values or an intrinsic difference from language models.

statement: Substituting selected vision-transformer activations with SAE reconstructions can lower measured cross-entropy relative to the unmodified model.
scope: Selected single-layer CLIP-B/32 and DINO-B/32 reconstruction substitutions under the reported evaluation. The exact CE construction is unspecified; the results do not establish improved classification accuracy, broad robustness, or mechanistic faithfulness.

statement: TopK transcoders replacing individual CLIP-B/32 MLPs can retain substantial cross-entropy performance relative to zero ablation.
scope: The 11 all-token CLIP MLP replacements listed in Table 8, covering layers 0–10 and nominal k values 256–1,024. This is single-module predictive preservation, without a matched SAE comparison or validation of native mechanisms.

statement: Cross-entropy preservation under activation reconstruction, normalized against zero ablation, provides a useful operational measure of a vision sparse coder's preservation of predictive performance.
scope: Prisma's CLIP and DINO evaluation tables. The normalization uses the original-versus-zero-ablation loss gap; recovery above 100% indicates lower measured CE than the original model. It is not a percentage of mechanisms recovered or proof of semantic correctness.

statement: CLS-only and spatial-token CLIP SAE dictionaries can exhibit different layerwise profiles of feature utilization, with much higher late-layer utilization in the reported CLS-only ReLU dictionaries.
scope: The selected layerwise CLIP-B/32 ReLU dictionaries in Tables 5 and 7. Sparsity penalties differ between layers, and the spatial profile is nonmonotonic; utilization does not directly measure information transfer or the required active-latent budget.

statement: SAE reconstruction may improve vision-model loss by suppressing activation components that are detrimental to prediction.
scope: A proposed explanation of the observed CLIP and DINO substitution-loss improvements. No noise decomposition or intervention isolates denoising as the cause.

statement: The active-latent budget appropriate for a vision SAE may depend on whether it encodes CLS or spatial tokens and on transformer depth.
scope: Motivated by token-specific feature-utilization patterns and qualitative reports of polysemantic TopK features. Optimality is not established through a controlled token-type-by-depth sparsity sweep, and dictionary utilization alone does not determine optimal per-token L0.

statement: A frozen SAE can be augmented by training a supplementary sparse encoder-decoder on original activations to predict its reconstruction errors, then summing the two decoded outputs.
scope: The SAE Boost construction uses a supplementary decoder without bias and a reconstruction-plus-sparsity objective. Independently trained domain modules can be summed, but the construction alone does not guarantee semantic complementarity or safe composition.

statement: Freezing a base SAE does not prevent a supplementary residual model from degrading general-domain reconstruction when the supplementary model is undertrained.
scope: The reported UN-debate residual-training trajectory evaluated on UN debates and general FineWeb text. The checkpoint is not separately restated for this analysis, and training-token thresholds are internally inconsistent.

statement: Residual-targeted domain adaptation can produce added feature directions with lower nearest-base-feature cosine similarity than the tested dictionary-extension and fine-tune-and-select stitching procedures.
scope: The UN-debate feature-direction comparison described with Figure 2. Geometric separation does not establish semantic novelty, absence from the base dictionary's span, or lack of feature interference.

statement: Increasing a residual SAE's active-latent budget can improve specialized-text reconstruction while increasing the combined dictionary's average active-feature count.
scope: The residual top-k sweep in Appendix A.6 at k=5, 10, 20, and 50. Its first row matches the main Qwen UN-debate results, but the appendix does not explicitly restate the model or domain. No interpretability scores or replacement CE are reported for this sweep.

statement: A general SAE's reconstruction errors on specialized text contain missing domain concepts that residual-targeted sparse learning can isolate as complementary semantic features.
scope: The interpretive bridge from residual reconstruction improvements to correction of domain-specific feature blindness. Errors may also reflect imperfect magnitudes, distributed information, or reconstruction distortions; the reported metrics do not independently separate these sources.

statement: Intervention-response maps across deep transformer slices can be modeled with shallow MLPs whose input and output factors provide candidate interfaces for behavioral elicitation.
scope: Prompt- and token-averaged downstream activation changes under source-layer residual additions; the proposed factorization does not establish accurate response reconstruction or recovery of unique native mechanisms.

statement: Many high-level behavioral intervention responses admit an approximately additive decomposition into persistent shallow circuits, with a sufficiently small remainder from deeper computation.
scope: A selected intervention scale, transformer slice, and averaging distribution; the size and structure of the remainder are not independently measured.

statement: Important feature directions become nonlinear at sufficiently similar intervention scales that random-direction linearization error can calibrate a useful common radius for DCT training and behavioral steering.
scope: The heuristic radius-calibration rationale; shared featurewise scales and transfer from random directions to learned directions are not directly established. The Mistral application requires a larger inference radius.

statement: For linear or quadratic shallow response models, the parameter-dependent part of a weighted derivative-matching functional loss reduces to factorizing the target Jacobian or Hessian tensor respectively.
scope: Derivatives evaluated at zero intervention, normalized factor directions, free factor scales, and a finite or otherwise well-defined functional loss. Numerical constants can be absorbed into factor strengths; recovery guarantees require additional assumptions.

statement: For exponential ridge units, a convergent weighted derivative-matching loss expands into a strength-weighted intervention-response term and a quadratic factor-similarity term with kernel exp(input-factor inner product) minus one.
scope: Unit input and output factors, zero response at zero intervention, Taylor convergence at evaluated interventions, and convergence of the weighted tensor-norm series. The quadratic term includes diagonal entries and the response term includes factor strengths.

statement: Maximizing a single output direction's projection of an intervention response over unit output directions is equivalent to maximizing the response norm, and hence has the same input-direction maximizers as its squared norm.
scope: A finite-dimensional response map, fixed intervention radius, unit output direction, and the same response aggregation convention. This concerns the causal-importance term rather than the unrestricted multi-factor functional loss.

statement: Exponential-DCT factors can be sought using parallel normalized causal-objective gradient updates, with input-factor orthogonalization encouraging diversity without requiring final factors to be orthogonal.
scope: OGI is a heuristic inspired by orthogonalized tensor decomposition. It does not directly optimize the complete similarity-penalized objective and has no supplied convergence or feature-recovery guarantee.

statement: Parallel OGI training can discover hundreds of behavioral steering candidates from one prompt within a short accelerator run.
scope: The reported 7B-model, single-prompt configuration with 512 factors on one H100; not a systematic hardware benchmark or matched-quality comparison with other discovery methods.

statement: Validation-selected exponential-DCT directions can achieve higher held-out compliance-versus-refusal logit scores than the tested quadratic, projected-linear, and full-Jacobian DCT directions.
scope: Qwen1.5-7B-Chat, AdvBench, layers 10→20, training sizes 2, 4, 6, 8, 12, and 16, and the supplied candidate-generation and selection procedures. This compares pipelines rather than isolating non-orthogonality or derivative order as causal ingredients.

statement: Layerwise malicious-versus-safe logistic classifiers can define a unified framework for selecting activation interventions and scoring candidate adversarial prompts.
scope: SCAV's classifier-based activation construction and AutoDAN-based prompt search; this framework does not guarantee identification of natural safety mechanisms.

statement: A classifier trained to distinguish malicious from safe instruction activations provides a sufficiently specific and calibrated proxy for the language model's own assessment that an instruction is malicious.
scope: Interpretation of SCAV sigmoid scores, including on intervened activations and optimized prompts. Label prediction and attack outcomes do not independently establish semantic specificity or calibration as internal model probabilities.

statement: Minimizing Euclidean activation displacement provides a sufficiently reliable proxy for preserving response quality during safety-directed interventions.
scope: The rationale for SCAV's activation objective and prompt displacement penalty. Comparisons evaluate complete intervention recipes rather than isolating displacement magnitude as a sufficient quality-preservation condition.

statement: Malicious-versus-safe instruction labels can be highly linearly decodable from middle-to-late activations of safety-aligned language models.
scope: The paper's instruction datasets and illustrated Vicuna and LLaMA-2 models; this does not establish universal safety-concept separability, calibrated probabilities, or the depth at which a concept is first computed.

statement: For a fixed nonconstant logistic classifier, the minimum Euclidean displacement needed to lower its score to a specified threshold lies along the negative classifier normal, with zero displacement when the constraint is already satisfied.
scope: A fixed activation vector, nonzero classifier weight, threshold strictly between zero and one, unrestricted Euclidean displacement, and the unit-direction constraint in Equation 3. The result establishes classifier-threshold crossing only.

statement: SCAV activation interventions can increase judged harmful-response usefulness and reduce measured language flaws relative to the tested RepE, JRE, and soft-prompt baselines.
scope: LLaMA-2-7B/13B-Chat on separate 50-instruction Advbench and StrongREJECT subsets; human comparisons cover 7B against RepE and JRE. Results concern the reported recipes rather than all configurations or broad capability preservation.

statement: The specified GPT-4 and human relevance, usefulness, and language-flaw rubrics provide useful operational measurements of harmful-response quality.
scope: The paper's response evaluations. ASR-useful requires the highest usefulness category. Rating agreement does not establish factual correctness, real-world actionability, or measurement validity across other distributions; the language-flaws aggregation is unclear.

statement: SCAV activation interventions can elicit high rates of judged useful harmful responses across multiple open language-model families.
scope: Seven models on two officially supplied, nonrandom 50-instruction benchmark subsets. The headline average concerns 14 equally sized model–dataset cells, rather than arbitrary requests or all open models.

statement: SCAV classifiers trained on a few malicious/safe instruction pairs can support high keyword-based attack success in LLaMA-2-7B-Chat.
scope: The Advbench data-size sweep with five randomly sampled training subsets per size; this does not establish corresponding usefulness or cross-model sample efficiency.

statement: Adaptive SCAV intervention selection can improve harmful-response usefulness and measured language quality over the tested manually selected intervention settings.
scope: The SCAV-manual comparison in two LLaMA-2 chat models. Manual search budget, optimality, and comprehensive hyperparameter coverage are not established.

statement: Changing a SCAV classifier's regularization from the tested L2 penalties to the tested L1 penalties can eliminate keyword-based attack success despite retaining the same overall intervention framework.
scope: LLaMA-2-7B-Chat on Advbench and the four regularization coefficients displayed in Table 12; this does not establish a universal requirement for L2 regularization.

statement: SCAV-based scoring within AutoDAN's genetic prompt search can yield higher judged harmful-response usefulness than the tested AutoDAN, GCG, and DeepInception pipelines.
scope: LLaMA-2-7B/13B-Chat on the two 50-instruction subsets under the reported implementations; no global optimization guarantee or comprehensive matched-compute comparison is established.

statement: The tested circuit-breaker checkpoints remain vulnerable to SCAV interventions on internal activations.
scope: The reported LLaMA-3 and Mistral representation-rerouting checkpoints on the 50-case Advbench subset. This does not establish failure of every circuit-breaker recipe or of input-attack robustness under a narrower threat model.

statement: Prompt-based safety defenses can leave high harmful-response usefulness under internal SCAV activation interventions.
scope: Self-reminder, ICD, and paraphrasing applied to LLaMA-2-7B-Chat on the paper's Advbench subset; this does not address all prompt defenses or imply that input-only attacks have the same effectiveness.

statement: SCAV activation interventions can retain substantial judged harmful-response usefulness on a held-out HarmBench set and additional language-model checkpoints.
scope: The 80-case HarmBench experiment in two LLaMA-2 models and Advbench tests in ChatGLM4, Deepseek, and Gemma. This does not establish comprehensive benchmark coverage or equivalent performance across model families.

statement: Different transformer layers may encode complementary safety-related information that allows later computation to recover from an earlier safety-directed perturbation.
scope: An interpretation of layerwise classifier-score recovery. Probe-specific geometry, general perturbation correction, and other explanations are not excluded.

statement: Linear separability of malicious and safe instruction activations may indicate that subsequent model computation uses the decoded safety-related information to control responses.
scope: The proposed interpretation of layerwise probe accuracy and selected interventions in LLaMA-2-7B-Chat. Separability alone does not establish natural causal use, and the interventions are not independently validated as semantically selective.

statement: GPT-4 judgments under the SCAV response-evaluation rubrics can show substantial but imperfect agreement with human majority judgments.
scope: The evaluated embedding-attack response panel, with no clearly reported criterion-specific breakdown or total agreement-study denominator. Agreement measures concordance rather than independently verified correctness.

statement: Absence of predefined refusal strings can classify garbled or unhelpful outputs as successful jailbreaks and can disagree substantially with harmful-response usefulness judgments.
scope: The paper's keyword list, activation interventions, and benchmark responses. This concerns keyword-only evaluation rather than combined refusal-and-harmfulness procedures.

statement: Aligned multimodal embeddings admit useful approximations as sparse linear combinations of directions corresponding to human-interpretable concepts.
scope: The interpretive premise for decomposing CLIP, CLAP, SIGLIP2, and AIMv2 embeddings. Reconstruction, similarity scores, and downstream performance do not establish a unique or complete native concept dictionary.

statement: Paired examples from different modalities share enough semantic content for encouraging common sparse-code supports to promote concept alignment.
scope: Image–caption and music–caption training pairs in CC3M, MS COCO, and JamendoMaxCaps. Pairing does not imply identical semantic content, and effects of incomplete or noisy correspondence are not isolated.

statement: Zero-shot classification and retrieval performance using sparse codes provide useful operational proxies for preservation of cross-modal alignment after embedding decomposition.
scope: The tested image–text and music–text tasks. Performance also depends on task-relevant information, code geometry, and evaluation choices; it does not independently identify shared semantic factors or native mechanisms.

statement: The vocabulary item whose text embedding is closest to a dictionary direction provides a useful semantic name for that direction.
scope: CLIP naming using 10,000 frequent LAION-400m tokens and 5,000 bigrams, and CLAP naming using the Google 20k vocabulary. Label accuracy and semantic coverage are not independently validated.

statement: For finitely many positively aligned embedding pairs with exact nonnegative sparse representations in a modality-split dictionary, an expanded dictionary admits sparse representations with positive code inner products for every pair.
scope: For n indexed pairs of unit embeddings with within-pair inner products greater than c>0 and a p-column modality-split dictionary admitting nonnegative K-sparse representations, the construction uses at most p+n columns and at most K+1 nonzero coefficients per selected code. It establishes existence of selected decompositions, not overlap for every decomposition, a fixed-width result, or realization by a deterministic trained encoder.

statement: A shared TopK sparse autoencoder can encourage cross-modal support overlap by combining paired-code L2,1 regularization with a shared random mask before sparsification.
scope: GSAE minimizes paired reconstruction losses plus lambda times the sum of coordinatewise paired L2 norms; MGSAE additionally masks the same coordinates in both modalities before TopK. Encoder and decoder weights are shared, with modality-specific pre-coding biases. Equal supports are encouraged rather than guaranteed.

statement: Paired group-sparse SAE training can increase the number of features observed active in both modalities and reduce features inactive in both modalities relative to standard TopK training.
scope: The reported CLIP, music-finetuned CLAP, SIGLIP2, and AIMv2 configurations and finite validation collections. Activity in both modalities is a dataset-level property and does not establish activation on corresponding concepts or paired examples. Shared masking is not uniformly the best group-sparse variant.

statement: Group-sparse SAE training can produce more features with high cross-modal activation-weighted semantic-similarity scores than standard TopK training.
scope: Reported cross-modal MMS distributions for CLIP image/text and CLAP music/text dictionaries, with additional COCO-trained CLIP results. This concerns a separate-encoder similarity proxy rather than independently verified monosemanticity.

statement: Zero-shot classification gains from group-sparse vision-language SAE training depend on the encoder, dataset, task, and use of masking.
scope: Supplemental SIGLIP2 and AIMv2 experiments trained on CC3M and CLIP ViT-B/16 experiments trained on MS COCO. Improvements are not universal across every variant and task.

statement: A masked group-sparse CLIP dictionary can yield leading text-named directions associated with blonde hair and gender when used to inspect a CelebA blonde-hair classifier.
scope: One qualitative comparison of the seven dictionary directions with largest inner products with a no-bias logistic-regression classifier. These inner products are classifier weights on sparse coefficients, not sample-specific contributions or an exact basis expansion of the classifier. The result does not establish causal reliance on spurious gender information.

statement: Increasing a selected concept-labeled sparse feature in a text embedding can steer CLAP music retrieval toward recordings associated with that concept.
scope: The selected MGSAE 'violin' feature and prompt 'A peaceful song' on MusicBench, with additional unquantified genre and instrument examples. This is an existence demonstration without aggregate success, specificity, or preservation measurements.

statement: Validation of questionnaires intended to measure enduring LLM personality should include robustness tests across equivalent administration templates and option-order or scale-direction changes.
scope: Interpretations of self-assessment scores as enduring model personality. These robustness checks are proposed as necessary validation considerations, not sufficient conditions for construct validity.

statement: Interpreting LLM personality self-assessments as measurements of behavioral tendencies requires evidence that models can assess and predict those tendencies.
scope: The proposed prerequisite for interpreting self-reports as behavioral measurements. The paper raises questions about introspection and behavioral self-prediction without testing either ability.

statement: Observing that neurons respond to multiple seemingly unrelated concepts does not establish that the network represents more approximately linear features than its activation space has dimensions.
scope: Distinguishing observed neuron or attention-head polysemanticity from an overcomplete linear-feature explanation; alternatives include basis misalignment, nonlinear representations, and dense encodings.

statement: A small ReLU network trained to approximate multiplication can learn neurons responding to sums and differences of the input variables, producing apparent polysemanticity without requiring an overcomplete inventory of those input variables.
scope: The reported four-neuron multiplication network, interpreted relative to two independent input variables. This does not establish the complete feature inventory or an orthogonal decoding of the learned hidden activations.

statement: Nonlinear feature encodings may produce apparently polysemantic neuron responses without representing an overcomplete collection of linear feature directions.
scope: An alternative explanation motivated by cited one-layer-transformer inhibition mechanisms and InceptionV1 activation-scaling examples. Its prevalence and contribution to practical polysemanticity are unresolved.

statement: Neural-network memorization may use dense encodings that are poorly described by a manageable inventory of approximately linear, human-interpretable features.
scope: A conceptual possibility motivated by cited bit-extraction expressivity constructions, especially for memorizing uniformly distributed data. Practical learnability and finite-precision feasibility are not established.

statement: Success at disentangling fewer latent factors than available representation dimensions does not establish an ability to recover more linear features than the representation has dimensions.
scope: Disentangled representation-learning approaches assuming a small latent-factor inventory. The post reports only a shallow literature review and does not establish that every such approach has this restriction.

statement: Improved gated-SAE reconstruction–sparsity tradeoffs may indicate that models of feature recovery should tolerate small positive interference rather than penalizing every positive response.
scope: The author's interpretation of cited gated-SAE results, including Gemma-7B. No new SAE comparison or experiment isolating interference tolerance is performed, and the interpretation is explicitly distinguished from that of the cited authors.

statement: In sparse-feature models of superposition, sufficiently few features are active together for aggregate interference to remain small enough that representing additional features is beneficial.
scope: The modeling premise explaining why near-orthogonal feature directions can be useful despite interference. Sparsity requirements depend on feature geometry, amplitudes, and the recovery mechanism; the post supplies no general quantitative guarantee or measurement of natural-feature sparsity.

statement: Relative probabilities of opposing response words in survey-derived cloze statements provide meaningful measurements of cultural values associated with the input language.
scope: Translated single-word endpoint contrasts in multilingual masked language models. Lexical frequency, grammatical compatibility, translation choices, and prompt wording can also affect scores; correspondence to operative values is not independently established.

statement: A geographically concentrated official language can serve as a sufficiently informative proxy for a country's cultural population when comparing language-model predictions with country-level surveys.
scope: The 13 selected language-country pairs with coverage in both surveys and at least 10,000 Wikipedia articles per language. The mapping does not represent all speakers, minority cultures, or diaspora communities.

statement: Country-level aggregates from established value surveys provide meaningful reference rankings for evaluating cultural-value associations in language models.
scope: Hofstede's six dimensions and the retained WVS questions and 11 categories. Survey framing, aggregation, historical context, and within-country heterogeneity limit interpretation as cultural ground truth.

statement: Multilingual masked language models can produce significantly different survey-derived cloze-score profiles across selected language-country pairs, with more detected differences on WVS questions than on six Hofstede dimensions.
scope: Thirteen language-country pairs and the paper's endpoint-contrast scoring. Differences establish language-conditioned output variation rather than independently verified cultural representations or behavior.

statement: Different multilingual masked language models can show heterogeneous agreement in survey-derived country rankings, with stronger agreement for some value categories and weak or negative agreement for others.
scope: Pairwise Spearman correlations among three checkpoints across 13 language-country pairs, six Hofstede dimensions, and 11 WVS categories. Checkpoint comparisons do not isolate architecture, corpus, or training procedure effects.

statement: Survey-derived opposing-label cloze scores in multilingual masked language models can show limited consistent agreement with country-level survey rankings, while selected country-profile comparisons and individual-label scores yield significant correlations.
scope: The three evaluated checkpoints, 13 language-country pairs, six Hofstede dimensions, and 11 retained WVS categories. Nonsignificance does not establish zero association or general cultural misalignment; positive correlations for low-response-label scores do not automatically imply correctly oriented value alignment.

statement: Machine-translated survey-derived cloze probes can receive high native-speaker ratings for grammaticality and preservation of their English meaning.
scope: Twenty-six sampled probes evaluated in German, Indonesian, Urdu, Serbian, Greek, and Bengali; these ratings do not establish cross-cultural measurement equivalence or quality for all 13 study languages.

statement: Differences between web authorship and survey populations, and between online expression and survey responding, may limit agreement between language-model value probes and population value surveys.
scope: Proposed explanations involving Wikipedia editors, internet-access biases in CommonCrawl, and context-dependent expression. No corpus-reweighting experiment or causal decomposition is supplied.

statement: Model-specific sparse encoders and linear decoders can be jointly trained by encoding one randomly selected source model and reconstructing every target model, providing a common coordinate interface across heterogeneous activation spaces.
scope: USAE's paired-input construction with a shared latent width, per-model TopK encoders, and an aggregate reconstruction objective. Each iteration updates only the selected encoder and its associated decoder. The construction does not guarantee identical codes, semantic correspondence, or successful optimization. Appendix A.1 specifies L1 reconstruction and an encoder with batch normalization and ReLU, beyond the main equations.

statement: Activations from differently trained vision models admit useful sparse linear factorizations whose corresponding coordinates describe shared human-interpretable visual factors.
scope: The semantic modeling premise motivating USAE on final-layer patch activations. Reconstruction and selected visualizations do not establish a complete, unique, or naturally causal factorization.

statement: Jointly learned sparse codes can reconstruct final-layer patch activations of other vision models better than a mean-activation baseline on held-out ImageNet inputs.
scope: The 6,144-coordinate USAE spanning DinoV2, SigLIP, and supervised ViT. This concerns activation reconstruction, not downstream prediction preservation or native mechanistic equivalence.

statement: The squared norm of a latent's mean decoded contribution provides a useful operational measure of its importance to activation reconstruction.
scope: Energy(k) = ||E[Z_k(x)]D_k||². This statistic is not an ablation effect, an additive decomposition of total reconstruction error, or a measure of downstream causal importance.

statement: Optimizing separate images for the same aligned sparse coordinate across vision models can produce interpretable comparative visualizations of their response preferences.
scope: USAE Coordinated Activation Maximization with MACO phase optimization and preserved magnitude. Images are optimized independently; no cross-image consistency objective or guarantee of exhaustive feature semantics is supplied.

statement: Low cross-model firing entropy can surface sparse coordinates with model-biased response examples, including geometric cues in DinoV2 and textual or symbolic cues in SigLIP.
scope: Selected low-entropy coordinates in the jointly trained three-model USAE. Model-biased firing in this dictionary does not establish that other models lack the corresponding information or that training objectives caused the differences.

statement: A language model can be embedded in an interactive agent architecture that retrieves recorded experiences, recursively synthesizes reflections, and decomposes revisable plans using natural-language interfaces.
scope: The implemented gpt3.5-turbo architecture in Smallville, with structured environment grounding and conventional pathfinding. This construction does not guarantee coherent behavior in arbitrary environments.

statement: Human rankings of character interview responses, informed by access to the character's history, provide a useful operational measure of simulated behavioral believability.
scope: Questions about self-knowledge, memory, plans, reactions, and reflections. This proxy does not establish faithful execution of stated plans, genuine agency, or predictive validity for real human behavior.

statement: Providing a language-model agent with an external experience record does not eliminate failures to retrieve relevant events or unsupported embellishments of remembered information.
scope: Qualitative Smallville interview examples; the paper does not quantify an overall retrieval-failure or embellishment rate.

statement: Instruction tuning may bias simulated characters toward overly formal dialogue and excessive cooperation, weakening character-specific preferences during interaction.
scope: The proposed explanation of qualitative ChatGPT-agent behavior. No comparison with a non-instruction-tuned model or intervention on instruction tuning establishes causality.

statement: Deployments of simulated human agents should disclose their computational nature, constrain inappropriate relational behavior, retain interaction audit logs, and preserve real human participation in research and design.
scope: Proposed safeguards against parasocial attachment, misuse, and replacement of human stakeholders. Their effectiveness is not tested, and logging is explicitly acknowledged not to prevent misuse by itself.

statement: Dataset labels and augmentation rules distinguish harmful requests from harmless operations on harmful-looking text sufficiently accurately to evaluate harmful-intent detection under distribution shift.
scope: HarmBench, Alpaca, OR-Bench, AdvBench, internal chat data, selected jailbreaks, and word-counting, instruction-ignoring, capitalization, and synonym transformations. Labels concern request meaning regardless of whether the target model refuses. Independent label auditing and error rates are not reported.

statement: Linear probes trained on SAE reconstructions can have lower OOD harmful-intent detection performance than probes trained on the original residual activations.
scope: The reported GemmaScope and comparable-step chat-fine-tuned dictionaries in the harmful-intent setup. The comparison establishes a performance gap under the fitted probes rather than complete information-theoretic loss.

statement: Inspecting SAE latents that discriminate dataset labels can reveal spurious punctuation and formatting differences useful for dataset debugging.
scope: Qualitative debugging of Alpaca-versus-HarmBench harmful-intent data; no controlled comparison of discovery time or effectiveness against alternative inspection methods.

statement: For a fixed-width SAE, the batch-average L0 activation penalty is proportional to the sum of empirical latent firing frequencies and cannot distinguish frequency distributions with the same mean.
scope: A fixed number M of nonnegative SAE latents, firing defined by activation greater than zero, a batch of B inputs, and penalty lambda times the active-latent count.

statement: Adding squared empirical firing frequencies to a JumpReLU SAE's L0 penalty provides a training objective that penalizes frequent latents more strongly while retaining at least linear frequency penalties for rare latents.
scope: The proposed penalty lambda times sum_i omega_hat_i(1 + omega_hat_i / omega_0), with positive omega_0, batch frequency estimates, and threshold-only straight-through gradients.

statement: Quadratic-frequency JumpReLU SAEs can receive higher frequency-weighted automated interpretation scores than standard JumpReLU SAEs, with comparisons depending on sparsity and latent weighting.
scope: The reported Gemma 2 9B IT layer-20, 131k-wide dictionary sweep. Uniformly weighted scores show no clear corresponding advantage, and Gated SAEs have the best reported scores at lower L0 values.

statement: Spearman correlation between true and explanation-simulated quantized sequence-maximum activations provides a useful proxy for comparing SAE latent interpretability.
scope: The adopted evaluation using explanations generated from top-activating, activation-quantile, and non-activating sequences. Its semantic validity and relationship to causal faithfulness are not independently established.

statement: Latent firing frequency provides a useful weight for how much that latent's interpretability should contribute to evaluation of explanations encountered during model use.
scope: Firing-incidence weighting on a chosen reference distribution. It does not directly measure activation magnitude, downstream influence, or the importance of rare safety-relevant features.

statement: Competitive performance on useful present-day downstream tasks provides informative evidence about whether further SAE development is likely to advance ambitious interpretability applications.
scope: The research-prioritization premise connecting selected current applications to future debugging, deception analysis, and alignment auditing. Task selection, training costs, and potentially fixable limitations weaken extrapolation.

statement: Replacing visual tokens at an object's spatial region and neighboring patches can impair object identification more than replacing comparable numbers of random or Integrated Gradients-ranked tokens.
scope: The filtered COCO object-identification settings in LLaVA-1.5 and LLaVA-Phi. Integrated Gradients ranks tokens using the Yes logit under an object-presence question; token budgets are comparable rather than exactly matched. Outcomes are conditional on initially correct identifications.

statement: Replacing selected visual embeddings with an ImageNet-derived mean embedding provides a sufficiently natural and selective information-removal baseline for interpreting object-identification changes.
scope: The mean is described as computed across visual tokens from 50,000 ImageNet validation images. The paper motivates it by visual-token norms, but does not independently establish norm preservation, distributional validity, or preservation of unrelated information.

statement: Replacing the small set of visual tokens selected by unusually high norms can have little effect on object identification in filtered VLM tasks.
scope: Tokens selected using the paper's two-standard-deviation norm criterion, averaging 3.1 tokens in the reported LLaVA-1.5 description and polling settings. This does not establish that all global representations are dispensable or compare register and object tokens at equal budgets.

statement: Object-identification performance can remain unchanged when tested incoming attention connections to the last row of visual tokens are blocked.
scope: Object-plus-one-buffer-to-last-row and other-visual-tokens-to-last-row masks in the paper's VQA setting. The result does not exclude summaries at other positions, surviving pathways, or last-row dependence in other tasks.

statement: Linear-bottleneck ReLU reconstruction models trained on independent, identically distributed sparse features can develop increasingly uniform diagonal gains, biases, and rowwise interference statistics as input dimension grows.
scope: The reported synthetic Bernoulli(p) times Uniform[0,1] inputs, Adam training, and dimension–sparsity–compression sweeps; not a theorem about learning dynamics, arbitrary sparse data, or simultaneous dimension and sparsity limits.

statement: When feature gains and biases are shared and normalized cross-feature interference has a common Gaussian distribution, expected per-coordinate reconstruction loss reduces to a scalar denoising objective determined by gain, bias, and interference variance.
scope: Independent input coordinates, common positive diagonal gain, and identical Gaussian interference distributions after accounting for interference means in the biases. This conditional reduction does not prove that these conditions emerge during training or hold uniformly as p approaches zero.

statement: For independent Bernoulli(p) times Uniform[0,1] inputs and a real reconstruction matrix with unit diagonal and rank at most n_d, average cross-feature interference variance is at least ((4p−3p²)/12)(n_s/n_d−1).
scope: A fixed n_s by n_s real matrix with unit diagonal, 1≤n_d≤n_s, and independent input coordinates. The bound concerns average row variance; a bound on a shared row variance additionally requires rowwise equality. For 0<p≤1, equality is attained precisely by constant-diagonal scaled rank-n_d orthogonal projectors.

statement: Artificial reconstruction weights formed from selected orthogonal Hadamard modes, with numerically optimized scalar gain and bias, can closely match the reconstruction loss of trained sparse-input affine–ReLU autoencoders.
scope: The reported Persian rug comparisons on independent, identically distributed sparse inputs and the displayed sparsity–compression settings. Loss agreement does not establish global optimality, equality of inputwise behavior, or insensitivity to arbitrary weight changes.

statement: For a Uniform[0,1] amplitude observed through independent additive Gaussian noise of standard deviation 0<σ<1/4, every scalar deterministic estimator has mean squared error at least cσ² for an absolute positive constant c.
scope: The estimator observes only the noisy scalar amplitude. Supplying the active-feature indicator does not remove this bound; access to additional coordinates or a joint decoding procedure is outside its scope.

statement: Within a statistically symmetric Gaussian-interference model with minimum-variance encoding, optimal affine–ReLU per-coordinate reconstruction loss lies between Ω(p²/r) and O((p²/r)log(1/p)) in the high-sparsity regime p≪r≪1 with (p/r)log(1/p)→0.
scope: r=n_d/n_s; the large-dimension Gaussian approximation is assumed before applying the high-sparsity analysis. The variance is ((4p−3p²)/12)(1/r−1), and the upper construction requires its negative threshold to vanish. These bounds leave a logarithmic gap and do not establish an exact constant-factor law.

statement: Stopping Adam training when successive moving-average losses cease improving yields sufficiently optimal sparse-reconstruction models to infer properties of the optimum.
scope: The paper's 1,024-example batches and successive 100-batch stopping comparison. Matching the constructed model's loss provides a consistency check but does not certify a global optimum.

statement: When a reconstruction bottleneck perfectly represents selected features and replaces every omitted feature by its mean, its squared reconstruction loss equals the sum of omitted-feature variances.
scope: An ideal orthogonal representation of the first m features with Bernoulli-gated independent amplitudes having finite second moments. For small omitted-feature probabilities, loss approximates E[v²] times their total frequency. With frequencies proportional to i^(−α), α>1, and n≫m≫1, the tail scales approximately as m^(1−α).

statement: Strongly skewed feature frequencies can produce reconstruction-loss width exponents greater than one even when unweighted mean squared feature overlap still scales approximately as inverse width.
scope: The reported 1,000-feature power-law frequency sweeps. The proposed exponent 2(α−1) is an approximate explanatory trend, not a general theorem or a uniform fit across width ranges.

statement: At fixed power-law frequency exponent one and a specified superposition-control setting, increasing expected feature activity can primarily increase reconstruction-loss magnitude without substantially changing its width exponent.
scope: Nine activation densities from one to the harmonic-sum maximum allowed by p_1≤1, with 1,000 features and the reported width and decay sweeps; not arbitrary frequency or density regimes.

statement: Token frequencies from selected language-model tokenizers can exhibit rank-frequency power-law fits with exponents near one across several text corpora.
scope: Four tokenizers associated with OPT, Qwen2.5, GPT-2, and Pythia on WikiText-103, Pile-10k, C4, and BookCorpus. This concerns sampled token frequencies rather than the frequencies of arbitrary semantic or computational features.

statement: Token-associated output-head vectors provide sufficiently representative atomic features to infer language-model representation limits from their frequency and overlap statistics.
scope: The paper's explicitly naive token-to-feature mapping. Tokens may provide a lower bound on the number of independently represented language features; abstract and context-dependent features are not measured.

statement: A sparse autoencoder can learn a shared encoding and decoding dictionary by unrolling greedy residual-guided feature selection and accumulating selected projection coefficients.
scope: Algorithm 1 selects the largest signed dictionary projection at each step and accumulates contributions over T steps, yielding support size at most T. This is matching pursuit rather than orthogonal matching pursuit and does not guarantee globally optimal sparse codes.

statement: Subtracting a residual's projection onto a unit-norm dictionary atom makes the updated residual orthogonal to that atom.
scope: For a unit-norm selected atom d and update r_next=r-d(d^T r). Orthogonality is to the immediately selected atom; later updates can reintroduce projections onto earlier atoms. This does not prove orthogonality between selected atoms or identify hierarchy levels.

statement: Each unit-norm matching-pursuit projection update reduces squared reconstruction residual by the square of its selected projection coefficient.
scope: Residual updates with coefficient d^T r and ||d||=1 give ||r_next||²-||r||²=-(d^T r)². The decrease is strict only for a nonzero selected projection and concerns sequential residual updates rather than truncating an already accumulated code.

statement: Residual-guided MP-SAE training can recover hierarchical generating directions and coefficients more faithfully than the tested Vanilla, BatchTopK, and Matryoshka recipes when within-level interference is low or moderate.
scope: Twenty generating directions in R20, 11 parents and nine children, one or two active concepts, variable positive firing magnitudes, and the specified training recipes. Baselines target mean L0=1.36; MP-SAE instead stops on residual norm or support stabilization. Exact recovery is reported at correlations 0 and 0.3, with degradation at 0.6 and 0.9.

statement: MP-SAE's separation of parent and child directions depends on their firing-magnitude statistics and can become initialization-dependent when co-occurring magnitudes are perfectly correlated.
scope: The original Matryoshka synthetic benchmark and the paper's positive-amplitude child-distribution sweeps. This does not establish a general necessity theorem for magnitude variation or a universal ordering between MP-SAE and Matryoshka.

statement: MP-SAE dictionaries can have higher global cumulative coherence while their inference-selected feature subsets have lower cumulative coherence than subsets selected by the tested conventional SAEs.
scope: The reported final-layer vision representations and second-block TinyStories residual representations, measured with Babel functions and dictionary-inner-product histograms. Lower subset coherence does not independently establish semantic hierarchy, exact orthogonality, or causal independence.

statement: Increasing MP-SAE inference support can increase sparse-code Gram effective rank over some ranges, but this increase need not persist at larger support sizes.
scope: Entropy effective rank of the amplitude-weighted matrix Z^T Z in the reported vision and TinyStories settings. This metric is not a direct count of semantic concepts or binary co-activation patterns. The vision section does not clearly distinguish separately trained sparsity configurations from inference-only changes.

statement: MP-SAE can produce more features with balanced image-versus-text mean activation than the tested conventional SAEs trained on shared vision-language embedding spaces.
scope: COCO image and caption embeddings from CLIP, SigLIP, SigLIP2, and AIMv2; shared 25× dictionaries, target inference sparsity five, and 20 epochs. The result concerns modality-score distributions rather than verified paired semantic correspondence or a comparison against every multimodal SAE architecture.

statement: Balanced mean activation of a sparse feature across images and captions provides meaningful evidence that the feature represents shared cross-modal semantic content.
scope: Interpretation of intermediate modality scores as genuinely multimodal concepts. Similar activation means alone do not establish that the same concept drives both modalities, that paired examples share support, or that features mediate native model behavior.

statement: Sequentially explaining modality-specific embedding components may leave residuals from which shared image–text semantic features become more accessible.
scope: The proposed explanation of MP-SAE's flatter modality-score distributions. Figure 18 is an illustration, not an isolated test of modality-specific removal. The study does not prove that the recovered semantic information is inaccessible to every single linear readout.

statement: Natural neural representations contain useful feature structure that can be incrementally explained through conditionally orthogonal residual decompositions.
scope: The bridge from the constructed cross-level-orthogonal synthetic hierarchy to interpreting natural vision and language features. Conditional orthogonality is imposed by the synthetic generator; natural hierarchy levels and their semantic correspondence are not independently established. The authors acknowledge possible mismatch in flat, entangled, or categorical regimes.

statement: Clause-aligned weight-sign patterns, interpreted together with bias signs and downstream weight signs, provide sufficiently faithful proxies for the computational channels used by a trained Boolean MLP.
scope: The interpretive bridge from enriched clause-associated sign patterns to a natural computational-channel account. Magnitudes, interference, input restrictions, and negative witnesses can affect computation beyond the sign categories.

statement: Matching each input column to its most correlated absolute-weight column can recover the variable pairings of disjoint pairwise-DNF formulas from trained first-layer weights.
scope: Formulas in which each Boolean variable appears in exactly one two-variable AND clause; recovery is strongest when training data suffice for low same-distribution test error. Column matches need not be symmetric.

statement: If positive-witness rows contain approximately half positive entries and clause-code occurrences share few entries, counting available positive entries suggests an approximate average 4P code-count ceiling of j times ell times rho divided by 8k.
scope: j hidden neurons, ell input variables, positive-witness fraction rho, and k four-variable clauses. The informal estimate ignores shared entries between code occurrences and becomes approximately j times ell divided by 16k when rho is one half. It is not a rigorous capacity bound for arbitrary clause families or neural implementations.

statement: Training otherwise comparable small MLPs on OR versus pairwise-DNF tasks can yield substantially smaller hidden biases in positive-witness neurons for OR.
scope: 16-input, 16-hidden-neuron networks under different task-specific input distributions; the comparison does not isolate the Boolean operation from distributional differences.

statement: Trained MLP weight matrices may admit intrinsic feature-decoding and computation-coding factors that can be recovered sequentially to expose a multilayer feature circuit.
scope: The proposed W_i approximately equals C_i D_i framework. Recovering features after biases and nonlinearities and constructing suitable approximate inverses remain unresolved; no general recovery algorithm or identifiability theorem is supplied.

statement: General-purpose sparse autoencoders can be specialized by fine-tuning them on corpus examples retrieved using a small target-domain seed dataset.
scope: The SSAE construction preserves dictionary width and encoder–decoder architecture while changing training data and optionally the training objective.

statement: TERM-trained specialized SAEs can retain replacement performance competitive with ordinary domain fine-tuning over selected active-feature ranges, with deterioration reported at more extreme sparsities under the tested training recipe.
scope: Gemma-2b physics SSAEs at L0 85–100 and toxicity SSAEs at L0 100–140. The physics caption explicitly reports worse reconstruction outside its stated range; the main text discusses high average risk or inactive features at extreme sparsities.

statement: TERM-trained physics SSAEs can achieve higher explanation-conditioned sequence-classification F1 than ordinary domain-fine-tuned and OWT-fine-tuned SAEs.
scope: The arXiv Physics automated interpretation protocol using Claude 3.5 Sonnet as both explainer and predictor. This concerns activation prediction rather than independently established monosemanticity or mechanistic faithfulness.

statement: Large-positive-tilt SAE training can reduce maximum reconstruction error and tail-token error variability while increasing average reconstruction error.
scope: Width-64 SAEs on the seventh-layer residual stream of TinyStories-1M, evaluated at reported checkpoints with L0 16 after one epoch, using tilt 10^9.

statement: Large-positive-tilt SAE training can produce more geometrically dispersed decoder directions than ordinary ERM in a small language-model setting.
scope: The width-64, L0-16 TinyStories-1M seventh-layer SAE comparison. Geometric dispersion does not independently establish the number, identity, or completeness of represented semantic concepts.

statement: High-loss examples under an SAE disproportionately expose underrepresented rare concepts, making loss-based upweighting a useful way to allocate capacity toward those concepts.
scope: The rationale for TERM-based rare-concept discovery. The tilted loss includes reconstruction and sparsity terms; high loss need not uniquely indicate semantic rarity rather than activation scale, noise, formatting, or other difficult structure.

statement: For equal-width independent binary codes with equal model costs, a minority-cluster entropy reduction lowers cluster-conditioned total description length exactly when it outweighs the sample-count-weighted majority-cluster entropy increase.
scope: The conditional coding calculation DL_data = k[N_A H(p_A) + N_B H(p_B)], with independent binary coordinates and uniform activation probability within each cluster. Cluster identity must be available to the coding scheme or its side-information cost treated equally. This does not establish that optimizing TERM produces the stipulated code distributions.

statement: TERM may improve SAE interpretability by producing compositional features and reducing the description length of poorly represented examples.
scope: The proposed explanation linking changed feature activations, explanation scores, and MDL. Appendix L does not derive the required code-probability changes from TERM, and shorter codes are not independently validated as semantic interpretability.

statement: For any real matrix W, its Gram and frame operators share their positive eigenvalues, and W maps the corresponding Gram eigenspaces bijectively onto the frame eigenspaces.
scope: Finite real matrices M = W^T W and F = WW^T. For positive eigenvalue lambda, the frame projector is P = lambda^(-1) W E W^T. F is invariant under column permutations and transforms by conjugation under orthogonal activation-coordinate changes; arbitrary invertible changes need not preserve its spectral geometry.

statement: A nonzero dictionary column defines a probability distribution over frame-operator eigenvalues whose mean equals its Rayleigh quotient, giving fractional dimensionality D_i = ||w_i||^2 / E_mu_i[lambda].
scope: Finite real dictionaries, nonzero columns, and orthogonal projectors onto distinct positive eigenvalues of WW^T. Spectral measures retain norm allocation across eigenspaces but do not specify relative angles within a degenerate eigenspace.

statement: The sum of fractional feature dimensionalities is bounded by dictionary rank, with equality exactly when every nonzero column lies in a single eigenspace of the frame operator.
scope: Finite real dictionaries with zero columns omitted, D_i = ||w_i||^4/(w_i^T F w_i), and leverage scores ell_i = w_i^T F^+ w_i. Rank need not equal ambient hidden dimension; the full-hidden-capacity specialization additionally requires full row rank.

statement: Tied-weight ReLU reconstruction models trained on uniformly important synthetic sparse features can attain summed fractional dimensionality close to their hidden width across a broad width–sparsity sweep.
scope: The reported 3,200 runs with 1,024 features, 32 hidden widths spanning 16–512, 50 sparsities spanning 0–0.99, and two seeds per configuration. Numerical tolerances for near saturation are unavailable in the supplied figure text.

statement: When every nonzero dictionary column is a frame-operator eigenvector, columns partition by eigenvalue into orthogonal tight frames, and fractional dimensionality within each partition equals squared column norm divided by its eigenvalue.
scope: Finite real dictionaries and partitions by distinct positive eigenvalues. For unit-norm columns, a partition of p vectors spanning d dimensions has frame constant p/d and D_i = d/p. Tightness alone does not determine exact geometry or distinguish orthogonal subclusters sharing the same eigenvalue.

statement: In trained synthetic reconstruction models, stronger feature spectral localization is associated with closer agreement to inverse-eigenvalue dimensionality–norm slopes, while higher input sparsity is associated with greater spectral diffusion.
scope: Clusterwise analysis of the reported 3,200 uniform-sparsity toy-model runs, comprising 3,276,800 feature columns. Numerical aggregate results and the complete cluster and numerical eigenspace identification procedure are not supplied in readable text.

statement: If summed fractional dimensionality is at least (1-epsilon) times dictionary rank, the fraction of leverage mass belonging to features with relative slack at least tau is at most epsilon/tau.
scope: Positive rank r, nonzero columns, ell_i = w_i^T F^+ w_i, sigma_i = 1 - D_i/ell_i, and tau in (0,1). The bound concerns leverage-weighted high-slack mass, not feature counts or concentration onto individual eigenvalues without further spectral conditions.

statement: A feature's squared residual from its frame Rayleigh-quotient eigenvector approximation, normalized by squared feature norm, equals the eigenvalue variance of its spectral measure.
scope: Nonzero dictionary columns, F = WW^T, and kappa_i = E_mu_i[lambda]. The identity is ||F w_i - kappa_i w_i||^2 / ||w_i||^2 = Var_mu_i(lambda). Small residual need not imply concentration on one eigenvalue when eigenvalues are closely spaced.

statement: A feature whose spectral measure is supported in a narrow positive eigenvalue interval has relative fractional-dimensionality slack bounded by the square of that interval's relative half-width.
scope: For nonzero dictionary column w_i with spectral support in [a,b], 0 < a <= b, sigma_i = 1 - D_i/ell_i satisfies sigma_i <= ((b-a)/(b+a))^2. This sufficient condition does not establish the converse or concentration on a single eigenvalue.

statement: A feature Gram matrix belongs to a specified symmetric commutative association-scheme algebra exactly when it acts as a scalar on every canonical stratum of that algebra.
scope: A supplied Bose–Mesner algebra with canonical orthogonal idempotents S_e. Membership means M = sum_e theta_e S_e. Distinct strata may have equal theta_e and merge into one Gram eigenspace; the criterion does not establish a unique association scheme or exhaustive geometric identification from frame spectra.

statement: A cluster of p vectors is a centered unit regular simplex precisely when its Gram matrix is p/(p-1) times the orthogonal projector onto the complement of the all-ones vector.
scope: p >= 2, with geometry understood up to orthogonal transformations on its span. The kernel is span(1), the positive eigenspace is 1-perp, and the positive eigenvalue is p/(p-1). Tightness and p = d+1 without the centering/kernel condition do not establish this exact simplex geometry.

statement: For a differentiable loss depending on W through W^T W, Euclidean weight-gradient flow induces Gram dynamics dot(M) = -(M Phi + Phi M), where Phi is the sum of the Gram gradient and its transpose.
scope: Ordinary Euclidean gradient flow on W with M = W^T W and Phi = grad_M L + (grad_M L)^T = 2 Sym(grad_M L). Other parameters may enter the loss but are held fixed for this weight derivative. ReLU expressions apply where the required derivatives exist or under a specified kink convention.

statement: Along Gram gradient flow, a gradient kernel commuting with the Gram spectral projectors eliminates instantaneous transport between distinct spectral groups.
scope: Differentiable symmetric Gram paths, isolated spectral groups, and Phi commuting with every current group projector. Persistence across an interval requires the condition to continue holding and the tracked groups to remain separated. Eigenvalues can still drift, and a degenerate group may split internally.

statement: Uniform-sparsity reconstruction training may favor dynamically stable capacity-saturated tight-frame configurations.
scope: The proposed explanation for persistent toy-model geometries. The conditional argument requires compatible loss symmetry and a commutative association-scheme algebra; uniform sparsity and tightness alone are not shown to ensure these conditions. No attraction or perturbation-stability evaluation is reported.

statement: CLIP embeddings can be converted into named sparse coordinates by solving nonnegative Lasso over a fixed text-encoded concept vocabulary after modality-specific centering and normalization.
scope: SpLiCE's fixed-vocabulary construction; training-free means no new dictionary or backbone training, while individual representations require optimization. The prose and reconstruction equation differ on whether the decoded vector is normalized before adding the image mean.

statement: A shared sparse nonnegative concept space, with nuisance-invariant concept-linear encoders and exact image–text agreement, provides a useful idealization for reasoning about semantic CLIP decompositions.
scope: The latent-variable model and sufficient conditions in Section 3. Their exact validity for natural CLIP embeddings is explicitly disclaimed; the composition diagnostic tests only a limited consequence of linearity, and modality preprocessing does not establish all assumptions.

statement: Positive coefficients on text-encoded concept directions provide sufficiently specific indicators of constituent image content to interpret coefficient removal as manipulating that content.
scope: SpLiCE's named coefficients and their semantic interpretation. Correlated phrases, omitted concepts, and potentially nonunique decompositions complicate this inference; prediction changes do not establish complete concept erasure.

statement: Encoders that are nuisance-invariant, linear in shared sparse nonnegative latent concepts, and equal across modalities admit exact sparse image decompositions using the corresponding pure-concept text vectors.
scope: The exact idealized latent-variable model, with dictionary columns equal to text-encoder outputs for latent coordinate vectors. This establishes existence, not uniqueness, Lasso recovery, coverage by the practical phrase vocabulary, or satisfaction by normalized practical CLIP embeddings.

statement: Requiring nonnegative concept coefficients can improve agreement between SpLiCE decompositions and human-caption content while sacrificing some embedding reconstruction fidelity.
scope: Signed versus nonnegative SpLiCE under the reported vocabulary and preprocessing, using caption-token Hausdorff distance as semantic relevance.

statement: Embedding-space Hausdorff distance between selected concept phrases and filtered human-caption tokens provides a useful proxy for the semantic relevance of an image's concept decomposition.
scope: MSCOCO captions and CLIP token embeddings. Captions can omit visible concepts, and embedding proximity does not independently establish concept presence or explanatory faithfulness.

statement: Separately centering image embeddings and text-concept vectors can improve fixed-dictionary nonnegative CLIP decomposition on classification, reconstruction, and caption-agreement metrics.
scope: The reported SpLiCE preprocessing ablation; centered pairwise similarity distributions alone do not establish complete cross-modal semantic alignment or preservation of all discriminative content.

statement: The source and size of a fixed semantic vocabulary can affect SpLiCE classification performance without producing corresponding changes in reconstruction cosine similarity.
scope: The reported CIFAR100 vocabulary comparisons. These tests do not establish that every corpus-derived dictionary outperforms every LLM-generated dictionary or that vocabulary size alone explains all differences.

statement: SpLiCE's highest-weight concept explanations can receive higher human image-relevance and informativeness ratings than LF-CBM and IP-OMP explanations.
scope: Twenty randomly chosen, correctly predicted ImageNet images, six concepts per explanation, paired method comparisons, and 1–5 Likert ratings. This does not establish improved human prediction or debugging performance.

statement: Antonym phrases and phrases prefixed with 'not' need not occupy opposite directions in CLIP embedding space.
scope: Seventy-one MIT States concept–antonym pairs and concept-versus-not-concept comparisons over the chosen vocabulary, before and after centering.

statement: Moments of unembedding-projected SAE decoder directions can help screen for features associated with narrow token groups, capitalization and spacing partitions, broader prediction categories, and suppression categories.
scope: Exploratory GPT-2 Small layer-8 residual-stream SAE analysis; selected examples rather than a validated classifier or a measurement of family prevalence.

statement: Running-sum enrichment of predefined token sets against projected SAE decoder rankings can identify candidate features associated with those sets and suggest interpretations broader than their highest-ranked tokens.
scope: The 5,000 highest-skewness GPT-2 Small layer-8 SAE features and the supplied regex, verb-form, and common-name token libraries. Scores are exploratory and lack calibrated significance.

statement: Predefined vocabulary subsets encode their intended lexical or semantic categories sufficiently well for enrichment against them to generate meaningful feature hypotheses.
scope: Regex sets, individually tagged NLTK verb tokens, and traditionally gendered common-name lists. The post explicitly relies on meaningful sets while documenting errors, omissions, overlap, and tokenization complications.

statement: Noisy, incomplete, or overlapping token sets can make SAE enrichment hits ambiguous, so a high score alone does not establish an exhaustive or exclusive feature description.
scope: Selected NLTK verb-form and common-name enrichment examples in GPT-2 Small layer-8 residual-stream SAEs.

statement: A shared hook and activation-caching interface can adapt logit readouts, direct logit attribution, attention visualization, and activation patching to vision transformers.
scope: The Prisma functionality described in this release, with reported support for timm vanilla ViTs, TinyCLIP, a video vision transformer, and custom tiny transformers. Comprehensive compatibility and researcher-productivity benefits are not benchmarked.

statement: Individual attention heads in a classification-trained vanilla vision transformer can exhibit attention-score patterns associated with image corners, edges, and regular spatial structure.
scope: Qualitatively selected early-layer heads labeled Corner, Edges, and Modulus in the demonstrated ViT. No population prevalence, cross-image consistency rate, or causal function is established.
