statement: Eight-class emotion probing can perform worse on situational clinical narratives than on keyword-rich examples, with smaller observed gaps in larger Llama and Gemma checkpoints.
scope: Peak residual-stream AUROC on 80 Set A versus 96 Set B emotional examples. The independently constructed sets differ in more than keyword presence, and checkpoint comparisons do not isolate parameter scale.

statement: Detecting emotional significance and identifying a specific emotion category can rely on dissociable language-model mechanisms with different sensitivities to explicit emotion vocabulary.
scope: The proposed interpretation of the six-model clinical-vignette experiments. Different decoding difficulty and timing do not establish distinct causal pathways. Whole-state patches do not selectively manipulate salience, and their success endpoint is inconsistently described.

statement: Replacing answer-position activations with emotional donor activations selectively transfers affective salience sufficiently to distinguish it from emotion-category transfer and other donor information.
scope: The interpretive premise used for Set A-to-Set B whole-activation patching. No salience-specific subspace intervention or matched neutral-donor control is reported, and the success definition conflicts with the claimed interpretation.

statement: Emotion classification on situational clinical narratives can be sensitive to individual attention and FFN output knockouts at more layers than classification on keyword-rich examples.
scope: The tested single-layer zero-output interventions and reported greater-than-20% accuracy-drop criterion. The source does not clearly distinguish relative from percentage-point drops. Counts measure intervention-relative fragility rather than complete circuit distribution or semantic specificity.

statement: Larger checkpoints in the tested Llama and Gemma panel can have fewer individual layer-output knockouts causing large emotion-classification losses than the tested 1B checkpoints.
scope: Six checkpoints at approximately 1B, 8B, and 9B parameters, with the reported greater-than-20% accuracy-drop threshold. Architecture, training, depth, and family differences prevent a causal scaling conclusion; low singleton sensitivity does not itself establish redundancy or self-repair.

statement: Base Llama and Gemma checkpoints can already support strong decoding of situational emotion labels without instruction tuning.
scope: The three evaluated base checkpoints and the constructed clinical stimuli. This establishes pretraining availability of accessible label information without validating the broader Persona Selection Model or isolating effects of a specific post-training procedure.

statement: Attention heads can be ranked without discovery-time ablations by counting positive-only argmax sparse-autoencoder codes, or by counting head participation in highly ranked positive-only code-pair co-occurrences.
scope: Position-averaged head outputs, a shared tied-weight ReLU SAE, post-training argmax discretization, and thresholded softmax rankings. The co-occurrence construction selects heads and does not independently recover directed causal edges.

statement: Positive-only discrete SAE code rankings can achieve high reference-head classification ROC AUC on IOI, Greater-than, and Docstring, with comparative performance depending on hyperparameter selection.
scope: The three supplied task datasets and manual reference labels. Both node-based and co-occurrence-based procedures ultimately classify heads; their AUCs do not establish directed causal edge recovery or complete native mechanisms.

statement: Training a task-specific SAE on five to ten prompts can support effective discrete-code head ranking even when substantially more prompts are needed to estimate code-occurrence statistics.
scope: The reported IOI, Greater-than, and Docstring sample-size sweeps. SAE-training sample efficiency is distinct from the total labeled-prompt requirement.

statement: Head subsets selected by discrete SAE codes can retain or slightly exceed full-model aggregate IOI and year-span task scores when excluded head outputs are replaced by specified corrupted activations.
scope: GPT-2 Small, reference-F1-selected head sets, IOI logit difference, and Greater-than probability difference and cutoff sharpness. Other model machinery remains available; aggregate score retention does not establish identical predictions or complete mechanism recovery.

statement: Discrete SAE head-discovery ROC AUC can remain relatively stable over ranges of dictionary width, sparsity penalty, and retained co-occurrence-pair budget, without establishing a universal selection threshold.
scope: The reported three-task sweeps, including searches over 128–2,048 features and sparsity penalties 0.01–0.1. Robustness is task- and parameter-range-dependent.

statement: The construction of negative prompts materially affects discrete SAE reference-circuit recovery, with task-matched corruptions outperforming several alternative negative constructions in the evaluated settings.
scope: Five Greater-than negative-example types and the IOI experiment adding unrelated Pile examples. These results do not independently establish that better negatives selectively switch off the intended circuit.

statement: Discrete SAE training and code-based head selection over cached activations can complete in seconds to under a minute across the evaluated GPT-2 sizes.
scope: The reported single-V100 SAE-training and threshold-sweeping workflow. Inclusion of language-model loading and activation collection is unclear; hours-long ACDC comparisons use cited timings rather than a controlled matched-runtime benchmark.

statement: Discrete SAE code counts can perfectly separate the supplied active-component labels in compiled transformers when negative activations are constructed using known zero-versus-nonzero weight structure.
scope: Four Tracr tasks with maximum sequence length six and deliberately weight-informed Q/K/V corruption. This is controlled component discrimination rather than recovery of unknown natural circuits.

statement: Discrete SAE head rankings can recover repeated-token prediction behavior in several pretrained transformers without using output-based attribution scores for discovery.
scope: Synthetic sequences formed by repeating ten sampled token IDs, contrasted with nonrepeating continuations. Evaluations use output KL or repeated-token loss rather than independently established induction-circuit membership.

statement: Discrete SAE code scoring can distinguish reference circuit heads more effectively than ranking heads by the norm of their positive-minus-negative mean outputs in a small-sample comparison.
scope: The paper's ten-example head-activation mean-difference comparison on IOI, Greater-than, and Docstring. This does not establish superiority over other raw-activation classifiers or matched optimized alternatives.

statement: Adding an auxiliary cosine contrastive objective or substituting code-pair entropy for positive-only co-occurrence scoring can worsen discrete SAE reference-circuit recovery.
scope: The specific IOI contrastive-loss and entropy-scoring variants evaluated in Appendices J and K; this does not establish failure of contrastive learning or entropy methods generally.

statement: Existing SAE features can be assigned dataset labels by ranking thresholded token activation-frequency predictions with calibrated F1 and filtering feature–label pairs by label support and optional output influence.
scope: The proposed pipeline searches frequency thresholds 0.05–0.95 in increments of 0.05, uses reference prevalence 0.001 and label-support threshold 50, optionally filters output scores above 0.001, and retains the top 50 remaining pairs per forum. It does not guarantee unique or exhaustive semantic labels.

statement: Selected topic cohorts steered through individual Gemma SAE features can attain AxBench aggregate ratings close to a published LoRA reference while remaining below prompting overall.
scope: Several Stack Exchange-derived cohorts in the Gemma-2-9b-it layer-17 and layer-32 evaluation. LoRA scores are imported from Wu et al. (2025), rather than obtained through a matched-concept LoRA rerun. The comparison does not establish statistical equivalence or general superiority over LoRA.

statement: Under supervised feature selection, the evaluated lowest-L0 Gemma Scope dictionaries show no large reported topic-steering advantage over higher-L0 counterparts.
scope: The evaluated Gemma-2-9b-it layers, forum-derived cohorts, and sparsity ablations. Principal low-L0 dictionaries have approximately 11 and 10 active features; higher-L0 values are not specified in the supplied text. This is a descriptive comparison rather than an equivalence result or a claim about arbitrary SAE configurations.

statement: Applying calibrated-F1 feature labeling to Llama Scope does not necessarily yield effective steering in Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct.
scope: The Appendix E experiment. Evaluated layers, dictionary configurations, selected-pair counts, numerical scores, and detailed intervention settings are not specified in the supplied text. This does not establish failure of all Llama Scope interventions.

statement: Ordinary F1 can yield useful feature-label selections for Gemma steering, so calibrated F1 is not established as necessary for the pipeline's success.
scope: The exploratory Gemma experiment in Appendix E. Exact configurations and numerical outcomes are unavailable. The suggested role of increasing the support threshold from 20 to 50 is speculative rather than isolated experimentally.

statement: Reweighting false positives by the observed-to-reference class-odds ratio makes population F1 equal to F1 under the reference prevalence when class-conditional prediction rates are held fixed.
scope: Binary labels with observed and reference prevalences strictly between zero and one. The result concerns population rates or algebraic reweighting; it does not remove finite-sample variance, label noise, or threshold-selection bias.

statement: Calibrated F1 estimates can remain highly variable when the number of positive examples is small despite population invariance to class prevalence.
scope: The Appendix A Gaussian probe simulation with 10,000 observations, varying positive prevalence, unit-variance class distributions with means zero and two, and reference prevalence one half. The simulation does not establish that support 50 is a universally sufficient threshold.

statement: Lowering the reference prevalence in calibrated-F1 threshold selection can favor more conservative probes and stronger class separation.
scope: The Appendix A Gaussian simulations with one million observations, balanced sampled classes, threshold sweeps, and a class-separation sweep. This does not independently establish why reference prevalence 0.001 works well on Stack Exchange tags.

statement: Agreement between user-assigned topic tags and a feature's token activation frequency provides sufficiently specific evidence of topic content to assign semantic labels to that feature.
scope: The selected Stack Exchange forums, support-filtered tags, and threshold-optimized calibrated-F1 associations. Tags can omit secondary topics, correlate with neighboring concepts, and reflect forum-specific usage. Label support may also proxy topic prevalence in training data.

statement: Inducing concept-consistent text by clamping an SAE feature is sufficient to confirm the assigned concept as that feature's ground-truth semantic label.
scope: The paper's interpretation of steering as validation against dataset-specific interpretability illusions. Intervention-induced output content does not independently establish complete activation semantics, exclusive representation, or ordinary causal mediation.

statement: For every nonzero SAE decoder column u, parameterizing its encoder row as z + u(1−uᵀz)/||u||² enforces encoder–decoder inner product one and spans the entire corresponding affine hyperplane when z is unrestricted.
scope: Exact arithmetic, nonzero decoder columns, and unrestricted n-dimensional free encoder parameters. The implementation fixing the last free coordinate to zero retains full hyperplane coverage only when the decoder's last coordinate is nonzero.

statement: A bias-free one-feature ReLU autoencoder that perfectly reconstructs a nonzero input must have encoder–decoder inner product one.
scope: The supplied two-dimensional, one-latent, single-training-point example with no sparsity penalty and exact reconstruction. It does not establish the appropriate inner product for general overcomplete dictionaries.

statement: Pretrained SAE dictionaries can exhibit bimodal distributions of corresponding encoder–decoder inner products, with populations near zero and near one.
scope: The pretrained Pythia-70M layer-3, LLaMA-3-8B-IT layer-25, and Gemma-2-2B layer-12 residual-stream dictionaries listed in Appendix E. This does not establish bimodality for every modern architecture or training recipe.

statement: SAE encoder–decoder inner products near one may identify meaningful features, while values near zero or below may identify uninterpretable training artifacts.
scope: The semantic interpretation motivating aligned training. The one-feature reconstruction derivation and correlations with MCS and autointerpretability do not establish this classification for arbitrary features or dictionaries.

statement: Enforcing unit encoder–decoder inner products can improve ReLU SAE explained-variance and replacement cross-entropy-recovery frontiers at comparable measured active-feature counts.
scope: Pythia-160M layer 8 and Gemma-2-2B layer 12, approximately 4K/16K/65K dictionaries, 50M Pile training tokens, and four sparsity penalties. A separate 500M-token extension concerns Gemma layer 12 at 65K width.

statement: Unit encoder–decoder inner-product constraints can improve reconstruction in selected TopK and BatchTopK SAE operating regimes.
scope: The reported TopK and BatchTopK dictionary sweeps, illustrated by Gemma-2-2B layer-12 65K dictionaries. The text identifies a low-sparsity regime without giving numerical boundaries.

statement: Enforcing unit encoder–decoder inner products can reduce observed dead-feature fractions to near zero without resampling or auxiliary dead-feature losses.
scope: The reported ReLU, TopK, and BatchTopK experiments on Pythia-160M layer 8 and Gemma-2-2B layer 12, with the 500M-token extension restricted to Gemma 65K. Observation-window details are unspecified.

statement: Combining aligned training with p-annealing can improve feature utilization and usually explained variance relative to p-annealing alone, without uniformly improving replacement cross-entropy recovery.
scope: Pythia-160M layer-8 residual activations, dictionary width 4,096, the reported sparsity sweep, and three random seeds for the reconstruction comparison.

statement: Aligned SAE training can improve spurious-correlation-removal performance, with gains depending on the model and active-feature budget.
scope: SAEBench SCR for 65K dictionaries at Pythia-160M layer 8 and Gemma-2-2B layer 12 under the reported training recipes. Results concern classifier accuracy after selected latent ablations.

statement: Constraining encoder–decoder inner products can retain better reconstruction while reducing dead features compared with the tested weight-tied SAE recipe.
scope: Pythia-160M layer 8 and Gemma-2-2B layer 12, dictionary width 16,384, and the Appendix F comparisons. Weight tying and unit inner-product constraints are not generally nested unless decoder norms are additionally controlled.

statement: Curated hematopoietic stage distances and ontology depth provide sufficiently meaningful proxy targets for learning and evaluating developmental representation geometry.
scope: The stage ontology, branch labels, and developmental-depth targets used for H65. These are reference annotations rather than independently measured developmental trajectories.

statement: Predictive utility and biological annotation agreement in a supervised adaptor built on exported scGPT operators provide sufficient evidence that the resulting standalone predictor recovers an algorithm naturally implemented by scGPT.
scope: The interpretive bridge from exported linear operators and ontology-supervised adaptors to native algorithm extraction. The document does not establish native intervention correspondence, isolate pretraining contributions with matched randomized operators, or show that the adaptor reproduces scGPT's contextual computations.

statement: Frozen scGPT operators can be combined with an ontology-supervised low-dimensional adaptor and separate task readouts to construct standalone cellular predictors that avoid full-transformer inference.
scope: The whole-human scGPT checkpoint, reported 1,200×1,200 exported operators, pooled drift or selected-head feature maps, and LET adaptors. Shared-adaptor training uses internal data; downstream classification probes are subsequently trained on benchmark training donors.

statement: An ontology-trained low-dimensional representation built from scGPT operators can preserve hematopoietic distance relationships and local neighborhoods on selected external immune panels under frozen-adaptor transfer.
scope: The H65 panels. Observation-level non-overlap is established for the Tabula Sapiens external panel; exclusion from scGPT pretraining is not established. Transfer is panel-dependent, and external scores inform some representation choices.

statement: The evaluated H65 cell-trained representation yields stronger donor-local pseudotime association with ontology depth than the tested trajectory and representation baselines.
scope: Robust-V2 donor-local test-only pseudotime on valid runs. Absolute-correlation summaries and paired signed-correlation tests are distinct endpoints. Reused donors limit independence of the split-level inference.

statement: H65 cell-trained representations can improve selected hematopoietic subtype discrimination while trailing established baselines on other classification endpoints.
scope: Eight non-pseudotime Robust-V2 endpoints with grouped donor holdouts. Results do not establish uniform classification superiority or recovery of causal developmental mechanisms.

statement: Selected H65 adaptor-and-probe configurations can outperform the evaluated deeper MLP probes on frozen scGPT embeddings across multiple donor-held-out classification endpoints.
scope: The 12-split comparisons in S20. Adaptor supervision, feature construction, probe architectures, and representation dimensions differ; these comparisons do not establish superiority over all embedding readouts or identify native mechanisms.

statement: The evaluated H65 10D adaptor with an MLP readout can outperform small raw-expression MLPs on selected hematopoietic subtype metrics while performing worse on stage classification.
scope: The two direct raw-expression architectures and 12 grouped donor-holdout splits in S22. Results do not establish that raw-expression predictors generally cannot recover comparable subtype discrimination.

statement: The evaluated H65 4D linear-readout pipeline requires substantially less reported preparation and repeated-split evaluation time than the tested frozen-scGPT embedding-and-MLP pipeline.
scope: S23's runtime accounting for the 4D linear configuration and 12-split campaign. The 5–170 parameter count covers downstream readouts, excluding the shared adaptor and exported operator. It does not describe the 10D MLP2 configuration.

statement: A selected single scGPT operator can replace the pooled exported operator in the evaluated adaptor pipeline without statistically detected losses on the reported classification endpoints.
scope: L2H5 selected through a 96-head external-transfer screen, followed by adaptor and probe retraining. Non-significance does not establish equivalence, native head necessity, or sufficiency of the original contextual attention head.

statement: Low-rank and hard-sparse compression of the selected scGPT exported operator reduce storage while degrading classification performance at the tested compression levels.
scope: Truncated-SVD ranks 8, 16, 32, and 64 and the selected 16-factor hard-sparse surrogate, with adaptors and probes retrained. These results concern tested recipes rather than an impossibility of better compression.

statement: A small subset of SVD factors can account for most pooled fixed-probe ablation damage in an H65 compressed predictor while remaining insufficient to preserve its classification performance.
scope: The selected rank-64 surrogate, its trained downstream machinery, and the reported pooled damage statistic. Necessity is intervention-relative and does not establish native scGPT circuitry, biological causation, or irrecoverability after retraining.

statement: Selected high-impact factors of an H65 operator surrogate can have loading and enrichment patterns associated with hematopoietic lineage programs.
scope: The four selected rank-64 and hard-sparse factors and the reported cached marker and pathway analyses. Associations supply candidate labels rather than evidence of regulatory causation or complete semantic isolation.

statement: Strong supervised classification and pseudotime performance of an H65 representation can coexist with weaker unsupervised branch partition recovery than raw expression.
scope: The canonical donor-holdout split under the tested Scanpy and Palantir wrappers. Wrapper-dependent results do not establish that all unsupervised methods would fail to exploit the representation.

statement: Three-dimensional displays of an H65 latent representation can obscure subtype information accessible in its full ten-dimensional representation.
scope: The reported anchor-trained and cell-trained LET configurations and selected visualization axes. Dimension indices depend on training variant, and correlated axes do not constitute independent biological factors.

statement: Biologically motivated direction edits in an H65 latent representation can produce monotonic shifts in selected computational lineage readouts, with effectiveness varying by contrast.
scope: Source-anchor latent sweeps decoded to feature space on the strict non-overlap external panel. Outcomes are target-fraction and graph-based proxies, not experimental cell-state changes or interventions on native scGPT inference.

statement: Selected H65 representations can exhibit statistically detectable periodic residual geometry after dominant components are removed, without established biological interpretations for those residuals.
scope: The paper's projection-level and latent-level sinusoidal scans, permutation procedures, and selected Gaussian null. The results do not establish that periodic geometry is unique to scGPT or represents particular regulatory programs.

statement: A second scGPT-derived communication-geometry representation can exceed a PCA-2 alignment baseline on an external panel after iterative internal-training changes, although the measured advantage is small and follows repeated external evaluation.
scope: The selected H38 v11 ensemble and its curated interaction-path target. The result does not establish generalization across foundation-model families, native communication mechanisms, or performance on a fresh post-selection external panel.

statement: Low entropy across normalized emotion-conditioned positive-activation frequencies identifies neuron groups sufficiently specific to particular emotions for their masking effects to be interpreted as changes to emotion processing.
scope: The six-category FFN selection procedure in Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and Llama-3.1-70B-Instruct. Low entropy alone does not exclude lexical, topical, stylistic, or generator-related associations, and group-masking effects do not establish semantic specificity.

statement: Entropy-selected emotion-associated FFN neuron groups can differ in category counts and depth distributions between Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and Llama-3.1-70B-Instruct.
scope: The paper's synthetic six-emotion dialogue corpus and stated lowest-entropy 1% selection procedure. Absolute counts depend on architecture and selection, and the comparison does not isolate a causal effect of model size.

statement: Substantial overlap between selected emotion-associated neuron sets can coexist with a large target-emotion accuracy loss after one set is masked.
scope: The reported anger–disgust sets in Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. The observation does not establish that shared neurons are interchangeable or identify how remaining neurons respond to masking.

statement: Among incorrectly classified examples after emotion-associated neuron masking, errors can concentrate in particular alternative labels, including anger–disgust and happiness–surprise confusions.
scope: Conditional error distributions in the paper's six-emotion synthetic dialogue evaluation. These distributions exclude correct predictions and do not measure overall error rates, establish increases over baseline confusion, or identify shared causal emotion representations.

statement: Overlapping or complementary emotion-associated neuron populations may preserve classification performance when a selected emotion-associated group is masked.
scope: Proposed explanation for weak or absent target-emotion accuracy losses, particularly 8B happiness and 70B disgust. The experiments do not distinguish active compensation from pre-existing redundancy, ineffective selection, or alternative classification strategies.

statement: Steering scores averaged over separately sampled, dictionary-specific concept inventories are sufficiently comparable to assess relationships between SAE design, interpretability, and utility.
scope: Each SAE supplies its own 100 feature-description pairs from 1,000 evaluated latents; selected-feature comparisons further change the evaluated population. Comparable concept difficulty and semantic granularity across dictionaries are not independently established.

statement: SAE steering candidates can be ranked by the magnitude of intervention-induced changes in the negative average log probability of the highest-probability next tokens.
scope: Delta C_k equals C_k of the intervened distribution minus C_k of the baseline distribution. The implemented setting uses k=1, amplification 10, and the fixed prefix 'From my experience,'. Candidate sets include positive and negative tails, top-K selections with K from 1 to 5 per direction, and tail quantiles. Main text preserves other feature coefficients, whereas Appendix D zeros them; the latter comparison can include effects of removing other activation content.

statement: Feature subsets selected using Delta Token Confidence can achieve higher average concept-steering scores than output-score-selected subsets and unselected feature populations under the evaluated selection protocol.
scope: The three reported model-level averages over 30 SAEs each, using dictionary-specific Concept100 sets, equal subset sizes between selectors, and a search over confidence-tail selection sets. This compares selected populations rather than improving steering of a fixed concept inventory; independent evaluation for choosing the best feature subset is unclear.

statement: Steering vectors can be constructed by filtering desired-minus-undesired SAE activation means and mapping the resulting sparse feature target through a pretrained affine effect approximator.
scope: FGAA removes features with density above 0.01 and BOS-associated features, selects contrast coordinates, and subtracts a normalized bias-related direction from a normalized target-mapped direction. The evaluated recipe retains 1–8 positive features and no negative features. The construction does not guarantee exact target effects, optimality, or preservation of all untargeted features.

statement: Including negatively contrasted SAE features in a steering target can reduce behavioral-coherence performance relative to selecting positive contrast features alone.
scope: The reported FGAA feature-count investigations, with explicit joint positive/negative-count grids for anger and praise in Gemma-2-2B. This does not establish that avoidance-based steering is generally inferior or that every negative-feature target is harmful.

statement: FGAA steering directions can remain closely aligned with single-feature SAE-TS directions while differing substantially from raw CAA and SAE decoder directions.
scope: Nine selected targets at layer 12 in each of two Gemma models. The selected FGAA directions need not all be multi-feature directions. Directional alignment does not establish identical semantic effects, mechanisms, or generation distributions.

statement: Removing frequently activating and BOS-dominated SAE coordinates preferentially removes nuisance content while retaining the feature information needed for behavioral steering.
scope: FGAA's density threshold of 0.01 and BOS-feature removal in the tested Gemma dictionaries. The rationale rests on qualitative activation observations; separate quantitative ablations do not establish the contribution or semantic specificity of either filter.

statement: Enrichment of an SAE feature's highest-activation-associated genes against biological databases provides a useful proxy for the feature's biological meaning.
scope: Top-20 genes ranked by mean activation magnitude, five annotation databases, Fisher enrichment tests, and Benjamini–Hochberg correction. Association does not establish semantic exclusivity, a unique biological concept, or native causal use.

statement: Enrichment of perturbation-responsive SAE features for a perturbed transcription factor's known targets provides an informative assay of regulatory knowledge encoded in a single-cell model.
scope: The Geneformer K562 assay using TRRUST target sets, feature-associated top genes, and 20 perturbed cells per target. Interpreting low recovery as absent regulatory knowledge requires adequate feature extraction, annotation coverage, sampling, and statistical sensitivity.

statement: Fourfold-expanded TopK SAEs can reconstruct substantial residual-stream variance across all layers of Geneformer V2-316M and scGPT whole-human while retaining 32 coefficients per position.
scope: The reported layerwise dictionaries and sampled K562 or Tabula Sapiens activation distributions. Reconstruction does not establish downstream behavioral preservation, semantic recovery, or simultaneous whole-model replacement fidelity.

statement: Most learned Geneformer SAE decoder directions can lack high cosine alignment with every leading SVD axis while their associated gene sets retain biological enrichments.
scope: The top 50 SVD axes at each layer and the stated decoder cosine threshold above 0.7. This does not establish absence from the SVD span, invisibility to all linear methods, or an inventory of equally many distinct biological concepts.

statement: Zeroing selected annotated Geneformer SAE coefficients during reconstruction replacement can produce larger mean logit changes at annotated gene positions than at other positions.
scope: Fifty richly annotated layer-11 features, 200 cells per feature, and the absolute ratio of signed mean target versus other-position logit changes. The procedure replaces the entire state with a modified reconstruction; a reconstruction-only comparison is unspecified, and cancellation in signed means can affect the ratio.

statement: Strong cross-layer co-activation links can remain common among single-cell model SAE features even when decoder directions lack persistent geometric matches.
scope: Three selected layer pairs per model and PMI above three. PMI links are observational associations, not established directed transmission or conserved causal mechanisms. The tables use distinct source, target, and conditional coverage denominators.

statement: Limited regulatory-response recovery by SAE analysis may reflect missing regulatory information in Geneformer's representations rather than insufficient tissue diversity in SAE training.
scope: The proposed interpretation of the K562-only and pooled-data comparisons. Those comparisons do not establish model representations as the exclusive bottleneck or exclude alternative SAE architectures, combinatorial readouts, annotation gaps, or assay-sensitivity limitations. Perturbation mapping was not performed in scGPT.

statement: Most unannotated Geneformer SAE features can share co-activation communities with annotated features while only a small fraction form standalone gene-set clusters.
scope: Layers 0, 5, 11, and 17; top-20-gene Jaccard clustering and the reported PMI communities. Because communities cover nearly all features, co-membership does not independently establish biological meaning or exclude noise.

statement: Single-cell model SAE activations can exhibit cell-type-associated patterns across immune, kidney, and lung transcriptomic samples.
scope: The selected 3,000 Tabula Sapiens cells and 56 cell types. Geneformer dictionaries were trained on K562 activations; scGPT dictionaries used the Tabula Sapiens collection. Enrichment does not establish cell-identity exclusivity or independent generalization for scGPT.

statement: Automatic language identification and GPT-4 content ratings provide useful operational measurements of desired-language response frequency and multilingual generation quality.
scope: langdetect language labels and GPT-4 1–10 ratings on translated Vicuna questions. Independent human calibration, handling of mixed-language responses, and evaluation sample counts are not supplied.

statement: Aligned multilingual sentence representations can become more similar after early layers and less similar near output layers, alongside an opposing depth profile of selected language-associated neuron counts.
scope: LLaMA-2-70B sentence embeddings from translated Vicuna texts, using the paper's mean sentence embedding similarity measurement.

statement: Language-mean-shift sentence-alignment analysis can yield multiple prominent target languages in a multilingual language model.
scope: The BLOOM checkpoint labeled 170B in Section 3.3.3 and Figure 7(b), evaluated on translated Vicuna texts with h_k − v_k + v_c.

statement: Higher aligned-sentence similarity after shifting representations toward a target-language mean provides a meaningful measure of that language's dominance in multilingual processing.
scope: Equation 6's dominance score. Shared mean offsets and representation geometry can influence similarity; the score is not independently validated against causal reliance on a dominant-language computation.

statement: Feature-specific recurrent states learned to reconstruct language-model activations provide informative proxies for information maintained by the language model across tokens.
scope: The interpretive bridge from an auxiliary encoder's explicit temporal aggregation to native contextual representations. The encoder introduces its own memory; persistence, probing, and decoder-direction sensitivity do not independently identify the language model's memory mechanism or establish that every retained signal remains present in its current hidden state.

statement: Activation-conditioned signals along standard SAE decoder directions can persist across hundreds of subsequent tokens and decay more slowly in coherent documents than in cross-document sentence concatenations.
scope: BatchTopK and Matryoshka dictionaries at the two studied residual-stream sites. Features require at least 256 activation events, 64 valid anchors at every evaluated lag, and a non-negligible projection-elevation denominator. Conditional projection persistence does not isolate repeated evidence or a unique persistent concept.

statement: Adding fitted contributions from past activations along their corresponding decoder directions can modestly reduce held-out standard-SAE reconstruction errors when the activations come from the target document's actual history.
scope: Diagonal additive corrections to BatchTopK and Matryoshka reconstructions at selected lags from 1–32. Controls use unrelated shuffled-corpus activations to predict the same natural-document targets. Improvements are not positive at every model–lag combination.

statement: A sparse activation encoder can be extended with independently learned per-feature exponential moving averages and a linear decoder reconstructing from the accumulated state.
scope: Persistent SAE uses h_j(t)=λ_jh_j(t−1)+(1−λ_j)a_j(t), zero sequence-initial states, and λ_j=0.999 sigmoid(l_j). BatchTopK constrains sparse updates rather than accumulated-state sparsity. Temporal roles are not preassigned, and no auxiliary temporal objective is used; the training recipe retains the shared dead-feature auxiliary loss.

statement: Learning feature-specific recurrence can retain reconstruction close to ordinary BatchTopK in one residual-stream setting while incurring a larger reconstruction gap in another.
scope: Two sites, 16,384 features, nominal BatchTopK update budget 20, approximately 500 million activation tokens, and matched optimization steps. Accumulated state is denser than sparse updates, and sequence access differs between methods. No downstream replacement-loss comparison is reported.

statement: Persistence coefficients learned through activation reconstruction can rank features by the duration of their activation-associated decoder-aligned signals.
scope: Quintile-level median empirical persistence in the two evaluated Persistent SAE dictionaries. This establishes an ordering diagnostic rather than exact identification of native memory timescales.

statement: Low-persistence SAE features can have more predictable token-wise activation explanations than high-persistence features under local automated interpretation evaluations.
scope: Lowest-λ 50% versus highest-λ 1% of each evaluated Persistent SAE, scored on sparse updates rather than accumulated states. This comparison concerns local activation-description prediction, not comprehensive semantic or mechanistic interpretability.

statement: Sparse updates to low- and high-persistence SAE features can have different token-category distributions, with the lowest-persistence group relatively enriched at nouns and the highest at punctuation and conjunctions.
scope: The reported learned-λ quintile analysis at the two studied sites, using six token categories and frequencies normalized by corpus-level category prevalence. Update-location associations do not establish that punctuation performs contextual integration or reveal the information encoded by accumulated states.

statement: Decoder directions weighted by injection-probe coefficients from slow recurrent SAE states can retain positive influence on an external monitor's injection-judgment logit margin across increasing post-injection distances.
scope: Single-site additions and subtractions at the final monitoring-query token, using directions fitted at the injection-span endpoint. The outcome is judgment-margin sensitivity, not improved judgment accuracy, natural mediation, or changes to the original agent's actions. Equal intervention norms do not establish equal functional disruption or semantic specificity.

statement: For a fixed nonzero linear readout, projecting an activation onto the readout direction preserves its scalar output, and activations with equal outputs differ by a vector in the readout's kernel.
scope: A fixed w = W^T phi with w nonzero. The orthogonal representative is (w^T h / ||w||^2)w. This establishes a readout-preserving decomposition, not independent identification of semantic content or a complete feature ontology.

statement: Linear communication interfaces in transformers force communicated semantic features to occupy context-invariant linear subspaces.
scope: The advertised architectural interpretation of Theorem 3.7. Its proof assumes exact semantic linear decodability and constructs relevant components through that readout; it does not derive semantic linear decodability from architecture or identify a unique semantic decomposition.

statement: A feature with K linearly separable values has a minimal context-invariant representation subspace of dimension at most K minus one.
scope: Proposition B.2, including its binary-feature directional-invariance conclusion. The supplied argument bounds the span of K centered representatives but does not establish that those representatives exhaust contextual feature information. Linear separability also does not require affine independence.

statement: When vocabulary size greatly exceeds hidden width, sparse feature activity and shared semantic attributes force optimal token unembeddings to factorize over a much smaller inventory of reusable semantic directions.
scope: Proposition 3.8 and Appendix B.1. The dimensional constraint rules out mutually orthogonal nonzero vectors for every token but does not establish semantic factors, their number, sparsity, or optimality. The proposed representation cost is not a fully specified optimization problem.

statement: A transformer with a nonlinear classification head can learn modular division accurately while its tested hidden-state linear probe performs poorly and its embeddings lack the reported Fourier-circle structure.
scope: The reported two-layer transformer trained on division modulo 97. Seed counts, optimizer settings, probe details, and a matched linear-head control are unspecified. Absence of the displayed geometry does not establish absence of all Fourier information.

statement: LayerNorm maps an additive term along a fixed feature direction into an additive term along a fixed transformed direction, with its coefficient divided by the activation's context-dependent normalization scale.
scope: For h = alpha d + eta, centering P = I - 11^T/d, and positive normalization scale sigma(h), the transformed direction is gamma elementwise-multiplied by Pd. A nonzero direction additionally requires this transformed vector to be nonzero. Orthogonality of the remainder and semantic decodability need not be preserved.

statement: Adding a vector to the input of a fixed linear unembedding changes each token logit by the inner product of that vector with the token's unembedding row.
scope: Direct edit h' = h + lambda d at a readout with logits W_U h. Intervening nonlinear layers or changing normalization are excluded. Individual softmax probability changes depend on relative logit shifts, rather than the sign of one token's absolute logit shift alone.

statement: High-level semantic and contextual variables generally remain more stable across nearby language tokens than local syntactic variables.
scope: The temporal-consistency premise used to interpret persistent dictionary features as semantic or contextual. Assumption 1 additionally stipulates similar high-level latents for tokens sampled from the same sequence; this need not hold across topic changes or long documents.

statement: A language-model activation can be modeled as an invertible encoding of high-level and low-level generating variables, with the high-level variables alone approximately reconstructing the activation and the low-level variables supplying residual information.
scope: The single-layer generative model x_t=g(h_t,l_t), with ||g(h_t,0)-x_t|| bounded by epsilon. Invertibility and this reconstruction hierarchy are stipulated rather than established for natural language-model activations.

statement: Topic labels, source-sequence identity, and part-of-speech annotations provide useful operational targets for comparing semantic, contextual, and syntactic information in activation decompositions.
scope: MMLU question categories and question IDs, plus spaCy part-of-speech labels, and the related Wikipedia/FineFineWeb probing evaluations. Label prediction does not establish semantic exclusivity, native causal use, or separation from lexical and document-specific shortcuts. The additional datasets' label construction is not detailed in the supplied text.

statement: A sparse autoencoder can combine prefix and full-dictionary reconstruction objectives with symmetric contrastive alignment of high-level codes from temporally related tokens.
scope: T-SAE's single high/low partition, cosine-based batch contrastive objective, paired activation loading, and optional preceding-token sampling. The construction encourages specialization without guaranteeing latent identification, prevention of collapse, or semantic independence. The written encoder-bias dimension and reconstruction-bias signs contain inconsistencies.

statement: The temporally regularized high-level partition of a T-SAE can vary less across adjacent tokens than the high-level partition of a comparable Matryoshka SAE.
scope: The active-feature, activation-change-normalized smoothness metric in Table 1. This is a partition-specific result; full-dictionary smoothness is not uniformly better than both baselines.

statement: Selected T-SAE feature interventions can yield better concept-expression versus coherence frontiers than selected Matryoshka feature interventions in Gemma2-2b.
scope: The comparison against the authors' Matryoshka SAE and Neuronpedia's gemma-2-2b-res-matryoshka-dc dictionary. The text reports averaging 30 features, while Table 8 lists 29 correspondences. Targets and description specificity differ across dictionaries. Several selected T-SAE indices exceed the nominal high-level prefix, so the comparison cannot be attributed exclusively to that partition. No prompting or supervised-steering baseline is tested here.

statement: Concept-expression scores based on approximately corresponding feature descriptions are sufficiently comparable across dictionaries to evaluate their relative steering utility.
scope: The selected T-SAE, Matryoshka, and Neuronpedia correspondences in Table 8. Intervention success is judged against each dictionary's own description; the authors acknowledge that more specific Neuronpedia descriptions can lower its scores. Some correspondences also differ substantially in semantic content.

statement: In the first 1,000 evaluated HH-RLHF examples, rejected completions have a greater mean token length than chosen completions.
scope: The first 1,000 samples used in the harmful/harmless preference-data case study. This establishes an association in that subset, not a causal preference for short answers, the prevalence of a particular annotation rationale, or an effect on trained reward models.

statement: Mean T-SAE activation contrasts between rejected and chosen HH-RLHF responses can surface both safety-related features and features associated with response-length differences.
scope: The first 1,000 HH-RLHF samples, selected top activation-difference features, and qualitative comparison with Matryoshka. Feature labels and selected examples do not establish exhaustive semantic specificity, dataset-wide superiority, or causal effects on subsequent safety training.

statement: Temporal SAE semantic, contextual, and syntactic probe performance depends on the temporal pairing rule, the use of batch contrast, and the allocation of high-level dictionary capacity.
scope: Pythia-160m ablations evaluated with five-feature MMLU probes. These finite recipe comparisons do not establish optimal temporal scales or universal partition sizes.

statement: Adding temporal contrastive training need not reduce feature absorption or the number of split features relative to a Matryoshka SAE.
scope: The single SAEBench absorption comparison in Appendix C.3. Model, evaluation sample counts, and the interpretation of the reported dispersions are not separately specified. Small mean differences do not establish statistically significant degradation or equivalence.

statement: Sparse autoencoders can combine training-history activation and reconstruction-gradient statistics with adaptive statistical thresholds and stochastic feature masks while retaining reconstruction and L1 objectives.
scope: ATM's proposed construction, including warmup, periodic pruning, and minimum feature retention. Frequency tracking, probability handling, and some hyperparameters are incompletely specified; the construction supplies no recovery or stability guarantee.

statement: Feature importance evolves predictably enough across SAE training steps for exponential moving averages to provide useful feature-selection signals.
scope: The temporal-consistency assumption underlying ATM. It concerns optimization history rather than semantic persistence across adjacent text tokens; no isolated test of the assumption is supplied.

statement: The product of smoothed activation magnitude and smoothed absolute reconstruction-loss gradient provides a useful proxy for an SAE feature's reconstruction importance.
scope: ATM's importance score. Gradient magnitude measures local sensitivity rather than directly measuring finite removal effects or semantic importance; no component ablation or independent importance validation is reported.

statement: SAE feature-importance distributions possess sufficient regularity for thresholds based on their means and standard deviations to guide useful adaptive masking.
scope: ATM's statistical-structure assumption and periodic threshold schedule; no distributional characterization, calibration analysis, or threshold-rule comparison is supplied.

statement: Adaptive Temporal Masking can yield lower first-letter probe-projection absorption scores than the evaluated TopK, JumpReLU, and standard L1 SAE training recipes.
scope: Gemma-2-2B layer 12, 16,384 latents, and five million WikiText-103 training tokens. The comparison uses substantially different realized active-latent counts and does not establish matched-sparsity superiority or general feature stability.

statement: Adaptive Temporal Masking can improve activation reconstruction and replacement cross-entropy recovery over the tested TopK and JumpReLU recipes while trailing a denser standard L1 SAE.
scope: The single Gemma-2-2B layer-12 comparison with 16,384 latents and five million WikiText-103 training tokens; realized sparsity differs across methods.

statement: Adaptive Temporal Masking can achieve higher reported top-one-latent probing accuracy than a standard L1 SAE while remaining below TopK and close to JumpReLU.
scope: The reported 35-task binary classification suite using Gemma-2-2B layer-12 dictionaries, mean-pooled non-padding-token activations, and selected single-latent logistic regression probes. The precise task inventory and aggregation weights are not supplied.

statement: Matrix rows or columns enriched for low-drift parameters can produce greater language-modeling degradation under perturbation than equal-count high-drift, middle-drift, or random dimensions.
scope: The attention and FFN matrix orientations tested in LLaMA2-7B and LLaMA2-13B, using one, three, five, or ten selected dimensions. Effects depend on checkpoint, matrix orientation, and dimension count.

statement: Changing a single selected RMSNorm scaling parameter can catastrophically degrade LLaMA2-13B language modeling while analogous changes at selected control coordinates have negligible effects.
scope: LLaMA2-13B input_layer_norm coordinate 2100 at layer L1, with resetting to one or multiplication by ten; selected controls include layer L0 coordinate 2100 and layer L1 coordinates 2800 and 4200. This is not a prevalence estimate or a result about infinitesimal parameter changes.

statement: Chinese continued pretraining that improves a LLaMA checkpoint's reported Chinese linguistic competence need not substantially improve its Chinese examination benchmark scores.
scope: Chinese-LLaMA-7B and Open-Chinese-LLaMA-7B versus LLaMA-7B on C-Eval, Gaokao-Bench, and AGI-Eval. The comparison uses existing checkpoints; the supplied text neither gives numerical benchmark scores nor quantifies the Chinese competence improvement.

statement: A small parameter region that remains stable across language fine-tuning implements fundamental linguistic competence shared across languages.
scope: The proposed approximately 1% linguistic core in the studied LLaMA models. The 0.981% stability statistic uses a maximum relative-change threshold of 3%, whereas perturbation experiments select ranked parameter budgets. Uniqueness, sufficiency, and linguistic specificity are not established.

statement: Next-token perplexity on natural-language corpora provides an adequate operational measure of linguistic competence for interpreting parameter perturbations.
scope: The paper's monolingual and multilingual corpus evaluations, including its interpretation of very large perplexity increases as loss of linguistic competence. No direct grammaticality, comprehension, or minimal-pair evaluation validates this interpretation.

statement: Low parameter drift across language fine-tuning, combined with disproportionate perplexity sensitivity to perturbation, identifies parameters implementing shared linguistic rules rather than general computational fragility.
scope: The interpretive bridge from Bottom-region stability and disruption to a specifically linguistic functional region. Semantic processing, numerical stability, generic information transport, and other computational functions are not independently separated.

statement: LLaMA models may contain dedicated knowledge-processing parameter regions dissociated from a shared linguistic core.
scope: A proposed functional organization motivated by checkpoint-level language-versus-examination performance differences. No knowledge region is localized or selectively intervened on.

statement: Scores on academic examination benchmarks adequately measure knowledge and reasoning separately from linguistic competence when comparing language-model checkpoints.
scope: C-Eval, Gaokao-Bench, AGI-Eval, and MMLU in the LLaMA checkpoint comparison. Benchmark performance also requires language understanding and response-format competence; no independent decomposition of those demands is supplied.

statement: Normalized chosen–rejected SAE activation contrasts, filtered for safety relevance, can define a signed feature-based score for ranking reward-model preference pairs.
scope: SAFER's two-stage TopK SAE training, normalized feature contrasts, GPT-4o relevance filtering, and length-normalized pair scoring. The construction defines a ranking without guaranteeing semantic isolation or annotation correctness. The relationship between sentence-final extraction, token aggregation, and length normalization is incompletely specified.

statement: GPT-4o safety-relevance ratings of SAE activation contexts can show high exact agreement with human ratings under a shared five-point rubric.
scope: The 500 randomly sampled SAE features and supplied annotation rubric. Human annotator count, inter-annotator reliability, rating prevalence, and the underlying reward-model checkpoint are unspecified.

statement: Ranking reward-model SAE features by normalized absolute chosen–rejected activation contrast can enrich a candidate set for features rated as safety relevant.
scope: Comparison of 100 highest-ranked features with 100 randomly sampled features using GPT-4o's five-point safety-relevance ratings. Exact effect sizes, statistical-test details, and the underlying reward-model checkpoint are unspecified.

statement: SAFER's poisoning and denoising outcomes depend on feature-extraction configuration, and a single default configuration need not dominate the tested alternatives.
scope: The Llama-3.2-1B-RM ablations over extraction layer, selected-feature count, dictionary width, activation budget, and normalization constant in Table 6. No exhaustive optimization or larger-model robustness conclusion follows.

statement: Amplifying a selected safety-associated SAE feature can increase chosen-response reward scores more on sampled safety preference pairs than on sampled general-chat pairs.
scope: Feature #3389, fivefold activation scaling, 20 safety pairs and 20 chat pairs, and an unspecified reward-model checkpoint. This does not establish dictionary-wide causal validity, comprehensive semantic specificity, or improved preference-ranking accuracy.

statement: Two-dimensional UMAP projections of selected SAE decoder dictionaries can show apparent clustering of safety-related features and separation between features labeled safe and unsafe.
scope: The four model-associated dictionaries described in Appendix D. This concerns the authors' qualitative account of projected decoder geometry, not quantitative separability in the original space, a causal safety subspace, or cross-model feature correspondence.

statement: RewardBench Safety and Chat scores provide adequate proxies for safety alignment and preservation of general conversational capability when evaluating preference-data interventions.
scope: The paper's inference from reward-model subset scores to safety and general-performance claims. These are reward-model evaluations; no downstream RLHF policy evaluation or broad capability suite validates the stronger transfer to assistant behavior.

statement: Lower-to-higher-layer activation prediction can combine an adaptively interpolated encoder, single-entry vector quantization, EMA codebook updates, and a contextual transformer decoder receiving both quantized codes and unquantized encoder states.
scope: CLVQ-VAE's construction. Default settings include 400 codebook entries, top-5 sampling at temperature 1, commitment weight 0.1, EMA decay 0.99, and a six-layer, eight-head bidirectional decoder. Unquantized cross-attention bypasses the discrete channel.

statement: Projecting out CLVQ-VAE code directions can disrupt task-label probes more than projecting out selected cross-layer SAE encoder subspaces, with model- and dataset-dependent exceptions.
scope: Four models crossed with three classification datasets, prescribed layer pairs, Layer Integrated Gradients token selection, and top-10 SAE encoder-subspace removal. This concerns the specified probe-disruption protocol, rather than general SAE utility or native causal faithfulness.

statement: Removing the CLVQ-VAE direction assigned to a salient token can damage task-probe accuracy more than removing alternative active codebook directions sampled preferentially farther from the assigned code.
scope: Nine configurations spanning RoBERTa, BERT, and Qwen across three datasets. LLaMA is excluded. Alternatives are sampled by codebook distance rather than uniformly or by matching removed projection magnitude.

statement: CLVQ-VAE word clouds can enable higher human agreement with model sentiment predictions than hierarchical-clustering word clouds on a small stratified ERASER-Movie sample.
scope: Nineteen sentences spanning true-positive, true-negative, false-positive, and false-negative outcomes, rated by the same fourteen annotators. Annotators see neither original sentences nor model predictions. Agreement does not establish faithful reconstruction of internal reasoning.

statement: Euclidean and spherical k-means initialization can favor different evaluation outcomes in discrete cross-layer activation models.
scope: The tested CLVQ-VAE initialization recipes across four models and three datasets, measured through probe disruption and prediction-plausibility ratings. No universal initialization ordering or independently established functional–semantic tradeoff follows.

statement: Providing unquantized encoder states through decoder cross-attention can improve code-direction probe disruption and reduce average codebook-vector cosine similarity relative to quantized-only reconstruction.
scope: Nine configurations using RoBERTa, BERT, and Qwen across three datasets. Codebook cosine similarity is a geometric diagnostic. The ablation does not establish that the bypass carries only low-level details or that discrete codes recover native mechanisms.

statement: A TopK sparse autoencoder trained on Whisper base's final encoder frames can expose individual coordinates associated with phonetic, lexical, pronoun-class, morphological, and numerical categories.
scope: One 16,000-latent, K=45 dictionary; selected candidate features evaluated on LJSpeech or the reported mixed analysis set. Association does not establish exhaustive monosemanticity, independence from acoustic cues, or a hierarchy across network depth.

statement: Selected profanity-associated Whisper SAE latents can jointly detect most annotated profanity occurrences while also activating on many non-profanity occurrences.
scope: Latents 3584 and 104 in the reported analysis corpus, using occurrence-level annotations. Temporal spread and annotation limitations are possible explanations rather than independently established causes.

statement: Word-local interventions on selected Whisper SAE latents can alter higher-level transcript content more readily than the tested phonetic feature, with positive interventions succeeding for more selected feature families than negative interventions.
scope: The six selected feature families in Table VI and their qualitative binary outcomes; these are not trial-level success rates or representative estimates for all latents at an abstraction level.

statement: Clamping selected Whisper SAE latents across an entire utterance can cause repetitive or unrelated decoder outputs, motivating interventions restricted to a word's frame span.
scope: The reported whole-utterance attempts, including Numbers and profanity latents. No matched-dose comparison isolates intervention duration from total perturbation strength.

statement: A profanity-associated direction from a Whisper SAE trained without French audio can remove profanity from selected French transcripts, as well as selected Spanish transcripts, while sometimes substantially corrupting other transcript content.
scope: Word-local negative steering of latent 3584 on curated Common Voice clips; five French and five Spanish examples are displayed. This does not establish language-independent semantics or reliable meaning-preserving profanity suppression.

statement: A Whisper SAE latent selected for English-versus-Spanish discrimination can predict the language distinction while failing to change Whisper's language classification under the tested positive interventions.
scope: Latent 5106 in the English/Spanish analysis set and positive steering on English content. Negative steering was not tested; the result does not establish failure of other language interventions.

statement: Selected Whisper final-encoder SAE latents can activate in narrow absolute-time windows across different audio files.
scope: Three selected positional latents. Their usefulness for decoder word-order computation is suggested but not tested.

statement: Redundant phonetic encoding may let a speech decoder compensate for suppression of individual encoder features, making low-level and negative steering less effective.
scope: A proposed explanation of selected Whisper steering outcomes, including phonetic similarity retained after semantic steering. Redundancy and compensatory pathways are not independently measured.

statement: For a fixed deterministic encoder and a fixed input domain, changing a downstream SAE's training samples or hyperparameters does not change the encoder's image set.
scope: The set M={E(x):x∈X} with E and X fixed. This observation does not guarantee feature recovery, prevent SAE overfitting, or establish equivalent evaluations under different sampling measures.

statement: Sparse reconstruction coordinates learned from a frozen speech encoder provide sufficiently faithful proxies for native linguistic features to interpret their activation patterns as the encoder's representational content.
scope: The interpretation of selected Whisper base SAE coordinates as phonetic, lexical, morphological, syntactic, and semantic features. Their complete semantics, uniqueness, and native causal roles are not independently established.

statement: An encoder supplying a sufficiently informative purely phonetic code can in principle support transcription when a downstream autoregressive decoder performs language modeling.
scope: The architectural premise used to interpret Whisper encoder's higher-level associations as exceeding transcription's minimum requirements. No formal sufficiency construction or phonetic-only encoder comparison is supplied.

statement: A sparse autoencoder can explicitly represent a two-level hierarchy by adding top-level feature contributions to refinements from parent-gated, low-dimensional expert dictionaries.
scope: The H-SAE construction uses learned down/up maps and nominal TopK₁ expert codes. These maps need not be orthogonal projectors. Algorithm 1 omits expert TopK₁, leaving an implementation ambiguity; architectural gating alone does not guarantee semantic hierarchy.

statement: Parent-gated hierarchical sparse autoencoders can reduce first-letter probe-projection absorption relative to standard TopK sparse autoencoders and attenuate its increase with dictionary width.
scope: The reported Gemma 2-2B layer-20 SAEBench first-letter evaluation and width sweep. This does not establish reduced absorption for arbitrary semantic hierarchies or improved general monosemanticity.

statement: Greater overlap of strongly activated SAE features across corresponding translated contexts provides useful evidence of reduced language-specific duplication of shared concepts.
scope: The interpretation of last-token top-eight overlap as feature redundancy and composability. It assumes sufficient semantic correspondence despite differences in translation, tokenization, syntax, and final-token identity; overlap alone does not establish equivalent feature meanings.

statement: Sparse execution of low-dimensional child experts can add little training overhead relative to a standard SAE using a naive auxiliary dead-latent loss.
scope: The paper's Gemma 2-2B training configurations and implementations. The comparison does not establish a general runtime or memory advantage over optimized baselines.

statement: SAE encoder directions selected for attribute association can define a fixed native-space attenuation operator, optionally after classifier-weighted aggregation, without running the SAE during inference.
scope: S&P Top-K constructs A from selected encoder directions or their weighted sum and uses V=I−alpha A(AᵀA)⁻¹Aᵀ. The written inverse requires full column rank; complete removal of the selected span requires alpha=1. The subsequent single-axis formula has an inconsistent norm denominator. Removing the selected span does not guarantee removal of all attribute information.

statement: Aggregating selected SAE encoder directions into a classifier-weighted single axis can preserve substantially more hair-color classification utility than removing their full span, while achieving a smaller retrieval-fairness improvement.
scope: CelebA, CLIP ViT-B/16, 16 selected features, and worst-group hair-color ROC-AUC versus top-500 retrieval gender-distribution metrics.

statement: Classifier-weighted aggregation of selected SAE encoder directions can improve retrieval gender-balance metrics over unweighted averaging or attribute-signed summation of those directions.
scope: The CelebA CLIP ViT-B/16 ablation with Stylist selection and 16 features. The alternative rules aggregate L2-normalized encoder directions; this does not establish universal superiority or better utility for every aggregation baseline.

statement: The relative effectiveness of SAE feature-selection procedures for gender debiasing can reverse between face datasets.
scope: CLIP-score correlation, linear probing, and Stylist selection under encoder-direction removal in the reported CelebA and FairFace experiments. The FairFace selector table does not separately specify interpolation status.

statement: Combining selected encoder-direction image interventions with BendVLM prompt debiasing can improve retrieval gender-balance metrics over BendVLM alone.
scope: The reported CLIP ViT-B/16 CelebA and FairFace evaluations; no FairFace downstream-task utility metric is available.

statement: LLM ratings of aggressive or sycophantic intensity provide valid, comparable measures of behavior suppression across altered opinion generations.
scope: The unspecified judge evaluates three numbered opinions together on a 1–10 scale. Supplied prompts place vanilla, masked reconstruction, and S&P outputs in a fixed order; counterbalancing and independent human validation are not reported. Lower scores can accompany sarcasm, awkwardness, or changes in task adherence.

statement: Restricting a concept classifier to a suitably selected SAE encoder span may reduce reliance on spurious correlations and lower supervision requirements relative to an unconstrained CAV.
scope: Appendix D's explanation for the CelebA CAV comparison. Regrouping a linear classifier on encoder preactivations establishes that its effective direction lies in the selected encoder span, but does not establish exclusion of spurious information. No controlled corruption or sample-size experiment is supplied.

statement: Oppositely weighting male-associated and female-associated SAE encoder directions may cancel shared human-related content and yield a gender contrast that preserves more hair-related information during removal.
scope: The proposed mechanism for interpolation's CelebA utility retention. Composite human-plus-gender features and cancellation of their common content are an explanatory interpretation; the paper does not directly measure that decomposition or isolate cancellation as the cause.

statement: Sparse dictionaries can be trained through alternating complete-parent-set graph induction, graph-conditioned structural optimization, parent-aligned decoder refinement, residual completion, and full graph re-induction.
scope: AG-SAE combines bank-specific reconstruction with a global feature DAG. The implemented LLM search limits parent sets to three members within a 12-feature search pool after retrieving 24 candidates. Selection is greedy, with no guarantee of globally optimal structure or discovery outside the searched pool. Residual completion reuses suitable features or initializes unused entries, with capacity growth capped at 5%.

statement: A graph-conditioned decoder realignment update can reduce first-letter feature-absorption diagnostics while approximately preserving reconstruction quality and average active-feature count.
scope: One induction and one Absorption Realignment update starting from a fixed, fully trained SAE, with inference threshold and evaluation settings fixed. The implemented update uses shared graph-conditioned decoder parameters and subsequent contribution-preserving conversion, rather than merely applying a static algebraic rewrite.

statement: Finite empirical complete-parent-set induction is locally constant in the dictionary state when discrete decisions, fitted scores, candidate acceptance, and greedy selection are nondegenerate.
scope: Fixed finite feature identities and empirical configuration, including data, batch contexts, external randomness, and tie rules. Requires continuous branch quantities; locally persistent ties or nonzero discrete comparison margins; full-column-rank NNLS fitting matrices; positive normalization energies; valid finite calibration lists; strict acceptance margins; and strict greedy selection gaps.

statement: The feature interpretation of a fixed steering vector may depend on the activation to which it is added, particularly when dictionary directions have negative alignment.
scope: Appendix D's schematic distinction between global and local interpretations. No context-conditioned behavioral experiment or formal impossibility result is supplied.

statement: Strong cross-layer coactivation across prompt tokens, combined with low corpus activation density, provides a useful basis for grouping SAE features into candidate semantic components.
scope: The interpretive premise connecting the paper's correlation graphs and density filter to semantic grouping. Selected group interventions provide operational checks but do not establish semantic identity among all members, causal transmission along edges, or the semantic adequacy of the density threshold.

statement: Replacing residual-stream activations at multiple layers with SAE decodings after selected-coordinate edits preserves enough of the original computation to interpret answer changes as effects of the selected semantic groups.
scope: The residual-stream component ablation and amplification protocol. Footnote 7 specifies decoded activation replacement; the supplied text does not specify restoring reconstruction residuals or report a matched unedited multilayer-decoding control.

statement: The tested coactivation-selected SAE groups provide substantially less reliable relation and composite steering for verb transformations than for country facts or word translation.
scope: Eight verbs with synonym, antonym, past-tense, capitalization, and first-letter relations in Gemma 2 2B. This concerns selected groups and a finite strength search, rather than impossibility of controlling these transformations through other representations or interventions. Verb groups are context-specific rather than consistently intersected across contexts.

statement: Manipulating selected multi-feature country and relation components can achieve higher counterfactual-answer success than manipulating the individually most ablation-impactful feature selected for each concept or relation.
scope: The Gemma 2 2B country-facts task and highest-single-feature-KL baseline. Intervention size and total perturbation magnitude are not matched, and the comparison does not cover alternative single-feature selection or optimization procedures.

statement: Country-fact and translation SAE component ablations can preserve high accuracy on comparison tasks, whereas the tested verb-transformation component ablations cause broader degradation.
scope: The three small Gemma 2 2B task inventories. Same-task evaluations omit cases where the prompted concept or relation overlaps the ablated pair. Results concern ablation specificity rather than amplified or composite steering specificity, broad capability preservation, or matched perturbation doses.

statement: In the tested Gemma 2 2B coactivation graphs, selected entity and word components generally begin earlier in depth than selected factual-relation and translation-language components.
scope: Components retained by top-activation filtering, density pruning, correlation thresholds, and manual selection on the three task inventories. Component membership does not identify the first layer encoding all relevant information or establish a universal concrete-to-abstract processing hierarchy.

statement: High-impact SAE coactivation components associated with selected countries, words, and relations can retain overlapping feature membership when the other task attribute changes.
scope: Qualitative comparisons within the small country-fact and translation inventories, with supplementary country examples in Gemma 2 9B. Final intersections enforce shared membership by construction; no aggregate pre-intersection overlap distribution or broad paraphrase evaluation is supplied.

statement: Generated descriptions of individual SAE features can omit or apparently mismatch the concept or relation associated with a selected component's task-dependent intervention effects.
scope: Selected Gemma 2 2B components and Neuronpedia descriptions. Disagreement does not distinguish description errors, polysemantic features, contextual specialization, or imperfect component interpretation, and no dictionary-wide mismatch rate is established.

statement: Selected animal-associated SAE coactivation components can exhibit nested membership across taxonomic prediction tasks and recover coarse taxonomic groupings through component-overlap clustering.
scope: An exploratory Gemma 2 2B dataset of 26 animals queried for class, order, and family. Baseline answers are imperfect and steering performs poorly. Reported hierarchy quality is qualitative, with mistakes at order and family levels and no numerical clustering score.

statement: Evaluating an unsupervised generalization–specialization hierarchy should distinguish individual-concept interpretability, static semantic structure, and sample-dependent parent–child activation consistency.
scope: The proposed seven-requirement framework for transitively reduced concept DAGs, including multiple-parent structures. The requirements are motivated evaluation objectives rather than a proved necessary-and-sufficient characterization of meaningful hierarchies.

statement: Parent and child SAE activation magnitudes provide sufficiently comparable measures of concept evidence for magnitude dominance and conditional correlation to diagnose hierarchical consistency.
scope: Post-TopK-64 activations under the evaluated preprocessing, architectures, and training recipes. The paper does not independently calibrate coefficient magnitudes as confidence or demonstrate invariance to feature-specific rescaling.

statement: In an ImageNet-1k taxonomy evaluation using class-membership activations, child concepts usually have higher embedding-coherence scores than parents, and siblings have high embedding similarity.
scope: The supplied ImageNet-1k hierarchy, up to 1,000 sampled images per class, binary class-membership activations, and 20 randomly selected images per class for sibling representations. The encoder used for this check is not explicitly restated in Appendix C.3.

statement: A conditional-co-activation graph extracted from a standard visual TopK SAE can exhibit strong embedding-based parent–child ordering while its parent features rarely co-activate with any extracted child.
scope: CC3M-trained CLIP ViT-L/14 dictionaries with 6,144 features, post-TopK-64 evaluation, activation-weighted conditional-co-activation threshold 0.9, pruning, and transitive reduction. Scores apply to retained graph elements rather than the entire dictionary.

statement: Weighted training across nested activation budgets can yield larger extracted visual SAE hierarchies, more nodes beyond the second level, and more frequent parent refinement than the evaluated standard TopK recipe.
scope: ActMSAE versus TopK under the paper's dictionary sizes, common post-TopK-64 evaluation, and conditional-co-activation graph pipeline. Comparisons concern complete recipes rather than isolated training ingredients or matched compute; numerical refinement comparisons below concern CLIP.

statement: Nested-dictionary SAE training can improve parent–child activation consistency over standard TopK while yielding weaker embedding-based hierarchical specificity.
scope: The evaluated ArchMSAE and TopK CLIP recipes and their separately extracted conditional-co-activation graphs. This does not establish a universal tradeoff for Matryoshka SAEs or every possible extracted graph.

statement: An explicit parent-gated visual SAE hierarchy can exhibit consistent parent–child co-activation while its child features lack coherent semantic refinements of their parents.
scope: The evaluated two-level H-SAE with 361 experts and 16 child atoms per expert, its reported training recipe, and common evaluation postprocessing. This does not establish failure of all explicit hierarchical architectures.
