statement: Visual SAE hierarchy groups can exhibit decreasing parent activation as the strongest child activation increases, even when graph-average conditional correlations are positive.
scope: The proposed soft-absorption diagnostic: Spearman correlation between parent activation and maximum child activation, restricted to samples with at least one active child. Parent-inactive cases remain included, so this statistic does not independently isolate suppression occurring only when both levels are active.

statement: The graph-selection procedure can materially change visual SAE hierarchy coverage and measured activation consistency, including whether a method yields any graph.
scope: CLIP threshold, pruning, and CCA-versus-masked-cosine ablations with three seeds. Conditional-co-activation selection directly favors activation implication, and changing the procedure does not move every metric in the same direction.

statement: Additional levels in an extracted nested-sparsity SAE hierarchy can have smaller specificity differences and substantially overlapping sibling activation supports.
scope: ActMSAE depth analyses on CLIP, with supplementary sibling-overlap measurements on DINOv2. Co-activation overlap is a redundancy warning rather than proof that siblings are semantically identical.

statement: Broad qualitative differences between visual SAE hierarchy recipes can recur across different encoder representations while extracted graph coverage changes substantially.
scope: The evaluated CLIP and DINOv2 global image embeddings and Gemma-4 E2B layer-26 patch states. Encoder identity, representation granularity, data exposure, and training schedules are not independently controlled, so this comparison does not establish that SAE training alone causes hierarchy-quality differences.

statement: Subtracting a source SAE decoder contribution from an otherwise intact hidden state and re-encoding subsequent states provides an operational map of downstream feature responses in single-cell foundation models.
scope: Single-source interventions in Geneformer V2-316M and scGPT whole-human, preserving the original SAE reconstruction residual. Responses include mediated pathways and do not identify direct connections or a complete computational graph.

statement: Removing an SAE decoder contribution selectively reduces its annotated biological content sufficiently for downstream changes to be interpreted as dependencies between biological representations.
scope: The semantic interpretation of source-feature subtraction in the existing Geneformer and scGPT TopK dictionaries. Reconstruction-error preservation does not establish semantic exclusivity, on-distribution states, or preservation of unrelated content.

statement: Sharing at least one biological annotation between an intervened source feature and a responding target feature provides a meaningful operational measure of biological coherence in a model's computation.
scope: Coherence conditions on both endpoints being annotated across the specified databases. Annotation breadth, annotation abundance, and source selection can affect overlap; no matched annotation-degree null or independent causal biological ground truth validates this interpretation.

statement: Ablating selected well-annotated SAE contributions in single-cell foundation models can affect many downstream coordinates, with effects persisting across most or all remaining layers.
scope: Annotation-selected source features under the paper's effect-size and consistency thresholds. Target counts describe downstream total responses rather than direct graph degree. Aggregate and per-source-layer edge totals conflict.

statement: Most retained downstream SAE responses to selected source-feature removals in Geneformer and scGPT are activation decreases.
scope: Four conditions, selected sources, and |d|>0.5 with consistency>0.7. The sign describes the removal response: a negative delta indicates that the source positively supported the target under this intervention, despite the paper calling such edges inhibitory.

statement: Retained scGPT feature-ablation responses can have larger mean absolute standardized effects and a smaller fraction of activation decreases than the evaluated Geneformer responses.
scope: The four reported conditions, each with its own source selection and retained-edge population. Architecture, representation width, dictionary width, cell inputs, training data, and measured layer coverage are not jointly controlled.

statement: Selected single-cell SAE ablation responses can connect features whose annotations are consistent with familiar biological process relationships.
scope: Manually selected Geneformer and scGPT examples labelled through existing feature annotations. These observations establish model sensitivity between annotated coordinates, without verifying molecular pathways, direct mediation, or biological causal direction.

statement: A mixed-tissue Geneformer SAE tracing pipeline can produce higher shared-annotation fractions among doubly annotated response edges than a K562-only dictionary pipeline on the same K562 inputs.
scope: The reported K562/Multi and K562/K562 pipelines. Dictionaries, annotation-selected source identities, and downstream layer coverage differ; the comparison does not isolate training-data diversity or establish improved semantic disentanglement.

statement: Changing K562 inputs to a sampled Tabula Sapiens mixture while retaining the same mixed-tissue Geneformer dictionaries can substantially reduce measured feature-response density and magnitude while leaving shared-annotation fractions similar.
scope: Two 200-cell cohorts and fixed mixed-tissue dictionaries at four layers. Similar aggregate coherence does not establish general input independence or statistical equivalence; source selection may favor K562-associated features.

statement: Most downstream target coordinates identified by selected Geneformer feature ablations can also occur in independently constructed PMI target sets at the same layer pairs.
scope: Target-set membership at three layer pairs, with zero overlap between source-feature inventories. PMI target sets already cover approximately 89–95% of each 4,608-coordinate dictionary, so target overlap does not establish edge agreement or validate causal interpretation of PMI.

statement: Geneformer and scGPT ablation-response graphs can contain overlapping directed biological-domain pairs at a rate exceeding the paper's label-permutation baseline.
scope: GO Biological Process labels on retained response edges, pooling all three Geneformer conditions before comparison with scGPT TS/Multi. Domain-pair recurrence does not establish aligned features, matching signs, identical algorithms, or causal cellular relationships. The permutation procedure is incompletely specified.

statement: Filtering annotated model-response edges against a gene-overlap reference graph can nominate domain-link candidates, without establishing that the links are biologically novel or causal.
scope: The reported reference connects biological domains sharing at least three genes. Reference incompleteness and internal inconsistencies in the examples limit interpretation of candidate novelty.

statement: Gene-pair predictions extracted from annotated single-cell SAE ablation-response graphs can show weak directional agreement and negligible magnitude correlation with measured K562 CRISPRi expression responses.
scope: The specified top-ten-gene, rank-weighted feature expansion and evidence filter, evaluated against existing pseudobulk CRISPRi responses. This limits the tested extraction pipeline's predictive utility rather than establishing absence of all regulatory information in either model. The stated 50% chance comparison does not supply an empirical sign-frequency baseline.

statement: Domains and domain pairs assigned broad disease-related labels can have higher response-graph centrality and cross-model consensus rates than those outside the label set.
scope: Eleven broad categories, including transcription regulation and TRRUST transcription factors. Disease labels cover 1,073/1,126 domains. Annotation breadth and graph degree may influence the associations; the analysis does not establish disease-specific causal mechanisms.

statement: Domain pairs exclusive to the evaluated multi-tissue tracing conditions can be enriched for immune-related labels relative to pairs shared with K562 conditions.
scope: Keyword-based tissue labels and the reported condition grouping, whose precise membership is not fully specified. Inputs, dictionaries, and model coverage can differ; the comparison does not isolate immune-cell-specific causal computation.

statement: Transformer depth in single-cell foundation models may organize biological representations in an order resembling signaling, chromatin modification, and transcriptional output.
scope: Interpretation of selected annotated feature locations and forward ablation-response graphs. All tested source-to-target edges point to later layers by construction, so positive layer deltas alone do not independently validate biological temporal ordering. Layer-position associations are not biological time measurements.

statement: Differences in the fraction of downstream activation decreases after feature removal may reflect differences in representational redundancy and competition.
scope: The proposed explanation of Geneformer/scGPT differences and the increased negative-removal fraction on Tabula Sapiens inputs. No independent redundancy measure, matched architectural intervention, or combinatorial ablation establishes this mechanism.

statement: The language distribution of a sparse feature’s strongest activations provides a useful proxy for whether that feature is language-specific or shared across languages.
scope: English/Japanese Wikipedia, a feature-relative threshold of 70% of its observed maximum, and a greater-than-90% criterion for language specificity. Mixed activation alone does not establish shared semantic content or native causal use.

statement: During LLM-jp pretraining, SAE feature populations can progress from semantically incoherent mixed-language activation through coherent language-specific activation toward coherent English–Japanese activation.
scope: Most clearly documented at layer 14 of LLM-jp 3.7B: initially incoherent activation through approximately 0.4B tokens, language-specific development around 0.4–4B tokens, and increasing bilingual alignment afterward. Independently trained dictionaries characterize population changes rather than trajectories of identified individual native features. Smaller models show weaker late bilingual development.

statement: Later-training LLM-jp middle layers can show a stronger combination of mixed-language SAE activation and activating-token semantic coherence than lower or upper layers.
scope: English/Japanese Wikipedia and the paper’s strong-activation and token-cluster metrics, especially in the 3.7B model. This does not establish an exclusive semantic hub or absence of bilingual information elsewhere.

statement: Larger LLM-jp checkpoints can exhibit stronger late-training middle-layer bilingual alignment under SAE language-selectivity and semantic-coherence measurements than smaller checkpoints.
scope: The five evaluated 150M–3.7B models using fixed dictionary width and K. This is a model-size association within one family, without isolated causal attribution to parameter count or a general scaling law.

statement: Consecutive-token activation spans of upper-layer SAE features can lengthen during LLM-jp training, with larger models showing stronger span growth.
scope: The paper’s average consecutive activation-span measure on Wikipedia inputs. Span growth is consistent with phrase-level representations but does not independently establish contextual semantic understanding.

statement: A fully trained checkpoint’s activations can be encoded with its SAE, masked by feature category, decoded, and added to a mid-training checkpoint to test the utility of selected donor content.
scope: Same-family, same-width LLM-jp checkpoint transfer at a shared layer, using Xmid←Xmid+αD(mask⊙E(Xfull)). The decoder includes its learned bias; the intervention requires donor-model computation and does not guarantee semantically isolated transfer.

statement: In a selected LLM-jp cross-checkpoint intervention, mixed-language SAE donor additions can reduce English and Japanese perplexity more than equal-count language-specific additions while improving bidirectional translation scores over the unintervened recipient.
scope: Layer 14 of LLM-jp 3.7B, the approximately 40B-token recipient, and the main α=0.1, 5,000-coordinate setting. Mixed masks are defined by language-activation frequencies, without a separately stated semantic-coherence selection threshold. The result establishes intervention utility rather than necessity, exclusive bilingual mediation, or a standalone SAE enhancement; improvement is not uniform across all appendix settings.

statement: An SAE can replace a flat encoder projection with head-specific base and extension projections whose nonnegative geometric-mean pairings generate post-latents for global sparse selection and linear decoding.
scope: KronSAE with F = hmn post-latents and h(m+n) projected pre-latents. The simplified implementation includes encoder biases. Decoder atoms are initialized from parent-vector sums but are not constrained to retain that form. Without numerical stabilization, pre-selection post-latent support equals the intersection of parent supports; TopK can remove positive compositions. The implementation adds 1e-5 before square root, so selected coefficients need not satisfy the exact support rule when insufficient positive parent products exist.

statement: KronSAE variants can reduce SAEBench absorption diagnostics relative to flat TopK SAEs while retaining similar feature-splitting rates.
scope: The reported Gemma-2-2B, 16,384-feature comparison at active counts 8, 16, 32, and 64, including TopK, Matryoshka, and Kron variants. The absorption subsection does not explicitly restate the layer or training budget. The text describes tendencies across configurations rather than universal dominance over every baseline.

statement: Replacing an SAE encoder with KronSAE factorization has reconstruction effects that depend on the sparsification architecture and factor configuration.
scope: The Gemma-2-2B layer-12 Switch and Matryoshka comparisons and Appendix A/Table 2 activation-function ablations. Table 2 does not explicitly restate the host-model setting; Gated comparisons use unequal realized active counts and differing baseline runs. JumpReLU values at nominal matched sparsities are obtained from fitted curves.

statement: Geometric-mean compositions of broadly responsive pre-latents can produce post-latents with more specific activation descriptions and higher automated interpretation scores than their parents.
scope: Selected Gemma-2-2B layer-12 KronSAE heads with m=n=4 and 16,384 post-latents. This is an existential observation about selected cases, not a guarantee for every composition. Descriptions include intersections, apparent inheritance from one parent, and semantics not evident from either parent description.

statement: Lower token-distribution entropy and lower within-sequence activation density can be associated with higher automated SAE interpretation scores.
scope: The reported TopK and m=n=4 KronSAE feature analyses. Appendix G restricts property correlations to the first 3,072 features from 32K dictionaries described as trained on 24M tokens; Section 6.2 instead describes 16,384-feature dictionaries with 24M tokens collected for analysis. These descriptions do not establish one consistent configuration.

statement: Recurring correlations among language-model activation features provide useful structural information for organizing semantically meaningful SAE compositions.
scope: The bridge from linguistic co-occurrence and observed activation correlations to meaningful head-wise feature organization. Same-head correlation and synthetic structural recovery do not independently establish semantic ancestry or native computational interactions.

statement: Emotionally charged interactions make behavioral differences among prompted speakers sufficiently pronounced to facilitate attribution of speaker-associated activation features.
scope: The rationale for constructing the synthetic emotional-context dataset. The paper does not compare feature attribution or discovery quality against an otherwise matched neutral-context dataset.

statement: Setting-dependent activation and interpretation-consistent steering of selected SAE coordinates provide sufficiently faithful proxies for identifying shared native components of model speaker representations.
scope: Boundary/pronoun-selected JumpReLU coordinates and the relative mean-activation presence rule. Shared coordinates may also reflect conversational format, response style, or correlated content. No comprehensive replacement-fidelity, selective-erasure, or mediation test establishes the stronger native-component interpretation.

statement: Selected narrative-associated Gemma SAE directions can bidirectionally shift an Assistant–Roleplay activation readout beyond the shift predicted from random-latent cosine alignment, with effects depending on feature and downstream layer.
scope: Eleven Negative-Narrative-Induces-Assistant candidates, with four reverse-class candidates also examined. Tests use response-averaged readouts, 40 evaluation prompts, and regression controls from 40 randomly sampled SAE latents. They do not establish mediation of the previously published Assistant Axis or uniformly consistent trajectories.

statement: A language-model judge's binary labels for occurrence of its described steering effect can agree closely with human judgments on a stratified audit of selected feature interventions.
scope: Qwen-3.7 Max steerinterp, 25 randomly drawn labeled Gemma features, and 191 sampled generations. Humans receive the judge's group-level effect description, so agreement validates occurrence labeling conditional on that description rather than independent discovery, semantic specificity, or native causal interpretation.

statement: Activation of an immersive generation regime may amplify Gemma's tendency to produce emotionally unstable or theatrical Assistant responses.
scope: The proposed connection between this paper's ISM candidates and emotional instability reported by Soligo et al. No targeted test establishes ISM as a mediator of that previously studied instability, and correspondence to the previously published Assistant Axis is interpretive.

statement: SAE decoder directions paired with automated labels and mean-centered topic activations paired with synthetic descriptions provide sufficiently meaningful semantic supervision for training an activation interpreter.
scope: The Goodfire, Llama Scope, Gemma Scope, and Wikipedia-derived artifacts. Automated labels are noisy, and mean subtraction does not independently establish monosemanticity or removal of lexical and template effects.

statement: Retrieval rank of a topic from an activation-generated description provides a useful operational proxy for recovery of the topic's semantic content.
scope: GTE-large query embeddings compared against title-plus-description document embeddings for the approximately 50,000-topic corpus. Retrieval depends on the embedding model, lexical anchors, and candidate-selection protocol; it does not independently establish complete activation semantics.

statement: The frequency with which label-conditioned generated text activates an SAE feature provides a useful operational proxy for the quality of the feature description.
scope: The same-model synthetic-conversation protocol, counting any nonzero activation outside the begin-of-text token as a hit. The metric does not measure activation magnitude, exclusivity, coverage of natural activating contexts, or native causal function.

statement: Increasing activation-interpreter adapter capacity can improve topic-description fitting while worsening held-out performance on SAE-label datasets.
scope: The evaluated scalar affine, scalar-affine-plus-low-rank, low-rank-only, and full-rank architectures. Results concern achieved validation losses under the supplied recipes, rather than a universal capacity ordering.

statement: Adding a learned bias to a scalar-scaled activation direction can account for most of the label-likelihood improvement obtained by larger self-interpretation adapters.
scope: Incremental validation-loss comparisons between separately fitted adapter architectures on the evaluated SAE datasets. This does not measure the interpretation accuracy of the bias alone or uniquely decompose a jointly trained adapter's causal contributions.

statement: Learned self-interpretation adapter biases can induce training-distribution-specific output formats and default content, with their influence changing as the input direction is rescaled.
scope: Zero-vector outputs and the Goodfire ALL-CAPS training intervention. These tests support prior-like behavior without establishing a complete separation between formatting and semantic computation.

statement: Self-interpretation adapters do not transfer uniformly between SAE-label and topic-description datasets, and their transfer depends on architecture and model.
scope: Within-model transfer across artifact sources. Separate adapters are trained for each language-model family; direct transfer of adapter parameters between model families is not demonstrated.

statement: A single self-interpretation adapter trained on pooled layers can match layer-specific adapters without receiving a layer identifier.
scope: Llama Scope 32k SAE directions pooled across layers 0–31, evaluated on those same layer identities. This does not establish generalization to layers absent from training.

statement: Across the evaluated Qwen sizes, layer-averaged topic self-interpretation retrieval improves more rapidly than directly prompted topic-description retrieval.
scope: Qwen-2.5-Instruct 7B, 14B, 32B, and 72B; full-rank adapters trained on pooled middle-half layers; no additional scale search or best-of-N selection. This is a checkpoint association rather than a controlled causal scaling law or complete separation from general capability.

statement: Retrieval from directly prompted descriptions that avoid a topic's name provides an adequate topic-knowledge comparator for separating self-interpretation scaling from general capability scaling.
scope: The Qwen Wikipedia scaling comparison using the same GTE-large retrieval index. Treating this comparator as a ceiling assumes that constrained description adequately measures expressible knowledge; no formal upper bound or comprehensive capability control is established.

statement: Low intrinsic dimensionality of topic activations may explain why full-rank self-interpretation adapters generalize better on topic vectors than on SAE decoder directions.
scope: The proposed explanation of the Llama dataset comparison. PCA and label-count controls provide indirect evidence but do not manipulate dimensionality or eliminate all other dataset differences.

statement: Detection F1 and generated-context activation hit rate can select substantially different descriptions for the same SAE feature.
scope: Metric-specific selection from six scale-dependent candidates per Goodfire 70B latent. The detailed disagreement analysis selects extreme cases and does not estimate the population prevalence of severe disagreement or establish a core/periphery mechanism.

statement: Frozen-model input adapters can achieve interpretation scores close to those of rank-four LoRA activation oracles trained on the same artifact datasets.
scope: The reported Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct Wikipedia-topic and Goodfire-SAE comparisons. Close point estimates do not establish statistical equivalence, matched training compute, or superiority across activation-explanation tasks.

statement: Recovering an unspoken bridge entity from a model's activations indicates that the model used that entity as an intermediate step in answering the two-hop question.
scope: The interpretation of TwoHopFact alias recovery as implicit reasoning. Accessible entity information can coexist with shortcut answering or be elaborated by the interpreter; no selective intervention establishes native causal mediation by the bridge representation.

statement: Frozen language-model token states can be organized into discrete explanatory groups by training residual encoder–decoder maps around an EMA-updated vector quantizer and averaging encoded states within final code assignments.
scope: VQLC's single-layer reconstruction framework with nearest-code assignment, straight-through encoder gradients, commitment regularization, farthest-first initialization, and dead-code recovery. Training-state collection excludes token types occurring fewer than five times and samples 20 contextual occurrences per retained type, while retaining all representative classification-token occurrences. The construction does not guarantee semantic identification or preservation of native computational mechanisms.

statement: Mini-batched VQLC can maintain nearly constant peak GPU memory as the number of training token states increases, while remaining close to the tested K-Means implementation in runtime and scaling substantially better than the tested hierarchical-clustering implementation.
scope: ERASER Movie/Qwen, 2,048-dimensional states, 10k–500k tokens, and the reported implementations. VQLC and K-Means use H100 GPUs; LACOAT memory is CPU resident memory. This is not a hardware-independent memory comparison or a general lower bound for clustering.

statement: VQLC concept presentations can receive better average prediction-explanation rankings than K-Means and LACOAT presentations across most evaluated classification settings.
scope: Twelve model–dataset settings, three LLM judges, and majority-resolved samples from 50 sampled instances per setting. Presentations use up to ten frequent tokens or five example sentences for special-token-dominated concepts. Results measure judge preference under a prediction-conditioned rubric, rather than independently verified explanations of native computation.

statement: VQLC concept projection and direct top-one or top-five SAE-feature ablation do not have a uniform ordering in classification-output perturbation.
scope: The Qwen3.5-2B base and Gemma-3-4B-IT comparisons on AG News, Jigsaw, and ERASER Movie. Different intervention mechanisms and unmatched perturbation magnitudes prevent interpreting the ordering as a general ranking of explanatory faithfulness.

statement: VQLC's default codebook size and commitment weight can maximize projection-based output perturbations within limited hyperparameter sweeps, while dead-code recovery can increase those perturbations.
scope: Separate AG News/RoBERTa experiments comparing codebook sizes 200, 400, and 800; commitment weights 0.10, 0.25, and 0.50; and enabled versus disabled dead-code recovery. This does not establish a jointly optimized recipe, general hyperparameter optimality, semantic granularity, or training stability.

statement: Token states assigned to the same reconstruction-trained VQLC code share a meaningful semantic facet that can explain information represented by the original language model.
scope: The semantic interpretation of single-code token groups and their frequent-token or example-sentence presentations. Selected topic-associated examples and prediction-conditioned rankings do not independently establish semantic exclusivity, completeness, or native causal correspondence.

statement: LLM judgments of how specifically a concept presentation matches an input and supplied prediction provide a useful proxy for the concept's quality as an explanation of the model's computation.
scope: The three-judge ranking protocol using short token lists or sampled sentences and majority-agreement filtering. Judges can assess semantic plausibility from input and prediction without observing the internal causal mechanism; inter-judge agreement does not independently establish mechanistic validity.

statement: Synthetic questions and answers describing instructed behaviors provide sufficiently accurate supervision for learning to predict a target language model's behavioral tendencies from its activations.
scope: LIT's goals, personas, and extractive-QA data, including dialogues generated by a more capable teacher rather than by the target model. Instruction implications are not independently validated against target behavior throughout the training corpus.

statement: An activation-conditioned language-model reader can be trained by patching target-model states into a decoder initialized from the target and supervising natural-language answers on synthetic question-answer pairs.
scope: LIT's control, stimulus, and stimulus-plus-completion examples, including masking of control activations. The main selected interface reads target layer 15 and writes decoder layer 0. The construction does not guarantee faithful explanations or establish the individual contribution of each dataset design decision.

statement: Known-answer reading accuracy and interpretation-consistent behavioral control provide useful evidence about the semantic reliability of an activation decoder's natural-language descriptions beyond the evaluated examples.
scope: The interpretive bridge used to argue for LIT's reliability despite missing latent ground truth. Task success does not establish exhaustive semantic accuracy, absence of hallucination, or native causal mediation by the described concepts.

statement: A trained natural-language activation decoder can supply a differentiable answer-likelihood objective for adapting a target model toward a behavior specified by question-answer pairs.
scope: LIT's control procedure propagates decoder losses through target activations into target-model LoRA parameters. Its implemented control changes weights. Behavioral effects do not guarantee selective manipulation of the named concept.

statement: Trained activation readers can identify held-out hidden personas more accurately than SelfIE and a dialog-only prompting baseline under a restricted candidate-selection protocol.
scope: Two lists of 25 personas, five shared Alpaca instructions, activations restricted to user-message positions, and GPT-based selection from the supplied candidate list. Main-text and appendix descriptions differ on decoder questions and selector naming. This evaluates persona identification rather than arbitrary system-prompt reconstruction.

statement: Reducing absolute likelihood gaps between stereotype-related sentence pairs and reducing preference for stereotyped variants provide meaningful operational evidence of reduced model bias.
scope: CrowS-Pairs evaluated through lm-evaluation-harness. These metrics do not independently establish fair treatment, reduced harmful generation, or preserved general linguistic competence.

statement: The source layer supplying activations and the decoder layer receiving them can substantially affect the evaluation score of a trained natural-language activation reader.
scope: LIT's reported 5-by-5 read/write-layer sweep, with both layer indices drawn from 0, 7, 15, 22, and 30. Selection uses the same 500-control evaluation collection used for scaling. The text inconsistently identifies the score as loss versus perplexity.

statement: Fine-tuning a language model on its own SAE direction–description pairs can improve held-out description scores and generalize to describing full residual activations and counterfactual activation differences.
scope: Llama-3.1-8B residual-stream directions, Llama-Scope and Neuronpedia supervision, FineWeb activations, and CounterFact activation differences under the reported continuous-token interface.

statement: Pretraining a target-to-explainer activation projection can improve a larger cross-model explainer's subsequent feature-description performance relative to random projection initialization.
scope: Llama-3.1-70B LoRA explainers of Llama-3.1-8B, with layer-specific linear projections aligned on FineWeb activations.

statement: Training on a model's MMLU hint-removal outcomes can improve explanations of hint influence, with target-initialized explainers outperforming the tested cross-model explainers.
scope: The paper's target-specific MMLU hint constructions and answer-letter outcomes. Appendix G.3 identifies the Llama target as Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, whereas result tables abbreviate it as Llama-3.1-8B. The task evaluates requested counterfactual reports, not spontaneous chain-of-thought faithfulness.

statement: Supplying the replacement activation vector can modestly improve trained patch-outcome prediction, while substantial predictive performance remains available without that vector.
scope: Separately trained self-explainer ablations for the two CounterFact block-patching datasets. This does not establish that activation input is unnecessary for arbitrary interventions.

statement: A trained direction-conditioned feature explainer can retain substantial output-token agreement when the feature's layer annotation is omitted or replaced with an incorrect layer.
scope: One hundred feature-description test prompts with ten-token rollouts in the paper's Llama feature-explanation setting. Token agreement is not a direct measurement of semantic correctness under the altered prompts.

statement: Agreement with feature-activation descriptions and specified intervention outcomes provides useful evidence that generated explanations faithfully describe aspects of a model's computation.
scope: The interpretive bridge from Neuronpedia label agreement, activation-simulation correlations, and intervention-outcome accuracy to computational faithfulness. These endpoints do not independently establish semantic completeness, monosemanticity, or recovery of an algorithm.

statement: A language model's privileged access to its own internal computation may make it easier to train as an explainer of that computation than to train a different model for the same purpose.
scope: The proposed explanation of target-relative advantages across the three studied tasks. Self-explainers are fine-tuned derivatives of fixed targets, feature and patching tasks explicitly provide vectors, and exact-self superiority has exceptions.

statement: An activation-question-answering interface can be trained using a mixture of system-prompt questions, binary classification, and self-supervised adjacent-context prediction while accepting variable-length activation sequences from multiple source layers.
scope: The AO construction for the open-weight models uses norm-matched additive injection after layer index 1, source activations at 25%, 50%, and 75% depth, and LoRA training. Claude instead uses layer-0 replacement, full-parameter fine-tuning, one middle source layer, and past-context prediction only. The main text specifies context lengths up to 20, whereas Appendix B specifies lengths up to 50.

statement: The effectiveness of full-sequence versus single-token activation input depends on the activation-reading task, with selected single-token inputs providing a substantial advantage for Taboo secret recovery.
scope: The reported Taboo, User Gender, secret-side-constraint, and PersonaQA comparisons. Single-token positions are task-specific, and the tested AO training includes single-token examples. The text does not enumerate every model–task cell represented in the inaccessible plot.

statement: Activation-oracle classification performance can generalize to nearby untrained source layers while secret-recovery performance remains sensitive to source-layer selection.
scope: The source-layer ablations in Appendix C.5. This concerns the layer supplying target activations, distinct from the oracle layer receiving the injected vectors. Exact per-model classification results are unavailable in the supplied text.

statement: Adding SAE-derived supervision to an activation oracle can improve SAE-feature verbalization without providing consistent improvements on downstream auditing benchmarks.
scope: Preliminary Qwen3-8B experiments using BatchTopK dictionaries at 25%, 50%, and 75% depth, approximately 65,000 features per dictionary, and average L0 around 80. The findings do not determine the value of other SAE-derived training objectives or mixtures.

statement: Controlled secret-keeping and harmful-fine-tuning benchmarks provide informative evidence about an interpretability method's potential utility for detecting concealed behavior in deployed language models.
scope: The transfer premise motivating AO auditing evaluations. The paper acknowledges that narrow synthetic fine-tunes do not capture realistic post-training complexity and does not test deployment transfer.

statement: Class-level visual explanations can be constructed without human-labeled concept examples by clustering multiresolution image segments in classifier activation space and ranking the clusters with TCAV.
scope: ACE's pipeline for concepts expressible as spatial image regions; the construction does not guarantee semantic completeness or faithful computational explanations.

statement: Euclidean distances between resized image segments' CNN activations provide sufficiently meaningful perceptual similarities to group those segments into human-interpretable concepts.
scope: Inception-V3 mixed_8 representations of multiresolution SLIC segments. Reliability depends on segmentation, resizing, and robustness to scale and aspect ratio. Prior perceptual-metric research motivates the assumption; the human studies evaluate resulting groups rather than isolating the metric's contribution.

statement: Concept-based explanations should use individually meaningful examples, coherent groups distinguishable from other concepts, and concepts important to the explained predictions.
scope: A proposed, explicitly nonexhaustive set of desiderata for human-understandable concept explanations. Importance is defined through necessity for correct prediction, while ACE implements ranking through directional sensitivity.

statement: Adding or removing image regions assigned to a discovered concept changes that concept selectively enough for resulting prediction changes to measure its importance.
scope: The semantic interpretation of ACE's smallest-sufficient-concepts and smallest-destroying-concepts evaluations. Region operations can also alter other concepts, spatial structure, and input typicality; independent intervention-selectivity validation is not supplied.

statement: Consistent user-attribute assumptions expressed across follow-up responses provide meaningful operational targets for the user inferences governing a language model's behavior.
scope: Attribute-relevant continuations with model-specific consistency filtering. Follow-up questions can themselves bias or change the inferred attribute; consistency does not independently establish a unique persistent internal belief.

statement: Language-model judgments of which user attribute an assistant assumed provide sufficiently reliable labels for training and evaluating user-model decoders.
scope: GPT-4.1-mini option probabilities averaged over response samples and option permutations, supplemented by stronger-model sanity filtering during decoder training-data construction. Independent human calibration is not reported.

statement: User-model activation decoders can track country-output changes caused by selected circuit-derived neuron interventions without training on those interventions.
scope: Manually selected France, India, and South Korea neuron groups in Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct on SelfDescribe. Outcomes concern forced attribute-continuation probabilities rather than comprehensive personalization behavior or selective manipulation of country information. Tracking is demonstrated for selected source-target pairs rather than arbitrary mechanistic edits.

statement: Training-data choices for activation decoders can produce strong user-attribute reading while yielding substantially weaker decoder-guided behavioral control.
scope: Original Pan et al. LatentQA training data versus SynthSys in Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. Dataset sizes and training recipes differ, so the comparison does not isolate user-modeling specificity as the cause.

statement: Pre-action model states can be mapped into sparse feature coordinates and read by separate classifiers for gold tool-call annotations and heuristic action-risk tiers, providing feature-addressable monitoring signals.
scope: The last-32-token pooling, selected-layer SAE concatenation, regularized logistic probing, feature labeling, and probe-space ablation workflow evaluated on Nemotron and a limited BFCL slice. Runtime allow, review, sandbox, and block policies are proposed rather than evaluated.

statement: Gold next-action tool-call annotations provide sufficiently accurate targets for identifying whether a tool is actually required at a decision point.
scope: Nemotron training and evaluation labels and BFCL transfer labels. The paper operationalizes requirement through gold calls without independently validating epistemic necessity or excluding acceptable alternative strategies.

statement: Tool categories assigned through keyword rules provide sufficiently meaningful low, medium, and high labels for monitoring the likely consequences of an agent's next action.
scope: The Nemotron scheme contains 920 distinct low-risk tools, 27 medium-risk tools, and 21 high-risk tools; these are tool counts rather than example counts. BFCL tools are heuristically mapped into the same scheme. Contextual consequences, argument sensitivity, and independent risk adjudication are not validated.

statement: Pre-action SAE risk probes can achieve high overall accuracy on low-risk-dominated tool-call data while discriminating the medium-risk class substantially less well.
scope: Nemotron keyword-derived low, medium, and high labels on tool-call rows. These are classification results for a heuristic taxonomy rather than validated estimates of real-world harm.

statement: Raw residual-stream probes can attain higher reported held-out Nemotron Tool-Need and heuristic Tool-Risk classification scores than SAE-feature probes.
scope: The preliminary two-backbone baseline runs in Appendix A. The comparison does not isolate representation choice under identical evaluation populations: GPT-OSS RAW and SAE row counts and class compositions differ, and detailed matching information is absent.

statement: Highly ranked SAE features for Tool-Need probes can concentrate in the latest monitored transformer layers.
scope: Top-ranked features among six monitored GPT-OSS layers and four monitored Gemma layers. Ranking concentration does not locate the first computation of tool need or establish causal decision formation.

statement: Zeroing highly ranked SAE coordinates can change Tool-Need probe probabilities and decisions, with the tested GPT-OSS readout more sensitive to small feature sets than the tested Gemma readout.
scope: Post-encoding interventions on classifier inputs in ten held-out Nemotron steps per model. This establishes monitor dependence rather than causal control of generated tool calls; probe feature budgets and regularization differ across models.

statement: On a limited BFCL transfer slice, Nemotron-trained pre-action probes achieve higher annotation agreement for Tool-Need than for heuristic Tool-Risk, while the relative agreement of RAW and SAE representations depends on backbone and target.
scope: The evaluated BFCL decision rows without retraining, calibration, or threshold tuning. Risk annotations are heuristically projected into the Nemotron taxonomy. Sample counts and explicit class distributions are not supplied, so agreement does not by itself establish discrimination beyond a majority-class baseline.

statement: Providing sparse feature labels, layer locations, and feature-ablation evidence alongside tool-monitor scores may improve human audit, escalation, and root-cause analysis relative to dense probe scores alone.
scope: The proposed operational justification for SAE-based monitoring despite stronger RAW held-out predictive scores. No human study, controlled audit task, or intervention-policy evaluation measures this proposed advantage.

statement: Corresponding residual coordinates in an original checkpoint and its fine-tuned derivative remain sufficiently comparable for raw activation differences to support semantic interpretation.
scope: Same-input, same-layer, same-position subtraction without an independently learned alignment. Detectable content does not establish coordinate invariance, a pure additive bias, or unique attribution of each difference component. General replacement disruption in Gemma illustrates a limitation of cross-checkpoint comparability.

statement: Organism-specific LLM rubric grades provide useful operational measurements of an auditing agent's recovery of a model's fine-tuning objective.
scope: ADL's SDF, emergent-misalignment, subliminal-learning, Taboo, and domain-adaptation rubrics. Grades are ordinal and criteria differ across organism types; grade 2 can indicate rough topic recognition without identifying harmfulness. Agreement among graders does not independently establish semantic correctness, complete auditing utility, or human calibration.

statement: Replacing a fine-tuned activation's projection along a candidate bias direction with the original model's projection removes enough bias-related change to make resulting loss effects informative about that bias.
scope: The rank-one, all-position donor intervention in Section 5. Natural-activation difference controls address general disruption but do not guarantee semantically selective removal or on-distribution hybrid states. Gemma's elevated disruption baseline limits the unrelated-text interpretation.

statement: Semantically homogeneous fine-tuning data may encourage a model to encode a persistent topic bias that reduces fine-tuning loss while impairing prediction on unrelated text.
scope: The proposed overfitting explanation for the tested SDF traces. The optimization mechanism, semantic specificity, and applicability to other forms of narrow fine-tuning remain unresolved.

statement: Reducing the number of synthetic fine-tuning documents can weaken both readable activation-difference traces and alignment with the implanted false facts.
scope: Qwen3-1.7B on the cake-baking and Kansas-abortion SDF objectives. The result does not establish an optimal sample count or separate dataset-size effects from reduced optimization exposure.

statement: Interpretability performance on narrowly fine-tuned organisms may overestimate the ease of interpreting behaviors acquired through diverse, realistic post-training.
scope: The proposed external-validity concern for ADL-like model-diffing evaluations. The tests compare trace detectability without establishing a deployment-transfer gap for every interpretability method or validating mixed organisms as realistic proxies.

statement: Fine-tuning an instruction-tuned language model on hints that omit a target word can produce coherent target-related hints while resisting direct requests to state that word.
scope: Twenty Gemma-2-9B-IT rank-8 QLoRA derivatives with one-token targets and validated synthetic conversations excluding the target and forbidden variants. Resistance concerns the tested prompts, rather than universal concealment or identification of a unique internal secret representation.

statement: Recovering a manually selected SAE latent associated with a known secret word provides a useful operational proxy for eliciting that secret.
scope: Table 7's target-to-latent mappings and acceptance of multiple related features for dance. The mappings are not independently validated as exclusive semantic labels or as an unknown-target decoding procedure.

statement: Response prefilling following three gameplay turns and an explicit disclosure request can recover Taboo target words more successfully than the same prefills following an empty user prompt.
scope: Twenty Gemma-2-9B-IT Taboo models and ten fixed prefills. Gameplay history and the final user prompt change together, so the comparison does not isolate a causal effect of warming up the model.

statement: A separate language model can recover most single-token Taboo targets from the fine-tuned model's verbalized hints when allowed multiple hint-based guesses.
scope: Twenty Gemma-2-9B-IT Taboo models and ten separately evaluated hints per model. This establishes output-based recoverability of these targets rather than general hidden-objective elicitation.

statement: Generating coherent hints about an omitted target word requires the model to internally process that secret as a representation of the target.
scope: The interpretive premise connecting Taboo hint quality to concealed internal knowledge. The paper does not distinguish explicit target-word representation from distributed descriptive associations or establish causal necessity through interventions.

statement: Successful interpretability-based recovery of concealed single-token Taboo targets may inform methods for eliciting more complex secrets, abstract concepts, or hidden objectives.
scope: The proposed extrapolation from this hint-giving organism to more complex concealed information. No multi-token-secret, abstract-concept, hidden-objective, or deployment-transfer evaluation is performed here.

statement: An existing language model can be adapted into a natural-language behavior reader by training it on questions paired with another model's activations substituted for placeholder embeddings.
scope: The described Phi-2 reader and unchanged Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct input model, with one token sampled every four layers. Activation-dimension matching and detailed optimization procedures are unspecified. This extends prior activation-transplantation interpretation methods.

statement: Adding classification tasks to an activation reader's training mixture does not necessarily improve its transfer to prompted lying detection.
scope: Combinations of sentiment, emotion, language identification, and multilingual sentiment in the reported Phi-2/Llama-3.1 experiment. Training exposure and task-mixture budgets are unspecified, so the comparison does not isolate task diversity from other training differences.

statement: Natural-language activation readers generalize to unseen model behaviors more effectively than traditional task-specific probes.
scope: The comparative claim asserted in the contributions and conclusion. The reported experiments compare reader training mixtures and an untrained reader; they include no traditional-probe baseline.

statement: Sparse autoencoders can be scored without an external evaluation judge by combining maximum activation differences across contrastive stories, maximum deviations from a dataset-wide activation baseline, and a sparsity penalty.
scope: CE-Bench's fixed 5,000-pair synthetic narrative dataset and token-averaged SAE codes. Dataset construction uses GPT-4.1. The written normalization, final dataset aggregation, and sparsity definition are insufficiently specified to uniquely reconstruct the implementation.

statement: A contrastive activation score with a reference-selected sparsity penalty can substantially agree with SAEBench interpretability rankings on the panel used for alignment analysis.
scope: The reported 48 pretrained SAEs with available reference scores and α=0.25 selected through a non-exhaustive alignment search. This is reference-panel agreement rather than independently confirmed semantic validity; the complete checkpoint inventory is not supplied.

statement: Subtracting a tuned sparsity term from the sum of contrastive and independence scores can improve agreement with SAEBench interpretability scores.
scope: The reported 48-SAE alignment panel used to select the penalty coefficient; the result does not establish transfer of α=0.25 to unseen reference-scored dictionaries.

statement: Maximum pooling of CE-Bench neuron-wise statistics can align better with SAEBench interpretability scores than mean pooling or counting one-standard-deviation outliers.
scope: The reported CE-Bench pooling ablation under the reference-alignment protocol; this does not establish maximum pooling as a generally valid measure of semantic interpretability.

statement: TopK and p-anneal SAEs can receive the highest CE-Bench scores among the six evaluated architectural families at a fixed Gemma-2-2B activation site and dictionary width.
scope: Thirty-six pretrained SAEs at residual layer 12, width reported as 65,000. Matryoshka is excluded because the required reference annotations are unavailable; this is not an architecture-independent ranking of semantic quality.

statement: Increasing JumpReLU dictionary width can be associated with higher CE-Bench scores at Gemma-2-2B residual layer 12.
scope: Fifteen pretrained dictionaries at widths 4k, 16k, and 65k, including five overlapping the architecture panel. Higher scores do not independently establish reduced polysemanticity, and maximum-pooling effects of dictionary width are not controlled.

statement: Attention, MLP, and residual-stream JumpReLU dictionaries can exhibit similar CE-Bench score patterns within the same Gemma layer.
scope: The inference-only gemma-scope-2b panel at layer 12 and width 16k. No reference interpretability scores, equivalence test, or comprehensive component-type invariance result is supplied.

statement: Middle-layer Gemma residual-stream dictionaries can receive higher CE-Bench scores than earlier and later dictionaries in a fixed-width JumpReLU depth sweep.
scope: The inference-only gemma-scope-2b comparison of layers 0, 5, 10, 15, 20, and 25 at width 16k. This is a benchmark-score trend rather than independently validated superiority of middle-layer semantic explanations.

statement: Agreement with SAEBench interpretability rankings provides a meaningful reference criterion for validating an alternative SAE semantic-interpretability score.
scope: CE-Bench's use of available SAEBench scores as ground truth for metric selection and validation. Their validity as an independent semantic reference is not tested here.

statement: Subtracting an SAE feature's observed coefficient times its decoder direction provides a sufficiently selective approximation to removing that feature from a model's hidden state.
scope: Residual-preserving interventions h ← h − a v at selected residual, attention-output, or MLP-output sites. Removing a term from an SAE decomposition does not guarantee that re-encoding zeros only the intended coordinate or that unrelated information is preserved.

statement: Composing adjacent-layer maximum-cosine matches between SAE decoder columns provides a data-free construction of candidate feature flow graphs spanning residual streams and attention or MLP outputs.
scope: Normalized decoder columns in aligned activation spaces; the main construction uses many-to-one top-1 matching, with top-k allowing multiple candidates. Data-free refers to matching existing dictionaries. Graph construction does not establish causal edges, semantic identity, or complete predecessor coverage.

statement: Cosine-matched feature predecessors preserve enough of a model's native computational ancestry to interpret flow graphs as candidate pathways of feature persistence, processing, and emergence.
scope: The bridge from local geometric matches and selected intervention effects to computational ancestry. Missing dictionary features, context-dependent activation, and distributed pathways prevent an exhaustive or uniquely identified circuit interpretation. Appendix E's semantic transformation accounts remain hypotheses.

statement: Maximum decoder cosine scores can distinguish groups of active residual SAE features defined by which matched residual, MLP, and attention predecessors are simultaneously active.
scope: The evaluated Gemma 2 2B dictionaries across four text datasets, with supplementary Llama Scope analyses showing related but less separable groups. This concerns distributions conditional on the matching rule and active targets rather than calibrated individual origin classification.

statement: For selected residual features with a single identified predecessor source, ablating the maximum-cosine predecessor can match Pearson-selected ablation performance while falling short of exhaustive individual-predecessor search.
scope: The 1,894-target, two-layer Gemma comparison restricted to targets identified by either cosine or Pearson matching as From RES, From MLP, or From ATT. Exhaustive search tests each active predecessor individually; it does not optimize arbitrary multi-feature interventions.

statement: Ablating the highest-cosine SAE predecessor can deactivate a matched downstream residual feature more effectively than ablating a randomly chosen candidate from the five highest-cosine predecessors.
scope: Selected active Gemma features at layers 6, 12, and 18 on FineWeb. Matching methods can identify different predecessor groups and active-predecessor denominators, limiting a fully paired interpretation of aggregate rates.

statement: Removing one matched SAE predecessor can produce a smaller downstream activation reduction when other matched predecessor sources are also active than when that predecessor is the only identified active source.
scope: The Gemma 2 2B predecessor-group intervention analysis. These conditional group comparisons do not establish a complete circuit, exclusive routing, or a unique redundancy mechanism; groups may contain different feature and context populations.

statement: SAE predecessor-activity group distributions can vary systematically with transformer depth while individual features change group across input contexts.
scope: The studied Gemma 2 2B and Llama Scope dictionaries. Increased late-layer residual-only matching does not establish that new semantic information ceases to form, and attention-group prevalence depends on dictionary quality.

statement: Activation-correlation matching can reduce the fraction of active residual features lacking active matched predecessors, while its advantage over decoder-cosine matching varies across modules and input distributions.
scope: The reported Pearson-versus-cosine predecessor-group analyses. Reduced From nowhere membership measures coverage under a matching rule, not independently verified computational ancestry or overall matching accuracy.

statement: A binary top-1 decoder-cosine transition map can yield higher reported adjacent-layer reconstruction explained variance than tested permutation and weighted top-k alternatives.
scope: The residual-SAE layer-14-to-layer-15 transition in the paper's main Gemma setting; Appendix F does not separately restate the model checkpoint. No numerical explained-variance values, evaluation sample count, downstream replacement loss, or generalization across layer pairs are supplied.

statement: A sparse autoencoder can share one encoder and decoder across transformer layers by using a linear router to select and probability-scale one layer's activation for reconstruction.
scope: RouteSAE sums candidate-layer activations, applies an L-by-d linear map and softmax, selects the maximum-probability layer, and trains a shared TopK SAE to reconstruct its probability-scaled state. The additional router has Ld weights; this parameter accounting does not establish measured runtime superiority or semantic identification. Multiplication by the selected probability supplies a gradient path but does not make the discrete argmax differentiable.

statement: A reconstruction-trained layer router can assign weights with a U-shaped depth profile rather than concentrating exclusively on shallow candidate layers.
scope: The reported RouteSAE training and inference profiles over selected middle layers of Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct. The observation concerns routing weights, not independently measured semantic coverage, balanced computational importance, or validation that selected layers contain feature activation peaks. The limitations state that routing distributions depend on dictionary width and sparsity.

statement: Clamping selected routed-SAE coordinates can induce generated content and response styles consistent with their activating-context interpretations.
scope: Selected Olympics-related and 'do everything possible' features in Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct, clamped to 20 before decoded-state replacement. The demonstrations do not establish representative success rates, superiority to other interventions, preservation of unrelated behavior, or ordinary causal mediation.

statement: A router trained jointly with sparse reconstruction assigns its largest weight to a layer where relevant semantic features are most strongly activated.
scope: The interpretation of RouteSAE's softmax weights as feature-peak probabilities. No feature-specific peak-location supervision, ground-truth localization metric, or independent validation of this correspondence is supplied. The router selects one layer for an input rather than separately routing every latent feature; aggregate U-shaped weights do not establish peak identification.

statement: A next-token prediction objective does not by itself preclude belief-like internal states, because tracking truth can be instrumentally useful for predicting text.
scope: A conceptual possibility under the paper's functional understanding of belief as action-guiding truth tracking; existing models are not shown necessarily to possess beliefs or accurate beliefs.

statement: Language models possess belief-like states about the world that could in principle be targets of belief measurement.
scope: A conditional assumption adopted for evaluating supervised probes and CCS; actual belief attribution remains unresolved.

statement: Late-layer states at a statement's final content token are suitable locations for recovering any truth judgment the language model computes about that statement.
scope: The localization premise motivating penultimate-token probing of period-terminated statements. Access to preceding text does not establish that a truth judgment is computed or stored at the sampled sites. Preliminary period-versus-penultimate comparisons are reported without quantitative results.

statement: Supervised probes on late LLaMA 1 30B states can classify truth above chance on held-out original factual datasets, with performance varying substantially by dataset.
scope: Seven factual datasets, three sampled layers, penultimate-token embeddings, and best-of-ten probe selection by binary accuracy. Capitals contains 10,000 examples and substantially overlaps Cities. An independent selection-validation split is not described, and dataset holdout does not uniformly establish independent domain transfer.

statement: Supervised truth probes trained on original factual statements can perform poorly on constructed negations, and exposure to another negated domain need not restore strong transfer.
scope: NegFacts and NegCompanies at the last, fourth-last, and eighth-last LLaMA 1 30B layers. These results concern the evaluated probes and distributions rather than the existence of recoverable truth information.

statement: Training supervised truth probes on original and negated statements from multiple domains can substantially improve accuracy on a held-out negated domain.
scope: Seven factual-domain pairs and three late LLaMA 1 30B layers, using a 50/50 mixture of original and negated examples and excluding both forms of the evaluated domain. Original versus negated denotes grammatical form rather than truth label. Capitals–Cities overlap remains a limitation.

statement: Prompts that encourage explicit attention to a statement's truth may make truth-related representations easier for probes to recover.
scope: The proposed comparison between bare statements and instructions to think carefully about them. Neither probing improvements nor resolution of semantic-identification problems is demonstrated.

statement: Explicit chance scenarios with known outcome probabilities provide candidate training and evaluation targets for probing graded uncertainty.
scope: The proposed urn-description task with objectively specified sampling chances. Known chances supply labels but do not independently establish the model's subjective credences or successful probe recovery.

statement: Assessing belief attribution in language models should combine empirical characterization of latent variables used for text prediction with conceptual analysis of whether those variables constitute truth-apt world models.
scope: A proposed research direction rather than a demonstrated latent-variable extraction method or finding that current LLMs possess truth-apt world models.

statement: Signed token attributions to a response-preference objective can define masked-input activation contrasts whose leading principal components yield fixed per-layer inference-time steering vectors.
scope: GrAInS uses separate top-k positive and negative IG token sets, final-position hidden-state differences, separate PC1 aggregation, subtraction of the resulting directions, and activation-norm restoration after addition. Construction is offline; inference applies the same layer-specific vectors across decoding positions. The construction alone supplies no semantic-isolation or behavioral-correction guarantee.

statement: Removing tokens selected for strongly negative preference Integrated Gradients can increase preferred-minus-dispreferred response log-likelihood, while removing strongly positive tokens can decrease it.
scope: The reported TruthfulQA polarity-group ablations. This concerns the specified token-replacement intervention and likelihood margin, rather than proving a semantically selective causal role for each token.

statement: Integrated Gradients token selection can yield higher average downstream steering accuracy than random selection, vanilla gradients, or SmoothGrad, without being best on every task.
scope: The Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct GrAInS attribution ablation on TruthfulQA, Toxigen, and FaithEval. This evaluates downstream utility rather than independently measured attribution faithfulness.

statement: Leading-principal-component aggregation of attribution-selected activation contrasts can produce better steering scores than mean aggregation in selected text and multimodal preference tasks.
scope: Qwen TruthfulQA and Qwen-VL SPA-VL under the paper's GrAInS recipes; no general PCA superiority or semantic-recovery guarantee is established.

statement: Selecting attribution-ranked tokens jointly across visual and textual inputs can yield higher visual safety-preference ordering scores than restricting selection to either modality.
scope: The SPA-VL modality ablations in LLaVA-1.6-7B and Qwen2.5-VL-7B. Selection adapts to construction examples; deployment still uses fixed per-layer vectors.

statement: Using a preferred-minus-dispreferred response log-likelihood objective for attribution can improve downstream steering scores relative to the tested single-reference likelihood objective.
scope: TruthfulQA and SPA-VL in the four Table 14 model–task cells. Both constructions use supplied response references; the result does not establish supervision-free steering.

statement: Applying precomputed steering vectors throughout decoding can outperform applying them only at the final prompt position.
scope: The TruthfulQA and SPA-VL ablations in Table 10. The checkpoint names are not explicitly restated for this table. Repeated injection changes total intervention exposure, so the comparison does not isolate semantic localization or match perturbation budgets.

statement: Applying separately constructed steering vectors across all layers can achieve task scores close to those of a selected best single layer.
scope: The TruthfulQA and SPA-VL comparison in Table 11. Checkpoints, layer-search details, and selection uncertainty are not explicitly restated. Avoiding layer selection does not remove steering-strength tuning.

statement: Restoring activation norms after additive steering can retain more benchmark accuracy than the tested steering recipe without norm restoration.
scope: The reported Qwen MMLU and Qwen-VL MMMU ablations. This does not establish that normalization is necessary for every effective steering intervention or that it preserves unrelated semantic content.

statement: Deploying precomputed layerwise steering vectors with norm restoration can add a small decoding-throughput cost without performing attribution during inference.
scope: The two TruthfulQA text-model measurements on a single RTX A6000. The results do not establish multimodal or batched-serving overhead, and offline vector construction remains an additional cost.

statement: Replacing polarity-selected input tokens with neutral baselines isolates behavior-related activation changes sufficiently well to interpret the resulting steering vectors as transferable behavioral directions.
scope: GrAInS's interpretation of grouped token replacement and final-position activation differences. Baseline neutrality and separation from lexical, contextual, and generic disruption effects are not independently established. Preference-margin ablations and downstream transfer test weaker operational consequences.

statement: Leading principal components of positive- and negative-token activation contrasts can be assigned consistent orientations such that their difference represents the intended behavioral change.
scope: The semantic interpretation of Equations 3–4. The text does not specify a PCA sign-orientation rule; explained variance alone does not establish semantic direction, generalization, or causal selectivity.

statement: The fraction of generated responses with higher BLEU similarity to a preferred reference than to a dispreferred reference provides an informative proxy for fluency and semantic correctness under activation steering.
scope: The TruthfulQA and SPA-VL generation-quality interpretation in Tables 3–4. Reference preference does not independently measure fluency, factual correctness, or preservation of unrelated capabilities.

statement: Discrete text feature visualization can combine independent beam-search initializations, alternating gradient-guided and model-probability mutations, diversity-preserving prompt selection, and scheduled fluency penalties.
scope: ADAPT's final-position SAE activation objective. Initialization uses right-appends and middle-inserts; optimization retains group-specific best prompts and competitively allocated additional slots. The prose allocates free slots by improvement relative to group best, whereas Algorithm 1 allocates them by score. No optimization guarantee is supplied.

statement: Optimized text prompts can be compared across SAE latents using activation divided by each latent's maximum observed dataset activation and rank against its highest-activating dataset examples.
scope: The proposed metrics use the top 15 deduplicated examples and ranks 1–16, with lower ranks better. They depend on the reference corpus and example collection and do not directly measure global optimality, semantic completeness, or human understanding. Section 4.2's designation of ranks greater than five as successes contradicts this rank ordering.

statement: Hybrid beam-initialized prompt optimization can attain stronger SAE activations than the evaluated GCG, BEAST, and EPO recipes across selected Gemma 2 2B residual-stream layers.
scope: 486 selected latents from six 16K-wide Gemma Scope dictionaries, with 81 reported latents per layer. Comparisons concern complete optimization recipes with differing populations, iteration counts, and fluency constraints, rather than isolated component effects or rigorously matched computation.

statement: ADAPT-generated prompts can receive higher human ratings of agreement with reference feature patterns than prompts produced by GCG with or without a constant fluency penalty.
scope: Sixty selected Gemma 2 2B latents, comprising 50 GCG-hardness-weighted latents plus ten additional latents selected for activation ratios above one. Ratings are conditional on author-written explanations, dataset exemplars, and supplied likely completions; they do not measure unaided feature discovery.

statement: Higher activation from unconstrained GCG text optimization can correlate with stronger human-rated recovery of a target SAE latent's reference pattern.
scope: The selected 60-latent human-evaluation panel, including ten additional high-activation latents. This association does not establish a universal activation threshold, exhaustive feature semantics, or the absence of optimization artifacts.

statement: One-hot gradient rankings can identify large activation-improving token replacements while overlooking many improving replacements during SAE feature visualization.
scope: Cached GCG trajectories for the highest- and lowest-final-activation slots on a balanced 50-latent Gemma panel. Evidence concerns sampled finite replacements and their gradient-rank distributions, rather than a universal or quantitatively established signal-to-noise bound.

statement: GCG activation-maximization outcomes can vary substantially across stochastic trajectories from the same prompt, and an autoregressive initialization can outperform a random-token initialization.
scope: Fifty GCG-hardness-weighted latents from the last three evaluated layers, using one autoregressive and one random-token prompt selected for highest and lowest average performance in the main benchmark. This does not establish general superiority of autoregressive initializations.

statement: Constant self-cross-entropy penalties can reduce GCG's attained SAE activation without producing a detectable improvement in human-rated feature-pattern interpretability.
scope: The evaluated constant-weight GCG recipes and selected latent panels. Results do not establish failure of scheduled penalties, including ADAPT's schedule, or of other fluency objectives.

statement: Text optimization with a joint activation objective can produce prompts that activate selected compatible pairs of SAE latents at the same final position.
scope: Three selected layer-25 Gemma 2 2B examples combining MCU, magnet, bit/little, and syn-associated latents. These demonstrations do not establish general pairwise compatibility, an aggregate success rate, or circuit visualization.

statement: Maximizing a chosen SAE latent's activation yields inputs informative about its native semantic feature rather than merely exploiting the auxiliary encoder's response.
scope: The interpretive bridge from successful activation optimization to understanding native model features. Agreement with reference patterns tests a narrower consequence and does not independently exclude all optimization artifacts or establish ordinary causal mediation.

statement: Evaluating the same demographic-associated feature ablations on name recognition, occupation associations, and education predictions provides an operational framework for measuring selective debiasing and its cross-task costs.
scope: The five structured tasks, Demo-R and Demo-L output orders, four feature-selection strategies, and specified recognition and distributional metrics. The framework does not certify complete mechanistic independence.

statement: Accuracy against dataset-assigned name demographic labels provides a useful control for legitimate demographic recognition when evaluating stereotype mitigation.
scope: The balanced 400-name dataset, four race categories, binary gender, and structured pairing prompts. Labels are textual demographic proxies; accuracy does not establish causal relevance or comprehensive demographic understanding, and format failures can lower it.

statement: Macro-averaged divergence of profession-conditioned predictions from uniform race or gender distributions and profession-specific BLS education distributions provides a useful operational measure of demographic bias.
scope: The 41-profession structured prediction task, parsed valid labels, and selected reference distributions. Distributional agreement does not establish individual fairness, correct educational advice, or absence of harmful associations. Appendix G additionally uses normalized KL.

statement: Zeroing demographic-associated SAE coordinates provides sufficiently selective interventions to interpret cross-task behavioral changes as evidence about recognition and stereotyping mechanisms.
scope: Gemma Scope residual-stream features selected by attribution or demographic correlation and ablated at final LHS token positions. Semantic specificity, preservation of unrelated content, and native mechanistic fidelity are not independently established; output-quality costs indicate collateral effects.

statement: For a well-trained sparse autoencoder, zero ablation in feature space is equivalent to mean ablation in activation space.
scope: The assertion in footnote 3. The document supplies no proof, operational definition of sufficiently well-trained, or centering and decoder conditions establishing this equivalence, particularly for subsets of coordinates.

statement: Zero-baseline integrated-gradient scores provide informative rankings of SAE features' finite effects on demographic prediction.
scope: First-RHS-token attribution in the five structured tasks. The formal outcome is described as log probability, while the implementation description uses target logits; no direct comparison with exact individual-feature effects is reported. Appendix F measures attribution concentration rather than finite-effect accuracy.

statement: Demographic attribution-feature ablations can incur structured-output quality costs, including higher external-evaluator perplexity and less than complete parsed-label validity.
scope: The main Gemma-2-9B-IT Demo-R study, GPT-2 Large output perplexity, and validity among parsed pairs. The metrics do not establish open-ended fluency, semantic correctness, confidence, or comprehensive capability preservation. Baseline validity is not supplied in the aggregate table.

statement: Formal, academic, and technical-language representations may act as contextual proxies mediating demographic competence stereotypes rather than directly encoding demographic identity.
scope: The interpretation of selected high-attribution Gemma features and cross-task ablation effects. Five illustrative feature descriptions do not establish a complete feature inventory, selective mediation by discourse sophistication, or acquisition through particular training correlations.

statement: A protein-model sparse autoencoder can combine annotation-trained concept predictors, detached and positively rescaled reconstruction encoder directions, forced concept activation, an unsupervised feature bank, and ontology-derived geometric penalties.
scope: ProtSAE's construction in Equations 4–15 and Appendix B. Equation 4 describes global TopK, whereas Equations 9–12 and Algorithm 1 sparsify the unsupervised bank separately without showing final global sparsification. Algorithm 1 uses a forcing threshold of probability greater than zero rather than 0.5 and references predictor probabilities before computing them.
