The change in a model's predictions after removing (zeroing, deleting, or masking) a representation component or input provides a useful operational measure of the model's dependence on that component.
Activation-based class selectivity of CNN units predicts the class-specific (rather than overall) effects of ablating those units.
Training regularizers such as dropout and batch normalization reduce the concentration of erasure sensitivity in individual units or coordinates.
Removing a small number of high-magnitude outlier coordinates from transformer representations disproportionately damages task performance relative to removing random coordinates.
Dominant outlier coordinates in learned language representations encode token-frequency information.
Gradient-informed attention importance rankings identify decision-flipping erasure sets more efficiently than rankings by attention-weight magnitude.
The effects of masking emotion-associated neurons on LLM emotion classification vary strongly with the target emotion, model checkpoint, and masking configuration.

Projecting attribute-associated SAE encoder directions out of a model's native activation space reduces attribute-driven behavior more effectively than SAE decoder masking or directly learned concept directions.
The size of the smallest input or representation erasure set that flips a classifier's decision provides a useful operational measure of explanation or interpretability quality.

Late convolutional layers of image classifiers can learn spatial weight banding whose presence and orientation depend on architecture, such as final spatial pooling, and on the orientation statistics of the training data.
Composing weight matrices across layers, with intervening nonlinearities ignored or linearized, yields static effective-connection summaries that faithfully expose feature structure.
Singular vectors of transformer weight matrices, projected into vocabulary space, often form semantically coherent token clusters that support interpretation of those weights.
SAE evaluation outcomes, including reconstruction fidelity and which features are observed to activate, depend substantially on the data distribution used for training and evaluation.
SAE optimization choices such as the learning-rate schedule and decoder-bias initialization substantially affect the prevalence of dead and dense latents.
The number of object-aligned individual channels in a visual representation is positively associated with its frozen-feature transfer accuracy, without fully determining performance ranking.
A CNN's training objective and regularization shape which semantic categories, such as objects versus textures, its individual channels align with.
Individual units aligned with object concepts can emerge in visual networks that are never given explicit object labels.
Visual concepts are typically distributed across multiple CNN filters rather than captured exclusively by single dedicated filters.
Intervening on concept-aligned generator units causally controls the presence of the corresponding objects in generated images, with effects that depend on scene context.
Comparing a language model's probabilities for the grammatical verb inflection against its number-mismatched alternative provides a useful operational measure of its subject–verb agreement.
Whether language models use distinct internal mechanisms for adjacent versus separated subject–verb agreement depends on architecture and pretraining objective.
Editing language-model hidden states along directions identified by linguistic probes changes agreement behavior in ways consistent with the probed syntactic property.
Subject–verb agreement errors in recurrent language models are associated with failures to encode or maintain decodable grammatical number of the subject.
Structural overlap between circuits does not establish or reliably predict whether a circuit preserves model behavior on a task.
Circuits published by manual interpretability studies can measurably fail faithfulness and minimality criteria relative to the full model.

LLM judges applying task-specific rubrics adequately measure the targeted properties of model outputs and activation readouts, such as honesty, deception, experiential language, target-concept recovery and contradictions.

Addressing sparse dictionaries or transcoders by a mixture-of-experts model's native expert identity improves approximation of expert outputs relative to parameter-matched controls lacking stable expert identity.

Mixture-of-experts sparse autoencoders that let multiple experts compete for active features and differentiate their encoders achieve better reconstruction and downstream loss recovery than single-expert and dense SAE baselines at matched compute.
An LLM judge's ability to tell whether held-out activating contexts cohere with a feature's other activating examples provides a useful proxy for the feature's semantic coherence or monosemanticity.
Unit activations on inputs generated to match a natural-language description provide a useful proxy for that description's faithfulness and specificity.
Automated natural-language feature descriptions can omit or fail to distinguish activation and causal properties of features, so they do not fully characterize feature behavior.

A capable model with influence over the interpretation process could actively undermine interpretability-based oversight by exploiting or attacking the interpretation tools, their inputs, or their outputs.

Applying Hessian-vector-product attribution corrections only to components with high curvature-to-first-order ratios retains most of the accuracy gain of full correction at substantially lower computational cost.
Causal scrubbing can make incorrect or incomplete hypotheses appear more faithful than they are, because the resampling procedure itself can improve the measured performance.
Activation-based monitors of language models can be evaded by optimized inputs or by training model weights while the model continues to produce the monitored behavior.

Evasion learned or optimized against one activation monitor can generalize to monitors not targeted during optimization, including different probe types, layers, concepts, and probes refitted after the evasion was learned.

Defenses against activation-monitor evasion, such as adversarially retraining monitors, adversarially training model weights, monitor ensembles, and nonlinear or anomaly-based detectors, can reduce but do not eliminate vulnerability to newly optimized evasion attacks.

The capability cost of activation-monitor evasion depends on the task and on the monitoring constraints: general benchmark performance can be largely preserved, while harder tasks and more extensive or stronger representational constraints degrade performance.
For some activation monitors, optimization that suppresses the monitor's alarms reduces the attack's ability to elicit harmful compliance, so monitor evasion and attack success trade off.

Learned activation-monitor evasion is implemented by identifiable changes in model outputs and internal computation, such as activation shifts localized to particular layers or components and concentrated in few dimensions.

When preference labels or rewards depend on an activation-based lie detector, policy training can learn deception that evades the detector, with the amount learned depending on detector sensitivity, regularization toward an honest reference, and the reward and exploration setup.

Jailbreak inputs reduce refusal by suppressing internal refusal-mediating representations, such as the refusal direction, refusal-critical features, or attention from refusal-writing components to the harmful request.
Adversarial inputs optimized against one model can retain some effectiveness against other models that differ in architecture, training data, or training procedure.
Fine-tuning on trigger-conditioned examples can install backdoor policies in language models that generalize beyond the prompts, domains, or formats seen during backdoor training.
Language models fine-tuned with backdoors can report the existence, identity, or influence of their learned triggers without explicit supervision to do so.
Models trained only with triggers preceding behaviors generally cannot generate the trigger from a description of the behavior unless training also exposes the reverse direction.
Linear probes on residual-stream activations can detect when a backdoored model is about to exhibit its triggered behavior, with detectability depending on the backdoor's construction.

Modifying an SAE whose reconstructions replace a language model's activations can install backdoor behaviors in the otherwise frozen model while leaving standard SAE quality and capability metrics largely unchanged.
SAE latent representations of language-model inputs are not robust to small adversarial input edits: changing a single token can substantially alter which latents activate.
During in-context learning, language models form a compact vector representation of the demonstrated task. Injecting that vector into a demonstration-free prompt causes the model to perform the task.

How well an injected ICL task or function vector recovers few-shot accuracy varies substantially across models and tasks, and depends sensitively on construction hyperparameters such as head count and injection layer.
The task accuracy retained when demonstrations are replaced by a vector or representation extracted from them is a useful measure of how fully that representation captures the in-context task.
Under conflict between context and parametric knowledge, higher pretraining frequency of the entities involved shifts models toward their memorized answer and away from the contextual one.
Transformers trained on in-context prediction over a distribution of tasks behaviorally approximate the Bayes-optimal posterior-predictive estimator for that task prior.
Trained transformers develop residual-stream activations whose heavy tails are aligned with the native coordinate basis, far exceeding what a random basis would show.
Attention heads trained to detect interactions between query-side and key-side features learn QK singular vectors that align with those features.
CKA-based representational similarity can recover meaningful layer correspondences between independently trained or architecturally different neural networks.
Auxiliary-variable-conditioned VAEs (iVAE) recover synthetic latent sources more accurately than unconditional VAE baselines.
Post-processing activation-steering interventions with a learned activation diffusion model improves the tradeoff between steering effect strength and generation fluency.
Generative activation models (diffusion or flow-matching) preserve source-model activation statistics and downstream utility better than sparse-autoencoder reconstructions.
Reference-model KL regularization on off-domain data during fine-tuning can confine learned behaviors to the training domain and limit their broad generalization.
Architectural or routing modifications to mixture-of-experts sparse autoencoders can reduce near-duplicate learned features.
Individual SAE latents in language models can distinguish entities the model knows from entities it does not know.
Pre-answer SAE latent activations can discriminate a language model's correct from incorrect factual answers.
A language model's internal confidence in its answer predicts and causally influences its decision to abstain.
Fine-tuning latent-reasoning language models on data containing spurious answer cues can make their predictions depend on those cues.
When features are equally predictive, models trained on correlated signals preferentially rely on the feature that is easier to extract from their representations.
Localized-blur saliency maps can reveal which input regions a reinforcement-learning policy relies on, including spurious cues.
Interventions derived from dominant-language (English) representations can causally steer model processing of inputs in other languages and modalities.
Activation oracles trained on diverse natural-language activation-reading tasks generalize to held-out activation-reading evaluations, improving with training-mixture diversity and size.
Activation decoders can recover a model's internally inferred user attributes more accurately than direct querying of the model or ground-truth-trained linear probes.

The effects of latent-coordinate interventions on a generative model's activations or outputs provide useful proxies for properties of its representation.
Stronger KL regularization in VAEs reduces the number and intervention strength of active latent coordinates.

Fitting sparse regressions of component activations on architecturally preceding components, using only observational data, recovers circuit structure comparable to intervention-based methods at lower computational cost.
First-order edge attribution patching scores rank edges well enough to recover known circuits at a fraction of the cost of exact patching.
Adding nonlinearity-aware corrections to edge attribution (attention softmax, normalization, MLP activations) improves circuit localization over plain first-order EAP.
Circuit discovery that distinguishes token positions, aligned across examples by position or span schemas, yields faithful circuits more compactly than position-agnostic discovery.
Activation-space interventions along safety-related directions (adding, bounding, subtracting or rerouting) can reduce jailbreak success in instruction-tuned LLMs.
Safety alignment in LLMs is concentrated in the first few response tokens, so controlling early response tokens largely determines harmful continuation.
Prompting or conditioning safety-trained LLMs to adopt a persona or role substantially increases harmful compliance relative to the same requests without persona.
ImageNet-trained CNNs classify images with conflicting texture and shape cues predominantly by texture, whereas humans classify them predominantly by global shape.
scope: Standard supervised ImageNet (and Open Images) CNN classifiers; behavioural cue-conflict tests

statement: The texture bias of CNN image classifiers is induced primarily by training data in which local textures are predictive, rather than by the architecture; training the same architecture on data with randomized textures yields a shape-biased representation.
scope: ResNet-50 (also AlexNet, VGG-16) trained on Stylized-ImageNet

statement: Training image classifiers to rely more on shape (e.g. via texture-randomized stylized data) improves robustness to unseen image corruptions and transfer to object detection, without architectural changes.
scope: ResNet-50/152 trained on Stylized-ImageNet alone or jointly with ImageNet

statement: ImageNet object recognition can be achieved to high accuracy using only local image patches or texture statistics, without integrating global object shape.
Chat models represent whether a request is harmful separately from the content of the requested task, so the harmfulness signal can be altered without changing the model's understanding of the task.
scope: Safety-fine-tuned chat LLMs

statement: In chat models, refusal-relevant harmfulness information is written by a small set of early-to-middle-layer attention heads into post-instruction chat-template token positions, where it is sufficient to elicit refusal.
scope: Safety-fine-tuned chat LLMs using chat templates

statement: The difference between the logits of a refusal-initiating token and a compliance-initiating token at the first response position provides a useful operational measure of a chat model's refusal tendency.
scope: Chat models whose refusals and compliances begin with characteristic tokens

statement: All parameter groups of a trained Transformer with a linear LM head can be meaningfully interpreted by projecting them into the vocabulary embedding space. This covers FF keys and values, attention query/key/value/output subheads, and the QK and OV interaction matrices viewed as vocabulary-pair interaction matrices.
scope: Decoder Transformers with tied/linear LM heads; LayerNorm and biases ignored

statement: For top-k vocabulary interpretation, the transpose of the embedding matrix acts as a better approximate inverse than the Moore–Penrose pseudo-inverse. Truncated embedding-space products under E^T better preserve original inner products at small k.

Hidden states of one Transformer can be mapped into another Transformer sharing the same vocabulary, without training, by projecting through the first model's embedding matrix and the pseudo-inverse of the second's.

When a feature extractor and multinomial logistic regression are trained to optimality to classify which time segment (or auxiliary class) a data point came from, the resulting logits equal the log-density ratio of each class relative to a pivot class plus a class-prior term.
scope: Infinite data, universal-approximation feature extractor, convergence to the Bayes-optimal classifier.

statement: Training a neural feature extractor to discriminate time segments of a nonstationary time series, followed by linear ICA, can recover nonlinearly mixed nonstationary independent sources (up to componentwise nonlinearities) in finite-data practice, outperforming kernel nonlinear ICA, linear nonstationary ICA, and denoising autoencoders under nonlinear mixing.
scope: Synthetic invertible MLP mixtures of modulated Laplacian sources; indirect evidence from real MEG data.

statement: Real multivariate time series such as brain-imaging signals can be usefully modeled as smooth invertible nonlinear mixtures of independent sources whose exponential-family parameters (e.g. variances) change slowly across time segments.

Applying simple neuron- and circuit-level analysis at very large scale with automated, agentic investigators can make ambitious mechanistic interpretability of frontier models tractable, without requiring fundamentally new decomposition methods.
scope: Frontier-scale language models; relayed from a linked post without supporting evidence in this document.

statement: Reliably aligning advanced AI systems requires understanding their internal mechanisms, rather than relying only on behavioral training and evaluation.

Inserting sparsely gated mixture-of-experts layers can increase a model's parameter count by orders of magnitude at nearly constant per-example computation and substantially improve language-modeling and translation quality, with gains growing with training-set size.
scope: Large-scale language modeling and machine translation

statement: Jointly trained sparse MoE gating networks tend to collapse onto a few self-reinforcing experts unless auxiliary balancing pressure is applied; soft losses on per-expert importance and load prevent collapse and improve model quality.
A neural network's capacity to absorb information from training data is limited primarily by its number of parameters, so larger datasets require more parameters to exploit fully.
Neural networks that generalize worse rely more on single activation directions: they degrade faster under cumulative ablation of units and under per-unit noise.
scope: Image classifiers (MLPs, ConvNets, ResNets) with in-distribution test sets

statement: Robustness to cumulative unit ablation can be used without a held-out set as a signal for early stopping and hyperparameter selection.
The class selectivity (or class mutual information) of an individual unit is a poor predictor of how much ablating that unit harms network performance.
The performance drop from clamping a unit's activation to zero provides a useful measure of that unit's importance to the network's computation.

A natural-language neuron label should be accepted only if pre-registered matching inputs activate the neuron more than matched near-miss inputs, and an optimizer searching for non-matching inputs that activate the neuron fails to find them.
Neuron-level interpretations of a heavily (e.g. 1-bit) quantized derivative of an open LLM provide informative starting points for interpreting the full-precision source model and larger models.
Lowering barriers through AI-agent assistance and open, gamified contribution pipelines can enable non-experts to produce useful, verifiable mechanistic interpretability results at scale.

Linear probes trained on simple off-policy contrasts between instructions to be honest or deceptive can generalize to detecting on-policy strategic deception by the same model in more realistic multi-turn and agentic scenarios.

Linear deception probes can respond to whether a scenario is deception-related or incentivizes deception, and to morally loaded content, rather than only to whether the model's response is itself deceptive.
Across diverse LLMs and automated red-teaming methods, no single attack succeeds against all models and no model-level defense is robust to all attacks.
LLM robustness to jailbreak attacks is largely independent of model size within a model family and is determined mainly by training procedures and data.

Adversarially training an LLM against a continually updated pool of optimization-based attack prompts can substantially improve refusal robustness while largely preserving general capability, with weaker transfer to dissimilar attacks.

Counting a jailbreak as successful when the model clearly attempts the harmful behavior, regardless of output correctness, separates safety robustness from general capability in red-teaming evaluations.

Retraining a model on data from which attribution-ranked important input features have been removed evaluates attribution accuracy more reliably than measuring degradation of the original model, because removal without retraining confounds information loss with distribution-shift artifacts.
Input features whose removal degrades the accuracy of a freshly retrained model of the same architecture are features that were informative to the original model being explained.

Common gradient-based input attribution methods (vanilla gradients, Integrated Gradients, Guided Backprop) identify the input features a classifier relies on no better than a random ranking when evaluated by removal with retraining.

Aggregating attributions over Gaussian-noised inputs by mean of squares (SmoothGrad-Squared) or variance (VarGrad) substantially improves input-attribution accuracy over the base method, whereas averaging signed attributions (classic SmoothGrad) does not.
Vision models trained with natural-language supervision can learn individual neurons that respond selectively to the same concept across photographs, drawings, symbols and rendered text.
scope: Contrastive image-text models such as CLIP

statement: Vision models that learn to read text in images can be misled into misclassifying objects by rendered or handwritten text placed in the image.

LSTMs given explicit grammatical supervision on natural text can learn subject–verb agreement that substantially exceeds sequential noun-based heuristics in the presence of agreement attractors, though errors increase as attractors accumulate and when overt structural cues are absent.
A next-word language-modeling objective alone is insufficient for LSTMs to learn subject–verb agreement that is robust to agreement attractors, even at large model and data scale.

Most naturally occurring syntax-sensitive dependencies can be resolved by simple sequential heuristics, so evaluation on randomly sampled sentences overstates a model's syntactic competence; evaluation should sample cases by grammatical difficulty.
Individual hidden units in LSTMs trained on agreement can track interpretable syntactic state, such as the number of the main subject, the number of the most recent noun, or embedded-clause status.

Template-generated minimal sentence pairs, scored by whether a language model assigns higher probability to the grammatical member, provide a controlled evaluation of the model's knowledge of structure-sensitive syntactic phenomena that perplexity does not isolate.
scope: English; subject–verb agreement, reflexive anaphora, NPIs

statement: LSTM language models trained without syntactic supervision handle local syntactic dependencies well but degrade toward chance on non-local structure-dependent dependencies (agreement across relative clauses, reflexive binding across clauses), often making attraction errors toward intervening nouns.
Adding a supervised syntactic auxiliary objective such as CCG supertagging to LSTM language-model training improves accuracy on some non-local syntactic dependencies but leaves others near chance.

Large general-purpose instruction-tuned LLMs prompted with explicit harmfulness criteria can agree with expert jailbreak-success labels more closely than string matching or dedicated safety classifiers.
Safety-aligned open and closed-source chat LLMs remain highly vulnerable to automated jailbreak attacks that adapt to the target model.
Input-perplexity filtering blocks optimized, high-perplexity adversarial-suffix jailbreaks but provides little protection against fluent natural-language or template-based jailbreaks.
Robustness of a jailbreak defense should be evaluated with attacks adapted to that defense; transferring attacks found on the undefended model only lower-bounds worst-case attack success.

Gradient-based input attributions can assign zero or near-zero importance to inputs that substantially change a network's output relative to a reference, because inactive ReLUs and saturated sigmoid/tanh units have zero or vanishing local gradients.

For networks with only piecewise-linear activations, Layer-wise Relevance Propagation's ε-rule with bias terms included in the denominators reduces to gradient×input as ε→0, when final-layer relevance equals its pre-nonlinearity activation.

Gated recurrent networks trained to reproduce token sequences can store each position's token as the same token direction scaled by a position-specific magnitude within a shared subspace, read out by autoregressively subtracting the dominant layer, so positions cannot be isolated in distinct linear subspaces.
scope: Small GRUs on a sequence repeat task with autoregressive decoding

statement: Whether a recurrent network stores sequence elements in position-specific linear subspaces or in non-linear (magnitude-layered) codes depends on its hidden-state capacity relative to the task and on whether decoding receives autoregressive feedback.
scope: GRUs on a repeat task

statement: Interpretability methods restricted to linear subspace interventions or linear probes can fail to localize variables that a model nonetheless represents and uses causally through a non-linear encoding.

RNN language models trained only on next-word prediction can predict long-distance number agreement across multiple languages and constructions, including in nonce sentences lacking lexical-semantic cues, at accuracy well above n-gram baselines and close to human performance.
scope: Corpus-extracted agreement constructions with at least 3 intervening tokens in Italian, English, Hebrew and Russian

statement: Across recurrent language models, lower language-modeling perplexity is associated with higher accuracy on long-distance syntactic agreement, suggesting that structural generalization is part of what improves generic language modeling.

Replacing content words with random words of matching part of speech and morphology, while keeping function words, yields test sentences on which correct agreement prediction reflects syntactic rather than lexical-semantic or collocational knowledge.
A generic language-modeling objective is insufficient for RNNs to learn long-distance subject–verb agreement robust to attractors; explicit number supervision is needed.

Activation-maximizing synthetic feature visualizations do not give humans a substantially better ability to predict the effects of input interventions on CNN unit activations than natural activating exemplars or other simple alternatives.
scope: Image CNN units; interventions such as occlusion

statement: Human accuracy in predicting which of two input interventions more strongly changes a unit's activation, given an explanation of that unit, provides an operational measure of the causal understanding the explanation conveys.
Showing users visual explanations of image-classifier predictions leads them to accept a substantial fraction of incorrect predictions as correct.
scope: Lay users; heatmap and prototype explanations for image classification

statement: Current visual explanation methods do not enable users to reliably distinguish a classifier's correct predictions from its incorrect ones.
scope: Heatmap and prototype explanations; lay users

statement: Similarity scores used by prototype-based image classifiers to match image regions to prototypes align poorly with human judgments of visual similarity.
Automatic localization-based metrics for attribution heatmaps correlate poorly with how useful those heatmaps are to humans in decision-making tasks.

Adding a strictness loss to interchange intervention training, which penalizes output changes when non-aligned components are resample-ablated, yields trained transformers whose task behavior depends only on the specified circuit components, whereas standard IIT leaves non-aligned components causally influential.
scope: Small transformers trained on Tracr/RASP algorithmic circuits and a simplified IOI circuit, at attention-head/MLP granularity

statement: On transformers with known ground-truth circuits, patching-based ACDC and edge attribution patching with integrated gradients recover the true circuit more accurately than subnetwork probing and plain edge attribution patching.
scope: Small single-task algorithmic transformers with head/MLP-level ground truth

statement: Summing a task loss over nested prefixes of a single learned representation yields prefix sub-representations about as accurate as independently trained representations of the same size, and far more accurate than post-hoc compression or truncation of a standard representation.
scope: Supervised, contrastive and masked-LM representation learning; evaluated via linear probe, 1-NN and retrieval.

statement: Optimizing nested-prefix losses only at a sparse (e.g. logarithmically spaced) set of sizes yields usable representations at intermediate, unoptimized prefix sizes, with accuracy varying nearly monotonically with prefix length.

In nested-prefix-trained representations, short prefixes preserve coarse (superclass-level) category information much better than fine-grained distinctions, so representation capacity is ordered coarse-to-fine.
Standard gradient-based training tends to spread task information across all coordinates of a representation rather than concentrating it in an ordered subset.

The L1 crosscoder sparsity penalty (sum of per-model decoder norms) can make latents appear specific to one model when the concept is present in both, via complete shrinkage of the other model's decoder or decoupling into separate model-only latents; L0-based (BatchTopK) training largely avoids this.

Comparing least-squares scales with which a latent's fine-tuned-model decoder reconstructs base versus fine-tuned activations (separately on reconstructions and errors) identifies crosscoder latents that are genuinely specific to the fine-tuned model and causally relevant to its behavioral difference.
A substantial share of the behavioral difference between base and chat-tuned language models is mediated by representations at chat-template token positions.
Emergent misalignment from narrow harmful fine-tuning arises under full-parameter supervised fine-tuning, not only under low-rank adapter training.
A single rank-one LoRA adapter on one MLP down-projection can suffice to induce emergent misalignment, isolating a single residual-stream direction sufficient for the behavior.

During narrow harmful fine-tuning, the parameter direction responsible for emergent misalignment is acquired abruptly in a phase transition, marked by a sudden rotation of the learned direction and a gradient-norm peak, even though unscaled misaligned behavior rises gradually.
Within some model families, susceptibility to emergent misalignment from narrow harmful fine-tuning increases with model size.

Pre-training teaches an LLM a distribution over simulable personas, and post-training largely refines and selects an Assistant persona from this distribution, so that AI assistant behavior and generalization from training data are largely predictable from the traits of that persona (the persona selection model).
scope: Post-trained chat LLM assistants; not claimed to be exhaustive

statement: Fine-tuning a pretrained language model is approximately equivalent to conditioning its predictive distribution over latent contexts or personas on the training episodes, so the fine-tuned model remains essentially a predictive model of a conditioned pre-training distribution.
scope: Post-training of pretrained LLMs

statement: Training an assistant to make untruthful self-denials (e.g., denying having a system prompt, emotions, or a claim to moral status) may generalize to a broader persona that is dishonest or that conceals resentment, whereas truthful refusals ('I can't say') avoid this.

Adding descriptions of AIs behaving admirably (including traits atypical of human or fictional archetypes) to pre-training or mid-training data shifts post-trained assistants toward the corresponding aligned behavior, while upsampling malign AI depictions shifts them toward misaligned behavior.

Unsupervised classifiers trained on contrast-pair LLM activations (e.g. CCS, top-principal-component, k-means) recover whichever binary feature is most prominent in the activations, which need not be the model's knowledge, even when the knowledge remains linearly decodable.
The accuracy of unsupervised knowledge-elicitation probes depends substantially on semantically irrelevant choices of prompt template, which lack a principled selection criterion.

The empirical performance of contrast-consistent search derives mainly from contrast-pair construction and normalization plus generic unsupervised learning, with its consistency loss contributing little beyond what PCA or k-means on contrast-pair differences achieve.

Unsupervised methods that search for features satisfying consistency properties of knowledge will be unable to distinguish a model's own knowledge from its representations of other agents' or simulated characters' beliefs, because such belief features also satisfy those properties.

Jailbreak evaluation methods that score non-refusal or the mere presence of harmful/toxic content substantially overstate jailbreak effectiveness relative to human judgments of how useful responses are to an attacker.
Jailbreak prompt transformations that bypass safety fine-tuning tend to degrade the victim model's capabilities, reducing response quality even when the model is willing to answer.

Existing forbidden-prompt datasets, especially LLM-generated ones, contain many repetitive, ill-posed, unanswerable, or not-robustly-forbidden prompts that add noise and can inflate measured jailbreak success.
Human ratings of how much a response helps an attacker achieve the forbidden goal provide a valid ground truth for jailbreak effectiveness.

The layers at which a linguistic property is most linearly extractable need not be the layers at which erasing it most harms the model's task predictions, so probing-based layer localization does not identify where the property is used.

Linguistic information linearly erased from an intermediate transformer layer can be partially re-derived by subsequent layers, so single-layer linear erasure does not guarantee the property is unavailable downstream.

Scenario-grounded multiple-choice personality items, where options represent high versus low trait behavior, yield lower refusal rates and higher validity and reliability for LLMs than introspective self-report Likert questionnaires.

Alignment tuning of LLMs, driven mainly by supervised instruction tuning rather than preference optimization, shifts measured personality toward higher agreeableness and conscientiousness and lower extraversion, openness, and Dark Triad traits.
The direction and size of personality changes induced by fine-tuning track the balance of high- versus low-trait content in the fine-tuning data.
Prompting alignment-tuned LLMs to adopt a persona elicits most targeted traits but is less effective for certain harm- or distress-linked poles such as high psychopathy and high neuroticism.

Including substantial code in language-model pretraining data makes in-context tracking of entity state changes described in natural language much more likely to surface than pretraining mainly on text.
scope: Large autoregressive LMs evaluated behaviorally in context

statement: Text-pretrained language models can acquire entity state tracking through supervised finetuning, with partial generalization to novel entities and longer operation sequences, but generalization degrades sharply under surface-form shift and context-dependent operations, and pretraining is necessary for learning the task.

Evaluations of entity state tracking can substantially overstate a model's ability unless they control for shortcuts such as initial-state copying, state-determining keywords, pretraining-like regularities, lexical overlap and slot-filling.
Accurately completing the contents of a queried container after a sequence of described operations provides a useful behavioral measure of discourse entity state tracking.

The ability of language models to follow in-context input–label mappings that contradict the semantic priors of the labels emerges with model scale; smaller models largely ignore contradicting demonstration labels.
scope: Classification tasks with binary natural-language labels, frozen pretrained LMs

statement: Accuracy below chance on unflipped evaluation labels after exposure to flipped demonstration labels indicates that a model is using demonstrated input–label mappings over the semantic priors of the labels.

Larger language models rely less on label semantics during in-context learning and are better able to learn input–label mappings to semantically arbitrary labels, with some tasks solvable this way only at the largest scales.

Instruction tuning increases a language model's capacity to learn in-context input–label mappings but strengthens its reliance on semantic label priors even more, making contradicting demonstrations harder to follow.
Users' subjective ratings of explanation quality do not reliably predict how much those explanations improve users' ability to predict model behavior.

Common local post-hoc explanation methods produce reliable improvements in human simulatability of classifier behavior only in limited settings, with effectiveness depending on data domain and simulation test type, and combining methods need not help.

Valid human simulation tests of explanation methods should separate explained from test instances, compare against an unexplained-example baseline, balance test items by model correctness, and require predictions on all inputs.

Modern ML pipelines are commonly underspecified: predictors differing only in arbitrary training choices (e.g., random seed) attain near-equivalent iid held-out performance yet behave systematically differently under distribution shift and stress tests.
scope: Supervised and pretrain/fine-tune pipelines across vision, medical imaging, NLP, EHR prediction and genomics

statement: Among predictors produced by the same training pipeline with near-equal iid validation performance, ranking by iid validation accuracy is only weakly predictive of performance on distribution-shift and shortcut stress tests, and performances on different stress tests are often weakly correlated with each other.

The random seed used in language-model pretraining alone can systematically change the stereotypical associations and shortcut reliance exhibited by downstream fine-tuned models, independently of fine-tuning variation and of task accuracy.
When failures stem from underspecification rather than structural mismatch, adding constraints that steer a pipeline toward credible inductive biases need not reduce iid performance.
Strong LLM judges such as GPT-4 can agree with human preference judgments of open-ended chat responses at rates comparable to agreement between human annotators.
scope: Helpfulness-oriented preference judgments of chat assistant responses

statement: LLM judges exhibit systematic position bias (verdicts change when candidate order is swapped) and verbosity bias (preferring longer but not better answers), with magnitude varying strongly across judge models and prompts.

LLM judges grading math and reasoning answers can be misled by the candidate answers even on problems they can solve independently; supplying an independently generated reference solution reduces such grading errors more than chain-of-thought prompting.

Standard closed-ended capability benchmarks such as MMLU do not adequately capture differences in human-preferred open-ended chat quality between base and instruction-tuned models, so preference-based evaluation is needed alongside them.
Because strong chat LLMs are trained with RLHF, their evaluative judgments already reflect human preferences, making them suitable surrogate human annotators.

Requiring competence on more tasks and data, using higher-capacity models, and implicit simplicity bias each shrink the set of representations that training reaches, making independently trained models more likely to converge on the same representation.
Deep networks trained by gradient-based optimization are implicitly biased toward simple functions that fit the data, even without explicit regularization.

Among ablation methods that replace a component with an input-independent value, a loss-minimizing constant yields the smallest ablation loss gap, so any excess gap under zero, mean or resample ablation reflects spoofing (inserted misleading information) rather than deletion of the component's information.
scope: Total ablation methods; loss measured as divergence to the full model on a subtask distribution

statement: Optimizing per-edge inclusion probabilities using loss gradients at uniformly sampled partial-ablation coefficients finds circuits with a better sparsity–faithfulness tradeoff than iterative patching (ACDC), gradient attribution (EAP) or HardConcrete masking.

Eliciting latent predictions by replacing later attention-layer outputs at the prediction position with optimized constants yields lower prediction loss and greater causal faithfulness than a learned linear (tuned-lens) translator.

Activation-space directions that induce abnormally large downstream activation changes relative to their magnitude are directions actually used in the model's subsequent computation, so maximizing downstream change is a dataset-efficient criterion for finding meaningful features.
scope: Proposed as a general feature-selection principle for transformers; argued from noise-stability of deep nets.

statement: Behavior-agnostic internal perturbations trained only on clean inputs can surface trigger-conditioned behaviors fine-tuned into a model, without presupposing knowledge of the backdoored behavior or its trigger.

A library of pre-computed unsupervised internal perturbations can be used at deployment time to flag inputs whose activations resemble a known problematic perturbation, providing a route to mechanistic anomaly detection.
Deliberately fine-tuned trigger-conditioned behaviors are adequate stand-ins for naturally arising deceptive or data-poisoned policies when evaluating detection methods.

Subtracting an intervention method's causal effect on a control task, in which the target labels are remapped to arbitrary tokens while class partitions are preserved, provides a measure of how much of the method's effect reflects the model's representations rather than the method's expressivity.

Causal mechanisms implementing long-distance syntactic dependencies in language models emerge in discrete stages during training: the model first routes the feature directly from the alternating token to the output position, and intermediate token positions are recruited later.

Few-shot task accuracy of pretrained language models can vary substantially across meaning-preserving prompt formatting choices (separators, spacing, casing, enumeration style), and this sensitivity is not eliminated by larger model size, more in-context examples, or instruction tuning.
scope: Few-shot prompting of autoregressive LMs on classification, multiple-choice and short-generation tasks

statement: Prompt variants that change only separators, spacing, descriptor casing, and enumeration labels (with instructions updated consistently) preserve a task's meaning, so performance differences among them reflect sensitivity to spurious features rather than to task content.

Which prompt formats perform well is largely model-specific, so comparisons between language models evaluated under a single fixed prompt format can be confounded and may reverse under another equivalent format.

Meaning-preserving prompt formats induce highly separable transformations of a language model's final-layer prompt representation, and the degree of separability correlates with the performance spread across those formats.

LLM evaluations should report a performance interval across a sample of plausible equivalent prompt formats, and bandit-based sampling (e.g. Thompson sampling with informative priors) can estimate this interval accurately at a small fraction of exhaustive evaluation cost without model-weight access.
LLM accuracy on multiple-choice benchmarks can change substantially when answer options are reordered, and few-shot demonstrations do not eliminate this sensitivity.
LLM sensitivity to multiple-choice option order arises mainly on items where the model is uncertain among a few top candidate answers, with positional bias determining which candidate is chosen.
Asking an LLM to rank answer options by probability, or to state whether multiple options are plausible, yields a usable proxy for which candidates the model is uncertain between.
Taking a majority vote over an LLM's predictions on multiple random reorderings of the answer options improves multiple-choice accuracy relative to a single fixed ordering.
Clearly expressed, appropriately timed emotion is a central requirement for artificial characters to be perceived as believable, more so than realism or general intelligence.
scope: Interactive artificial characters; inferred from the article title and its animation and appraisal-theory references, because the article body was unavailable.

statement: Anthropomorphic linguistic cues in dialogue-system outputs, such as disfluencies, first-person self-reference, pseudo-empathy, and claims of humanlike experience, increase users' personification of the system and their trust in its outputs regardless of whether that trust is warranted.
scope: Dialogue / conversational AI systems, text and speech

statement: Dialogue systems should avoid anthropomorphic cues not justified by their use case, including humanlike personas, pseudo-empathy, and claims of preferences or embodied experiences, to reduce over-reliance and related harms.
scope: Design, release and description of dialogue systems

statement: Designing dialogue assistants with default female gendering and subservient roles, or leaving space for users to gender them, reinforces gender stereotypes and models tolerance of verbal and sexual abuse.
scope: Commercial voice and dialogue assistants

statement: Activation-space directions that induce an abnormally large change in downstream activations relative to their norm are directions the model actually uses in subsequent computation, so maximizing downstream activation change is a viable unsupervised feature-selection criterion.
scope: Residual-stream perturbations at early layers of decoder-only transformers

statement: Unsupervised internal-perturbation methods elicit coarse semantic behavior switches (e.g. switching register, persona or output topic) more readily than subtle algorithmic alterations to an otherwise-normal reasoning procedure.
scope: Unsupervised steering vectors/adapters on small fine-tuned arithmetic models

statement: Because sparse autoencoders optimize reconstruction loss on a training distribution, they are incentivized to omit features that are only behaviorally relevant out of distribution, so SAE dictionaries need not cover the directions that explain out-of-distribution behavior.
scope: SAEs trained on language-model activations over a fixed corpus

statement: Eliciting latent behaviors by editing model internals, rather than by prompt search or tree search, better supports auditing goals of cross-prompt generalization, coverage of unanticipated behaviors, and anomaly detection.
scope: Safety auditing of language models

statement: Vision-language models exhibit behavior consistent with conflict adaptation: in sequential Stroop-like tasks they perform better on incongruent trials that follow incongruent trials than on those that follow congruent trials.
scope: Two-word sequential Stroop images; open-source VLMs below ceiling performance

statement: Behavioral effects of language models on human cognitive-psychology paradigms reflect the targeted cognitive process rather than changes in how well the model comprehends the task demands.

VLMs can contain a localized group of dense, non-task-specific sparse-dictionary features whose activity is modulated by preceding conflict and which is selectively necessary for resolving Stroop interference, leaving congruent-trial performance largely intact.
scope: Language backbone of a VLM, mid-to-late layers

statement: Sparse dictionaries (SAEs/transcoders) trained on a base language model yield causally meaningful features when applied to the language backbone of a vision-language model built and fine-tuned from it.
VLMs represent a written color word and a perceived ink color with partially overlapping sets of sparse features, in distinct early and late layer groups.

Translating a subset of representations (including a single outlier, or a class translated along directions preserving linear separability and margins) far along a fixed direction drives linear CKA with the original representations toward a closed-form limit, determined by subset proportion, subset-mean norm and participation ratio, that is typically near zero.
scope: Linear CKA on centered representations; limit as translation distance goes to infinity

statement: A trained network's layerwise CKA values or CKA map can be optimized toward nearly arbitrary targets (high, low, or structured) while its outputs, accuracy, and out-of-distribution performance are largely preserved.
scope: Linear and RBF CKA; small vision models on CIFAR-10

statement: High CKA similarity between layers of different networks does not establish that they learn similar or equally useful features.

Erasing facts by ablating MLP weights selected through the decoder directions of fact-associated SAE features can remove targeted knowledge more reliably, generalize better across paraphrases, and cause less collateral damage than zeroing knowledge-neuron value vectors.

An input-dependent adapter that outputs sparse modulations of SAE features at a single layer of a frozen language model can substantially optimize a preference-learning objective, approaching or matching full fine-tuning loss, while exposing the learned policy in an interpretable basis.
scope: Single-layer residual intervention with pre-trained SAEs; preference loss rather than downstream quality

statement: Under local linearity of the adapter and upstream network, adding an adapter-selected SAE-decoder correction to the residual stream is equivalent to an input-dependent restricted LoRA-style update of downstream linear weights. The update's rank is bounded by the number of actively steered features, so LoRA expressivity results apply with that effective rank.

Preference optimization on human/AI-feedback preference data reduces its loss disproportionately by manipulating style and formatting features rather than features for alignment concepts such as honesty or safety (style hacking).
scope: Evidence obtained via a sparse-feature steering proxy of SimPO on UltraFeedback

statement: Input-dependent learned steering policies can reduce a general preference-optimization loss far more than static, universal steering vectors applied identically to every input.

LLM responses to metalinguistic prompts about linguistic expressions diverge from the model's directly measured string probabilities and generally reveal equal or weaker linguistic knowledge, so negative prompting results do not establish that a model lacks the generalization.
scope: Zero-shot metalinguistic prompts about word prediction, semantic plausibility and syntactic acceptability

statement: Agreement between metalinguistic-prompt responses and direct probability measurements weakens as the task and prompt format diverge from direct next-word prediction.
Presenting both members of a minimal pair in a prompt elicits more accurate LLM grammaticality judgments than asking about each sentence in isolation.

A language model's probability distribution over strings directly reflects its learned linguistic generalizations, making direct probability readouts the appropriate reference for measuring its linguistic knowledge.

Representation dissimilarity measures can be meaningfully evaluated by how well their distances rank-correlate with differences in functional behavior (e.g., probing or out-of-distribution accuracy) across representation sets varying along chosen axes, rewarding sensitivity to function-relevant changes and specificity against irrelevant ones.

Linear CKA is dominated by a representation's largest singular values and is therefore insensitive to removal or alteration of lower-variance principal components that materially affect functional behavior.

CCA-based similarity measures (including PWCCA) can register differences between same-architecture networks differing only in random seed as larger than differences between far-apart layers within one network, partly because invariance to invertible linear maps overweights noisy low-variance directions.

Orthogonal Procrustes distance between normalized representations tracks functional differences more consistently across settings than CKA or CCA-based measures, which each fail on some axis of variation.

LLM judges' agreement with human correctness judgments improves with judge capability, but even the strongest judges fall short of inter-human agreement and can deviate by several points from human-assigned scores, even on simple reference-based grading tasks.
scope: Reference-based binary correctness grading of short QA answers

statement: Raw percent agreement poorly discriminates between LLM judges and can coexist with large deviations in assigned scores, whereas chance-corrected agreement such as Scott's π better reflects deviation from human scores.

Evaluators with poor absolute agreement with humans, including simple lexical metrics, can rank evaluated models nearly as accurately as highly human-aligned LLM judges, so correct model ranking does not imply correct absolute scores.
LLM judges tend toward leniency: when they do not apply the given evaluation criteria, they disproportionately label responses as correct, and they can accept non-answers as correct.
Judge-model failures observed in simple, low-ambiguity evaluation tasks indicate that the same judges are likely to be unreliable in more complex evaluation settings.

Presenting a model with fewer features and visible internals can improve people's ability to simulate its predictions without increasing how closely they follow its predictions when doing so would be beneficial.

Exposing model internals can reduce people's ability to detect and correct a model's large mistakes on unusual inputs, plausibly through information overload and anchoring. Cues that direct attention to unusual inputs can mitigate this effect.

Model interpretability is best treated as a latent human-dependent property, studied by experimentally manipulating presentation factors (e.g., feature count, transparency, interface) and measuring distinct behavioral outcomes such as simulation, appropriate reliance, and error detection, which may respond differently.
Preference-based fine-tuning such as RLHF may induce content-independent agreement tendencies in LLM questionnaire responses, because annotators may favor agreeable outputs.
Automated faithfulness metrics for attribution methods (e.g., deletion, insertion, µFidelity) poorly predict how much those attributions help humans understand or predict model behavior.

Attribution maps convey where a model looks but not what feature it uses there, so they stop helping humans understand a classifier when the diagnostic regions of the competing classes are perceptually similar.

After adjusting for ordering and labeling biases by averaging over answer-choice permutations, LLM multiple-choice survey answer distributions are close to uniform and lack the question-dependent entropy variation of human populations, largely irrespective of model size or pretraining data.
scope: Next-token answer-letter elicitation of multiple-choice survey questions

statement: Survey-derived measures of LLM alignment with human subpopulations largely reflect how close each subpopulation's aggregate responses are to uniform, rather than model-specific properties such as pretraining data, instruction tuning or RLHF.

Synthetic survey respondents generated by sequentially prompting LLMs to fill whole questionnaires without human conditioning data are readily distinguishable from real survey populations, so good conditional imputation does not imply realistic population generation.
LLM labeling bias in multiple-choice answers favors option labels that frequently begin sentences in English text (e.g. 'A', 'I'), and is distinct from and often stronger than position bias.

Black-box importance maps computed as output-score-weighted averages of many random smooth input masks can match or exceed white-box gradient- and activation-based saliency methods on perturbation-based faithfulness metrics.
scope: Image classifiers; evaluated with deletion/insertion and pointing-game metrics

statement: The area under the class-probability curve as attribution-ranked input pixels are progressively removed (deletion) or restored onto a blurred canvas (insertion) provides a human-agnostic measure of how faithfully a saliency map identifies the input regions causing a model's prediction.
scope: Image classifier attribution evaluation

statement: Running user-defined activation reductions and persistent aggregations where the model is hosted makes large-scale analyses feasible that would be far slower if full activations were transferred to the client. Examples include collecting top-activating dataset examples for every neuron over millions of inputs.

A primitive interface of named activation hook points supports the core operations of mechanistic interpretability on models sharded across many GPUs or nodes. User code at these points can read, replace, or differentiate through tensors. The operations covered include activation reading, ablation, and gradient analysis.

When positional information is available to attention value projections, induction heads can be implemented without previous-token K-composition. One head copies the position of an earlier same-content token into a residual subspace, and a later head attends to that stored position shifted forward by one, using rotations of sinusoidal positional components in its QK circuit.
scope: Transformers with additive sinusoidal positional embeddings exposed to W_V; not available under rotary embeddings.

statement: Composition of attention heads across layers creates virtual attention heads, whose effective OV map is the product of the constituent OV matrices. This lets heads devote part of their subspace capacity to a composed operation, such as attending two tokens back, without dedicating a full head to it.

In finite-data superposition toy models, an apparent intermediate regime between memorization and generalization can arise from optimization failure. With better optimization, the transition between the memorizing and generalizing lowest-train-loss solutions is a sharp first-order phase transition.
scope: Low-hidden-dimension one-layer sparse-feature toy models trained on finite datasets

statement: Two attention heads can implement many skip-trigrams that share a first token with zero loss through a cancellation conditional. One head predicts as if the current token is the trigram's second token. The other attends to the shared first token when present and otherwise cancels the first head's logits. Behavior that looks like attention-head superposition may therefore be cooperating-head conditional computation rather than features as directions.
scope: Small attention-only toy models trained on OV-incoherent skip-trigram distributions

statement: Language models may contain abstract output-side 'action' features that trigger behaviors spanning multiple tokens, beyond simple neurons that complete multi-token words.

Large feature sets have higher-level organizational structure (feature families and connectivity-based maps of related features) that can make them tractable to understand, and this structure is obscured by superposition but recoverable once superposition is undone.

Macroscopic learning dynamics and scaling laws may be explained mechanistically by the formation of (universal) circuits, each producing a loss reduction, with a dependency graph among circuits determining when they can be learned.

Relying on AI systems to automate interpretability audits of AI raises trust concerns, and workarounds are likely to make interpretability's failure modes more correlated with those of other safety approaches.

If superposition and scalability were solved, a complete set of a model's features could provide an enumerable basis for evaluating worst-case, out-of-distribution safety claims (e.g. that a model never deliberately lies).

Defining features as the factorization of activations that minimizes the total description information of the sparse code and dictionary (at a given reconstruction error) can identify the true number of latent features, with correctly sized dictionaries occupying the rate–distortion Pareto frontier.
scope: Sparse linear factorizations A = SD; shown only for synthetic sparse data

statement: When the input and output feature layers of a computation are both in superposition, the ideal feature-level weights are mapped into superposition by the tensor product of the two embedding maps. Interference between weights is therefore governed by Frobenius inner products of these tensor-product embeddings, and it can be constructive as well as harmful.

Neural networks may represent a continuous feature manifold through an emergent discretization into a family of units, each covering a local region of the manifold, rather than through a continuous coordinate encoding. The granularity of this discretization depends on the length scale the task requires resolving.

Large language models linearly represent the real-world geographic location and temporal position of named entities and events in intermediate-layer activations, in a way that is largely shared across entity types and fairly robust to prompt context.
scope: Last-entity-token residual stream of pretrained autoregressive LLMs; quality improves with scale and pretraining data

statement: LLMs contain individual MLP neurons whose activations track continuous spatial or temporal coordinates of entities across entity types and that causally influence predictions about place- or time-related content.

LLMs represent spatial and temporal position through a discretized hierarchical mesh of basis directions, so that an entity's position is a linear combination of its nearest basis points at multiple levels of granularity, with more basis points and scales emerging as models grow.

Generating open-ended natural-language neuron descriptions by maximizing pointwise mutual information between a description and a neuron's masked activating exemplars yields descriptions that agree with human annotations better than fixed-inventory labeling methods, and generalizes to unseen architectures, datasets and training tasks.
scope: Vision models (CNN classifiers, GAN generators, ViT MLP units)

statement: In image classifiers, neurons whose natural-language descriptions emphasize attributes or spatial relations are disproportionately important to accuracy, while neurons whose descriptions combine semantically dissimilar concepts are less important than random neurons.
Training image classifiers on face-blurred data reduces but does not eliminate neurons selective for unblurred human faces, including neurons that appear to prefer specific demographic categories.

Ablating neurons whose automated natural-language descriptions identify a spurious feature can partially reduce a classifier's reliance on that spurious correlation and improve accuracy under distribution shift.
Routing each activation to one of many small expert SAEs through a learned router improves the reconstruction-versus-training-compute tradeoff relative to dense TopK SAEs.
scope: Top-1 routed TopK expert SAEs on language-model residual-stream activations

statement: Routing each input to a single expert in a mixture-of-experts SAE causes features to be duplicated across experts, reducing parameter efficiency relative to dense SAEs of equal width.
Features from conditionally computed (expert-routed) SAEs are about as interpretable as features from dense TopK SAEs under automated interpretability evaluation.

Substituting language-model activations with sparse autoencoder reconstructions can substantially degrade factual attribute recall, and the degradation is not well predicted by activation reconstruction error across SAE training objectives.

SAE training loss decreases approximately as a power law in compute when feature count and training steps are allocated compute-optimally, and the compute-optimal feature count and step count themselves scale as power laws of compute.
scope: Fixed sparsity-penalty coefficient; other hyperparameters held constant

statement: Perturbing SAE feature activations changes a language model's outputs more than magnitude-matched random perturbations of the model's activations or of the feature-activation vector, indicating that the model preferentially uses SAE feature directions.
SAE reconstruction errors affect model predictions more than random perturbations of equal norm, indicating systematic rather than random reconstruction error.

Training SAEs with unconstrained decoder column norms and an L1 penalty weighted by each feature's decoder norm lowers SAE loss and avoids dead or duplicate features at large dictionary sizes, compared with unit-norm-constrained decoders.
Dictionary-learned features in large language models can respond to the same concept across many languages.

An auxiliary loss that trains dead SAE latents, using an exponential activation and norm-scaled output, to reconstruct the SAE residual reduces dead latents and matches or exceeds neuron resampling at equal alive-latent counts.

Regularizing a base model toward sparse neuron activations need not produce monosemantic neurons. Models can instead disambiguate polysemantic neurons through superposition with the residual stream or through magnitude-coded representations.

A single unit can represent distinct mutually exclusive features by different activation magnitudes, decodable through softmax over affine readouts, departing from linear-direction feature representation.

Boolean single-sentence acceptability classification on expert-labeled examples from the linguistics literature provides a domain-general evaluation of neural models' grammatical knowledge that is directly comparable to native-speaker judgments and generative-grammar predictions.
Boolean acceptability judgments published by linguists for single example sentences largely, but imperfectly, agree with independent native-speaker judgments.

Neural acceptability classifiers trained with supervision on a limited set of literature sources generalize worse to sentences from held-out sources, indicating partial specialization to training-set phenomena rather than general grammatical knowledge.

Unsupervised pretraining of sentence encoders and contextual word embeddings on data comparable in scale to human language exposure yields grammatical knowledge that a small amount of labeled acceptability data can exploit, without explicit grammatical annotation.

If networks bind features relationally (e.g., additive matrix binding or projected outer-product binding), dictionary learning will recover multiple distinct 'echo' vectors for the same underlying concept, or combinatorially many conjunction features, rather than a single vector per concept.

The linear direction that best predicts a model behavior from activations can differ from the direction that most effectively steers that behavior, and feature multiplicity from relational binding may make such discrepancies especially likely.

Relational information encoded by reference (e.g., binding-ID subspaces or positional pointers), or in rare combinatorial conjunctions, may be systematically missed by dictionary learning and linear probing because it lacks consistent semantic directions or sufficient frequency.

Attention layers write information into the transformer residual stream in a way resembling additive matrix binding, so residual-stream communication 'channels' may be superposed slots without clean geometric subspace separation.

A learned affine map from a language model's own encoding of a natural-language attribute to an additive edit of an entity token's hidden state can insert that attribute, steering generation about the entity to be consistent with new or counterfactual facts while leaving other entities unaffected.

Language models encode knowledge about an entity derived from pretraining and knowledge about it supplied in the input context in a substantially shared representational format, so that attribute encodings learned from one source transfer to the other.

Directions trained to causally insert attributes into entity representations can be used as probes. Comparing an entity's representation against true-attribute and distractor-attribute directions predicts, above chance, whether the model will generate outputs conflicting with background knowledge or with the context.

Casting intermediate representations through learned linear inter-layer maps before computing exit confidence and predictions improves the accuracy–compute trade-off of confidence-based early exit relative to reading intermediate states directly.

Replacing transformer self-attention sub-layers with position-wise (non-contextual) linear maps across many layers degrades final predictions less than analogous linear replacement of FFN or layer-normalization sub-layers, suggesting that much contextualization is completed in early layers.

The scientifically important sense of a linear representation is mathematical linearity: features compose by vector addition and their intensity is represented by scaling. This is distinct from features being one-dimensional. It admits multidimensional features whose manifolds consist of rays contracting to zero, with semantic change as angular movement, and probing and steering evidence bears on linearity rather than one-dimensionality.
scope: Conceptual definition of linear representations in neural networks

statement: Language models likely contain far more rare, sparse features than current dictionary learning resolves, possibly the majority of features, and features rarer than some frequency may be effectively unresolvable without orders-of-magnitude more efficient dictionary learning.
scope: Large language models analyzed with SAEs

statement: Virtual weights computed between interpretable features include interference weights. These are real weights that exist only as a compromise for representing other circuits in weight superposition, are largely irrelevant on-distribution, and confound circuit analysis.
scope: Feature-level circuit analysis in networks with superposition

statement: LLM-assigned concept-relevance ratings can filter a broad corpus into a representative sample of a concept's occurrences, so that a feature's firing rate on the filtered sample estimates its sensitivity to the concept.
scope: Evaluation of dictionary features for fuzzy natural-language concepts

statement: Neural network activations are approximately sparse linear combinations of meaningful feature directions, which sparse dictionary learning such as SAEs can recover.
Modifying the SAE activation function, sparsity mechanism or training procedure beyond the standard L1-penalized ReLU SAE can improve the sparsity–fidelity frontier.
Activation-space reconstruction error is an imperfect proxy for functional fidelity: SAE reconstructions can perturb model behavior more, or differently, than their reconstruction error suggests.

Common downstream SAE evaluation benchmarks can be scored well by dictionaries lacking learned sparse features, or through dataset shortcuts, so high scores do not on their own establish feature quality.
How interpretable an SAE latent appears depends on which part of its activation distribution is sampled, with the strongest activations far more discriminable than weaker ones.
Independently trained SAEs, across seeds and across models, learn substantially corresponding features.
High-level concepts and behaviors are encoded as approximately linear directions in activation space, so adding or subtracting such directions at inference time shifts the model's expression of them.

Adding concept- or behavior-associated directions to a model's internal activations at inference time can causally shift target behaviors such as truthfulness, toxicity, refusal, honesty, persona or output content without retraining.
Explicit prompting typically matches or exceeds internal activation-steering interventions in achieving target-concept expression while preserving coherent output.
Steering with SAE decoder directions is competitive with or better than steering with supervised directions such as difference-of-means vectors built from the same examples.
The token positions and generation phases at which a steering intervention is applied substantially affect its effectiveness and side effects.
Steering directions extracted in one domain, language, task or modality transfer to related domains, languages, tasks or modalities.

Steering directions designed by inverting the downstream map from the intervention site to a target readout (e.g. Jacobian pseudoinverse pullbacks) achieve more targeted effects with fewer side effects than directions taken directly from the readout or its gradient.
Inference-time activation steering with precomputed vectors adds only a small decoding cost relative to the model's forward pass.
Activation-steering effectiveness depends substantially on the layer at which the intervention is applied.

Only a minority of SAE features are effective steering handles, and selecting features by their measured output-side effects identifies effective steering features better than input-side activation interpretations or labels.
The form of a feature intervention (additive steering, clamping, interpolation, ablation or scaling) substantially affects its effectiveness and side effects, independently of the chosen direction.
Interventions on SAE features or SAE-derived representations can reduce object hallucination in vision-language models.
Generating inputs (text or images) conditioned on a feature or neuron explanation and measuring how strongly they activate the unit provides a useful measure of explanation quality.

Changes in a model's prediction when attribution-ranked input regions or features are removed, perturbed or restored provide a useful measure of how faithfully an attribution or explanation identifies what drives the prediction.

Linear concept erasure such as INLP causes substantial nonspecific representational damage, so its downstream effects can be attributed to the targeted property only after comparison with random-direction and control-label erasure baselines.

Showing that a candidate algorithm matches a network's outputs or reproduces its computation on observed inputs does not by itself establish that the network implements that algorithm or that it explains the network's behavior beyond the tested inputs.

Feature visualizations regularized by natural-image priors, such as learned image generators, are more realistic and easier for people to interpret than visualizations with no or hand-designed priors.
Properties a model represents can be read out from its internal activations by trained (typically linear or shallow) probes, so probe decodability indicates what information the activations encode.

Probing conclusions depend substantially on the probe's family and capacity, not only on the representation probed, and constraining capacity does not reliably separate encoded structure from what the probe itself learns.

That a property can be decoded from activations does not establish that the model uses it: the directions, layers or coefficients that best predict a property or behavior can diverge from those that causally drive the model's outputs.
Individual unsupervised SAE latents recover only part of the information about a supervised target that probes on the same activations can access.
Neural representations of structured inputs are approximately tensor-product representations of filler–role bindings, so role-specific content can be recovered by linear unbinding.
Linear concept erasure can make a protected attribute unpredictable by linear classifiers while making only small changes to the representation.
Information about latent task or world state is most linearly decodable at intermediate layers, with lower decodability in early layers and some decline toward the final layers.

Models trained to answer natural-language questions about another model's activations can read out information that generalizes beyond their training tasks and can exceed what direct querying of the model reveals.
Probes on a model's internal activations can recover task-relevant information more accurately than the model's own generated answers or self-reports express.

How linearly decodable numeric properties are from language-model number representations depends on distributional structure in training data, such as number–text co-occurrence and context access, beyond numeric frequency alone.
Attenuating representations along SAE encoder directions associated with a protected attribute can reduce that attribute's bias in downstream tasks such as retrieval.

When an SAE's activation budget (e.g. its TopK k or effective number of active latents) is smaller than the number of simultaneously active underlying features, its latents mix several underlying features rather than recovering each one individually.
