Features of SAEs trained independently at adjacent layers or modules can be matched, by decoder similarity or activation correlation, into cross-layer correspondences that trace how features propagate through the network.

Keeping the SAE reconstruction residual fixed when editing SAE latents confines an intervention's effect to the decoded latent change, so its downstream effects are not confounded by reconstruction error.

A network's behavior on a task is implemented by a sparse subgraph (circuit) of its components, which can be identified by ablating or patching components and checking whether the retained subgraph reproduces the full model's task behavior.

Networks can reach near-perfect training accuracy long before they generalize to held-out data, and then generalize abruptly with continued training (grokking), with whether and when this happens depending on training-set size, task structure and optimization.

Delayed generalization arises because a generalizing mechanism forms gradually while memorizing components dominate the network's outputs, and held-out performance improves sharply once the generalizing mechanism overtakes or replaces the memorizing ones.

Fine-tuning on data that exhibits an unwanted trait while prompting with an instruction that elicits the trait (inoculation prompting) reduces the trait's expression under neutral evaluation, and instructions that elicit the trait more strongly before training inoculate more effectively.

Properties of the training procedure, such as the optimizer's coordinatewise normalization, numerical precision, noise statistics or activation regularization, can align learned representations with the network's coordinate basis independently of architectural nonlinearities.
During training, low-level features (e.g. token-level or edge-like features in lower layers) form earlier than higher-level, more abstract or contextual features.

Knocking out a candidate circuit and measuring the residual behavior of its complement does not reliably establish the circuit's completeness, because redundant pathways, the ablation values used and the choice of reference circuits all affect the outcome.
Circuit components can be identified from activation statistics alone, such as co-occurrence of sparse codes across components, without output-based attribution or patching.

Unregularized activation maximization yields noise-like, high-frequency images, and regularization or reparameterization (transformation robustness, decorrelated parameterization, blurring, informed initialization) is needed to produce recognizable feature visualizations.

Task-relevant information in trained networks is often carried by distributed, non-axis-aligned directions rather than individual unit coordinates, and high selectivity of individual units is not necessary for good task performance.
Representations learned by pretraining on one task or domain transfer as frozen features to other tasks, with transfer strongest for tasks and domains close to the pretraining data.

A feature or neuron explanation can be scored by how well activations simulated or predicted from the explanation match the unit's actual activations, with the scoring scheme affecting which explanations are judged correct.

Automated feature-interpretability scores computed without human raters (e.g. LLM intruder detection, activating-example consistency, explanation-conditioned detection or embedding-space separation) track human judgments of interpretability closely enough to compare decomposition methods.
Language models carry contextual entity–attribute bindings in localized activations that can be patched or edited to change which value is bound, while preserving other associations.
Fine-tuning or reinforcement learning on a narrow misaligned behavior (e.g. insecure code or incorrect advice) can induce broad misalignment across unrelated domains (emergent misalignment).
Broad emergent misalignment is mediated by a small number of persona-associated directions in activation space, so adding them induces and subtracting them suppresses broadly misaligned behavior.

Representation-similarity measures can disagree with each other and with functional correspondence: their invariances and sensitivities determine whether networks computing the same or different functions are judged similar.
Independently trained networks on the same task learn substantially similar hidden representations, with the degree of similarity varying systematically by layer.
Re-expressing network activations as sparse dictionary codes can increase measured representational alignment between independently trained networks relative to their native activations.

Personality expression measured by self-report questionnaires in language models does not reliably carry over to their behavior in realistic scenarios, free-text generation, or changing conversational contexts.

The transformer residual stream is a shared linear communication channel: components read from it and write to it additively, so their contributions can be analysed as vectors in a common space and decomposed into sums of paths.

When dictionary atoms are non-orthogonal, an encoder that infers each latent from one fixed input projection (as in standard SAEs) cannot perform optimal sparse inference. Inference that lets latents interact, for example iterative or competitive inference, recovers the generating dictionary better.

In finite-data sparse-feature models, networks shift from memorizing training examples to representing generalizing features as the dataset grows. Feature occurrence frequency and regularization set where this transition happens.

Transformer components partly counteract changes in the residual stream: later components or normalization can oppose earlier components' contributions or compensate for their ablation, so a component's isolated effect can differ from its effect in context.

Conditionally computed sparse autoencoders, which route each activation to one or several expert sub-dictionaries, achieve better reconstruction per unit of compute than dense SAEs without loss of feature interpretability.

SAE features are organised into parent–child hierarchies of general and more specific concepts, which flat standard SAEs represent poorly and which explicitly hierarchical or nested-budget training recovers more fully.

Language-model task accuracy is highly sensitive to meaning-preserving prompt variations, such as formatting choices and answer-option order, and this sensitivity persists with larger models, more demonstrations or instruction tuning.

When in-context information conflicts with knowledge from pretraining, whether a model follows the context depends on the strength of the conflicting prior, such as the pretraining frequency of the entities involved or the semantic prior of labels, and on model scale.

Intermediate residual-stream states can be read out in the model's output vocabulary space by applying the (possibly recalibrated) unembedding, so that these readouts show how the model's prediction develops across layers.

Ablating identified concept directions from activations during fine-tuning can control which behaviors a model generalizes from its training data, for example reducing broad misalignment while preserving the intended narrow task.
Networks trained on the same task with different architectures, implementations or input domains converge on similar internal representational structure.

High-level causal variables can be encoded in distributed, non-neuron-aligned representations, so alignments between a network and a high-level causal model must allow representation changes such as rotations or other bijections rather than mapping variables to individual neurons.

Coherence among a unit's or direction's highest-activating examples provides a useful proxy for its semantic interpretability, whether that coherence is judged by humans or measured by perceptual or semantic similarity.

Explanations inferred from a unit's or direction's top-activating examples on one dataset can be misleading or incomplete. They often fail to generalize to other datasets or to lower activation ranges, and they can omit other inputs that also activate the unit.

Features tracked across pretraining checkpoints form progressively, with initially diffuse activations organizing into coherent token or concept groups, and a feature's semantic association can stabilize while its decoder direction is still changing.

Contrasting SAE latent activations between model responses that exhibit and lack a target behavior or persona identifies latents relevant to that behavior, which can then be amplified, attenuated or ablated to shift it.

Parameter-space decomposition methods (such as APD, SPD or sparse gradient decomposition) can recover known ground-truth mechanisms from a trained network's weights, including computations distributed across neurons or layers and computations that share parameters.

A network's input-output function, or an interpretability method's training objective, determines its internal weights or features only up to a group of symmetries (such as permutation, phase, unitary or invertible linear transformations), so interpretations are well-defined only for properties invariant under that group.

Next-token predictors that induce the same conditional output distribution necessarily share certain linear representation properties, such as vector parallelism and relational linearity, within the subspaces that affect token log-odds, while their representation geometry outside those subspaces is unconstrained.

Koopman spectra of transformer activation dynamics, estimated from finite observable dictionaries, converge with sample size at roughly root-sample rates, but their values depend on analysis choices such as the observable dictionary, the layer analysed and the state–control decomposition.

Representational similarity geometry alone underdetermines a system's mechanisms and feature content: distinct mechanisms or encodings can produce the same similarity structure, so geometry-based comparisons need controls that relate internal states to external stimulus properties.

Individual attention heads in pretrained transformers specialize in specific, recognizable functions, such as tracking syntactic dependencies, coreference or rare tokens, that can be identified from their attention patterns.

A large fraction of a trained transformer's attention heads can be removed with little or no loss, or even a gain, in task performance, and the heads that survive pruning concentrate in particular attention types and layers.

Statistical enrichment of a feature's most strongly associated items (such as genes or tokens) against curated annotation sets provides a useful, though not exhaustive or exclusive, proxy for the feature's meaning.

Sparse autoencoders trained on activations of biological foundation models, such as single-cell transcriptomic models, recover features corresponding to known biological structure such as cell types, pathways and annotated gene sets.
Language-model task performance is sensitive to semantically equivalent prompt-format changes (separators, spacing, casing, enumeration labels), and which formats work best is model-specific.

Multimodal models represent semantically corresponding visual and textual inputs with partially shared internal features, so that individual features, such as SAE latents, can respond to the same concept across images and text.

Representations learned from different modalities converge toward a shared statistical representation, so that cross-modal representational alignment increases with model capability and with the amount of information the paired data share.

Conflicts between information supplied in context and knowledge memorized in parameters are mediated by a small number of attention heads, so scaling those heads at inference time shifts the model toward contextual or memorized answers without weight changes.

Attribution graphs from replacement-model circuit tracing give incomplete accounts of model computation: they can omit decisive mechanisms (such as how attention selects information) and record influence strengths without specifying the functions that compute outputs, so the absence of a mechanism from a graph is weak evidence that the model lacks it.

Successful jailbreaks shift the internal representations of harmful requests toward those of benign requests, reducing the activation of harmfulness- or refusal-related directions that would otherwise trigger refusal.

Cross-seed feature consistency of sparse autoencoders varies substantially with architecture and sparsity mechanism, dictionary capacity, training duration and auxiliary objectives, and with the layer or activation site being reconstructed.

Language models solve indirect object identification with a recurring circuit of functionally specialised attention heads: duplicate-token/induction heads detect the repeated name, S-inhibition heads suppress attention to it, and name-mover heads copy the remaining name. Independent analysis methods and different models recover this circuit.

Communication between attention heads is carried by a small number of low-rank (singular-vector) components of their QK and OV weight matrices, so head-to-head interactions can be localised to, and causally intervened on in, small subspaces.
Sparse mixture-of-experts routing reduces neuron polysemanticity relative to dense feed-forward layers, and the reduction grows as the fraction of active experts falls.

Multilingual language-model hidden states approximately factor into a language-identity component and a language-independent content component (concept, relation or fact). Patching or vector arithmetic can separate and transfer the two components independently.

Safety fine-tuning ties refusal partly to incidental surface features of its training requests, such as jailbreak framing, so refusal generalizes poorly to unfamiliar formulations or contexts of harmful requests.

Interventions guided by interpretable internal concepts, such as ablating units or features tied to a spurious attribute or routing predictions through human-interpretable concepts, can reduce a model's reliance on spurious correlations and improve accuracy under distribution shift.

Interpretability tools such as saliency maps, feature visualizations, sparse concept decompositions and attribution graphs can surface spurious correlations or dataset artifacts that a model relies on or that its training data contains.

Refusal in instruction-tuned chat models is mediated by low-dimensional directions in activation space: removing them suppresses refusal of harmful requests and adding them induces refusal of harmless ones.
Chat models represent a request's harmfulness separately from the decision to refuse, so harmfulness can remain recognised internally while refusal is suppressed.
Assigning personas through system instructions can substantially change a chat model's toxicity and refusal behavior, with effects that depend on the assigned identity and the framing of the request.

Transformer language models develop induction heads: attention heads that attend to the token following an earlier occurrence of the current token and copy it ([A][B]...[A] -> [B]), typically by composing with a previous-token head.

Models typically contain multiple induction heads that act as a redundant, partly specialised ensemble rather than isolated one-to-one previous-token/induction pairs, so knocking out a single head understates the ensemble's contribution.

A network's weights can be decomposed into additive parameter components of which only a small, input-dependent subset is needed to reproduce its output on each input, and these components correspond to identifiable mechanisms that can be ablated or edited selectively.

Attention layers can be approximated by overcomplete sparse attention replacements, with many low-rank attention units of which few are active per token, that predict the native attention outputs while exposing more interpretable attention features.

Targeted edits to a small set of weights or directions, such as low-rank MLP or attention-projection updates or selected neurons' value vectors, can insert, change or erase specific factual associations or behaviors while largely leaving unrelated behavior intact.

Likelihood-based model-editing metrics can overstate edit quality: high efficacy and locality scores on reference completions can coexist with degraded fluency or failure to express the edit in free generation.

A limited set of exact activation-patching measurements can calibrate and correct attribution-patching estimates for unmeasured components, provided the measured components are representative of the unmeasured ones.

Attention weights alone do not faithfully measure input tokens' contributions to a model's outputs; attributions that also account for the transformed value vectors and surrounding computation measure those contributions more faithfully.

Widely used gradient-based input-attribution and saliency methods can fail basic faithfulness checks. Their maps may change under model-invariant input transformations, resemble the input regardless of what the model has learned, or rank features no better than random when evaluated by removal.

Post-hoc explanations of classifier predictions, such as attribution maps and local explanations, give humans only limited and setting-dependent improvements in predicting model behavior or in telling correct predictions from incorrect ones.
Automated evaluation metrics for attributions, including localization, deletion/insertion and fidelity scores, poorly predict how useful those attributions are to humans.
Aggregating attributions over noise-perturbed copies of the input improves attribution quality relative to the base attribution method.
Probes on a language model's internal activations can detect harmful or jailbroken generations, including attacks they were not trained on, when attackers do not optimize against the probes.

Latent generating factors are identifiable from the observed data distribution, up to permutation, scaling or simple invertible maps, when the generating process satisfies sufficient structural conditions such as sparsity, independence, incoherent dictionaries or diverse auxiliary conditioning; without such conditions, rotational or other ambiguities remain.

Sparse dictionaries whose decoders sum independent feature directions capture compositional structure such as feature binding or conjunctions poorly, and adding explicit interaction or composition mechanisms over sparse latents can capture compositional concepts better.

Matched SAE features from independently trained dictionaries, including dictionaries trained on different language models, share similar relational geometry: their decoder directions are arranged similarly as measured by representational-similarity metrics such as SVCCA.

Recall of specific factual associations in language models can be localized to a small set of mid-layer MLP components or FFN neurons whose activations causally modulate whether the fact is expressed.

Transformers trained on structured tasks can implement their task behavior largely by aggregating many localized, individually imperfect heuristics (such as pattern-specific neurons or location-specific update rules) rather than through a single coherent algorithm.

Language models bind entities to attributes in context through abstract binding vectors added to the entity and attribute representations. The binding is carried by these vectors rather than by token position, can be redirected or restored by vector arithmetic on them, and is shared across tasks.

Language models contain dedicated final-layer neurons that regulate overall output confidence rather than promoting specific tokens. They do so by writing to directions with little direct unembedding effect that act through final normalization, or along a unigram-frequency logit direction.
Safety fine-tuning changes a model's activations by an approximately low-rank transformation concentrated in a few directions, which unsafe inputs engage more strongly than safe ones.

The reliability of contrastive mean-difference activation steering varies substantially across behaviors and inputs. Properties of a behavior's training contrasts predict it, such as how consistently and separably the contrast activations align with the steering direction.

Interpretability methods such as probes, sparse dictionaries, causal alignment, patching and explanation techniques can produce apparently meaningful structure on randomly initialized or weight-randomized networks, so attributing such structure to learned computation requires comparison against randomized-network controls.

Shallow ReLU networks can compute far more sparse Boolean functions of superposed features, such as pairwise conjunctions, than they have neurons, with the outputs approximately linearly readable from their activations.
Clustering activation vectors groups inputs that share coherent, human-recognizable properties, and such cluster features can be more interpretable than individual units.

Trained neural networks typically contain much smaller subnetworks of components (attention heads, weights, neurons or kernels) that preserve most of their task performance, so a large fraction of components can be removed with little loss.
Pruning a network to preserve a chosen internal feature's responses yields a sparse subcircuit of upstream components that implements that feature.

Interpretability readouts such as feature visualizations, attribution rankings and the circuits derived from them can be substantially altered by training or fine-tuning while the model's task behavior is largely preserved.
Training-time interventions such as dropout, spectral or locality regularization and modular initialization can increase the structural modularity (clusterability) of a network's weight graph.

Language models built with interpretability-oriented architectural constraints (activation sparsity, SoLU, discrete codebook bottlenecks, modular experts) can retain most of the performance of standard architectures trained on the same data.

A language model's verbalized chain-of-thought need not faithfully reflect the computation that determines its answer: answers can stay unchanged when the reasoning is removed or truncated, or can be driven by cues and context that the reasoning does not mention.
Language models can carry task-relevant computation or information in reasoning or filler tokens beyond what those tokens' surface meaning expresses (hidden or encoded reasoning).

Monitoring a model's verbalized reasoning for explicit statements of intent, concerning plans or contradictions can detect a useful fraction of its harmful, deceptive or incorrect behavior, even when that reasoning is not fully faithful.

SAE architectures or training objectives that go beyond a flat sparsity penalty, notably those that model feature hierarchy (nested prefixes, parent gating, structured or pursuit-based decoders), can reduce feature absorption relative to standard flat SAEs at comparable width and sparsity.

Framing an undesired behavior as requested or acceptable in training prompts (inoculation prompting) reduces how much the learned behavior is expressed or generalizes when that framing is absent at test time.

Several apparently distinct input-attribution rules, such as derivatives with respect to multiplicative input masks and LRP's epsilon-rule with biases in the denominators, reduce exactly or in a limit to gradient-times-input, so they inherit its properties and failure modes.

Units that are more interpretable tend to have closer activation-matched counterparts in other independently trained networks or brains, so feature universality and unit interpretability are positively associated.

Neural networks reuse shared components, such as attention heads or sub-circuits with the same functional roles, across related tasks or repeated instances of a function, rather than implementing each with disjoint task-specific components.

Apparent bias reductions from activation interventions on question-answering bias benchmarks can arise mainly from increased abstention or flattened answer confidence rather than from reduced stereotype preference among substantive answers.
Linear probes on a language model's activations can detect when the model's own responses are deceptive, including in settings that differ from the contrasts the probes were trained on.

Language models perform arithmetic not with a single exact algorithm but by combining several imprecise heuristics, such as approximate magnitude estimates and modular or periodic number features, whose interaction yields precise answers.

Faithfulness checks based on aggregate task performance can rate incomplete or incorrect circuit hypotheses as faithful, because omitted or resampled components with opposing effects can cancel out or even improve the measured metric.
Units or features that recur across independently trained models or initialization seeds are disproportionately interpretable and causally important to model behavior.

Sparse dictionary features of language-model activations carry temporal dependencies across token positions, so dictionaries that use a sequence's history (recurrence, past-activation terms or temporal objectives) can improve reconstruction or feature quality without sacrificing standard SAE quality.

In continuous latent-reasoning language models, how much the answer depends on the latent chain, and what structure the chain shows (decodable content, step ordering, state dynamics), depends substantially on the training recipe, task and backbone.

Networks can emulate many sparse computations (Boolean circuits or subnetworks) in superposition, with width or parameter count scaling with the number of simultaneously active computations rather than the total number of computations.

Networks computing on superposed representations perform interference or error correction, which produces activation-space plateaus where small perturbations along feature directions change outputs little.

Language models trained only on next-word prediction, without syntactic supervision, learn structure-sensitive subject–verb agreement that tracks the syntactic subject rather than relying solely on surface heuristics such as the most recently encountered noun.

Latent generating factors are not identifiable from the observation distribution under unrestricted nonlinear latent-variable models, but become recoverable (up to permutation and componentwise transformation) under additional restrictions such as auxiliary-variable conditioning.

How readily interpretability methods recover a behavior installed in a model organism depends substantially on the organism's construction recipe (data-generation pipeline, training objective, data mixture), not only on the installed behavior and its expression rate.
Training with regularizers that penalize dense or long-range connectivity yields sparse, modular networks whose module structure exposes interpretable task structure.

Models encode task-relevant information redundantly across overlapping units or features, so ablating, masking or suppressing a selected subset can leave behavior largely intact, and a small ablation effect does not show that the subset is unused.

Nested-prefix (Matryoshka-style) SAE training orders latents hierarchically: earlier prefix latents capture more general, frequently active concepts and later latents encode more specific refinements.
Increasing SAE dictionary width does not monotonically improve downstream feature-quality measures such as sparse probing or interpretability coherence, even when it improves reconstruction.

Hidden conditional harmful policies in language models can be detected by measuring how readily perturbations, such as random activation noise or brief restricted fine-tuning, raise harmful-action probability on inputs where the model initially behaves benignly.

Plain input-gradient attributions are unreliable measures of input importance, because they are noisy and vanish at saturated or inactive units; modified backward-pass rules can yield more faithful attributions.

Learned image representations, including deep network layers, can be inverted by regularized optimization into inputs that reproduce the representation, so the reconstructions reveal what information the representation retains and what it discards.

The input region that actually drives a CNN unit, as measured by occlusion or by reconstruction from its activations, is substantially smaller than the unit's theoretical architectural receptive field.

Sound certificates of transformer attention behaviour over input perturbation sets, such as target stability, evidence mass and entropy bounds, are attainable, but whether they are non-vacuous depends strongly on how bounds are composed across factors and layers: independently bounded terms are often vacuous, while bounds that track correlations between terms are much tighter.

Interpretability conclusions such as replacement-model fidelity, feature rankings or model-wide approximation guarantees can be formally certified over input perturbation sets by composing sound local bounds (e.g. Lipschitz constants, interval bounds, per-block approximation errors) across components.
SAE reconstruction error is structured rather than unstructured noise: much of it is predictable across dictionary sizes and persists as dictionary width grows at fixed sparsity.

Whether training produces learned optimization (internal search) depends on task and training properties, such as instance diversity with shared structure, reachability and representability of optimizer implementations, penalties on runtime computation, and whether explicit optimization or reward models are supplied to the system.

Feature properties other than task difficulty, such as feature complexity, label balance, input extent and the number of output labels, systematically affect how much activation variance a network allocates to a feature, even when all features are classified perfectly.

Selective state-space models admit an exact input-dependent causal token-mixing representation analogous to attention, so attention-style interpretability analyses can be applied to them, while their expressivity differs from that of transformer attention.

Periodic (Fourier/harmonic) structure in numerical representations does not by itself establish that periodic properties such as residue classes are linearly decodable; decodability depends on how that structure is distributed between and within classes.

Behavioral fine-tuning of language models mainly shapes how responses begin, so trained behaviors can be bypassed by continuing generation from a prefilled response that already exhibits the untrained behavior, unless training covers recovery from such prefixes.
Routing predictions through a bottleneck of human-specified concepts costs little task performance relative to end-to-end models while yielding accurate intermediate concept predictions.

A model's output sensitivity to activation-space steering perturbations is concentrated in a low-dimensional, strongly anisotropic subspace that need not align with the dominant directions of activation variance.
SAE feature activations can guide the selection, filtering or synthesis of training data so as to change targeted safety behaviors more efficiently than untargeted data selection.
Groups of co-activating SAE features form reusable components whose membership is shared across tasks that involve the same entity or attribute.
Scaling language models on sufficiently diverse data drives them toward more accurate representations of the statistical structure of the world underlying their training observations.
Image classifiers trained on natural-image datasets such as ImageNet rely predominantly on local texture cues rather than global object shape.

LLM-generated survey responses do not reproduce the distributional properties of human survey populations, such as question-dependent answer variability and population-level response structure, even when individual answers or conditional imputations look plausible.
